story:
Scarlett was playing in the yard with Baani. They rolled a red ball down the hill. The ball stopped by the fence.

Scarlett ran to get it. Then she saw something small on the grass. It was a little stick with a button. It looked like a lighter.

Baani came over. "What is that?" she asked.

"I think it's a lighter," said Scarlett. She did not pick it up. "Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use," she said.

"Let's go tell a grown-up," said Baani.

They ran to Scarlett's dad. He was watering the flowers. Scarlett held his hand and showed him the fence. Dad picked up the lighter and put it in his pocket. "Good job, girls," he said.

The sun went down. The ball went back in the toy box. Scarlett got tired and went to her bed. Dad tucked her in. "Night night, Scarlett," he said. She smiled and closed her eyes.

Charlie stood in the kitchen. The toast was on her plate. Her dad had made it hot, and now it was cool enough to touch.

"You can try the butter," her dad said. He gave her a small knife with a dull edge. He stayed right beside her. Charlie held the knife. She poked the toast with the tip. The toast got a hole in it. Butter went on in one big lump. "Why did that happen?" she asked. Her dad said, "Try the flat side. Watch what it does."

Charlie turned the knife over. She laid the flat side on the butter. Then she pushed it across the bread. The butter spread out thin. The whole toast turned yellow. "Look!" said Charlie. "One push, then two, then three." She counted her pushes. Three pushes made it smooth.

Next came the milk. Charlie held the cup with both hands. She poured slowly. The milk went up the side, one inch, then two. Not one drop spilled. There was a flower on her cup, and now the flower looked like it was swimming. "Can I make more toast tomorrow?" she asked. Her dad smiled and said, "Yes, butter girl."

Emilia went to the store with her dad. She wanted to pick a present for her grandma. Near the bread, there was a little play spot. Saanjh from her class was there. He was building a tall block tower.

Emilia ran over fast. Her elbow bumped the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. All of them. Saanjh's mouth went wobbly. "My tower," he said.

Emilia felt hot in her face. She took a big, deep breath. "Sorry, Saanjh," she said. "I bumped your tower." Then she got down on her knees. She put one block on the bottom. Then another. Saanjh put the top block on. The tower stood tall again.

Saanjh smiled at her. Emilia smiled back. She held her dad's hand. "Present time," she said, and off they went to the card aisle.

Andrew went to the park with his mom. They walked past the swings first. The slide was long and silver. Andrew slid down, down, down. The metal felt cold under his hands. "Nice sliding," said his friend Axton.

Then they went to the little farm stand by the gate. A snowy white pig lived there. Andrew patted the pig with one finger. The pig made a happy oink. But then Andrew looked around. He could not see his mom. Too many people. His tummy felt tight.

Andrew remembered something. He saw a lady at the stand with a big red vest. She had a cash box. She worked there. Andrew walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The lady held his hand. "Let's look together," she said. They stepped past the pig, past the swings. There was Mom, right by the slide. Mom hugged him tight. "You found a helper," Mom said. "I did," said Andrew, and he waved to the lady in red.

Joshua was in bed. The room was dark. Then he heard a noise. Tap, tap, tap. It came from the window.

Joshua felt scared. He pulled the blanket up. The noise came again. Tap, tap. His tummy felt tight.

Joshua got out of bed. He went to Mommy's room. "I heard a noise," he said. "I feel scared."

Mommy took his hand. Her hand was warm and soft. "Come on," she said. "We can look together."

They walked down the hall. Mommy turned on the light. The room felt less dark. Then they heard the noise again. Tap, tap.

Mommy opened the curtain. A tree branch was tapping the glass. The wind was moving it. "That is a cool branch," said Joshua. He was not scared now.

They saw Grandpa's dog outside in his bed. The dog heard them and began to bark. "Woof!" he said.

Mommy tucked Joshua back into bed. The blanket smelled like clean laundry. "If you feel scared again, you can tell me," she said. "I will help you."

Joshua closed his eyes. Tap, tap, went the branch. He smiled and went to sleep.

Avery sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump over the road. "Where are we going now?" she asked. Mom said, "To the park. Today we play at the park." Avery clapped her hands. She wanted to see the ducks.

At the park, Avery found her friend Gwendolyn. Gwendolyn was throwing thin little sticks into the pond. "I came to this park tomorrow," said Gwendolyn. Then she stopped. She put one ear toward Avery. "No, wait. Yesterday. I came yesterday." Avery blinked. Yesterday was the day already done. Tomorrow was the day not here yet.

"I want to do that too," said Avery. She picked up a thin stick. She threw it in the water. A duck swam fast to the stick. Splash! "Look! My stick made the duck come!" said Avery. Gwendolyn threw her stick too. Another duck came. Two ducks, two sticks.

"Now it is time to go home," said Mom. Avery waved to the ducks. "Can we come back tomorrow?" she asked. Mom smiled. "Yes. Tomorrow we will come back." In the car, Avery looked out the window. "Bye, park," she said. "See you tomorrow."

Myles went to his mom's office. The office was on a busy street. Myles saw a tablet on the desk. "Can I use it?" he asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Let me turn it on for you." She pressed the button. The screen lit up. Mom tapped a drawing app. "You can draw," she said. Then she went back to work.

Myles looked at the big white screen. He moved his finger across the screen. A green line followed his finger! He moved his finger again. More lines, like squiggles. Then he stopped. The squiggly line looked like a snake. "A snake!" said Myles. He drew one eye. He drew a long tail. His friend Logan came by with his own mom. "Wow," said Logan. "Draw another one!"

Myles drew two more snakes. His finger got tired. "All done," he said. He pressed the button like Mom did. The screen went dark. He folded his hands in his lap. "I put it away," he said. Mom smiled. "Good job, Myles." Logan waved goodbye. Myles waved back and held his mom's hand.

Lily stood in the restaurant kitchen with her dad. The cook, Mr. Wright, made hot toast on the big stove. "Can I help?" Lily asked. "You can spread the butter," said her dad. Lily took the knife. He helped her hold it. She spread the soft butter. The toast turned shiny and yellow.

"Now the milk," said Mr. Wright. He set a cup on the table. Lily picked up the jug. She poured fast. Milk splashed out onto the table. "Oh no," said Lily. Her dad wiped the table. "Try again," he said kindly. He gave her a new cup. This time Lily poured slowly. The milk went in, and not one drop came out. The cup was high and full.

Lily carried the cup with two hands. She set it by the toast. "Look, Dad!" she said. Dad smiled at her. Lily drank some milk and ate her buttery toast. "More toast, please?" she asked. Mr. Wright laughed and gave her a slice.

Jaxson wanted to bake cookies with his dad. His tummy was hungry for warm cookies. First they had to shop for butter and sugar. Jaxson helped carry the small bag home.

In the kitchen, Dad turned on the oven. "The oven is hot," Dad said. Jaxson stayed back and watched. Dad mixed the dough. Jaxson helped stir. He was not lazy about stirring. He stirred and stirred.

Then Jaxson moved the chair to reach the counter. He saw a little hole in the wall. It was an outlet. He wanted to put his finger in it. "Dad, look at this hole," Jaxson said. Dad came right over. "That hole is an outlet," Dad said. "Never put fingers or things into it." Jaxson nodded. He kept his fingers on the spoon instead.

The cookies went into the hot oven. Only Dad touched the oven. Jaxson waited by the table. Soon the cookies were done. "You kept everyone safe today," Dad said. Jaxson took a big bite of his warm cookie.

Sienna ran into the community centre. It was a sunny day after a stormy summer morning. Mr. Hassan had a big box of crayons.

"Let's count!" said Mr. Hassan. He put crayons on the table. He put four crayons in one pile. He put two crayons in another pile.

Sienna pointed at the piles. "Which pile has more?" asked Mr. Hassan. Sienna counted the big pile. "One, two, three, four." She jumped up and down. "Four! The last number was four!"

Benjamin counted the small pile. "One, two. Two!" he said.

"Four is more than two!" said Sienna. She hugged the big pile of crayons.

"You can use them all," said Mr. Hassan. Sienna drew a big sun. Benjamin drew a stormy cloud with rain.

Jenny came over. "How many pictures?" she asked. Sienna counted. "One, two. Two pictures!"

"Two crayons each," said Sienna, and she shared them out.

Daniel sat in his car seat. He held his red doll tight. "Are we at Grandma's now?" he asked. "Not now," said Dad. "Later." Daniel looked out the window. One cow. Two cows. Three cows. "Is it later yet?" he asked. "No, not yet," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Daniel watched the trees go by. Yesterday he played with Antonio. Today he was in the car. Tomorrow he would see Grandma again. "Is it later now?" he asked. Dad laughed. "Almost! Count the cows for me." Daniel counted. One more cow. Two more cows.

Then the car slowed down. Dad did not pull into a farm. He pulled into Grandma's driveway. Her door opened. "Now it is later!" said Daniel. Grandma waved. "Come here, little one!" Daniel hugged his doll and ran to her.

Hazel went to the grocery store with her dad. She held her little bunny toy. Then she let go to help pick apples. When they walked on, her hands were empty.

"Where is Bunny?" Hazel asked. She looked by the apples. She looked under the cart. She looked at the bread. No bunny.

Mr. Sánchez worked at the store. "Let me help you look," he said. They walked slowly past the milk and the lake of spilled peas nobody had swept yet. Then Hazel stopped.

She looked at her dad's big coat pocket. The pocket was bumpy. Bunny could be inside a pocket! She reached in. Out came Bunny, soft and warm.

"Bunny was hiding in your pocket, Daddy," Hazel said. Dad laughed and hugged her. At home, Hazel put Bunny in her own pocket. Then she ran outside to play.

Aiden ran into the community hall. His boots went clomp, clomp, clomp. Hiba and Daksh were already at the little table. Ms. Iyer was setting out rice and warm soup. Aiden was very hungry.

"Before we eat, we say a special word," said Hiba. "My grandma taught me. In Japan, people say 'itadakimasu' before eating. It gives thanks for the food." Aiden opened his mouth. "Itchy donkey mouse!" he said. Daksh laughed and laughed. "That is not it! Not it at all!"

Aiden tried again. "Ita... daki... masu." Hiba clapped. "Almost! Say it with me. Itadakimasu!" They all said it together. "Itadakimasu!" Then Ms. Iyer put the food on the table. Aiden took a big bite of rice. "Yum," he said. "I said the true word, and now I can eat!" He wiggled his boots under the table. "Itadakimasu," he whispered to his bowl. "Thank you, rice."

Maya ran into the garage with her recorder. Travis was already there, waiting by the big blue bag of toys. "Listen to this!" said Maya. She blew into her recorder. It made a loud squeak. Travis covered his ears.

"That was a bad sound," said Travis. Maya looked at her recorder. She saw the little holes on top. She tried again. One finger was not covering its hole all the way. She pressed that finger down hard. She blew. Now the recorder sang a real note.

"It works!" Maya shouted. She lifted her finger off the hole. She blew again. A different note came out. She put it back. The first note came back. Travis laughed. "Let me try!" he said. He pressed all the holes down hard. His recorder sang too. The two friends played their notes together, loud and happy.

Lily sat in the reading corner. She hugged a big red book. It was about a dragon who could not fly. She loved every page.

"You have to put it back now," said Isha. "The book lives here."

Lily did not want to put it back. Her lip went down, down, down.

Ms. Buchanan came over. She held out a small card. It was blue with Lily's own name on it. "This is a library card," she said. "A library card lets you borrow books and take them home to read."

Lily's eyes went big. "Even the dragon book?"

"Even the dragon book."

Ms. Buchanan zapped the card on her desk. Beep! Then she zapped the book. Beep! "Now it can go home with you."

Lily held the book tight. The cover felt rough under her fingers. "Come on, dragon," she said. "You can hang out at my house."

Isha giggled. "The dragon sleeps at your house tonight!"

"He snores," said Lily. "You will hear it tomorrow."

At the door, Lily waved the blue card high. "See you soon, library!" she called.

Blake went to the garden center with her dad. She picked out small tomato plants. "We will plant them at home," said Dad. Blake held a plant in her little hands.

At home, Blake dug a hole in the dirt. Then she saw a weed. She pulled it up. "Whoa!" said Blake. Long stringy roots hung down from the weed. Her friend Rocco came to play. "Look at the strings!" he said. "Those are roots," said Dad. "A plant's roots grow down into the soil."

So Blake put her tomato plant in the hole. She made sure the roots went down into the dirt. She patted the soil on top. Every day she gave it water. After some days, small green tomatoes grew. "A big number of tomatoes!" said Blake. Rocco laughed. "Can we taste one?" he asked. Dad smiled and picked one red tomato for them.

Sophie dug a little hole at the community garden. Ms. Kim handed her pea seeds. "Drop them in," said Ms. Kim. Sophie dropped them and patted the dirt. Every day she came back with her watering can. Green shoots popped up. Then tall vines grew. Sophie watered and watered, but she saw no peas anywhere. "Where are my peas?" she asked. "I don't see them!"

Paris came over to look. He picked a long green pod. "Is this a bean?" he asked. Sophie was worried. Was it the wrong plant? Ms. Kim smiled. "Open it and see," she said. Sophie pressed the pod with her thumb. It popped open. Inside lay a neat row of little round peas, like green beads.

"Peas!" Sophie shouted. "They grow inside the pod!" She picked pod after pod and filled her basket. She gave one to Paris and one to Marion, who was watering the carrots. A pig puppet sat on the fence post, and Sophie made it sniff the pods. It was getting late, so Ms. Kim said, "Time to go home." Sophie held her basket tight. "We can eat these at dinner," she said.

Logan ran into the baby store. "The baby needs things!" he said. Mom said, "We need a cozy blanket." Logan followed her down the big aisle. He saw tiny shoes. He saw tiny socks. He saw a little bed with soft sides.

Then Logan saw something wonderful. His friend Sehaj was there too! Sehaj held a demo baby doll. "My mom has a real baby at home," Sehaj said. Logan patted the doll's head. Pat, pat, pat! He patted hard. Sehaj's eyes got big. "Too hard!" Sehaj said. "The baby is little. A new baby must be touched very gently."

Logan tried again. He stroked the doll's tiny hand. Soft, soft, soft. The doll's hand wiggled, just a little. "It moved!" Logan said. Sehaj smiled. "Gentle hands make the baby happy," he said.

Mom held up two cozy blankets. "Pick one, Logan." Logan picked the blue one with stars. At home, the real baby lay in the crib. Logan reached out slowly. He stroked the baby's hand, soft, soft, soft. The baby's tiny fingers curled around Logan's finger and held on. Logan laughed. "She likes gentle hands!" he said. "Hello, baby. I am Logan."

Brooks sat in his cozy car seat. His dad was driving to the dentist. It was Brooks's first time going. A big plane flew over the car. Brooks watched it zoom away. He felt a little worried.

"I will sit still," said Brooks. "But what do I do with my mouth?"

His dad smiled. "You open your mouth wide so the dentist can see every tooth," he said.

At the dentist, Brooks sat in a big chair. The dentist said, "Say hello, Brooks." Brooks closed his mouth to talk. The dentist could not see any teeth then. Brooks tried again. He opened his mouth wide, like a lion's roar. Now the dentist could see every tooth.

"Very nice teeth!" said the dentist. Brooks got a sticker of a plane. He jumped down from the chair. "I want to come back!" he said.

Levi's class had a big basket. It sat by the cubbies at school. Levi put his muddy socks on the floor. He wanted to play, not clean.

His friend Ahaan picked up a sock. "Watch this," Ahaan said. He tossed the sock. It went into the basket. Swish! Levi laughed loud. "My turn!" said Levi.

Levi lifted his other sock. He threw it. It hit the edge and fell out. Sasha giggled. "Try again," she said. Levi tried again. This time it went in. Swish! "Basket!" he shouted.

Ms. Wijaya clapped her hands. "Good work," she said. "Now those dirty socks can get washed." Levi felt proud. He gave the basket a gentle pat, like a hug.

The next day, Levi wore his clean socks. They smelled like flowers. He wiggled his toes inside his shoes. "My socks got washed!" he told Sasha. She wiggled her toes too. At play time, Levi aimed one more sock. Swish! Right into the basket.

Gabriel wanted to go to the park. He held his red ball by the door. Then the sky turned dark. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"No park today," said his mom. "We need to stay inside."

Gabriel felt sad. His lip went down. His eyes felt watery. He sat on the floor and hugged his ball.

Then his mom brought a big blanket. "We can build a fort," she said. Gabriel jumped up. He felt excited now!

They put chairs together. They spread the blanket on top. Gabriel crawled inside. It was cozy and dark. His mom gave him a little flashlight.

"Wow," said Gabriel. "My fort!"

He shined the light on the red ball. The ball glowed inside the fort. Gabriel laughed and laughed.

Just then the phone rang. It was Iqra from school. "Come to my house tomorrow," she said. "We can play at the park together."

"Okay!" said Gabriel. He was happy.

The rain still tapped outside. But inside the fort, Gabriel smiled. He gave his mom a big hug through the blanket door.

The rain tapped, and Gabriel laughed.

Benjamin was at daycare. He dropped his teddy bear on the floor. The bear went bump on the tiles.

Benjamin felt scared. "Is my bear hurt?" he asked.

Ms. Baptiste picked up the bear. She gave it a big hug. "The bear cannot really feel," she said. "But you can pretend it does."

Benjamin hugged the bear too. He patted its head. He made a little bed from a scarf.

Jasmine came over with her doll. "My doll is hungry," she said.

"Pretend it can eat," said Benjamin. He held a toy cup to the doll's mouth. Jasmine made slurp sounds. Then they built a pretend mountain of soft blocks. The doll climbed to the top.

"More soup, please," Jasmine said in a tiny doll voice. Benjamin laughed and poured again.

Clara lay on her little mat at school. One mat, one blanket, one bear. She closed her eyes for rest time. The room went very quiet. Then it went very dark.

Clara woke up and opened her eyes. She could not see the sun. She could not see the blocks or the easel. She saw only black. "It is morning," she said. "Time to play!" She stood up fast and bumped her toe. "Ow," she said, and sat down slow.

Mr. Moretti came over with a small lamp. He helped her look out the big window. "The sky is dark," he said. "It is night, not day." Paige was awake too, holding her bird with one paper wing. "Night and day are opposites," said Paige. "Night is dark. Day is bright." Clara held her bear and watched the wild wind move the tree.

Mr. Moretti brought warm milk. First it was too hot, so Clara waited. Then it was just right, not hot, not cold. She took small sips. One sip, two sips, three. Outside, a car went by fast. Then all was slow and still again. The lamp made a little circle of light on the floor.

Clara looked out at the dark sky one more time. "Night," she whispered to her bear. Then she lay back down. One mat, one blanket, one bear. She closed her eyes and waited for day.

Miles sat in the family car. His hair was wet from a quick bath. Today he would get his first haircut at a salon. "I want to look like Dad," he said.

At the salon, the hairdresser put a blanket around Miles. Snip, snip went the scissors. A little curl fell down. The hairdresser was careful, and Miles sat very still.

Then Dad picked up the little curl. He put it in a small envelope. "Why?" asked Miles. "Some families keep a small lock of hair from a first haircut," said Dad. "We keep it to remember this day."

Back in the car, Miles held the envelope. He saw one small curl. Now it sat in paper, saved. "I want to see it at home," said Miles. Dad smiled and buckled him in.

Lillian went to the cultural center with her dad. There were red lanterns on the wall. Edmund and Asees were there too. "Come look!" said Edmund.

Then the drums began. Boom! Boom! They were very noisy. Lillian put her hands on her ears. "Too loud," she said. A big lion came out. It was gold and red. The lion jumped and shook its head.

Asees clapped her hands. "Watch the lion," she said. Lillian looked. The drums went boom, and the lion jumped. The drums went boom again, and the lion jumped again. The lion moved to the beat of the loud drums! Lillian let go of her ears. She clapped too. Clap, clap, clap. The lion danced faster, and Lillian clapped faster. "The lion hears the drums!" she said. Mr. Russo smiled and gave her a little red paper lantern. Lillian held it up high and clapped one more time.

Billie stood in the bakery kitchen with her mom. The oven door was open. It was hot inside. "Can I touch it?" Billie asked. "No, it needs a grown-up," her mom said. "You stay back here."

The kitchen lights were bright. A big door swung open and shut. Billie peeked through it. There were shelves and shelves of bread. She walked a little way. Then a little more. She turned around. She could not see her mom.

Billie looked and looked. Her tummy felt small. Then she saw the checkout counter. A worker stood there with a red apron. Billie walked to her. "I can't find my grown-up," she said. "Can you help me?" "Yes, I can," the worker said. She held Billie's hand and called out. Mom came running from the kitchen door. She hugged Billie tight. "You told the store worker," Mom said. "That was just right." Billie smiled and held on all the way to the car.

Hayden wanted to wash his hands. He stood on his step stool by the sink. His toy lion sat on the edge, watching him. "You wait there," Hayden told the lion.

Dad turned the tap. "Hot water is for me," said Dad. "Cold water is for you." The cold water ran over Hayden's hands. It felt cool and nice.

Then Hayden saw something small and red by the soap. It looked like a little candy. He wanted to pick it up. But he stopped. He kept his hands in the water. "Dad, there is a candy," he said.

Dad looked. "That is not candy. That is medicine. Only a grown-up gives you medicine." Dad picked it up and put it away high in the cabinet. Hayden washed and washed, slow and careful. He dried his hands all by himself.

Dad clapped. Hayden hugged his lion. "You are special," he whispered.

Edouard wanted to find the dog page in the book corner. The book was big and red. He sat on the soft rug and opened the cover. The pages felt smooth and cool. "Where is the dog?" he asked. "I will look and look," he said.

He put his finger at the right side of the page. He slid it left to left, back to the front of the line. His friend Amiyah came to sit with him. "One page, two pages, three pages," they counted together. But no dog.

Ms. Liu knelt down beside them. "Start here," she said. She pointed to the left side of the page. Edouard put his finger there. He slid it from left to right, word by word. "One word, two words, three words," he said. Then he turned to the next page. Then the next.

There it was. A big brown dog with a tight red collar. "A pet dog!" said Edouard. He patted the picture with his hand. The dog looked soft. Amiyah laughed and clapped. Edouard turned one more page, from the front of the book to the back. "Good dog," he said. "Good book."

The wind blew hard at the park. Riley held her hair with both hands. Sand flew up from the sandbox. "Ow," said her friend Salem. "Something went in my eye!" He blinked and blinked. A bit of dirt fell out on his cheek.

Riley blinked too. She blinked fast, like a butterfly. Nothing went into her eyes. "How come?" she wondered. She looked at Salem's face. He had little hairs above his eyes. She had them too. She could feel them when she touched her eyelids, soft as a feather.

Riley sniffed the air with her nose. She smelled popcorn. She heard the popcorn cart, boom, boom, going over the bumps. "I hear it with my ears!" she said. Ms. Reddy, her neighbour, was buying a bag. She gave Riley one warm piece. Riley tasted the salt on her tongue. Yum.

Then a big gust of wind came. Sand flew everywhere. Riley shut her eyes tight. She felt her little hairs stand out like a fence. When she opened her eyes, they felt fine. No dirt inside. "The sand stopped at my lashes," she said. Salem leaned close and looked. "My hairs stopped it too," he said. "Our eyes stayed clean!" Ms. Reddy smiled and held out the popcorn bag for one more piece.

Hailey was at the grocery store with her dad. It was cold outside. Hailey wanted to wear her red coat. "Can I put it on all by myself?" she asked. "Yes, you can," said her dad.

Hailey sat down on the bench. She pushed one arm into one sleeve. Then she pushed her other arm in too. But it went into the same sleeve! Both arms were stuck in one sleeve. "Look, I am a one-arm snake!" she said. Her dad laughed. A lady with carrots laughed too.

"Where does my other arm go?" Hailey asked. She wiggled her arm and looked. The other sleeve was empty. So she pulled her arm out. She put one arm in this sleeve. She put her other arm in that sleeve. One arm in each sleeve. The coat sat just right on her!

Now the zipper. Hailey pulled it up, up, up. Click, it closed at the top. "I did it!" she said. Her dad gave her a big smile. Outside, snow was starting to fall. Hailey stuck out her tongue to drink a snowflake. It was cold and tiny. "Snow is true," she said, and they walked to the car.

Emmett woke up from his nap. He was hungry. He ran to the kitchen. His dad was there, and so was the big blender.

Emmett looked at it with his eyes. He touched the cold counter with his hands. He sniffed with his nose. "I smell strawberries," he said.

"I smell them too," said Dad. "Smoothie time."

Then Dad turned the blender on. Whirrrr! It was so loud. Emmett's ears hurt. He put his hands right over his ears. The loud sound got quiet, just like that.

Emmett tried it. Ears open. Whirrr! Ears covered. Quiet. "Dad! My hands make it quiet!" he said.

"That is a good trick," said Dad. "One, two, three, four, five. Count your fingers over your ears." Emmett counted. One, two, three, four, five.

The blender stopped. Emmett took a taste of the smoothie with his tongue. "Yum," he said. "Can we sweep the crumbs too?"

"Sweep later," said Dad. "First, drink your wild pink drink."

Everett sat at the dinner table. He sniffed with his nose. "Mmm, soup!" he said. He touched his cup. It felt rough on the side. He tapped it. Tink, tink! He heard the sound with his ears.

Then Everett looked down. His teddy was gone! "Where is Ted?" he cried. He ran to his room. The room was dark. He could not see Ted anywhere. He froze like a statue.

"I can't see in the dark!" said Everett. His dad came in. Dad turned on the lamp. Click! The room filled with light. There was Ted, under the bed. Everett grabbed him and hugged him tight. He kissed Ted's soft ear. "Found you!" he said.

Back at the table, Everett took a big bite of soup. "Yum! I taste carrots," he said. Dad laughed. "You used your tongue, too! What a busy summer day for your eyes, ears, nose, hands and mouth."

"Taste it, Ted," said Everett. He held the teddy up to the bowl. "Ted says it tastes like carrots," he whispered. Dad smiled and gave him one more spoonful.

Logan stood by the big hotel pool. The water was blue and shiny. His dad held his hand. Logan wanted to swim like the big kids. But the water looked deep. He felt a little scared.

His dad said, "Hold the edge, Logan." Logan put his small hands on the cool wall. Then his dad said, "Kick your legs." Logan kicked and kicked. His legs made big splashes. The splashes were white and cold on his chin. He kicked so hard, water flew up and hit Mr. Esposito, the pool teacher. "Splash!" said Mr. Esposito, laughing and wiping his face. Logan laughed too. He was not scared anymore. He held on tight and kept kicking.

Then his dad picked him up. "You did it," his dad said. Logan looked at his cute yellow float toy bobbing in the water. "Kick more tomorrow?" he asked. His dad hugged him with a warm, soft towel. "Yes," he said. "Kick more tomorrow."

Grandma came to stay at Jaxon's house. She stayed for a whole week. They played in the backyard every day. They dug in the dirt. A long snake lay in the sun. "Is the snake afraid of us?" Jaxon asked. "No," said Grandma. "It slides away because we are big."

Then the week was done. Grandma packed her bag. She waved and drove away. Jaxon felt sad. He sat on the back step.

"What can we do now?" he asked his dad. "We can call her," said Dad. "On the phone?" asked Jaxon. "Yes. We can hear her voice." Jaxon called Grandma. He heard her say hello. The next day they made a video call. Jaxon saw her face on the screen. Then Jaxon drew a snake in the sun. Dad put the picture in an envelope. It was a letter for Grandma. Jaxon ran to the mailbox with it.

Sienna was at Grandma's house. Grandma said, "Time for your first haircut!" Sienna patted her curls. "My hair is big like a mountain," she said. Grandma laughed. "Off we go."

At the salon, there was a big chair. Sienna climbed up. But she was small. The hairdresser bent down low. She bent lower and lower. "I cannot reach your hair," she said. Sienna thought hard. Then the hairdresser brought a booster seat. "Small children sit on a booster seat," she said, "so I can reach." The booster seat went on the big chair. Sienna sat on it. Now she was up, up, up!

"Now I can reach your hair," said the hairdresser. Snip, snip, snip. The curls fell like soft little pieces. "Snip, snip, snip!" said Sienna. Grandma held up the mirror. "Look at you!" Sienna grinned. "Grandma, do you need a booster seat too?" Grandma laughed and laughed. "Not yet," she said. Sienna hugged her tight. "Maybe tomorrow!"

Oliver walked home with a small cage. Inside was a white rabbit. "His name is Snowy," said his dad.

At home, Oliver fed Snowy a carrot. He cleaned the cage with his dad. Snowy had soft fur. Oliver patted him a lot.

Then Oliver ran to the kitchen. He wanted his crackers. His mom stopped him at the door. "Wash your hands first," she said. "You touched Snowy and his cage." Oliver looked at his hands. He could not see anything on them.

Oliver washed his hands with soap. The water felt nice and warm. Then he ate his crackers.

The next day, Elijah came over. Elijah patted Snowy too. Then Elijah ran to the snack plate. Oliver called, "Wait! Wash your hands first." Elijah washed his hands. Then they shared the crackers and laughed.

"Snowy is a good rabbit," said Oliver. He gave Snowy one more gentle pat.

Cooper ran onto the soccer field. The grass was still wet. His red shirt felt bright in the sun. His friend Jolene ran beside him. She kicked the ball to him. Cooper kicked it back. The coach blew the whistle.

The other team scored a goal. Then they scored one more. The whistle blew again. The game was over. Cooper's team had lost. He sat down on the grass. He did not want to talk. His face felt hot. Jolene sat next to him. "We lost," he said.

Mr. Kaya clapped his hands. "Line up, everyone," he said. "We say good game to the other team." Cooper stood in the line. Each player walked past. Each player said, "Good game." A boy from the other team said, "Good game, Cooper." Cooper said it back. Then a small surprise. The boy smiled and held out his hand for a high five. Cooper laughed and clapped it. Jolene took a drink of water. "Good game," she said again. "Good game," said Cooper. The sky was turning pretty and pink.

Rosalie ran into the art room. Big paper waited on the table. Mr. Castillo held up a jar of paint. "This is red," he said. "Say it with me!" "Red!" shouted Rosalie. Shea pointed at another jar. "Blue!" said Shea. "Yellow!" said Rosalie. Mr. Castillo smiled. "Those are the primary colours."

Rosalie dipped her brush in the red paint. She made a big red circle. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue paint. She touched the paper. "Look!" she cried. The circle turned purple. "Purple! I made purple!" Shea ran over to see. "Make more!" said Shea. Rosalie painted purple all over the paper.

At home time, Rosalie set her brush down in the paint cup. She wanted to hurry and show her father. "Wait," said Mr. Castillo. He showed her the sink. "Paintbrushes are washed with water and left to dry when painting is finished." Rosalie rinsed her brush in the cool water. She laid it on the rack to dry.

The next day, Rosalie ran back to the art room. Her brush was soft and clean. It was true! She picked it up fast. "My turn for yellow and red," she said. She painted a yellow sun. She added red on top. "Orange!" she yelled. "Orange like a pumpkin!" Shea clapped. Mr. Castillo gave her a fresh sheet of paper. Rosalie dipped her clean, soft brush and wrote her name at the top in orange paint.

Jules stood in the kitchen. He was hungry. He wanted warm toast. Mom put bread in the toaster. Jules watched with his eyes. The bread popped up high. "Pop!" said Jules.

Then he heard a knock at the door. He used his ears. It was his friend Rhea. "Toast!" said Rhea. "I smell it with my nose." Jules sniffed too. The toast smelled warm and good. Mom gave them each a piece. Jules touched it with his fingers. The top was bumpy. He took a bite. It tasted sweet with jam.

"Rhea, how many openings does your nose have?" asked Jules. "I don't know," said Rhea. Mom said, "Those openings are called nostrils." Jules ran to the little mirror. He looked and looked. He counted one, two. "Two nostrils!" he said. "Me too!" said Rhea. Then they sniffed their toast at the same time. "I can smell with both," said Jules. They giggled and ate the last bite.

Grandma had a big soft bag. "Put your hand in," she said. "Do not peek. Tell me what you find."

Milo put his hand in the bag. He felt something round and smooth. "A ball!" he said. "A red ball!"

Grandma smiled. "Take it out and look."

Milo pulled out the ball. It was blue! He laughed. "I felt it was a ball. But my fingers did not know the color."

Wade and Miraal were there too. They wanted a turn. Wade put his hand in. "A spoon! A yellow spoon!" He looked. The spoon was red. "My fingers cannot see," he said.

Miraal had a turn next. She felt something small and smooth. "A car! A blue car!" She peeked in the bag. "No, it is green!"

"Close your eyes," said Milo. "Now look at the ball. What color is it?" Miraal opened her eyes. "Blue. I see blue with my eyes."

Grandma yawned. She looked tired. "Time for my nap," she said. The children hurried to be quiet.

Milo held the bag shut. "No peeking," he whispered. "You have to look. Looking is how you see."

Miraal put her hand back in. "I feel it! It is a yellow duck." She pulled it out fast.

It was yellow! She jumped up and down. "I guessed it! My eyes and my hands both helped me!"

Zoe sat in the big waiting room chair. Her sneakers swung back and forth. The room smelled like soap. A fish tank bubbled softly in the corner. Today Zoe had to get a shot.

Hanna from her class sat there too. "I am not even sick," said Hanna. "Why do we need a shot?"

The doctor came in and smiled. "Shots help protect your body from getting some sicknesses," she said.

Zoe thought about that. So the shot was like a special shield. It kept her body safe before any sickness came.

"Me first," said Zoe. She held Hanna's hand. The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then it was done!

Afterward, Zoe got a shiny band aid and a sticker of a star. She and Hanna skipped down the hall together, holding their stickers up high.

"I am protected," said Zoe.

Max put on his little blue apron. Today he would make pancakes for his family. Mr. Santoso held up a big card. "This is the recipe," he said. "One, mix the flour. Two, add the milk. Three, add the egg. Four, cook the pancakes."

Max looked at the card. He could not read yet. So he mixed the flour. He added the milk. Then he thought, "The egg is too cold!" Max skipped the egg. He skipped step three.

Mr. Santoso poured the batter onto the pan. The pancakes stayed flat, flat, flat. "Oh no," said Max. His tummy felt sad. "My pancakes are flat like the rain on the sidewalk!"

Kieran looked at the card. "Step three is the egg," he said. Max got the egg. He cracked it in the bowl. Kieran laughed. "You have batter on your nose!"

They mixed again. One, the flour. Two, the milk. Three, the egg. Max said each step out loud. "One, two, three!"

This time the pancakes puffed up big and fat. Kelly clapped her hands. "They look like little clouds!" Max carried the plate to his family. Dad took a big bite. "Yum," said Dad. Max grinned. "I read the recipe, Dad!"

Edouard ran to the playroom. Atreus was there with five toy monkeys. "Let's sing!" said Atreus. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed!"

They sang together. Then one monkey fell off. Atreus put it under the bed. "Now we sing four!" he said. Edouard counted the monkeys on the bed. "One, two, three, four," he said. Four monkeys were left.

They sang again. One monkey fell off again. Atreus put it under the bed too. "Four, then three!" said Edouard. The number got one smaller each time! He jumped up and down. "Sing more! Sing more!"

They sang and sang. Three, then two, then one. At last the bed held one monkey all alone. Edouard put the last monkey under the bed. "Zero monkeys!" he said. Atreus laughed. Meadow came over with a small broom. She swept pretend dirt off the bed. "Time for new monkeys!" she said. Edouard turned the bed around. He put all five monkeys back on top. "One, two, three, four, five!" he sang.

Nathan stood at the edge of the lake. The water was cool and clear. Small waves went tap, tap, tap on his toes. He wanted to jump in. He wanted to splash and kick.

His friend Vincent came running. "Let's jump now," said Vincent. Nathan looked around. No grown-up was there. Not Ms. Kaya. Not a parent. Nobody was watching the water. So Nathan sat down on the grass. "We wait," he said. A cow stood far away by the trees. It looked at them with big soft eyes.

Soon Ms. Kaya walked up. "I am here and I can see you," she said. "Now we can bathe in the water and practice swimming." Nathan held her hand. He stepped in slowly. He kicked his legs. The water went splash, splash. "You are swimming," said Ms. Kaya. Nathan was happy. Vincent clapped his hands by the shore.

Madelyn sat at the table. She wanted juice. "Give me juice!" she said. Dad did not get the juice. He just looked at her.

Madelyn tried again. "Give me juice, please." Dad smiled. He got the cup. He poured the juice. Madelyn drank it all up.

The next morning, Madelyn wanted her red shoe. It was under the chair. She could not reach it. "Help, please," she said to Dad. Dad got the shoe. "Thank you," said Madelyn.

Later, Madelyn ran fast in the hall. She bumped into the cat. The cat woke up. It was not asleep anymore. "Sorry, cat," said Madelyn. She patted the cat softly. The cat purred.

At nap time, Madelyn wanted her bear. It was on the bed. "Bear, please come here," she said. Dad laughed. He got the bear for her. Madelyn hugged the bear tight. Then she closed her eyes. Outside, a dog began to bark. Madelyn did not hear it. She was fast asleep.

It was a cold, windy day. Snow had begun to fall outside. Mia and her mom went to the baby store. A new baby sister was coming soon!

Mia had a big idea. "I will pick a blanket," she said. She picked a soft yellow one. Then she saw a little bed for dolls. She put her doll in it. The doll's head rolled to one side. Then it rolled the other way.

"Uh oh," said Mia. The doll's head would not stay up.

A lady walked by with a real baby. She carried the baby in her arms. She put one hand under the baby's head. She kept it there the whole time.

Mia looked at her doll. She picked the doll up. She put her hand under the doll's head. The head stayed still now.

"Look, Mom!" said Mia. "I hold her head too!"

Mom smiled big. "That is just right," she said.

Mia carried her doll all through the store. She held the yellow blanket in her other hand. At the door, the snow swirled outside.

"Baby sister is so lucky," said Mia. "I will carry her like this every day."

Ava sat at the art table. She had a small wooden block. She wanted to make it pretty. "I will put a sticker on it," she said.

Ava put one red sticker on the top. Then she turned the block over. There was another flat side! She put a blue sticker there. "How many sides are there?" she wondered.

Maria came to help. "Let's count them," said Maria. They turned the block again and again. One, two, three, four, five, six. Six stickers, one on each side. Every sticker was a square! "The block has six sides," said Ava. "They are all squares!"

Mr. Novák smiled. "Ava, look at your block. You made a cube." Ava held it up. Each square sticker was a face. Six flat faces, six square stickers.

Then Ava pressed the block onto her paper. She took some paint and stamped it. A square appeared! She stamped again and again. Squares on the paper. She stamped one corner down. Now it looked like a triangle!

Tia ran over. "Ava made shapes with her block!" she said. Ava laughed and stamped one more square. "My block can paint!"

Gabriel was at home with his friend Noam. They were building a big block tower. It was very tall. Gabriel ran to get his bear. He ran too fast. He bumped right into the tower. Crash! The blocks fell down. Noam's mouth turned down. His eyes looked wet.

"Sorry, Noam," said Gabriel. "Sorry, sorry." Noam sniffled. Then Gabriel picked up a block. He put it on the carpet. Noam picked up a block too. Would they build it again? Yes! One block, two blocks, three blocks. The tower grew tall again. It stood tight and straight, like at school.

Noam gave the bear a little tickle. "He can watch," said Noam. Gabriel smiled. He held the bear very still this time. "No bumping," said Gabriel. The tower stayed up. "Yay!" said Noam, and he clapped his hands.

Ruby is at Grandma's house. Grandma has made warm rice and peas. Ruby picks up her spoon fast. She wants the first bite right now.

Grandma holds up one hand. "Wait, Ruby," she says. Ruby stops her spoon in the air. Grandma puts her hands together. "We say Bismillah first," she says. "It means in the name of God. Many Muslims say it before we eat." Grandma says "Bismillah" in a soft voice. Then she takes her bite.

Ruby pats her fuzzy sleeves. She forgot yesterday. She forgot the day before, too. But today she remembers. She puts her hands together. "Bismillah," Ruby says. Grandma claps. "My smart girl!" Ruby takes a big bite of rice. "Yum," she says. "The rice tastes happy today." Grandma laughs and gives her more peas.

Ryan sat at the little desk in the library. Mr. Haile gave him a fat pencil and paper. "Time to write your name," said Mr. Haile.

Ryan held the pencil in his fist. It felt funny. Mr. Haile sat next to him. "Rest it here," he said, "on your fingers." Ryan tried it. The pencil sat nicely now.

Ryan began to write. He started at the right side of the paper. He made an R, then a Y. Then the paper ended. His name did not fit! Ryan made a sour face. "No room!" he said.

Mr. Haile pointed to the left side of the paper. "Start here," he said. "We go from left to right." Ryan looked at the left side. Then he looked at the right. He thought about the paper ending.

Ryan put his pencil down at the left. He wrote R, Y, A, N. The letters went across. His whole name fit! Ryan smiled big. He lifted the paper up high. "I did it!" he said. Mr. Haile clapped. "Read it to me," he said. Ryan pointed at each letter. "R, Y, A, N!"

Isabella wanted to sing the whole rhyme. It was about a cat with a shiny tail. She wanted to sing it all by herself.

At the music studio, Ms. Baptiste clapped her hands. Clap, clap, clap. Isabella clapped too. But the rhyme was tricky. One cat, two cats, three cats with shiny tails. The words were hard to remember.

Mason sang it very fast. He got all tangled up. "Three cats one tail two shiny," he sang. Leonel laughed and fell over sideways.

"Let's try it slow," said Ms. Baptiste. She clapped very slowly. Clap. Clap. Clap. Isabella sang one word for each clap. One cat. Two cats. Three cats with shiny tails. The slow words came out just right.

Then Isabella tried it fast. She got tangled too, like Mason. So she went back to slow, and it was easy.

"Now the fast one!" she said, and clapped her hands.

Paisley put on her little apron to wear. Ms. Bianchi took hot toast out of the toaster with a big glove. She set the toast on a cool plate.

"Now you can help," said Ms. Bianchi. Paisley picked up the knife of butter. She spread it slow, slow, across the toast. Then she stopped. The butter looked shiny. Then it was gone! "My butter is lost!" said Paisley. She looked at the plate. She looked at the floor.

Ms. Bianchi smiled. "Look at your toast," she said. Paisley looked. The toast was wet and glossy. She touched one corner with her finger. It felt soft and slippery. The butter had not run away. It had melted into the warm toast. Paisley put on more butter. She watched it melt again, just like before. "It melts!" said Paisley.

Next, Ms. Bianchi held the milk jug. Paisley held her cup with two hands. She poured slow, slow. One small drip ran down the side. She wiped it with a cloth. All the milk was in the cup.

Outside the window, a bird sat in a tree. Paisley took a sip of milk. "More toast, please," she said.

Clara ran to school with her red scarf. Today was scarf day! Genevieve had a scarf too. It was blue.

"Look at my scarf," said Genevieve. She spread it out wide.

Clara spread her scarf out too. Genevieve's scarf went on and on. It touched the floor. Clara's scarf was small. It did not touch the floor.

"Your scarf is long," said Clara. "My scarf is short. Long and short are opposites."

Genevieve clapped her hands. "Let's go show Ms. Qureshi!"

Ms. Qureshi was drawing a big ocean on paper. It had a big wave and a small fish. The girls held up their scarves side by side.

"A long scarf and a short scarf," said Ms. Qureshi. "What fun!"

Then Clara had an idea. "Can we use the scarves in your ocean picture?"

"Yes!" said Ms. Qureshi. The long scarf became the big wave. The short scarf became the small fish. Clara laughed and pointed.

Armaan came over to look. "The wave is so big!" he said.

At nap time, Clara was sleepy. She laid her short red scarf on her mat like a little blanket. "Good night, scarf," she whispered.

"I will wear you again tomorrow."

Jake had a runny nose. He was at home in his bedroom. He did not feel well yet. He blew his nose into a tissue. Then he put the tissue on his pillow.

"Where should that go?" his dad asked. Jake wondered. Maybe on the bed? Maybe on the floor?

Dad pointed at the bin by the door. "Try the bin," he said. Jake dropped the tissue in. It fell right down. Plop!

Jake blew his nose again. He got a new tissue. He held it up high. He dropped it in. Plop! He laughed.

Soon there were three tissues in the bin. "I can fix my messy bed," Jake said. He put his stuffed bear back on the pillow too. His shoe was under the bed. He put it by the door.

Was Jake still a little shy about missing school? Maybe. But he waved at the bin and said, "Plop, plop, plop."

Elijah wanted to play hide-and-seek at school. Lilly said, "I will count, and you hide." Elijah ran to the toy shelf. He hid behind a big toy horse.

Lilly counted, "One, two, three, four, five." She counted very, very fast. She got to ten in a blink. Elijah peeked out. His legs were still showing. Ember popped up from behind a tiny chair. She was not hidden at all.

"Lilly, you counted too fast," said Ember. "We need time to hide." Lilly nodded. "Okay," she said. "I will count slowly this time."

They all started again. Lilly put her hands over her eyes. She counted, "One... two... three..." Each number came slow, like a soft song. "Four... five... six..." Elijah squeezed behind the horse. He froze like a statue. "Seven... eight... nine... ten!"

Lilly opened her eyes. "Ready or not, here I come!" She tiptoed past the shelf. Elijah held his breath. Ms. Martínez smiled from her desk. Lilly looked behind the tiny chair. She looked under the table. Then she looked behind the horse.

"Found you, Elijah!" said Lilly. Elijah laughed and jumped up. "You counted slow," he said. "Now let me hide one more time!"

Charlotte went to Ophelia's house. Ophelia had a tablet. Charlotte wanted to draw on it too.

"Press the round button," said Ophelia's mom. Charlotte pressed it. The screen lit up. The tablet made a little sound. "I hear it!" said Charlotte. She tapped the drawing app. A green hill grew under her finger. She drew a big sun over the hill. Then she drew a cat on the hill.

The screen went dark. "Oh no," said Charlotte. "The battery is low," said Ophelia's mom. Charlotte found the charger on the shelf. She carried it over, carefully, with both hands. "Here," she said. Ophelia's mom took the charger and plugged it into the wall. Charlotte watched. Then she pressed the button again. The screen lit up once more. Her cat was still there, sitting on the last hill she had drawn.

"Time to put it away," said Ophelia's mom. Charlotte pressed the button and held it. The screen went dark. She laid the tablet down flat on the table. "I did it all by myself," she said. Ophelia clapped.

Nicholas was at Grandpa's house. He found a big cardboard box under the bed. He put his teddy bear inside it. "Now teddy has a bed," he said.

Colin came over to play. Colin stood at the door. He looked at Nicholas and the box. "What are you doing?" Colin asked. Nicholas wanted Colin to play too. But Colin just stood there. Then Nicholas had an idea. "Let's pretend this is our house," he said. Colin smiled. Colin ran over fast. "I will be the dad," said Colin. "I will cook soup." He stirred a toy pot.

Louana came in next. She looked confused. "What is this game?" she asked. "How do we play?" Nicholas said, "Just say let's pretend." Louana said, "Let's pretend I am the grumpy baby!" She made a funny face. Everyone laughed.

Grandpa heard them from the kitchen. He peeked in the door. "Can I count the soup?" he asked. "One, two, three bowls!" said Nicholas. Grandpa sat down in a small chair. He pretended to slurp the soup. "Best soup in town," said Grandpa. Teddy watched from his box bed. Nicholas tucked him in with a soft blue sock.

Zoe sat at the paint table with Ivaan. Mr. Castillo put out three pots. Red, yellow, and blue. "Make a new colour," he said.

Zoe wanted to make orange. She dipped her brush in red. Then she put the brush in the yellow pot. She stirred and stirred. But the yellow turned brown and muddy. Not orange at all.

Zoe looked at her brush. The red was still on it. She remembered the water cup. She dipped the brush in the water. She swished it until it was clean. Then she dipped it in the yellow pot. She stirred. This time the pot turned bright orange, like a fox.

"Look!" said Ivaan. "You made fox colour!"

"It's magic paint," said Zoe. She painted a big orange circle. Then she painted a small green leaf with blue and yellow, after she rinsed her brush again. Alessia clapped her hands.

Zoe held up her wet brush. "Next, I will make purple."

Florence sat on the grass in her pink hat. She wanted to learn her five senses. "I will name them all," she said. "One, two, three, four, five!"

First she touched a leaf. "Hands are for touch," she said. Then she heard a bee buzz. "Ears are for hearing!" She sniffed a flower. "Nose is for smell. That is fun."

Then Florence looked up at the sky. "I want to see the sun up close," she said. She began to peek. The grown-up ran over fast. "Stop! Never look straight at the sun. It can hurt your eyes." Florence shut her eyes tight.

"So eyes are for seeing," said Florence. "But not the sun!" The grown-up laughed. "Good guess. Look at the roses instead." Florence looked at the pink roses. "Eyes see safe things," she said. Then she ate a snack the grown-up gave her. "Mouth is for taste! Five senses, all done!"

Connor ran to the sandbox. He had the big red truck all to himself. He filled it with sand. He poured the sand out. Then he filled it again.

Carmelo came to the sandbox too. Carmelo had no truck. He just stood there. He dug with one hand.

Connor looked at his truck. He looked at Carmelo. "Do you want a turn?" Connor asked. "Is that sharing?" Carmelo asked. "Yes," said Connor. "Sharing means letting someone else use something too." He pushed the truck across the sand.

Carmelo filled the truck. It was hard to pour with one hand. He tried again. He tried once more. Then all the sand came out in a big pile. "Good pouring," said Connor. Carmelo smiled.

Dania came over next. "My turn too?" she asked. "Yes," said Connor. "We can all use the truck." The three friends sat in a row. Fill, pour, pass. Fill, pour, pass. The sand pile grew and grew.

The sun began to go down. The kids waved goodbye. "Come back tomorrow," said Connor. "I will bring the truck again. It is a present for the whole sandbox."

Zayn stood on the ferry with his dad. The boat went slow across the water. Zayn held his little blue bag. Inside the bag was a snack, a seed he had found, and his red shoes.

"Look, Dad," said Zayn. "The waves make the boat go up and down." The big boat pushed the water. The water made little white waves by the side. Zayn laughed and held the rail with both hands.

On the beach, Zayn took off his shoes. He ran in the sand. Then it was time to go home. The trip was done. Zayn was very tired.

At home, Dad said, "Now we unpack." Zayn put his cars away. He put his shirt in the basket. Then he picked up his red shoes. Something made a funny sound. Shake, shake. Sand came out! Sand from the beach was hiding in his shoes.

"It's stinky sand," Zayn said, and he giggled. Dad helped him sweep it up. Zayn put his shoes by the door, all clean, ready for tomorrow.

"Next time, I'll shake my shoes at the beach," said Zayn.

Noah sat on the mat at team practice. Mr. Sánchez put one big red ball in the middle. Noah wanted it first.

Noah ran and grabbed the ball. He held it tight. Lucie stood there with no ball at all. Her face looked sad.

"Noah," said Mr. Sánchez. "Sharing means letting someone else play with it too." He knelt down next to Noah. "You can have a turn. Then Lucie can have a turn."

Noah looked at the ball. He looked at Lucie. Then he rolled the ball across the mat. Lucie caught it. She laughed and kicked it back.

They took turns. One kick for Noah. One kick for Lucie. Noah counted the kicks out loud. One, two, three.

After practice, the team sat at a little table. Noah picked crayons to write his name. Lucie had none. Noah pushed the crayon box to the middle of the table. Lucie took a blue one. She drew a big ocean with waves.

Noah was not mad. He drew a boat on the ocean too. Lucie drew a fish beside it.

"I like sharing," said Noah.

Mr. Sánchez smiled and gave them each a sticker.

Rehmat woke up and saw white everywhere. "Snow!" she said. School was closed today. It was a snow day at home.

Rehmat stood in the kitchen. She was hungry. Her dad made warm toast. Then they heard a sound outside. It was the mail carrier. She was walking on the snowy path. Her feet slipped. Slip, slip, slip.

"Uh oh," said Rehmat. Dad got the big shovel. Rehmat got her small red shovel. They pushed the snow away. One scoop. Two scoops. Three scoops. Rehmat pushed and pushed. Then the path was clear. The mail carrier walked on it. She did not slip at all. She waved and said, "Thank you!"

Inside, Rehmat looked out the window. The sun came out. The snow on the steps began to melt, drip by drip. Rehmat ate her toast and smiled. "Snow day," she said, "one, two, three scoops of fun." Dad laughed and gave her one more piece of toast.

Everly walked into the big library with her dad. She held his hand. Today she would get her very own library card.

At the desk, the librarian typed on her computer. Then she handed Everly a small blue card. "All yours," she said.

Everly hugged the card. Then she heard a voice from the next room. A librarian sat in a low chair, holding a book up high. Children sat on the floor all around her.

"What is she doing?" Everly asked.

"She reads books out loud," Dad said. "It is called storytime."

Everly tiptoed to the door. The librarian opened a book about a frog. She read it in a big, funny voice. The children laughed.

Everly picked out a bear book. The librarian beeped it. "Bring it back soon," she said.

Everly blew a kiss to the storytime room. "Next time I will sit down too," she said. She waved her new card all the way home.

Ryan ran into Ms. Dela Cruz's music studio. A big guitar sat on a stand. "Can I play it?" he asked. Ms. Dela Cruz smiled and said yes.

Ryan tapped the guitar like a drum. Pat, pat, pat. The strings stayed quiet. No music came out. "Why is it so quiet?" he asked. Ms. Dela Cruz said, "Watch me." She swept her fingers across the strings. Pluck, strum! A happy sound filled the room.

Ryan's tummy did a little jump. He tried it too. He plucked one string. Ping! He strummed them all. Waaaah! "It works!" he shouted. His friend Clovis clapped from the corner. Ryan strummed again, faster this time. Ms. Dela Cruz clapped too, and Ryan sat up tall and proud. "One more song!" he said.

Arnaud did not want to sleep. His favorite stuffed cow sat on the pillow. Arnaud held it tight. His tummy felt funny. Tomorrow was the class party, and he was excited.

"Too much thinking," he said to the cow. He got out of bed. He padded to the big mirror by the door. He looked at his face.

Arnaud smiled a big smile. The mirror smiled back. "That is my happy face," he said. Then he made his mouth turn down. The mirror looked sad. "That is my sad face," he said.

He made a scowl. His eyebrows went down. The mirror looked angry. Then he made big wide eyes. The mirror looked scared. Arnaud giggled. His face could change, and the mirror showed it. He made the happy face again. The mirror smiled at him.

Dad came in. "What are you doing, little one?" Arnaud said, "Watch!" He made his sad face. Then he made his happy face. Dad laughed and made a happy face too. Arnaud yawned. He got back into bed. He hugged the cow. His eyes closed slowly.

"Good night, cow," he whispered. "See you at the party."

Abigail was staying at Grandma's house. It was time to sleep. Grandma said, "Pick your socks in the dark room, so we don't wake Grandpa." Abigail tiptoed in. The room was very dark. She felt for socks with her hands. Two socks felt soft and warm. She pulled them on and went to sleep on the big cozy bed.

In the morning, light came in the window. Abigail looked down at her feet. One sock was red! One sock was green! "Grandma, look!" she said. "They looked the same in the dark." Grandma laughed a friendly laugh. "The dark room hid the colors," she said.

Abigail wondered about the dark room. What else was hiding in there? She peeked in again. In the light, she saw a blue blanket and a yellow hat. "In the dark I could not tell," she said. "Light helps me see!" She ran back to show Grandma her two funny socks, one foot at a time.

Jules had a cold. His nose was red. His throat felt scratchy. He sat at the kitchen table in his pajamas. His blanket was around him.

Jules wanted to hide his throat. It felt bad. But then he thought of Grandma's house. At Grandma's house, his throat had hurt too. He had told Grandma. Grandma had helped him. So Jules took a big breath and said, "Mom, my throat hurts."

Mom put her hand on his head. "Thank you for telling me," she said. "Let's fix that."

Mom got out a pot. She filled it with warm water. The stove was hot, so Jules stayed back. He watched from his chair. Mom added noodles to the pot. They were small noodles shaped like hearts. Jules smiled. "A heart!" he said.

Mom stirred the soup. Steam went up, up, up. Jules closed his eyes and smelled it. The smell was warm and good.

Mom set the bowl down. "Blow first," she said. Jules blew on his spoon. Then he took a little sip. The warm soup went down his throat. His throat felt softer now. Not scratchy.

Jules took another sip. Then he saw something at the bottom. He dug his spoon in. It was the biggest heart noodle of all. It had been hiding under the small ones.

Jules held it up. "Mom! Look!" he said. "The biggest one for me."

Axel sat at the big table. He wanted to paint a picture of the sky. He picked up a gray crayon first. He drew one gray line. Then he looked out the window.

The sun was shining bright. The day was clear. The sky did not look gray. The sky looked blue, all over.

Axel put the gray crayon down. He picked up the blue crayon instead. He drew blue at the top of his page. "Blue," he said. He drew a big blue sky.

Then he painted a yellow sun in the corner. He painted red flowers down low. He painted green grass under the flowers. Each color was different. "Look, Mama," said Axel. His mama looked at the paint. "What a sunny blue sky," she said.

Axel held his picture up to the window. The blue on his page sat next to the blue in the sky. They looked the same. Axel smiled. "Sky match," he said.

Mya sat on the playroom rug. She had a bowl of grapes. Auston sat next to her with his own bowl.

Mya counted her grapes out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." She pushed each grape as she said the word. Five grapes sat in a row.

Auston looked at his bowl. His grapes were very big. "My grapes are big," he said. "Maybe three big grapes are really five grapes."

Mya shook her head. "No. Three means three." She picked up his grapes. "Watch. One, two, three." Three big grapes sat in a row. "Three is three. Big or small, it is three."

Auston counted them himself. "One, two, three," he said. He laughed. "Three grapes are three grapes!"

Klara came over. "Can I have some grapes too?" she asked.

Mya looked at her bowl. She had five. She gave one to Klara. "Now I have four," she said. "One, two, three, four."

They played a counting game next. Mya hid grapes under a cup. "How many now?" she asked.

Auston lifted the cup. "One, two, three!" he said. "Three grapes!"

Klara hid grapes next. Auston guessed, "Four!" Klara lifted the cup. "No, it was two!"

They played until the grapes were gone. Then they counted blocks instead, all the way to ten.

"One, two, three, four, five," said Mya.

"Six, seven, eight," said Klara.

"Nine, ten!" said Auston. He stacked the last block on top.

"Lucky us," said Mya. "Ten blocks." The tower wobbled. Auston held it steady with one finger.

Mia was thirsty after her walk to shop with Dad. She wanted cold milk. She opened the big fridge door. It was open. Cold air came out onto her nose. "Ooh, cold," said Mia.

Dad was stirring hot soup on the stove. He turned fast. "The fridge is open," he said. "It should be shut. Open and closed are opposites." Mia looked at the door. Open meant she could see the milk. Closed meant she could not.

Could she make it closed all by herself? Mia pushed the door. Click. Now it was closed. She opened it again, quick and slow, then slow and fast. Open, closed. Open, closed. Dad laughed. "One, two, three pushes," he said. Mia took out the small milk cup. She shut the door and drank. "Cold milk," she said. "My door is closed."

Owen ran to the playground early. The sun was warm on his face. He wanted the big swing. But Mannat was on it. Mannat sat with her head down. She did not swing at all. Owen felt angry inside. He wanted to shout. Instead, he took a breath. He asked, "Why do you sit so still?" Mannat said nothing. She looked at her shoes. Owen waited. He heard the swing creak. He smelled the wood chips. He waited some more.

Then Mannat said, "I feel sad. My dog ran away." Ms. Tehrani was nearby. She heard the words. She sat on the swing next to Mannat. She helped her look for the dog by the fence. And there he was, wagging by the slide! Mannat clapped her hands. "I feel happy now!" she said.

Owen got his turn on the swing. The wind pushed his hair back. He felt excited, way up high. Then Aviraj came to ask for a turn. Aviraj frowned and stomped his foot. Owen remembered the quiet waiting. He asked, "Do you feel sad?" Aviraj said, "Yes. I want a swing." Owen said, "You can have my turn." They took turns, up and down, until the sky turned orange. "Best playground day," said Owen.

Nathan was going on a trip. He and his brother rode the ferry across the big water. The boat went bump, bump, bump. The wind smelled like salt. Big black birds flew over the deck. Nathan counted them. One bird, two birds, three.

They were going to the snow. But Nathan had packed his swimsuit. "For swimming," he said. His dad smiled. He unpacked the little bag. Out came one swimsuit. Out came two sandals. Out came nothing warm.

"You pack for the place you go," Dad said. "Snow needs a warm coat." He found Nathan's red mittens instead. Nathan pulled them on. His hands went warm and cozy. He put the mittens on his brother too, one for each little hand.

That night, Nathan had a dream. He dreamed he wore his swimsuit in the snow. A penguin slid by on its belly. "Nice suit," said the penguin. Nathan laughed and laughed. Then he woke up, held his mittens tight, and ran to the window to look for snow.

Rose sat at the big table. Grandpa had a new book. Rose wanted him to read it now.

Grandpa picked up the book. He held it far away. He squinted his eyes. "The words look cloudy to me," he said.

Rose watched Grandpa find his glasses. He put them on his nose. Then he smiled. "Now I can see the words," he said. The glasses helped his eyes see clearly.

Rose looked at the pictures with her eyes. She heard Grandpa's voice read the story. She smelled the warm cookies in the kitchen, because her mom was baking them.

Then Grandpa stopped reading. "Where is the cat?" he asked. Rose reached out her hand. She touched something soft. "Here she is!" she said.

Later, Mom gave Rose a small cookie. Rose tasted the sweet cookie. "Yum," she said.

Rose took her crayons. She wanted to color a cat. She drew big round circles for the cat's eyes. "These are cat glasses," she said.

Grandpa put his glasses on the cat picture. He laughed a kind laugh. "What a smart cat," he said. "Now open the book again," said Rose. "I want to hear the rest."

Hunter had a slide in his backyard. He wanted to slide down fast. His friend Zayden came over to play. Zayden brought his blocks, and they made a messy tower by the fence.

Hunter climbed up the slide ladder. He held on with both hands. He started to lie down with his head at the top. "Feet first," said Zayden. Hunter turned around. He put his little feet at the edge. Then he let go and slid down, feet first, whee!

They could smell the warm grass in the sun. Zayden went next. He went feet first too. They slid and slid until the sky turned orange. "One more time," said Hunter, running to the ladder.

Lillian ran to the playroom. Yousuf was building with blocks. "Look, a snake!" he said. His blocks made a long, curvy line.

Lillian wanted to add a house. She found a square block. "The house needs a roof!" she said. She put a triangle block on top. Then she found a rectangle block for the door.

Yousuf turned a square block on its corner. "Look, a new shape!" he said. He put it next to Lillian's house.

Lillian frowned. "That is not the same." She took the block. She turned it back flat. "It is a square again!" she said. Then she turned it back on its corner. Still a square! She laughed. "A square turned so a corner points up is still a square."

Ms. Taylor came in with paper. "Let's color!" she said. Lillian drew a circle sun and her silly square house.

"Time for the snake to visit," said Yousuf. The snake slid up to the house, right through the rectangle door. "Welcome!" said Lillian.

Charlie sat in her reading nook with a big letter card. It was the letter S. "I can't remember this one," she said. Her dad sat down next to her on the soft cushion.

"Make the sound with me," said Dad. "Ssss." Charlie tried it. "Ssss," she said. Then she looked around the nook. Her sun picture hung on the wall. "Sun," she said. "Ssss, sun!" Dad nodded. Charlie pulled off one stinky sock and laughed. "Ssss, sock!" She tipped over her toy bucket, and sand poured out onto the mat. "Ssss, sand!"

Charlie hugged her feather pillow. "Sun, sock and sand," she said. "They all go ssss." Dad smiled and pointed at the card. "Yes, Charlie. That is the letter S." Charlie traced the curvy shape with her finger. "Hello, S," she whispered.

Ava packed her small red bag. Grandma was taking her to the beach. It was a long drive in the car. Ava watched trees go by. Then she watched more trees. Her tummy felt funny. "I need the bathroom," she said. "The beach is still far away," said Grandma. Ava felt worried.

But then the car slowed down. It pulled into a big rest stop. "Here we can use the bathroom," Grandma said. "And we can stretch our legs." Ava held Grandma's hand. They walked in. Ava used the little bathroom. She washed her hands. Then they stretched outside. Ava reached her arms up high.

Back in the car, Ava felt better. Soon the water came into view. At the beach, Ava let a short stick float on a little wave. It bobbed up and down. "Look, Grandma, it floats!" said Ava. Grandma smiled and sat close by her on the warm sand.

Aaron stood in the pool changing room. He pulled on his swim shorts all by himself. Then he sat on the big bench to wait.

"Where is Mr. Ong?" Aaron asked his dad. "He will meet us by the pool," Dad said. Aaron felt worried about the water. "It looks so big," he said. "Will I float today?"

At the pool, Mr. Ong smiled. "Lie back in the water," he said. "I will hold you while you learn." Aaron lay back. Mr. Ong's hands were under his back. Aaron did not sink. He floated like a little boat!

"Can you let go now?" Aaron asked. "Yes, just a little," said Mr. Ong. His hands stayed close. Aaron looked up at the huge ceiling and the bright lights.

Back in the changing room, Aaron saw a poster of a painted house by a lake. "Dad, I floated!" he said. "I saw a bird fly past the window!"

Leon was at Grandma's house. Snowy fields sat outside the window. Leon wanted to make bread for the whole family.

Grandma helped him mix flour and water. The dough felt sticky. It stuck to his fingers. "Oh no," said Leon. "Is it ruined?"

Grandma smiled. "Watch me show you what cooks do," she said. She pushed the dough with her hands. Then she folded it over. Push and fold. Push and fold.

Leon tried it too. He pushed. He folded. The sticky dough came off his fingers. It turned smooth and soft.

"Why does it feel different now?" Leon asked.

"Because you pushed and folded it, just like a cook," said Grandma.

The dough made a quiet noise when Leon pressed it. Grandma put the bread in the oven. Leon watched from far away.

Soon the bread was warm and ready. The whole family ate it together. "Leon made this!" said Grandma.

Leon took a big, happy bite.

Wyatt wanted to be a rocket ship. He put a small box on his head. The box was his nose cone. His friend Veronica came over to play.

"We need blast off," said Wyatt. "But I don't know how."

"My big brother does it," said Veronica. "He counts backward from ten. It's called a countdown. Then he jumps!"

Wyatt tried. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." He wiggled his toes. "Six, five, four." A bug crawled by his shoe. "Three, two, one. Blast off!" Wyatt jumped up high.

The box fell off his head. It made a big bong sound on the floor. Wyatt laughed. Veronica laughed too.

"Again!" said Wyatt.

Veronica put the box back on his head. "Ten, nine, eight," she started.

Wyatt jumped again, even higher.

Leah was three today. Her party was in the backyard. Balloons sat near the fence. Danny and Mallory came to play. They hopped on the grass with bare feet.

Then Mom brought out the cake. It had three candles. Leah wanted to light them herself. She reached for the matches. Dad took them up right away. "Lighting candles is a grown-up job," Dad said. "You get to make a wish."

Dad lit the candles one by one. The little flames wiggled. Leah blew out each candle with one big breath. Danny and Mallory clapped. Mom cut the cake and gave everyone a slice. Leah took a bite and smiled at her friends.
"Best cake ever," said Leah.

Grayson ran to the window at daycare. "Look, look!" he shouted. Big white flakes were falling. "It is snowy today," said Ms. Nielsen. Grayson jumped up and down. He loved snow.

"Snowball time!" said Billy. They put on their boots. Grayson put on his red mittens. Billy had no mittens. "I forgot mine," Billy said. His voice sounded shy.

Outside, the wind blew. "It is windy too!" said Kaitlyn. She held her hat tight. Grayson scooped up snow. He patted it into a ball. It was cold, but his hands stayed warm inside his mittens.

Billy made a snowball too. Then he stopped. "My hands are cold," he said. He held his hands under his arms. Grayson looked at his own warm, red mittens. Then he looked at Billy's cold hands. "Take one of mine," Grayson said. He pulled off a mitten and gave it to Billy.

Billy put it on. He smiled big. "Now my hand is warm!" He patted a new snowball with his mitten hand. Kaitlyn glued a snow sign onto the classroom door when they went back in. It said hello, snow. Grayson clapped his mittens together. "Snowy days are the best days," he said.

Quinn went to the pet store with her dad. She saw fish and birds and one small black kitten. "This one," said Quinn. Her dad smiled. They took the kitten home in a little box with holes.

At home, Quinn gave the kitten a soft blanket. The kitten drank and drank. Then Quinn saw the water bowl. It was empty. The kitten looked sad and licked the bowl.

"We need fresh water," said Quinn. "Every day, right Dad?" "Yes," said Dad. "Dogs and cats need a bowl of fresh, clean water every day." Dad held the bowl under the tap. Quinn could not reach the sink, so she watched from her step. Dad filled it up with cool, clean water.

Quinn set the bowl on the floor. The kitten ran to it. Slurp, slurp, slurp. "You were thirsty," said Quinn. The kitten drank it all. Then it curled up on Quinn's lap and went to sleep. "Good night, kitten," Quinn whispered.

The car ride to the library was a little bumpy. Felix sat in his big seat and looked out the window. "I see a cow!" he said. "One, two, three cows." His dad smiled. Soon Felix said, "I see a dog. And a bird. And another dog." He wanted to find a book about animals, all about cows and dogs and birds.

The car stopped. They were at the library. Felix held his dad's hand and went inside. It was quiet and warm. It smelled like paper. Ms. Oliveira was there. "I want an animal book," said Felix. She walked with him to a shelf. "Here are the animal books," she said. "They sit together in a group."

Felix looked and looked. Then he saw it. A book with a cow on the front, a big brown cow. "This one!" he said. He hugged it tight. Next to it was a shelf of toy books, and then a shelf of food books. "Books about food live together too," said Ms. Oliveira. Felix laughed. It was a surprise, like a big family of books.

In the car, the ride home felt bumpy again. Felix held his cow book on his lap. "Cow, dog, bird," he said, one finger up for each. His dad said, "We can read it at bedtime." Felix patted the cover gently and whispered, "Book goes home with us."

Avery sat at the little table. It was art time at school. Outside the window, snow was falling. The snow piled up on the grass. The snow looked white and soft.

"I want to paint the snow," said Avery. She got white paper. She painted a big white snow hill. But the white paint did not show. The white paint looked like nothing at all. Ms. Smith came over. "Try blue paper," said Ms. Smith. Avery was careful as she got a blue sheet. She painted a white hill on the blue paper. Now the white snow showed up. "I see it!" said Avery. Waylon leaned over. "The snow looks so soft," he said.

Avery mixed yellow and red. She painted a red mitten. She painted a green tree. "Almost done," she said. She reached for her cup of water. The cup began to tip. "Careful," said Enoch. Avery caught it. Not one drop did spill. Then she painted one last thing. A small yellow sun, way up in the sky. "Snow day," said Avery. "All done."

Beatrice stood by the blocks at school. She wanted to play with Jayke and Penny. But they were busy feeding a teddy bear with a tiny spoon.

Beatrice did not know how to start. She looked at her shoes. She looked at the toy shelf. Then she had an idea.

"Let's pretend I am the bear's doctor," she said. Jayke looked up right away. "Okay, doctor!" he said. Penny handed her a toy phone. "The bear is sick," said Penny. "He needs one hug, two pats, and three songs."

Beatrice got to work. She bent down low. She listened to the bear's tummy with a block. "Hmm," she said. She gave one hug, two pats, and three little songs. The bear smiled. Then the bear jumped up and danced.

"Now let's pretend the bear is a pirate," said Jayke. "Let's pretend I am the pirate's parrot," said Penny. Beatrice laughed. She flapped her arms like wings.

The teacher, Mr. Han, walked by. "A pirate, a parrot, and a doctor," he said. "What a happy crew." Beatrice held the bear up high. "Sail the ship!" she called.

Brooklyn went to the library with her dad. She wanted to find the letter M. It was the first letter of her name. But the big letter rug had all the letters mixed up. Brooklyn could not find M anywhere.

Adriano was there too. He sat on the letter B. "I found my letter," he said. Brooklyn looked and looked. She sat down on a letter, but it was a W. "Oh no," she said. "That is not my letter. This feels bad."

Then Mr. Dela Cruz came over. He was the library man. He sat down on the rug with them. He began to sing, very soft. "A, B, C, D, E, F, G." Brooklyn knew that song. She sang along too. The song went on and on, all the way from A to Z. When the song got to L, Brooklyn looked at the rug. L was next to a letter. And after L came M. There it was.

Brooklyn jumped up and put her feet on the M. "This is mine," she said. "M is for Brooklyn." The sun did shine in the window. It made the M on the rug bright. Then Mr. Dela Cruz said, "What letter comes after M?" Brooklyn took a deep breath and sang, "N, O, P."

Eli sat on his bed. He had lots of books. He wanted the dog book. But which one was it?
