He looked at a birthday card on his shelf. The card was from Naya. On the front it said Eli. The letters were E, L, I. Mom opened the card. She read the first page, then the next. "She reads it front to back," Eli thought.

Then Eli saw a paper tag on his toy box. It said Eli too. E, L, I. The same letters. The same order. He held the card next to the tag. "It looks the same!" he said. His name always looked like that.

Eli picked up a book. He opened the front cover. The dog on the cover looked ready to jump over a big red ball. Inside, a little note said Eli. The same letters again. E, L, I. This book was his! He put his toy pot back on the shelf to make room.

Eli held the book on his lap. He turned the first page, then the next. He went front to back, just like Mom did with the card. Mom sat down beside him. "That one," said Eli. "It says me."

Charles sat at book club with Cade and Abygael. Ms. Goldberg held up big letter cards. She held up A. "A," said Charles. She held up P. "P," said Charles. "P is the last letter," he said. "The alphabet is done!"

Cade laughed. "No way," he said. Ms. Goldberg kept going. She held up more cards. Q. R. S. Charles counted them. "Four more letters," he said. T. U. V. W. X. Y.

Then Ms. Goldberg held up the last card. "What is this one?" she asked. Charles looked hard. "Z," he said. "Z! The alphabet ends at Z!"

"I thought it ended at P," said Charles. "It ends at Z," said Abygael. Ms. Goldberg smiled.

"Now sing the song," she said. Charles sang it all the way. He sang A, and he sang Z. His itchy sweater made him wiggle, but he kept singing. After the song, his hands were dry from clapping.

"Does the alphabet end at P now?" asked Cade, teasing.

"No, it ends at Z," said Charles. "A first, Z last, forever!" He turned over the Z card and made a sleepy animal snore. "Zzz," he said, and everyone giggled.

Elizabeth went to the park with her dad. Her class was having a picnic. Ekam and Luca were there too. A man had a little stove on a table. He was making warm soup for everyone.

Elizabeth wanted to see the soup. She walked to the table. She looked at the stove. It did not look hot at all. Nothing was red. Nothing was smoking. She wondered, is it still hot? Her hand came up close.

"Stop there," her dad said, gentle and quick. He took her hand. "Only grown-ups touch the stove," he said. "A stove can be hot even when it does not look hot."

Elizabeth watched from far back. The man put his hand near the stove. "Still hot," he said. He poured the soup with a big mitt on. The soup steamed and steamed.

Ekam got his cup. Luca got his cup. Then it was Elizabeth's turn. The cup felt warm in her two hands. She blew on it, one big blow. "Not too hot now," she said. She sat on the bench and took a little sip. "Warm soup is the best," said Luca.

Avery went to the store with her dad. Zoravar and Sadie were there too. They saw a big bin of apples. Avery wanted to pick the first apple.

But Sadie was already talking. She was telling Mr. Ferreira about her new shoes. Avery opened her mouth. Then she closed it. She looked at her dad.

"Do I have to wait?" Avery asked.

"Yes," Dad said. "When someone is talking, we listen and wait until they finish."

So Avery waited. She kept her hands still. She watched Sadie's face. Soon Sadie was all done talking. Then it was Avery's turn. "I want a red apple," said Avery. "The shiny one, please."

Mr. Ferreira smiled. "Good waiting, Avery," he said. "Now you can pick."

Avery reached into the bin. There were sharp stickers on some apples. She picked one without a sticker. She put it in the basket, not in her pocket. Then Zoravar picked an apple. Then Sadie picked one too. Everyone got a turn.

At the checkout, Dad used his phone to pay. Avery held the basket with both hands. The apples did a little dance when she walked. Bump, bump, bump.

"That was fair," said Zoravar. "Everyone got an apple."

Avery bit into hers on the way home. It was sweet and crunchy. "My turn came fast," she said.

Isaiah sat on the big rug in the living room. Dad sat beside him. Brendan and Eden sat on the floor too. The big game was on TV.

The players ran and kicked. One player kicked the ball. It began to spin through the air. "Watch!" said Isaiah. "The ball will go over the net!"

Then the ball went into the net. The crowd cheered loud. Everyone in the room jumped up.

"Goal!" Dad shouted, arms open wide.

Isaiah's mouth fell open. He showed a missing tooth and grinned. "It went in the net! That's how they score!"

"Goal again!" said Eden, pointing.

The referee blew the whistle. Isaiah clapped and clapped.

"They kick it in," Isaiah said. "I want to try that at the park tomorrow."

"Then that's our plan," said Dad, and he held up his hand for a high five.

Arya went to the library with her dad. She saw a big box of toys. Inside were five little monkeys. "Look, monkeys!" she said. Her friend Nova was there too. "Let's sing the monkey song," said Nova.

They put the five monkeys on the top of a little bed. "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed," they sang. Then one monkey fell off! Nova took that monkey away. Now they sang four. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed." One fell off again. Arya laughed. "The number gets one smaller!" she said. They kept singing. Four, then three, then two, then one.

At last all the monkeys were off the bed. "No more monkeys jumping on the bed!" they sang. Arya lined the monkeys up on the rug. She counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." Mr. Pritchard, the library man, clapped. "Sing it again!" he said. So Arya put all five monkeys back on the bed.

Eloise sat high in the big stadium. Her dream was to see a real game. Her friend Oliver sat beside her. Ms. Chaudhry sat on her other side.

The players ran out onto the green grass. Eloise frowned. "I can't tell who is who," she said. "Everyone is running fast. I see so many players. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight!"

Ms. Chaudhry pointed. "Look at the shirts," she said. "This team wears red. That team wears blue."

Eloise looked hard. Yes! The red team had the ball. A red player kicked it. The blue team ran after him.

"Red team, red team," Eloise said. "Blue team, blue team." She named every player on the field.

A red player kicked the ball into the net. The crowd jumped up. Eloise clapped and clapped.

Oliver wiped his seat with a napkin to clean off some spilled juice. Then he clapped too.

"My favorite team is the red team," Eloise said. "They won because I kept watching them!"

Ms. Chaudhry laughed. "They won because they kicked the ball well," she said. "But you watched very well too."

Eloise looked down at the field one more time. The red players waved. "Goodbye, red team," she whispered.

Leah sat in the living room. She held the tablet in her two hands. "How do I make it turn on?" she asked. Her dad sat beside her. "Press the round button," he said. Leah pressed it. The screen lit up. "It worked!" she said.

Next she wanted to draw. Her dad helped her tap the little paintbrush. A big white page appeared. Leah wanted to draw a red sun. She looked at the colours at the top. She tapped the blue. Her finger made a blue line. "That is not red," she said. She tapped the red spot. Now her finger made a red line. She drew a big round sun. "I did it!" she said.

Then Leah drew green grass. She drew a yellow bird. Her picture was full. "Time to put the tablet away," said her dad. "Where does it go?" Leah asked. "On the shelf, next to your bed things," he said. Leah pressed the button and the screen went dark. She carried it slowly with both hands. She set it on the shelf, safe and snug. "Goodnight, tablet," she whispered.

Violet zipped up her red coat. Dad took her hand. They walked to the playground.

Violet wanted to play on the slide. But the slide was busy. Laurie was there, and Amyra too. Violet hid behind Dad's itchy scarf. She peeked out with one eye.

A grown-up waved from the bench. It was Mr. López from next door. He said, "Hello, Violet!"

Violet stayed behind Dad. Her tummy felt small and tight.

Then Amyra slid down the slide. She ran to Violet. "Hello!" said Amyra. "Want a turn?"

Violet looked at Amyra's big smile. She stepped out. She said, "Hello, Amyra."

Amyra laughed and clapped. "Yes! Come on!"

Violet went up the steps. She slid down, fast. "Again!" she said. Amyra held her hand in the line.

Soon Violet saw Mr. López again. This time she did not hide. She waved her hand. "Hello, Mr. López!" she said.

Mr. López smiled a big smile. He gave a little wave back.

"Time to go," said Dad. Violet held his hand. "Bye, Amyra! Bye, Laurie!" she called.

They waved all the way to the gate. Violet skipped all the way home.

Mia was ready for bed. Her toy horse was missing. She looked under the bed. No horse. She looked in the toy box. No horse. Mia felt angry. She stomped her foot. "My horse is gone!" she said. Her dad sat down next to her. "Try a slow, deep breath," he said. "Will that help?" Mia asked. "Yes, it helps your body calm down," said Dad. Mia took a big breath in. She let it out slowly. She did it again. Her foot felt still. Her tummy felt calm. Then she saw something white by the window. Snow was falling outside. And there, on the sill, sat her horse. Mia smiled. She hugged her horse tight. "Goodnight, little horse," she whispered.

Lucas sat at the kitchen table. He had a big new pencil. It was yellow and shiny. "I will write my name!" said Lucas.

He gripped the pencil in his fist. His mom smiled. "Try two fingers on top," she said. "Like this." Lucas changed his grip. One finger, two fingers, thumb below. The pencil felt smooth and cool. He started to write. L, U, C. He began at the right side of the paper. He wrote and wrote. Then his pencil bumped the edge. No room! No more letters! Lucas frowned. "My A is stuck!" he said.

"You ran out of room," said Mom. "Watch me." She wrote her own name. She started at the left side. The letters marched across, left to right, all the way to the right. Lucas gasped. "Start here!" he said. He put his pencil at the left edge. L, U, C, A, S. Five letters! They all fit!

"It's beautiful!" said Lucas. He clapped his hands. The letters sat in a row like little friends. Then he grabbed a new sheet. "Now a story about my name!" said Lucas. The pencil went scratch, scratch on the paper. He began at the left again.

Josephine sat at Emma's table. Emma's mom put a tablet in front of her.

"Press the round button with your finger," said Emma. "Then tap the little paint box."

Josephine pressed the button. The screen lit up. Then she tapped the paint box. A drawing app opened.

"I did it!" said Josephine.

She drew a thin green snake. Then she drew a big red sun. Then she drew Emma with yellow hair.

Emma laughed. "That looks like me!"

"Can I draw a cat too?" asked Josephine.

"Yes," said Emma. "There is lots of time."

Josephine started the cat. She drew one ear. Then two ears. Then the screen went black.

Josephine sat very still. "Is it broken?" she asked.

Emma's mom came over. "No, it ran out of power after being used," she said. "It needs charging. Watch me."

She plugged the charger into the wall. Then she plugged it into the tablet. A little picture of a battery showed up on the black screen.

"See?" said Emma's mom. "It is getting power now."

"It was tired," said Josephine. "Like me at bedtime."

Emma giggled. "It has to rest and eat!"

Emma's mom said, "You can draw more later. Can you put the tablet away now?"

Josephine picked up the tablet. She set it down on the shelf, right next to Emma's crayons.

"Bye bye, tablet," said Josephine. "Rest well."

Emma took her hand. "Come play blocks until it is full again."

Josephine smiled and followed her friend to the toy corner.

Jackson sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down a pencil and paper. "Can you write your name?" she asked. Jackson grabbed the pencil and stood up. He waved it in the air. He wanted to run to the door and show Dad.

"Hold the point down," said Mom. "A pencil can poke if it faces up." Jackson looked at the point. He turned it down toward the floor. Then he walked to the door, slow and careful.

Dad smiled. "Show me your name." Jackson sat back down. He held the pencil the right way. He missed some lines at first. He tried again. There it was. A J. Then an a. "That's me!" said Jackson. Dad clapped, and Jackson laughed.

Grayson walked on the nature trail with Ms. Hoang. She held a bag of things. "Let's play a puzzle," she said. "Tell me which things are soft and which are rough."

Grayson pulled out a feather. He touched it with his fingers. "Soft," he said. Then he touched a pinecone. It poked his skin. "Rough!" he said. Next came a small purple blanket. He rubbed it on his hand. "Soft," he said. He had solved the puzzle with his skin.

"Now close your eyes," said Ms. Hoang. She put something in his hands. It was bumpy and hard. Grayson laughed. "Rough! My skin can tell!" His skin could feel soft things and rough things, even with his eyes shut.

They walked on. Grayson touched a smooth gray rock. "Rough?" he asked. He felt it again. "No. Smooth. That's a new one!"

Alexander dug a little hole in the backyard. His dad helped him pat the seeds into the dirt. "Now we water them," said Dad. Alexander tipped the can. The water made dark spots on the soil.

The next morning, Alexander ran outside. He saw only dirt. No sprout. "Where is my plant?" he asked. His tongue poked out as he thought. He watered the seeds again. A bird swung on the fence and watched him.

Ila came to play. They watered the seeds together. Still only dirt the next day. And the next day. Then one morning, Alexander looked down and gasped. A tiny green sprout stood in the dirt. "Ila! Come see!" he called. Ila ran over fast. "It's new," she whispered. Alexander watered it again, very carefully.

It was game morning at Charles's house. Dad put snacks on the table. Salem and Flavie came over to watch the big game with Charles. Everyone sat on the rug.

"Who is that man?" Flavie asked. She pointed at the TV. A man in a striped shirt ran back and forth. He kept watching the players. He blew his whistle, and everyone stopped.

Charles felt a little scared of the loud whistle. Dad said, "It's okay. Come sit by me." Charles sat close.

"He is the referee," said Salem. "A referee watches the game and makes sure players follow the rules."

Then a player pushed another player. The referee blew his whistle. He pointed his finger. The player put his hands up and said sorry.

Charles counted the players. "One, two, three, four, five," he said. He counted the referee too. "Six!"

The whistle blew again. The game went on. Dad gave Charles a snack.

"That man helps them play nice," said Flavie.

Charles waved at the TV. "Good watching, referee!" he said.

Gabriel was at Grandma's house. Snow had fallen in the night. The snow covered the grass and the trees. Gabriel looked out the window. The snow was white, all white.

"I will draw the snow," said Gabriel. Grandma gave him white paper. Gabriel picked a crayon. He found a red crayon. Red was not snow. He found a yellow crayon. Yellow was not snow. He found a white crayon. He drew and drew. But nothing showed up on the white paper. Gabriel frowned. "Where did my snow go?"

Grandpa was looking at his map by the door. He waved Gabriel over. "Try this," said Grandpa. He gave Gabriel a blue paper. Gabriel drew with the white crayon. White lines showed up on the blue paper. "I see the snow!" said Gabriel. He drew white snow on the blue sky. He drew a green tree under the snow. He drew a red hat on a little yellow bird.

"Time for lunch," said Grandma. The soup was warm and salty. Gabriel waved at his picture while he ate. Outside, the real snow was still white on the grass. "Snow matches my crayon," said Gabriel, and he took one more bite.

Willow had a little bunny toy. She loved that bunny very much. But one morning, bunny was gone. Willow looked in her toy bag. Bunny was not there. She wanted to run to the big attic all by herself.

Then she remembered something. If you lose something, you tell your grown-up first. So Willow found her mom in the kitchen. "Bunny is lost," she said. "Will you look with me?"

Mom wiped her hands on a towel. "Yes, let us look together." They walked through the house side by side. They peeked under the bed. They found a yucky dust ball, but no bunny. Willow heard a scratch, scratch sound by the couch. Mom lifted the cushion. There was bunny!

Willow hugged bunny close. "We found her together," she said. Mom smiled and kissed the top of Willow's head. "Next time, tell me first too," said Mom. Willow nodded, and bunny's soft ear tickled her chin.

It was Blake's first day of school. She marched down the hallway with her new lunchbox. It was blue, with a huge dog on the front. Her tummy felt like popping corn.

At lunch, Blake saw a boy with the same blue lunchbox. "That is mine!" said the boy. "No, it is mine!" said Blake. Then Arnav opened the lid. "Look," he said. "My name is here. Arnav." Blake opened her lid. Her name was not there. Uh oh. Her lunchbox looked just like his. Which one was hers?

After lunch, Mr. Ramos helped. "Whose sandwich is this?" he asked. "I have cheese," said Arnav. "I have jam," said Blake. Mr. Ramos looked in both boxes. Arnav's name was on the jam box. So the jam box was Blake's! Mr. Ramos wrote Blake's name on her lid with a marker.

At pickup time, Blake's mom gave her a hug. "Will your lunchbox get lost again?" she asked. "No," said Blake. "My name will bring it back to me." Then she held up her lid and smiled at the letters.

Victor sat at the little table in the school library. Ms. Walker gave him a pencil and paper. "Now we write your name," she said.

Victor held the pencil in his fist. He pushed hard on the paper. The first letter came out wobbly and big. It did not look like a V at all. Victor felt sad. "My letter is wrong," he said.

Ms. Walker put a pink thing in his hand. "This is called an eraser," she said. "Try it." Victor rubbed the pink eraser on the wobbly letter. He rubbed and rubbed. The wobbly line went away! The paper was clean again. What a surprise!

Victor held the pencil the new way, with his fingers. He made a V. It was a good V. He made an i, a c, and more letters. His friend Anayat came to look. "You wrote Victor!" said Anayat. Victor smiled and rubbed the eraser on his sleeve like a little drum. Then he wrote his name one more time.

Charles went to the art studio with his dad. He brought his box of crayons. He wanted to draw a big red sun.

Charles sat at the little table. Clemence sat next to him. Elia sat next to her. "I will draw the sun," said Charles. He opened his box.

Uh oh. The crayons were soft. They bent like noodles. Charles tried to hold one. It flopped over in his hand. "My crayons are bendy!" he said.

"I left my box in the car," said his dad. "It was sunny and hot today." Charles touched a red crayon. It was warm and shiny. He pushed it on the paper. The soft crayon made a thick, shiny red mark. It did not look like a line. It looked like a fat red sun!

Charles pushed the crayon again. The red sun grew bigger. Elia said, "It looks like a real sun!" Clemence clapped her hands. Charles mixed the red sun with a soft orange crayon. The colors mixed into one big glow.

Ms. Bighorn came to look. "What a big sunny picture," she said. Charles held up his bendy crayon. He smiled at it. "You are my sun crayon," he said. He gave it one more push across the paper.

Olivier was going to the dentist for the first time. His mom took his hand at the door. The waiting room had a picture of a lion on the wall. The lion had big white teeth. "I wonder how many teeth a lion has," Olivier said.

A kind dentist called Mr. Rahman came out. "Hello, Olivier," he said. "Let's look at your teeth." The chair went up and down. That was funny. The light was bright, not cloudy at all. Mr. Rahman counted Olivier's teeth one by one.

Then it was time to brush. Mr. Rahman put minty toothpaste on a little brush. He brushed all around. Soon Olivier's mouth was full of white foam. It tasted like mint. Olivier was about to swallow it.

Then he remembered what Mr. Rahman had told Georgia at school. Georgia had asked about the foam, and Mr. Rahman had said, "You spit it out, not swallow it." Olivier turned his head. He spat the foam into the sink. It went down with a swirl.

"Good job," said Mr. Rahman. "Your teeth are clean and shiny." Olivier looked in the little mirror. His teeth were white like the lion's teeth. "Can I take a sticker?" he asked. "Yes," said Mr. Rahman, and handed him a shiny gold tooth sticker.

Mila sat on the school rug. Mr. Bui had big news. "A puppet show is coming today," he said. Mila felt so excited. Her legs wanted to bounce. Her mouth wanted to shout. She bounced and bumped into Amber. Amber dropped her red crayon and looked sad. "Sorry," Mila said. She picked up the crayon. Then Mila felt excited again. She jumped up high and shouted, "Puppets!" Maeve covered her ears. Mila saw that her shouting made Maeve scared. Mila sat down. She put her hands in her lap. She squeezed them tight and counted, "One, two, three." The bouncing feeling got small and slow, like ice cream starting to melt. The door opened. The puppets had big yellow shapes on them. Mila clapped her hands softly. "I waited," she whispered to Amber. Amber smiled and made room on the rug.

Maverick stood in the school hallway. His shoes were new and red. He held his dad's hand tight. There were so many doors. One, two, three doors, and more.

A boy stood by the wall. He looked at the floor. He did not talk to anyone. Maverick let go of his dad's hand. He walked over to the boy. "My name is Maverick," he said. "What is your name?"

The boy looked up. "I am Raphael," he said. "I have a furry cat at home. And a baby sister." Maverick smiled. "My dad bakes banana bread," said Maverick. "Maybe your cat would like to smell it."

Mr. Clarke opened the classroom door. "Time to come in," he said. Raphael held out his hand. Maverick took it. They walked in together, side by side.

"Sit by me," said Raphael.

Theodore ate his sandwich at daycare. "I am thirsty," he said. Angel gave him his cup. After lunch came naps. Theodore lay on his mat and closed his eyes.

At nap time, he thought about his morning. He had brushed his teeth after breakfast. "Why did I do that?" he wondered. He asked Ms. Whitehead when he woke up. "You brush in the morning," she said. "And before bed too."

That night, Theodore got into his pajamas. He pulled his blanket up. Then he sat up tall. "Wait!" he said. He hopped out of bed. He ran to the sink. He brushed and brushed. His teeth felt clean and shiny.

"Did you brush?" his dad asked from the hall.

"Yes! Morning and night," said Theodore. He climbed back into bed and smiled his clean smile.

Sebastian ran to the toy shelf at daycare. He wanted his red car. But the big toy bin was a mess!

"Where is my car?" he said. Samrath came to help. "Let's sort the toys," Samrath said. Sebastian put all the red blocks in one pile. Samrath put all the blue blocks in another pile. Then Lydia came with a big smile. She took the same blocks and made a new pile. "Look," she said. "Big blocks here. Small blocks here." The same blocks, but now they were sorted by size!

Sebastian stared. Wow! One pile was red and blue. One pile was big and small. Then he saw something. Under the small pile was a slow, shiny snail toy. And right next to it was his red car!

"My car!" he shouted. He held it up high. Mr. Mensah hung a sign on the shelf. It said "Sort by color or sort by size." Lydia laughed. "Next I will sort by shape!" she said. Sebastian put the car on the floor and pushed it to her.

Arlo stood at the park with a red beanbag. A wooden hoop lay on the grass. He wanted the beanbag to land inside it.

Arlo threw the beanbag over his shoulder. It flew high and far. It landed in the dirt, way past the hoop. Nellie ran to get it for him.

"Try it like this," said Ms. Wu. She held her arm down low. Then her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the hoop. "That is an underhand throw," she said.

Arlo held his arm down low. He swung it forward and up. The beanbag sailed and fell into the hoop. "I did it!" said Arlo.

Then Ms. Wu tossed him a big ball. Arlo hugged it with both hands. It did not fall. Nellie clapped, and Arlo laughed.

Aaron went to the store with his dad. Aaron wanted a cookie. Where were the cookies? Aaron saw a sign on a shelf. The sign had words on it. Dad read the words out loud. "It says cookies are here," said Dad. Wow! The words told Dad something.

Aaron wanted to make a sign too. At home he drew one for his friend Laurier. He wrote all his letters in one long line. IMADEACOOKIEFORLAURIER. "Can you read my sign?" Aaron asked. Laurier looked and looked. "No," said Laurier. "It is all squished."

What could Aaron do? He looked at a book. The book had words too. Aaron opened the front cover first. He saw little gaps between the words. A space here. A space there. Aaron copied that. He put spaces in his own line.

I MADE A COOKIE FOR LAURIER.

"Spaces between the words," said Aaron. Laurier read it out loud, slow and happy. "A cookie for me!" Then Laurier took a big chew of the cool cookie Aaron had saved. "Your words work," said Laurier. Aaron smiled and drew one more sign. It said AARON.

Theodore put on his little apron. He was at the big community kitchen with his dad. Today he would make cookies for his family. Ms. Sinclair smiled at him. "One, two, three scoops of flour," she said. Theodore counted along. "One, two, three!" He poured the flour into the bowl. Then he cracked two eggs. A bit of shell fell in. His dad helped him fish it out. "Good try," Dad said. "Try again." The next egg came out clean.

Theodore mixed the dough. He mixed and mixed. His arm got tired, but he kept going. Then the dough was ready. Dad slid the tray toward the oven. Theodore wanted to open the oven door himself. He reached out his hand. Dad caught his arm gently. "A grown-up is in charge of the hot oven when children help cook," Dad said. "You can watch from here." Theodore stepped back and nodded.

The kitchen window rattled. It was windy outside. A paper napblew off the counter and sailed across the room. Theodore giggled and chased it. He caught it and set it back down. Then the oven beeped. Dad put on big mitts. He opened the door. The cookies were golden. But there was a surprise. One cookie had a hole in the middle, shaped like a little star. "Look, Dad!" Theodore said. "A star cookie!" He counted the tray. "One, two, three, four, five, six cookies for my family." He carried the plate, walking slowly, all the way home.

Today was Maria's birthday. She wore a paper hat with stars. The party was at the bowling alley. Zackary and Alaina came too.

Maria rolled her ball. One pin fell, then two pins, then three pins. Zackary clapped. Alaina clapped. Maria wanted to see her balloons float. Dad had blown up three balloons with his own breath.

Maria let go of a red one. She watched the sky. The balloon did not go up. It went down, down, down to the floor. It sat by Zackary's shoe.

Maria picked it up. She let go again. Down it went again. It drifted like a soft leaf. Ms. Smith, from next door, smiled and gave it a little sweep with her hand. The balloon slid across the floor.

Alaina found one gold balloon on a string near the party table. That balloon pulled up on its string. Maria held the red one up high and let go. It fell right onto her hat.

"This one stays with me," Maria said. She hugged the red balloon. Zackary yawned and rubbed his eyes. The little ones at the next lane were asleep in their strollers.

Maria carried her red balloon to the car. She held it tight all the way home.

Hayden rode the bus with his mother. The floor was slippery, so he held her hand tight. Today he would get a library card.

At the library, Ms. Malik smiled. "Here is your card, Hayden." Hayden took it. The card had his name on it. He picked a big red book about buses.

A cat in the book went scratch, scratch on a tree. Hayden laughed.

Then he had to give the book back. He felt sad. "All done?" he asked Ms. Malik.

"No, no," she said. "Watch this."

She slid his card again. Beep! Out came a new book, a green one about frogs.

"My card works again!" said Hayden.

He hugged the card all the way home on the bus.

"Next week, more frogs?" asked his mother.

"Next week, more buses!" said Hayden.

Luka loved the dress-up corner at school. Today the basket was all mixed up. "Where did my red hat go?" he asked. Saint looked too. "Maybe it is under the heavy crown," said Saint.

Luka dug in the basket. He found a shirt. He found a sock. He found another sock. But no hat. Then he looked at the toy shelf. Something soft was sticking out of the truck bin. It was his hat!

"Why is a hat with the toys?" Luka wondered. Rehmat laughed. "That was my joke," she said. "I hid it there." Luka laughed too. He put the hat back in the basket. He put the shirts and socks in too.

"Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes," said Ms. Xu, peeking in. "They live together." Luka looked at the toy shelf. Trucks and blocks are toys, he thought. They live over there.

He carried the heavy basket to the shelf. The dress-up corner looked just right now. "Tomorrow can I wear the red hat?" he asked Ms. Xu. She smiled and said, "Yes, at play time."

Rose and Alaya found a small house in the forest. It was made of sticks and old plastic bags. "Let's play house here," said Alaya. "Yes!" said Rose.

They set out leaves for plates. They set out pinecones for babies. Rose picked up a pinecone. "I am the parent," said Rose. "I feed the baby." "No, I am the parent," said Alaya. "I want to feed the baby too."

Both girls wanted to be the parent. Both girls stood still. The baby pinecone sat on the ground. Nobody fed it. Mr. Nasser, their neighbour, was walking by with his dog. He stopped and smiled. "You can both be the parent," he said. "Just not at the same time. One of you can be the baby, and then you can switch halfway."

"Alaya first," said Rose. "Then me." Alaya held the pinecone. She rocked it and sang. "Baby, baby, time to eat." Rose got down on her knees. She was the baby now. She drank pretend soup from a leaf. "More, please," said Rose. Alaya laughed and filled the leaf again.

Then they switched. Rose was the parent now. She held the pinecone up high. "Time for a hug, baby!" Alaya was the baby. She yawned a big yawn. "Sleepy, sleepy," said Alaya. Rose patted her back, very soft.

They played all afternoon. Parent, then baby. Baby, then parent. "Best house ever," said Rose. Alaya hugged the pinecone tight and said, "See you tomorrow, baby."

Arnaud wanted to win the guessing game. Ms. Cho had a big box on the table. Ewan and Jay stood in a line. Ms. Cho held up a long string. "Tie it on your eyes," she said. Arnaud could not see. He heard Jay giggle next to him.

Ms. Cho put something in Arnaud's hands. It was small and heavy. He touched it with his fingertips. His fingertips felt it all over. Smooth. Very smooth. "A stone!" he said. "Yes," said Ms. Cho. She gave him a new thing. His fingertips felt little bumps everywhere. Bumpy, bumpy, bumpy. "A pinecone!" he said. Jay clapped.

Then Arnaud held something light. His fingertips said soft, like a tickle. He smelled it too. It smelled like nothing much. He touched it again, soft and smooth. "A feather," he said. Ms. Cho took off the string. There it was, a white feather. Arnaud touched it one more time with his fingertips. "Soft," he said.

Rosalie went to the store with her dad. Evaan and Crew were there too. They saw a big box of toy bears near the door. One bear had soft brown fur. Rosalie wanted that bear so much.

Rosalie grabbed the brown bear fast. But Evaan was holding it first. Evaan's face went sad. He started to cry. Rosalie heard him sniffle. Her tummy felt funny and tight. She did not want that.

Then Rosalie remembered. She put the bear back in Evaan's hands. "Can I have a turn, please?" she asked. "When you are done?" Evaan wiped his eyes. "Yes," he said. "You asked. Okay." He hugged the bear once. Then he gave it to Rosalie.

Rosalie held the soft brown bear. "Your turn now," she said after a bit. She gave it back. Evaan smiled big. Crew clapped his hands. Dad came close and smiled too. "Time to go," he said. Rosalie waved to Evaan and Crew. "Bye, bear," she said. "Bye, friends."

Elizabeth wanted to make muffins for her family. Her mom said, "Yes, let's cook in the backyard." They set a little table by the friendly oak tree.

Elizabeth grabbed the sugar bag. She poured it straight into the bowl. Sugar went everywhere. Too much sugar sat in a big hill. "Oops," said Elizabeth. Her back felt sticky.

Mom held up a small cup. "This is a measuring cup," she said. Elizabeth scooped sugar with it. She filled it up and tapped it flat. Then she used a measuring spoon for the vanilla. Just the right little bit went in. Not too much. Not too little. The batter looked smooth and good.

Mom put the pan in the hot oven. Elizabeth watched from her chair, far away and safe. Soon the muffins were done. The family sat on the grass to eat. "Yum," said Dad. Elizabeth caught a crumb in her hand and smiled. "I made these," she said.

Connor woke up and looked out the window. "Snow!" he said. The grass was gone. White snow was everywhere. No school today! It was a snow day at home.

Connor put on his boots and his coat. He ran out the door to play. But the sidewalk was icy. His feet went slip, slip, slip! Down he went, right on his bottom. "Oof," said Connor.

His dad came out too. Dad did not run. Dad took small, slow steps. His feet went tap, tap, tap. "Watch me," said Dad. Connor stood up. He took small, slow steps too. Tap, tap, tap. His feet did not slip! "I did it!" said Connor.

Connor stomped in the soft snow. The snow was bumpy in some spots. He found a surprise under a bush. Little bird tracks, like tiny stamps! "Who made these?" Connor wondered. He followed them, slow and careful, tap, tap, tap, all the way to the fence.

Claire was in the playroom. There was one big rocking horse. Claire wanted to ride it. But Lyana wanted to ride it too.

They both held the horse. It did not rock at all. Claire looked at Lyana. Lyana looked at Claire. "We can take turns," said Lyana. "You go first, one after another. Then me." Claire nodded.

Claire climbed on. She rocked and rocked. The horse went squeak, squeak. "Silly horse," said Claire, and she laughed. Lyana counted to ten. Then Claire got off. Now it was Lyana's go. Lyana rocked fast, and her hair flew up. Claire waited. She tapped her toes on the grass-green rug. It was hard to wait. But then Lyana got off, and Claire got another go.

Ms. Choi came over with two scarves. She tied a red scarf on the horse. "It looks like a knight's horse now," said Ms. Choi. Claire gasped. A surprise! Lyana rode the silly knight horse first. Then Claire rode it after her. One go, then another go, all the way to snack time. "My turn again?" asked Claire. "Yes," said Lyana. "After me!"

Raphael ran to Manuel at daycare. "Can I come to your house now?" he asked. "I want to see your beach ball."

Manuel smiled. "Not now," he said. "We go after a sleep. Tomorrow."

Raphael frowned. "What is tomorrow?"

Ms. Toussaint knelt down beside them. "Tomorrow comes after today," she said.

"But I want to go now," said Raphael.

"Now we play here," said Manuel. "Then we sleep. Then it is tomorrow."

Raphael looked out the window. The sun was up. Today was now.

After school, Raphael ate his snack. Then he slept in his bed. When he woke up, the sun was up again. "Is it tomorrow?" he asked his dad.

"Yes," his dad said, smiling. "Today is the new day."

At Manuel's house, they threw the beach ball high. Raphael held up his drawing with the sharp point of his pencil.

"I waited, and now it is today!" he said.

Austin stood by the lemon tree in his backyard. His eyes saw four yellow lemons on a branch. His ears heard a bee buzz by. His nose smelled something sharp and fresh. "Lemons," said his dad. "They are ready to pick."

Austin wanted lemonade. He thought lemons would taste like orange juice, sweet and yummy. His dad picked one lemon and cut a thin slice. Austin put the slice in his mouth. His tongue tingled. His whole face scrunched up. "Sour!" he said. "So sour!"

His friend Evan came over with a big grin. "You made a sour face," Evan said. Austin laughed and gave Evan a tiny taste. Evan's face scrunched up too. Then the boys touched the lemon skin. It was bumpy and cool.

Dad squeezed the lemons into a jug. He added water and sugar. Austin stirred it with a long spoon. The juice and the sugar sank and swirled together. They drank cold cups in the shade. Austin took a sip and smiled big. "Sweet now!" he said. "And a little bit sour too."

Gabriel sat in his car seat. Dad was driving to the park. Gabriel had a little bag of grapes.

"You can have three grapes," said Dad. "Not more."

Gabriel looked at his grapes. Some were small. Some were big. Did big grapes count as more?

"Is a big grape still one?" he asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Three means three grapes. Big or small."

Gabriel picked three big grapes. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three." Then he ate them, one by one.

He heard rain tap the roof. One tap, then more taps. The rain made a song. Dad sang, "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten."

A grape fell from Gabriel's hand. It rolled under the seat. He could not reach it.

"I will pay attention and hold on tight," Gabriel said. He held the next grape with both hands.

The rain stopped. The sky looked beautiful and blue.

"We are here," said Dad. He helped Gabriel out of the car. They held hands and walked to the swings.

"Can I have three grapes later?" asked Gabriel.

"Yes," said Dad. "Three is three, every time."

Gabriel smiled. He swung his arms and counted the swings. "One, two, three!"

Eliana wanted to zip her own coat. But the zipper was stuck at the bottom. She pulled and pulled. It did not move.

She called her dad. "Count while you pull," he said. "One, two..." Then Eliana forgot what came next. She stood very still.

Then she remembered a song. "One, two, buckle my shoe," she sang. "Three, four, shut the door." Dad smiled and clapped the beat. The words rhymed, so they came out easy. "Five, six, pick up sticks." On "pick," she grabbed the zipper tab with her fingers. "Seven, eight, lay them straight." The zipper slid up, up, up. "Nine, ten, a big fat hen!" The coat was zipped all the way to her chin.

Eliana picked up her red hat. "I did it with my song," she said. Dad gave her a real hug. "Sing it at school for Krew," he said. Eliana ran to the door. "One, two, buckle my shoe!" she sang.

Theo sat at the art table. He wanted to make a robot. Ms. Bondarenko gave him a wood block and a sheet of stickers. "What can I do with these?" Theo asked. "Count and see," said Ms. Bondarenko.

Theo put a red sticker on the front of the block. Then he turned it. Another flat side! He put a blue sticker there. He turned the block again and again. Top. Bottom. Left. Right. "One, two, three, four, five, six!" said Theo. Six stickers on six flat sides. Each sticker was a square, and each flat side was a square too!

Alexis came over. "How many sides does it have?" she asked. Theo held up the block. "Six! Count my stickers!" Alexis clapped. Theo glued the block onto his robot for a head. He drew two circle eyes and a triangle nose. "My square-headed robot has a tail," said Theo. He taped on a paper rectangle. The robot waved its arm.

Arnaud loved the big red blocks at school. Today he got to the block corner first. He stacked one, then two, then three. The tower grew tall.

Hallie and Matheo came over. "Can we play too?" Hallie asked. Arnaud looked at his tower. "These are my blocks," he said. "All of them?" Matheo asked. "All of them," said Arnaud.

Hallie walked away. Matheo walked away. Arnaud built alone. The room felt quiet. He looked at Hallie. She was drawing with her finger in the air. He looked at Matheo. He was spinning in a circle. Nobody was building.

Arnaud pushed the blocks into one big pile. Then he stopped. What if he made three piles? He counted them out. "Hallie! Matheo!" he called. "Look. One pile for me. One pile for you. One pile for you."

Hallie ran back fast. Matheo ran back fast too. Each child built a small tower. "Can I put my block on top of yours?" Arnaud asked. "Yes," said Hallie. "You say please, that's polite." "Please," said Arnaud.

The three towers stood side by side in a row. Matheo clapped his hands. Hallie moved her tower closer so they touched. Arnaud grinned and said, "Blocks for everyone."

Miles sat at the table. Mom put down a big pot. It smelled warm, like rice and peas.

"Tonight we say the blessing first," said Mom. "It is special. We fold our hands."

Miles wanted to eat right now. The rice smelled so good. But Mom said, "Watch Grandpa."

Grandpa bowed his head. He closed his eyes. Miles peeked. He saw Grandpa's eyes shut and Grandpa's head down. Miles closed his eyes too. He bowed his head. "Thank you for our food," he said, in his little voice.

Then Miles opened one eye. Grandpa was still bowing. Miles closed his eye fast. He waited. The room was very quiet. He could hear the pot steam going tss, tss.

"Amen," said Grandpa. Everyone said "Amen." Mom smiled big. "Miles said it with us!"

Miles clapped. The blessing was done, and now it was time to eat. Miles took his spoon. "I did it!" he said. "Can we say it again tomorrow?"

Eleanor went to the corner store with her dad. Apples sat in a big box. "Can I count them?" she asked. "Yes," said Dad. Eleanor pointed at the apples. "One, two, three, four, five, six." But she pointed at one apple two times. "Six!" she said. Dad shook his head. "Count again," he said. "Point to each apple one time."

Eleanor tried again. She tapped one apple and said one number. "One, two, three, four, five." Five apples! She had said one number for each apple. She jumped up and down. "Five apples!"

Next, Eleanor looked at two little piles of pears. She counted the first pile. Four pears. She counted the second pile. Seven pears. "This pile has more!" she said, pointing. Mr. Korhonen, the store man, smiled. He put one pear in the middle of the small pile. "Now count again," he said. Eleanor tapped each pear one time. "Five!" she said. Still not more than seven. She giggled and gave the pear back.

At home, Eleanor counted her toy cars. One car got two taps by mistake. She lifted her finger and started over. "One, two, three, four." She ran to Dad with all four cars. "I counted just right!" she said. "Can we go back tomorrow?"

Harper wanted to bake cookies with Dad. She asked, "Can we bake now?"

"Not now," said Dad. "We will bake later."

Harper frowned. "Is it later yet?" she asked.

"No, not yet," said Dad.

Harper followed Dad to the laundry room. He put a shirt in the washer. Then he put a towel in. "One shirt, one towel," he said.

"Is it later yet?" asked Harper.

"Not yet," said Dad. "Later means some time after now, not right away."

Harper waited. She counted the socks. "One sock, two socks, three socks."

The washer went swish, swish. Then it stopped.

"Now is it later?" she asked.

Dad smiled. "Yes! Now it is later."

They washed their hands. Harper helped pour the sugar. She was careful and stood back from the hot oven. Dad put the cookies in.

"One cookie, two cookies, three cookies," said Harper.

"Tomorrow we can bake more," said Dad.

"Tomorrow!" said Harper. "I love tomorrow."

The bookmobile stopped on Myles' street. Myles ran up the steps with his dad. Mr. Mansour smiled and handed him a card. "Your very first library card," he said. Myles held it with both hands.

Myles picked a book about tools. There was a hammer on the cover. He read it in the corner. Then he slid it onto a shelf by the door.

"Wait," said Mr. Mansour. "See that little white label on the spine? That label shows where the book belongs." Myles looked at the letters. He pulled the book out and matched the label to the shelf. It slid right into its spot.

"Did the label do that?" Myles asked. His dad nodded. "It did."

Then the bookmobile began to beep. "Time to go," Mr. Mansour spoke softly. "Take your book home. Bring it back soon."

Myles carried the hammer book down the steps. He held his card up high.

Madelyn sat in the family car. Her tummy felt jumpy. Today she would get a shot at the doctor.

"I think the needle is big," said Madelyn. "Big like a boat!"

"Say what you see at the doctor," said Mom. "Then we will come back to the car."

At the doctor, Madelyn held her bear tight. The doctor held up a thin, thin needle. "One quick poke," said the doctor. "Ready?"

Poke. Done. Madelyn blinked. "It was tiny! Not big like a boat. Just a quick poke in my arm." She looked at her arm. A small bandage sat there like a little white boat.

"That was so fast!" said Madelyn.

"Very fast," said Mom. "You did it."

Back in the car, Madelyn grinned. "Shots are just a quick poke with a thin needle. That is all!" She waved her bandage out the window. "Can we get a tasty snack now?"

"Yes," said Mom, starting the car. "You earned it."

Madelyn hugged her bear. "Quick poke, thin needle, all done!"

"Home we go," said Mom, and the car rolled down the road.

Aurora sat in the family car. She was going to the dentist. It was her first time. She held her little bag on her lap. Inside was her toothbrush, ready to show.

"One toothbrush, one girl," said Aurora. She liked that.

Mommy started the car. Aurora peeked in her bag. She saw a toothbrush. But it was blue. Her toothbrush was green. This one was not hers. It was the baby's toothbrush. "Not mine, not mine," said Aurora.

Mommy looked in the mirror. "The baby uses that one," she said. "Each person uses their own toothbrush." Then the car went on. Aurora held the blue toothbrush. She did not use it. She just looked at it.

At the dentist, Aurora opened wide. The dentist counted her teeth. One, two, three, up to twenty. Then Aurora smiled a big smile. "No bad teeth today," said the dentist. "Good brushing!"

Back in the car, Aurora held her bag tight. At home, she ran to the bathroom. She put the blue toothbrush back by the baby's cup. She took her own green one. "One toothbrush, one girl," said Aurora. She gave it a big hug.

Eleanor ran to the kitchen with muddy hands. "Soup time!" she called.

Her dad pointed to the sink. "We wash our hands before we eat," he said.

Eleanor looked at her hands. They were brown. "My hands are wearing mud shirts!" she said. Her dad laughed.

She went to the sink. He turned on the water. It was warm, not hot. Eleanor rubbed her hands together. The mud went down the drain. Now her hands were pink and clean.

Back at the table, there was soup and bread. Eleanor dipped the bread in. "Salty!" she said, and made a funny face. "Salty soup, clean hands."

Her dad held up his own hands. "Wash first, eat after," he said, and winked. Eleanor giggled and took another big bite.

Brooks was in the playroom. The sun made a warm spot on the rug. His friend Dexter was there too.

"Let's put things in piles," said Dexter. "Animals here. Toys here. Food here."

Brooks picked up a cow. It went in the animal pile. He picked up a banana. It went in the food pile. He picked up a little red car. It went in the toy pile.

Then Brooks found a soft brown dog. He put it in the animal pile. Dexter shook his head. "That is a toy," he said. "It is not alive."

Brooks looked at the dog. It did not bark. It did not wag. It just sat there, soft and quiet.

The real dog at home barked. This one did not. Brooks picked it up. He put it in the toy pile, next to the red car.

"Now it is not lost," said Brooks.

"Wait," said Dexter. "The food pile is empty."

Brooks smiled. He ran to the toy kitchen. He came back with a apple, a carrot, and a egg. They went in the food pile, one by one.

Mr. Jung looked in the door. "Nice tidy piles," he said.

The soft brown dog sat with the toys. It was quiet. It was not alive. It was right where it belonged.

Declan sat in his car seat. He was going home from the park with his dad. His tummy rumbled. He wanted a warm bath and his pillow right after.

"Big bath tonight," said Dad. "You got very muddy."

Declan smiled. At home, Dad turned on the water. Declan wanted to jump in. He stopped. "Wait," he said. "You check first."

Dad put his hand in the water. "Too hot," he said. "Watch this."

Dad turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Steam went up, then it stopped. Dad checked the water again. "Now it is warm," he said.

Declan put in his toes. Warm, not hot. He slid in all the way.

Declan had an idea. "Does the tap make cold water too?" he asked.

Dad showed him. Declan put his hand near the cold tap. Brrr. He pulled back fast.

"So taps can be hot or cold," said Declan. "And you check first."

"Check first," said Dad. "Every time."

Declan splashed and played. His rubber duck floated past his knee. Then he hugged his towel, warm and soft like a big pillow. "Bath time is the best," he said. "After you check first."

Jaxson went to the library with his dad. A big sign said "Story Time Today." Jaxson wanted to sit in the front row. But the front row was full.

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya held up her hand. "Let's count the chairs," she said. "One, two, three, four, five." Then Francesca counted too. "One, two, three, four, six." She frowned. "That sounds funny."

Jaxson listened hard. "Six comes after five," he said. Francesca tried again. "One, two, three, four, five, six." She smiled big. "Now it sounds right!"

Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya gave Jaxson a job. "Count the mats for me," she said. Jaxson touched each mat. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." Ten mats for ten kids. Everyone sat down. Finley patted the mat next to him.

The story was about ten little ducks. Jaxson counted them on the pretty blue pages. One duck went away, then two, then more. At the end, all ten ducks came back.

Story time finished. Jaxson gave back his mat. "One," he said, putting it on the pile. He waved to Ms. Silva-Jayasuriya. "Ten tomorrow?" he asked. She laughed and said, "Ten tomorrow."

Jackson sat at the dinner table. He had ten green beans on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself.

He touched a bean. "One," he said. He touched the next one. "Two." His mom smiled and waited. "Three, four, five." The beans were round and little. "Six, seven, eight, nine." One bean was left. "Ten!" Jackson clapped his hands.

Then Jackson wanted to write the number ten. He had a paper and a crayon. He wrote a big 4 first. No, that was four. He rubbed it out. He drew a huge 7. No, that was seven. He looked at his mom.

"Ten is written with two numbers," she said. "A 1 and then a 0." Jackson drew a small 1. Then he drew a round 0 right after it. He held up the paper. "Ten!" he said.

At school the next day, his friend Zaya was counting sheep on a card. "One, two, three," she said. Jackson sat next to her. He wrote 1 and then 0 on his paper. "That means ten sheep," he said. Zaya counted the last sheep and laughed. "Ten!"

Nora wanted to play the flower fairy game with Wren and Mivaan. The rules were simple. You pick a flower card. You hop two hops. Then you send your fairy to the flower house.

Nora picked a card. She hopped four hops. She zoomed straight to the flower house. "I win!" she said.

Wren put down her card. "That is not the game," she said. Mivaan folded his arms. He sat down on the smooth rug. Nobody hopped. Nobody picked a card.

Nora looked at the empty flower house. Her fairy sat all alone. "Okay," she said. "Two hops. Then I send my fairy."

She picked a new card. She hopped two hops. She sent her fairy to the flower house. Wren clapped. Mivaan jumped up and picked his card. All three fairies sat in the flower house together. "Now we all win," said Wren.

Ryan woke up early. He found his toy monkeys on the rug. "Five monkeys for my song," he said. He set them on his bed.

Ryan sang, "Five little monkeys jumping on the bed. One fell off and bumped his head!" He pushed one monkey off the bed. It fell on the rug. Now he counted. "One, two, three, four. Four monkeys left!"

He sang the next part. "Four little monkeys jumping on the bed!" Another monkey fell. He counted again. "One, two, three." Hmm. Was it three now? Yes, three monkeys sat on the bed.

"One fell off and bumped his head!" Ryan laughed. He counted, "One, two." Then one more monkey fell. "One," said Ryan. Then that monkey fell too. "Zero monkeys! All done!"

Mack came over to play. "Where are the monkeys?" he asked. Ryan pointed at the rug. "They all fell off. Want to put them back?" Mack put five monkeys on the bed. "Sing it again," said Mack. "One, two, three, four, five. Ready?" Ryan smiled. "Ready!"

Ivy sat on her bedroom floor. She had paper and a fat red crayon. She wanted to write a note for Grandpa. Grandpa was coming today.

Ivy made letters. She made them big and small. She made them all in one long line. The letters were squished together like peas in a pod. She held up the paper. "Look, a note!" she said. Then she put it on the bed for Grandpa.

Mom came in. She picked up the note. She turned it upside down. She looked and looked. "Hmm," said Mom. "My eyes feel weak today. I cannot find the words." Mom tapped her toe, thinking. Then she smiled. "Ivy, there is a space between one word and the next." She showed Ivy with two fingers. A little gap. Like that.

Ivy tried again. She wrote a word. She left a gap. She wrote the next word. Gap, word, gap, word. "Dear Grandpa, let us play," the note said now. She did not forget the gaps at all. She ran and put the note by the door, face up, so Grandpa would see it first.

The door opened. Grandpa came in. He picked up the paper. He read it right away. "Dear Grandpa, let us play," he said out loud. He laughed a big laugh. Ivy jumped up and down. "You read my words!" she said. Grandpa held out his hand. "Come on," he said. "Let us play."

Edouard loved basketball day in the school gymnasium. His team was the Blue Foxes. His friends Khalid and Abir were on the team too. But Edouard had a problem. The ball never went in. He threw it high. It hit the wall. He threw it low. It rolled away. "The hoop is playing tricks on me," he said.

Mr. Do blew his whistle. "Watch Abir," he said. Abir held the ball up. She bent her knees. She let it fly. Swish! The ball went through the hoop. The scoreboard changed. Two points! A shy boy on the bench whispered, "That's how our team scores." Edouard opened his eyes wide. The ball had to go through the hoop.

Edouard tried again. He bent his knees like Abir. He aimed up. The ball sailed through the net. "I did it!" he shouted. Khalid laughed and gave him a high five. Mr. Do clapped. After the game, they helped clean the floor. Edouard put the ball in the bag. "Same time next week?" said Abir. Edouard grinned. "Yes! I want more hoops!"

Penelope ran out to the playground. The sun was big and bright. "Sunny today!" said Dax. Penelope looked up. The sun made her eyes go small. She could not see the slide. She held Emmitt's hand tight.

"Why are my eyes squinting?" she asked. Ms. Sokolov smiled. "Try a sun hat," she said. She got a blue hat. Penelope put it on. The hat made shade over her face. Now her eyes opened wide. She could see the whole slide. She could see Dax waving. She could see the swing.

It was windy too. The wind blew Emmitt's scarf. It flapped like a tail. "Your scarf looks funny," said Penelope. Emmitt laughed and held it.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain came down. Rain was not scary. Ms. Sokolov opened umbrellas. "Rainy days need umbrellas," she said. They walked inside. Penelope kept her hat on. "My hat helps in the sun," she said. "I want to wear it again tomorrow." Dax said, "Me too!"

Juliette sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was full of warm soup. "One more bite," said Dad. Juliette took a big bite. Yum.

"I want to stay up late," said Juliette. "I want to play with my blocks." Dad said, "Okay, a little late." Juliette played and played. She did not sleep much.

The next morning, Dakota came over. They ran out to the yard. Juliette tried to run fast. Her legs felt slow. Her eyes felt heavy. She sat down on the grass near the swing. "I am too tired," she said.

That night, Juliette ate her dinner. She had a bath. She put on her soft pajamas. Then she said, "I will go to sleep now. Sleeping at night gives my body rest for the next day."

She slept and slept. In the morning, Dakota came again. Juliette ran fast in the yard. Her legs felt strong. "My rest worked!" she said. Dakota laughed, and they ran to the swing together.

Hudson sat in a big chair. It went up, up, up. Ms. Chanthavong put a cape on him. It was soft and it fit just right. "Time for your first haircut," she said.

Hudson's dad stood close by. Ms. Chanthavong picked up her scissors. Snip, snip, snip. Little bits of hair fell down. Some landed on Hudson's neck. Hudson began to wiggle. He scratched his neck with his hand.

"Why are you wiggling?" Ms. Chanthavong asked. "My neck feels itchy," Hudson said. She smiled and picked up a soft brush. She brushed the little hairs away, tick tick tick. The itchy feeling went away too. Hudson sat very still. "Where did the hairs go?" he asked. "Into my brush," she said. She tapped it over a bin. The bin was empty, and now tiny hairs fell inside.

Snip, snip, snip went the scissors. When a hair landed on his neck, Hudson said, "Itchy!" Ms. Chanthavong brushed it off right away. Then the haircut was all done. Hudson looked in the mirror. "I see a big boy," he said. Dad gave him a thumbs up, and Hudson grinned all the way home.

Eva went to Zeke's house. Zeke's mom put on a song. It had a bumpy, jumpy beat. Eva wanted to sing "Twinkle, Twinkle" with Zeke and clap too.

Eva clapped whenever she liked. Clap! Clap! Clap! Zeke shook his head. "You are clapping too fast," he said. "It sounds all mixed up." Eva got upset. Her claps and the song did not match. It was like a dream where her feet ran the wrong way.

"Listen first," said Zeke. "The song goes boom, boom, boom. Clap at the same time as the boom." They stood still and listened. Boom, boom, boom. Eva waited. Then she clapped on the boom. Clap, clap, clap. Her claps landed right on the song! She felt her hands find the music like a friend holding hands.

Then they sang. "Twinkle, twinkle, little star." Eva sang it all by herself. She did not miss one word. Zeke clapped along with her singing. Eva laughed and clapped too, right on the beat, all the way to "what you are."

Evan went to the library with his friend Kacey. Mr. Kerr had a big box of new books. "One book each," said Mr. Kerr. Evan picked a book about trucks. Kacey picked a book about a bear.

Kacey read fast. Soon she wanted Evan's truck book too. Evan held it close. Then he looked at her book. The bear had a big, wide yawn. Evan wanted to see it. "You read mine," said Evan. "I read yours." They swapped books. That worked well.

At the desk, Mr. Kerr stamped Evan's book. Evan took it and ran to the door. Kacey stopped him. "Wait," she said. "What do we say?" Evan thought hard. He ran back to the desk. "Thank you, Mr. Kerr," he said. Mr. Kerr smiled a big smile.

"Thank you too," said Mr. Kerr. "For remembering." Evan gave his book a little kiss and hugged it tight.

"Can we cook pretend soup with the bear book?" Kacey asked. Evan laughed all the way to the car.

Milan ran to the big tire swing at the playground. His friend Liam was already there. "Let's play rocket ship," said Liam. Milan wanted to be the rocket ship. But he did not know how to start it.

Liam held the tire with both hands. "Watch me," he said. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Liam jumped high on "blast off." The tire swing swung back and forth. Milan clapped his hands.

"My turn," said Milan. He got in the tire and held on tight. The tire felt bumpy under his tummy. Liam counted, "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Milan giggled. "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Milan jumped up and the swing went whoosh.

Ms. Thompson was sitting on a bench. "That is called a countdown," she said. "You counted backward from ten down to one." Milan smiled a big smile. His fuzzy hair blew in the wind. "Again!" said Milan. Liam laughed. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!"

Kinsley ran into the big room at the cultural center. There were rows and rows of little clay cups. Her mom held a box of them. "Can I help?" Kinsley asked. "Yes," Mom said. "Put them in a long row."

Kinsley set out the little cups one by one. She counted them as she went. Her friend Ryder came to help too. He put wicks in each cup. Then a grown-up poured oil into them.

"What are these called?" Kinsley asked. Mom said, "They are called diyas." Ryder rolled a diya across the table to Kinsley. She laughed and set it back in the row.

Soon Mr. Kelly came with a small flame. He touched it to the first wick. A little light popped up. Then he lit the next one, and the next. Kinsley watched from far back, where it was safe.

The whole row glowed now. One little cup had made one little light. Then all the little lights made a big bright line. "Look, Ryder!" Kinsley said. "They all shine together!" The diyas blinked like tiny stars on the table.

Emma put on her swim class suit. It had little ducks on it. Her mom took her to the big hotel pool.

Emma hoped she could swim today. Her class was by the steps. Mr. Bui was the teacher. "Hello, Emma," he said. "We will kick and blow bubbles."

Chelsea ran fast to the pool. "Wait," said Mr. Bui. "The floor is wet. Wet floors are slippery. Walk, please." Chelsea stopped her feet. She walked very slow, like a turtle. Emma laughed. "Slow turtle feet," she said.

Emma got in the water. She held the rail. She kicked and kicked. She blew ten bubbles. Then she let go. She kicked all by herself. "Look at me!" she called.

After class, Emma felt fresh and clean. She walked, not ran, to her towel. Chelsea walked too, turtle style. "See you next time," said Mr. Bui. Emma waved and waved.

Xavier waited by the gate. Ms. Grewal called the names. "Yunus! Neo! Xavier!" Xavier ran to his dad.

At home, Dad said, "First we wash hands. Then we eat." Xavier looked at the soap. It felt smooth. He rubbed it. Nothing happened. "Where are the bubbles?" he asked.

Dad turned on the tap. Water ran cool and fast. Xavier held his hands under it. He rubbed the soap again. Bubbles! Lots of soft, white bubbles covered his fingers.

"Look, Dad! Bubbles!" Xavier piled them on his chin. "I have a beard!" Yunus made one too, at school. Xavier giggled and giggled.

He washed the bubbles off. His hands were clean and shiny. Then he ate his lunch. After that came a bath, with more bubbles. Then he would wear his soft pajamas with the little animal on the front.

"Soap and water," said Xavier. "Bubbles every time."

He rubbed his soapy tummy and blew one bubble off his hand.

Scarlett was awake early. She wanted to wash her face all by herself. Dad put a small ice cube in her cup of water. Scarlett picked up the ice cube with her fingers. It felt so cold! She dropped it into the cup fast. Plop! Her ears heard the little splash. Then she washed her hands with warm, soapy water. The soap smelled like strawberries. She touched the soft towel to dry off. Dad held out his hand. "Here is your toothpaste," he said. It tasted like mint on her tongue. Scarlett looked in the mirror. Her eyes saw the ice cube floating in the cup. She touched it once more, very quick. Still cold! She laughed and poked it with her toothbrush. "Brrr," she said, and waved at the girl in the mirror.

Ayla went to the store with her mama. She held the shopping list. The list was small. The cart was big.

Ayla saw Ms. Do in the store. "Hello, Ayla," said Ms. Do. Ms. Do was buying soup. The soup can was cold from the shelf. Mama picked a warm loaf of bread. "Hot and cold," said Ms. Do with a smile.

Then Ayla saw it. A toy drum sat on a shelf. It was red and round. "Can we get it?" asked Ayla. Mama said yes. Ayla tapped the drum. BANG! It was so loud. A man by the bread put his hands over his ears. A baby began to cry. Ayla made her hands go fast on the drum. Loud, loud, loud.

Ayla stopped. She made one small, slow tap. Tap. That was quiet. The baby stopped crying. The man took his hands down. "Loud and quiet are opposites," said Ms. Do. Ayla tapped loud. Then she tapped quiet. One drum, two sounds!

A cart rolled by, fast. A old man walked by, slow. A box began to drop from a shelf. A worker caught it. He put it back in a tidy line.

At home, Ayla played her drum. She tapped quiet like a little rain. Then she tapped loud like a big storm. Mama laughed. "Play your quiet rain for me," she said. Ayla tapped, tap, tap, tap, soft as a spring day.

Arya sat on the rug at school. Amari had a shiny red kite. It had a long tail. Arya wanted to hold it very much.

She reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She looked at Amari's face. She put her hand in her lap. "May I have a turn?" she asked.

Amari smiled big. "Yes! You said may I!" He put the kite in her hands. Arya felt the string. It was smooth and long. "Thank you," she said.

Jose ran over too. He grabbed for the tail. "No, no," said Ms. Sinclair softly. "Try asking, Jose."

Jose thought for a moment. "May I hold the tail?" he said. "Yes, you may," said Arya. She held the kite safe and snug. Jose held the tail. They walked round and round the rug, humming a little song. "Zoom goes the kite!" said Amari, pushing it through the air.

Evelyn sat on the rug at home. Her blocks were all around her. She wanted to give her best block a sticker on every side. But she did not know how many sides it had.

First she looked at her snack. Her cookie was a circle. It was round like a ball. She stuck out her tongue and licked a crumb from her lip. Then she put the cookie down and looked at the block.

"One," said Evelyn. She put a red sticker on a flat side. The side was a square. She turned the block over. "Two." She put a blue sticker there. That side was a square too. "Three, four, five." A sticker went on each flat face. Her socks were stinky, so she wiggled her toes and kept going. She turned the block one more time. "Six." The last sticker was yellow.

"Mom, how many sides does a block have?" Evelyn asked. Mom came to look. "Count your stickers," said Mom. Evelyn lifted the block up high. "One, two, three, four, five, six," she said. Six stickers. Six flat faces. Each one was a square, just like her red sticker.

Evelyn held the block to the window. The sunlight made six shiny squares glow. "Six," she said again, and gave the block a hug.

Luca was at the ice rink. His team wore blue hats. Luca held his stick with both hands. He saw his friend Lyra on the red team.

The red team won the game. Luca sat down on the cold bench. He felt grumpy. Why did he feel like that? Then Mr. Mokoena blew his whistle. "Line up, everyone," he said.

The blue team stood in a line. The red team stood in a line too. The lines came close together. Each player tapped gloves with a red player. "Good game," said Luca. "Good game," said Lyra.

Luca skated off the ice. His grumpy feeling had gone away. He looked back at the closed rink door. "Can we do that again?" he asked. Mr. Mokoena laughed. "Next game," he said. "Good game, Luca."

Jake sat in the family car. He held his toy dinosaur tight. "Dentist today," said Dad. Jake's tummy felt jumpy. "The dentist will count my teeth," said Jake. "Roar," said the dinosaur, in a small voice.

At the dentist's office, Jake climbed into a big chair. It went up and up, like a ride. Then a bright light turned on above him. Jake squeezed his eyes shut. It was too bright! "Here, these will help," said the dentist. She gave Jake little sunglasses to wear. Now his eyes felt fine. The dentist leaned close. The bright light helped her see inside Jake's mouth.

"Open wide," said the dentist. Jake opened wide. "One tooth, two teeth, three teeth," she counted. "Ten teeth! So clean, like after a bath." Jake grinned. "The chair is slippery," he said, sliding down. "Roar!" said the dinosaur, riding on his lap.

Audrey wanted to find her red ball. The playroom was messy. Blocks were on the floor. Dolls were on the rug. The toy box was empty.

Mckinley came to help. "Let's put them away," she said. Audrey picked up a block. It felt hard and cool. She put it in the box. "Blocks," she said. Mckinley held up a doll. The doll had soft yellow hair. "Dolls," said Mckinley. She put it in the box too.

Walter rolled something across the floor. It bumped Audrey's toe. It was the red ball! "Balls," said Audrey. She put the ball in the box with the blocks and the dolls. "Blocks, dolls and balls," said Mckinley. "They are all toys." Audrey clapped. "We win! The box is full."

Mr. Silva peeked in at the door. "What a clean playroom," he said. He pointed at the rug. A little bug was sitting there. "The bug needs a home too," said Audrey. She put her hand down low. The bug crawled onto a leaf by the window. Audrey waved. "Bye bye, bug. Bye bye, mess."

Theodore sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy hurt a little. "May I wash my hands?" he asked. The nurse said yes. Theodore saw the little sink. He turned toward the tap. The nurse stopped him fast. "Wait. I check the water first." She put her hand under the tap. "Warm, not hot," she said. Theodore waited. Then she nodded. "Now you." Theodore put his hands in. Warm! He got soap. "How long do I scrub?" he asked. "Twenty seconds," said the nurse. "That is two happy songs." Theodore sang and scrubbed. Bubbles, bubbles, bubbles. He saw a spotted fish on the soap bottle. Then the doctor came in with a sticker shaped like a seed. "Clean hands!" she said. Theodore smiled and clapped his soapy hands.

Ruby ran to the gate at school pickup. Her tummy made a little growl. She saw her grandma waiting with a bright yellow bag.

"Can I have cookies now?" Ruby asked. Grandma shook her head. "Not yet. First we eat breakfast."

Ruby stopped. "What is breakfast?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "Breakfast is the first meal of the day."

They walked home. The sun felt warm on Ruby's face. Grandma's shoelace came untied, so they had to wait while she tied the string into a bow.

At home, Grandma said Ruby could help. Ruby looked in the cupboard. She saw cookies on the top shelf. "Those come later," said Grandma. Ruby saw oats in a big jar. She picked the jar up with both hands.

Grandma cooked the oats on the stove. Ruby stood far away and watched. The oats went pop, pop, pop. They smelled sweet like warm honey.

Ruby ate her bowl of oats all up. Her tummy felt happy and full. Then it was time for the rest of the day. Grandma helped her get dressed in a red shirt and blue pants.

"Can I have a cookie now?" Ruby asked. Grandma laughed and put one cookie in her hand. Ruby took a big bite. It was soft and sweet.

"This is the best cookie," said Ruby. Grandma wiped oat milk from Ruby's chin with a warm cloth. "That is because your tummy is full," said Grandma. Ruby held the cookie up to the window, and the light shone through the little hole in the middle.

Hannah had a big bag of blocks. She wanted to build a tower now. "Can Bowie come play now?" she asked. Her dad was folding clothes. "Later," said Dad. "First I make the beds."

Hannah sat on the rug. "Is it later yet?" she asked. "Not yet," said Dad. Hannah looked at her blocks. She could not touch them yet. She made a little song instead. "Wait, wait, wait," she sang, softly.

She watched Dad pull the sheet. The messy bed got smooth. One pull, one smooth side. Then he did the next bed. Then the last bed. Hannah sang her song all the way through.

"Now it is later," said Dad. Hannah clapped her hands. She poured out the blocks. Bowie came in and they stacked them tall. The tower wobbled and did not fall. When bedtime came, Hannah sank into her pillow. "Tomorrow we build it again," she said. "Yes," said Bowie. "Tomorrow."

Jaxson stood in a big circle of people at the festival. Long tables were set with open boxes of warm bread. His friend Hallie waved at him. Her whole family stood beside her.

"Hands, everyone," said Hallie's grandma. "We say our blessing first."

Jaxson folded his hands. The blessing said thank you for the food. Everyone said it together. Then it was time to eat, but Jaxson did not move.

"Where does bread come from?" he asked.

"A farmer grew the wheat," said his dad. "The sun helped it grow tall."

So Jaxson cleared his throat. "Thank you for the food," he said. "And thank you to the farmer, too."

Hallie smiled and clapped. Her grandma blew him a little kiss. Then everyone took warm bread, and Jaxson took the biggest piece he could find.

Victor ran to the playground. He wore his red socks today. He loved his red socks. He took off his shoes to feel the soft sand. Then he ran to the slide. One red sock fell off in the sand. Victor did not see it.

He sat down for his juice. He felt his foot. One foot had a sock. One foot had no sock. Victor looked upset. "Where is my sock?" he said. His friend Luna came over. "We can find it," she said. Mr. Moretti sat on the bench. "One, two," he counted Victor's feet. "A pair means two," said Mr. Moretti. "You need two socks."

So Victor went looking. He took a step. Then another step. Luna came too. They looked by the slide. They looked by the swings. "One, two, three, four, five," counted Luna, touching the flowers. "Six, seven, eight," said Thatcher, who joined the hunt. "Nine, ten," said Victor, counting the stones.

Then Luna pointed. "Look!" There was the red sock, half under the sand. Victor picked it up. He put it on his foot. Two red socks. A pair! "Thank you," said Victor. He gave Luna a big hug. Then they ran to the swings together.

Wren stood at the edge of the pool. She held her teacher's hand. Mr. Yoon smiled at her.

"Time to try bubbles," he said. "Swim teachers have kids practice blowing bubbles into the water through their mouth."

Wren looked at the water. It was blue and shiny. She did not want to put her face near it.

"What if the water tickles me?" she asked.

"Maybe a little," said Mr. Yoon.

Wren leaned over. She took a big breath. Then she blew through her mouth into the water. Bloop, bloop, bloop! Big bubbles popped up. They tickled her chin. Wren laughed and laughed.

"Look, Willa!" she called. "I made bubbles!"

She blew again. More bubbles came. Willa ran over to see.

Then a bubble popped right on Wren's nose. It felt like a tiny kiss.

"Do it again," said Willa.

So Wren did.

"Hello, bubbles," she said.

Isabella was at Grandma's house. In the corner stood a little piano. Grandma gave Isabella a soft smile. "You can play it," Grandma said.

Isabella pressed one key. Plink. She pressed two keys. Plink, plink. Then she tried a song. It came out wrong. The song ran away from her fingers. Isabella frowned. "It is too hard," she said.

"You can try again tomorrow," said Grandma. So Isabella did. One day, she played three keys. Plink, plink, plink. The next day, she played four keys. Then five. Then the whole line of the song. Outside, soft rain tapped the window. Isabella was careful with her fingers, slow and small.

On the last day, Isabella sat up tall. She played the song all the way to the end. Plink, plink, plinkety, plink. Grandma clapped. "Play it again," she said. Isabella laughed and put her fingers on the keys.

Beatrice had a toy kitchen at home. She wanted to play house with her toy duck. "You be the baby," she told the duck.

She put the duck in a pot. She stirred with a spoon. Clang, clang, clang! Then she gave the duck a pretend bottle. The duck was a rough baby. It fell on the floor. Beatrice picked it up and patted its back. "One pat, two pats, three pats," she said. The duck felt better.

Then her friend Angad came over. He wanted to play too. He made pretend soup with round buttons. Slurp, slurp! They fed the duck together. "We win at playing house," said Angad. They laughed and laughed.

Soon Angad had to go home. But the kitchen was a big mess. The pot was on the floor. The spoon was under the chair. The buttons were everywhere. Her mom said, "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." So Beatrice and Angad cleaned up. One pot, two spoons, three buttons. They counted each toy into the box.

Then Angad went home. Beatrice hugged her duck. Mom tucked them both in for a cozy rest. "Night night, baby duck," said Beatrice.

Elizabeth sat at the dinner table. She wanted the apple pie. It sat on the counter, far away.

"Can I have pie now?" she asked.

"Not now," said her dad. "We eat pie soon."

Elizabeth frowned. "Soon is a long time," she said.

"Soon means in a little while," said her dad.

Elizabeth took one bite of her chicken. She took another bite. She drank some milk. She looked at the pie again. It was still there.

"Now?" she asked.

"Not yet," said her dad. "Eat a little more."

Elizabeth ate her carrots, one by one. She waited some more. Then her dad stood up. He cut the pie. He put a big piece on her plate.

Elizabeth looked at her plate. The waiting was done. The pie was here now.

"Yesterday I had bread," she said. "Today I have pie. Tomorrow I can have pie again?"

"Maybe tomorrow," said her dad, smiling.

Elizabeth took her fork and played a little game. She made her pie into a moon shape. Then she ate it all up.

"Now pie is all gone," she said.

Her dad laughed. "And tomorrow," he said, "we can bake a new one together."

Emile looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. "No school today," said his dad. "A snow day!"

Emile put on his boots. He put on his big coat. Then he walked into the snow. His boots made marks. Each step left a shape in the snow. Step, step, step.

Then Emile saw more marks. They were not his marks. They looked like little feet. "Look, Dad!" said Emile. "Little feet walked here!"

The little footprints went across the yard. Emile followed them. Step by step, he walked. The footprints went past the swing. They went under the big tree. They stopped at the fence.

The footprints led to a small door in the fence. It was the neighbour's door. Emile heard a sound. "Neigh!" A huge white horse stood there!

"Hello, horse," said Emile. The horse was gentle. It did not hurt Emile at all. The neighbour came out. "She escaped this morning," she said. "But her feet left footprints in the fresh snow."

Emile looked back at his own footprints. His feet made marks too. "My feet made footprints, Dad!" said Emile. Dad smiled. "You found the horse all by yourself."

Emile patted the horse's soft nose. "Good feet," he said. "Good footprints."

Alexis ran fast across the playroom at daycare. His shoes slip on the shiny floor. He fell right into Sultan's tall block tower. Crash! All the blocks fell down.

Sultan's mouth turned down. His eyes got big. "My tower," he said. Alexis felt his tummy go tight. He did not mean to knock it down. Mr. Toussaint knelt down next to them. "Alexis, do you have words for Sultan?" he asked softly.

Alexis took a big breath. "Sorry, Sultan. I did not mean it. Sorry means I know I hurt you." He looked at the fallen blocks. "Can I help build it again?" Sultan nodded. "Okay. Let's build it big."
