They stacked the red blocks first. Then the blue ones. Then the yellow ones. Joey came over with a cold juice cup from snack time. "Can I help too?" he asked. "Yes!" said Sultan. "It is going to be a birthday tower for my dog."

The tower grew tall, taller, tallest of all. "It did not fall," said Alexis. "We built it together." Sultan smiled and put one more block on top.

Ethan went to the garden center with his dad. He wanted to grow vegetables. He picked little seeds and a big bag of soil. "I will plant them all by myself," he said.

At home, Ethan put soil in a pot. He poked holes with his finger. He dropped the seeds in. He covered them up. Then he watered them. Every day he looked at the pot. Nothing was there. "Where are my plants?" he asked. "Maybe it is a big problem," he said. His dad said, "Not yet. Just wait a little more."

Ethan waited and waited. One morning he saw something tiny and green. It poked up out of the soil! Ethan ran to his dad. "Come see!" he shouted. His dad smiled. "That is called a sprout," he said. "A sprout! A sprout!" Ethan sang. He watered it again. "Grow big, little sprout," he said. "You will be a silly big carrot soon."

Benjamin ran into the kitchen. It was morning, and Dad was making breakfast. Benjamin saw big red strawberries in a bowl. He touched one with his finger. It felt bumpy and cold.

"I want a crunchy apple too," Benjamin said. Dad washed an apple. Then Dad turned on the blender for the smoothie. The blender was very loud. It was too loud for Benjamin's ears. He put his hands over his ears. His hands covered his ears. Now the loud sound was quieter. That was better. Benjamin smelled the strawberries. They smelled sweet.

The blender stopped. Benjamin took his hands off his ears. Dad gave him a slice of apple. Benjamin tasted it. Crunch, crunch. "Can Josh and Luna hear the blender?" Benjamin asked. "No, it stopped," said Dad. Benjamin listened. The kitchen was quiet again. "All done," said Dad.

Eva was at home in the kitchen. Her dad was washing strawberries. Eva wanted to taste one.

First she used her eyes. She saw the red strawberries. She saw the little green leaves on top.

She used her nose next. She sniffed a strawberry. It smelled sweet. Then she used her ears. She heard the water splash in the sink. She touched the strawberry with her fingers. It felt bumpy with little seeds.

Her dad let her have one. Eva bit it. "Yum!" she said. It tasted big and sweet in her mouth.

Then Eva held her nose closed. She bit the strawberry again. She chewed and chewed. The taste was very small now. It tasted plain, like nothing much. She let go of her nose. The sweet taste came back! Eva laughed.

She tried it again with a second strawberry. She held her nose. Plain again. She let go. Sweet again.

Her dad peeked over her shoulder. "What are you doing?" he asked.

Eva held up her strawberry. "My nose helps it taste big," she said.

Then her little bike bell rang in the hall. Ding, ding! Eva had not touched it. It was the cat, batting the bell with her paw.

Thomas sat at the dinner table. He had ten green peas on his plate. He wanted to count them all by himself.

He pointed at each pea. "One, two, three," he said. Then he counted some more. "Four, five, six, seven." His friend Ananya sat next to him. She held up her milk cup.

"Eight, nine," said Thomas. He looked at the last pea. "Ten!" He was so proud. But then he wanted to write the number ten on his paper.

He wrote a big 1. He stopped. "Where is the ten part?" he asked. Ananya laughed, not in a mean way. "Ten is two numbers," she said. "A 1 and then a 0."

Thomas was afraid he would forget. So he looked at his plate. He pushed one pea away from the rest. Then he pushed another pea next to it. One pea, then a round pea alone. They looked like his numbers!

"That is my ten!" said Thomas. His dad smiled and gave him a marker. Thomas wrote 1, then 0. "Ten!" he shouted. Ananya clapped and Thomas ate the round pea last.

Harper wanted to be a mommy today. But she felt too small. Her mom gave her a big blue coat. "Dress-up clothes help you pretend," Mom said. Harper put it on. Now she was Mommy Harper, big and tall!

Mommy Harper got to work. One spoon for Bunny. One spoon for Bear. "Time to eat," she said. Bunny had weak little arms, so Mommy Harper held him. "One more bite," she said. "Then we bake a cake." She patted air in a pan. Pat, pat, pat. The cake was pretend, but it smelled like rainbows.

Then the baby cried. "Waa, waa," said Mommy Harper for Bunny. She rocked him fast. She sang low. Bunny stopped crying. Mommy Harper smiled. She fixed Bear's hat too. Then she looked up at Mom and said, "Can I be a firefighter next?"

Ivy sat at the school table. Mr. Çilik put a bowl of ice cubes down. "We will use our five senses," he said.

Ivy peeked at the cubes with her eyes. They were shiny and white. She heard them clink in the bowl with her ears. She smelled them with her nose. They smelled like water, like nothing at all.

Then Ivy picked one up. She touched it with her fingers. "Ooh!" said Ivy. The ice cube felt so cold. She dropped it into her cup fast.

Bo tried it too. "Cold, cold, cold!" said Bo. He dropped his cube in too.

"What is in the cup now?" asked Khadija.

Ivy took a little sip with her tongue. "Cold water!" she said. "Ice makes it cold."

Ivy picked up one more cube. She was not alone at the table. All her friends held the ice, then let it go. "So cold, so fast!" they said, and laughed together.

Romy stood at the school gate. Her bag had a star on it. Her tummy felt jumpy.

"Have a lucky first day," said Mom. She gave Romy a hug. Then the gate opened with a click.

Romy walked in. Kids ran everywhere. They laughed and played. But Romy did not know anyone. She stood still by the wall.

Then she saw a girl. The girl stood alone too. She looked at her shoes.

Romy took a big breath. She walked over.

"My name is Romy," she said. "What is your name?"

The girl looked up. "I am Alexandria," she said. "Want to play?"

"Yes!" said Romy. They held hands and ran to the slide.

The bell rang. Mr. Costa came to the door. "Line up, friends," he said.

Romy and Alexandria lined up together. Romy waved at Mom outside the gate. Mom gave a big wave back.

"See you after school," said Alexandria.

"Lucky day," said Romy. They walked in side by side.

Leo went to the farm with his class. Anika and Blaire came too. Ms. Jung said, "We will find our five senses today."

First Leo touched a sheep. Its wool was soft. "We touch with our hands," he said. Then he heard a cow. "Moo!" went the cow. "We hear with our ears," said Blaire. Then Leo saw a red barn. It was a big shape like a box. "We see with our eyes," said Anika.

Then Ms. Jung held up a lemon slice. Leo put it on his tongue. His face went tight. "Sour!" he said. Then she held up a strawberry. Leo tasted that too. It was sweet. "The strawberry is sweet and the lemon is sour," said Leo. "My tongue knows both!" He stuck out his tongue and looked at it.

On the way home, Leo sniffed the air. "I smell hay with my nose," he said. Anika laughed and sniffed too. "I smell it too," she said. Leo counted on his fingers. Eyes, ears, nose, hands, tongue. "Five senses," said Leo. "All mine."

Quinn sat in her car seat. She looked out the window. "When do we eat?" she asked. "Soon," said her dad. "Soon means in a little while." The lamp posts went by, one by one. The car went into a deep, dark tunnel. Quinn waited. She counted the lights. One, two, three. Then the tunnel ended. The sky was bright again.

Soon, soon, soon. Quinn said the word to herself. The car turned a corner. Then she saw it. Grandpa's house! There was Grandpa, waving by the door. "We are here!" said Dad. "It was not a long wait," said Quinn. She climbed out of her seat. Grandpa hugged her soft and warm. "Did you bring cookies?" he asked. "Yes," said Quinn. "We will eat them soon." Grandpa laughed. "Then just a little while," he said, and held the door open wide.

Noah ran to the playground after dinner. He was not sleepy yet. He wanted to play on the swing. But the swing was taken. A girl was on it. It was Hannah from his class.

Noah waited by the fence. He watched the swing go up. He watched the swing come down. Hannah pumped her legs hard. Then the swing went slower. Then it stopped.

"Can I have a turn, please?" asked Noah. Hannah slid down off the swing. "Sure," she said. "Thank you!" said Noah. Hannah stood still. She did not know what to say next. Her mouth opened, then shut.

Dane was close by, sharing his crackers. He gave one to a small boy. "Thank you," said the small boy. "You're welcome," said Dane. Hannah watched too. Her eyes got big.

Noah pushed the swing with his legs. Up he went. Down he came. Then a ball popped out of the sand and rolled to his feet. "Can you help me?" called the small boy. "Sorry, I can't reach it alone," said Dane, who tried and missed.

Noah jumped off the swing. He picked up the ball. He handed it to the small boy. "Thank you," said the small boy. "You're welcome," said Noah. Then Noah looked at Hannah. She smiled. "Want to push me now?" she asked. "Yes, please," said Noah.

Myles was playing in the backyard with Flavie. They were digging in the dirt. They wanted to feed the birds later with the seeds they found.

Myles saw something shiny under the leaves. He bent down to look. It was a little lighter. It had a button on the side.

"Look, Flavie," said Myles. "What is it?"

Flavie shook her head. "Don't touch it. Let's show a grown-up. Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use."

They ran to Myles's father. "We found something!" said Myles.

His father came to the leaves. He picked up the lighter with care. "Good job not touching it," he said. "That was smart."

Myles felt tall and proud. His father put the lighter in his pocket, far away from little hands.

Then they fed the birds together. The birds came flying down, wild and fast. They pecked at the seeds on the grass.

"Again tomorrow?" asked Flavie.

"Yes," said Myles. He waved at the birds.

Eleanor went to the park with her friend Maci. Ms. Whitehead brought a hoop and a big red ball. She put the hoop on the grass. "Toss the beanbag in," she said.

Eleanor held the beanbag up high. She flung her arm over her shoulder. The beanbag flew far, far away. It landed near a little butterfly. The butterfly flew off fast. Maci laughed and laughed. "Too far!" she said. Eleanor ran to get the beanbag. She felt a bit cross.

Ms. Whitehead knelt down beside her. "Watch me," she said. "This is an underhand throw." She held the beanbag down low. Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag went up, up, up. Then it dropped right into the hoop. "Yay!" said Maci.

Eleanor tried it. She held the beanbag low. She swung her arm forward and up. The beanbag sailed into the hoop. Eleanor jumped up and down. "I did it!" she said. Then the beanbag fell out of the hoop and rolled on the grass. Eleanor shut her eyes and giggled. "Silly beanbag," she said.

Then it was ball time. Maci threw the big red ball to Eleanor. Eleanor held out both hands. The ball was too big for one hand. Both hands caught it, hug tight. Maci clapped. Ms. Whitehead clapped too. "Throw it back," said Maci. Eleanor hugged the ball, swung low, and let it fly up to Maci.

Jasmine found a big cardboard box in the backyard. She wanted to play with it right away. Her friend Mya came over to play too.

"A car!" said Jasmine. She sat in the box and turned a pretend wheel. "Beep, beep!"

"A boat!" said Mya. She wanted the box to be a boat. "Row, row!"

They both wanted the box. Mya frowned. Jasmine frowned too. Then Mya had an idea.

"Let's take turns," said Mya. "First a car. Then a boat."

Jasmine smiled. She drove the box car around the grass. "Vroom!" The wheels were loud in her head. Then she climbed out and gave the box to Mya.

Mya rowed the box boat across the grass. "Splash, splash!"

Jasmine got her teddy bear. The bear needed a house. "The box can be a house now," she said. She put the bear inside and patted its head. Mya added a leaf for a blanket so the bear could dry off after the pretend bath.

"Time for bed, little bear," said Jasmine softly.

Then the girls climbed in together. The box was a house for everyone.

Ms. Holloway peeked over the fence and waved. "What a fine house," she called.

Jasmine waved back. "Come to our house!" she said.

Eli went to the park with his mom. It was a big festival day. There were flags and drums and lots of people. There were food stalls too.

Eli saw a food stall with sweet bread. He let go of his mom's hand. He walked toward the smell. The crowd was big. People walked in front of him. He could not see his mom. His tummy felt dizzy with worry.

Then Eli remembered. At a big crowded celebration, children stay close to their grown-up. He stood still and looked around. His mom was not far away. She was waving at him. He ran back and held her hand tight.

"Stay close now," his mom said. "The crowd is too big for little feet." They walked to the sweet bread stall together. His mom bought one piece. Eli took a bite. It was soft and warm. A little crumb fell, and a cloud of birds flew down to peck at it. Eli laughed and licked his sticky fingers. He held his mom's hand all the way home.

Dylan was in his bedroom. Maxime was coming to play today. Dylan felt so excited. His tummy was bouncy like a frog.

"I want to jump!" said Dylan. He jumped on the rug. He bounced on his bed. He shouted, "Maxime is coming!" He was so loud. His teddy fell over. Teddy looked angry about the big noise.

Dylan stopped. He sat down on the rug. He took a big, slow breath. He gave teddy a hug. "Waiting is hard," he said softly. He patted his bouncing legs, one pat, two pats. The frog in his tummy got small and still.

Then the door went ding-dong. Dylan walked slowly, slow like a snail. He opened the door. "Maxime!" said Dylan. "Come see my bedroom!" Maxime ran in, and they both laughed.

Thomas ran into the yard. The grass was wet and cold on his toes. Then he saw it. A small grey feather lay by the big tree.

"Look, Mommy, look!" he called. He picked it up. It was soft like his cat's tail. He petted it with one finger.

"Birds are animals that have feathers," said Mommy. "So a bird lost this one."

Thomas looked up. He looked at the tree. He looked at the roof. "Bird!" he shouted. A fat bird sat on the fence. It had grey feathers, all over!

The bird flew down. It hop, hop, hopped. It found a crumb. Then it flew away. Thomas waved.

"Come back!" he called. He held the feather up high. He was proud of it.

Inside, Mommy gave him toast and apple slices. Thomas ate his food. He put the feather on the window sill.

"Maybe the bird will see it," said Thomas. He watched and watched the yard. The toast was warm and good. Then he saw something move outside.

A bird was back on the fence. "It came back!" Thomas shouted. He ran to the window and tapped the glass, very soft. "Hi, bird. Hi!"

Harper sat on the big rug in the living room. Theo and Oceanne sat next to her. On the TV, a big game was on. Lots of people were running with a ball.

"Which team is mine?" Harper asked. She pointed at the TV. "They all look the same to me!"

Theo laughed. "They do not look the same. That team is red. That team is blue."

Harper looked hard. She saw one group in red shirts. She saw one group in blue shirts. "Oh! Red team and blue team!"

"Each team wears its own colors," said Mr. Kaur from the couch. "So you can tell the two teams apart."

The red team ran fast. A red player kicked the ball. It went into the net. "Goal!" everyone shouted. Harper jumped up and down.

Then the weather outside turned rainy. Rain tapped on the window. But inside, the game went on.

"Now I can help," Harper said. She clapped for the red team. "Go red! Go red!"

The blue team got the ball. "Oh no," said Oceanne. "I like blue."

"That is okay," said Theo. "You pick blue. I pick red."

Harper made a kind offer. "You can share my team too, Oceanne."

Oceanne giggled. "No thank you. Blue is mine."

The game went on and on. Harper watched the red shirts run. She watched the blue shirts run. She never mixed them up again.

Mr. Kaur passed out cups of juice. Harper took a big sip. On the TV, the red team kicked the ball again.

"Here it comes!" Harper shouted. "Watch the red one!"

Brielle sat in her car seat. The car went bump, bump, bump down the road. She could see the pizza shop near the corner. "Pizza," said Brielle. "Yes," said her dad. "We will get pizza soon."

Brielle was thirsty. There was a juice box in the bag by her feet. "Give me juice!" she said. Her dad did not pass it to her. He kept both hands on the wheel. "Try again," he said. Brielle thought for a moment. "Juice, please," she said. Her dad smiled in the mirror. Then he reached back at the red light and gave her the juice box.

Brielle drank her juice. It did not hurt her tummy. It felt good and cold. "Thank you," she said. "You are welcome," said her dad.

At the pizza shop, the man gave Brielle one warm slice. "Please may I have more?" she asked. The man laughed and gave her a second slice. Brielle took a big bite. "Yum," she said. "More, please!"

It was bedtime. Jackson brushed his teeth in the bathroom. Then he ran to his room.

Jackson had a plan. He took out his crayons. He wanted to write a note for his dad. Jackson loved the playground, so he wrote, "LETSGOTHEPLAYGROUND." He put the paper under his pillow. His tummy felt happy and jumpy.

Dad came in to tuck him in. Jackson held up the note. "Read it, Dad!" Dad looked and looked. He turned the paper sideways. "Hmm. I cannot read this yet." Jackson's face went sad.

Dad picked up Jackson's bedtime book. He opened the front cover first. He turned the pages one by one. He pointed at the page. "See the words? There is a space between one word and the next." Jackson leaned in close. He saw the little gaps. The words sat apart, like friends on a bench.

Jackson took his crayon. He drew little gaps in his note. Now it said, "LETS GO THE PLAYGROUND." Dad read it out loud. "Let's go the playground! Yes, tomorrow we can go." Jackson laughed and clapped. Dad kissed his head. "Sleep now, my writer."

Jackson hugged the note to his chest. "Goodnight, words," he whispered.

Elijah stood at the train station. He held a big red sign. It said GRANDMA in wobbly letters. It was hard to write letters that big.

The train rolled in. It was long and shiny. The doors went whoosh. People walked out one by one.

Then Elijah saw her. "Grandma!" he shouted. Grandma hugged him tight. Her coat smelled like flowers.

"Grandma, you are staying at my house for a whole week," said Elijah. "Are you my friend Andie's grandma too?"

Grandma laughed. "No, sweet pea. I am your mommy's mom."

Elijah blinked. "My mommy has a mom?"

"She does," said Grandma. "I am her mommy, just like your mommy is your mommy."

Mommy came over with the car keys. "Hi, Mom!" she said, and hugged Grandma too.

Elijah looked at Mommy. Then he looked at Grandma. Mommy's mom. Grandma was Mommy's mommy!

On the walk to the car, Elijah held Grandma's hand. "Grandma," he said, "when we get home, can we have warm milk?"

"We can have warm milk," said Grandma. "Your mommy can heat it. She learned that from me."

At home, Mommy heated the milk. Elijah held his cup with two hands. It was warm and sweet.

"Grandma," he said, "tomorrow can you read me a book? The train book?"

Grandma sat down beside him. "Every day for a whole week," she said.

Elijah snuggled close. The book had a shiny train on the cover. "That train looks just like your train," he said.

"It does," said Grandma. She opened the book to page one.

Leo sat on the big red couch at Mr. Wu's house. Everyone was watching the game on TV. Leo's friend Willa sat next to him with her milk.

"Who is winning?" asked Leo.

"I forgot," said Willa. She spun her cup and got a little dizzy. "Maybe the blue team. Or the red team!"

Mr. Wu laughed. "Look up there," he said. He pointed at the TV. "That is the scoreboard."

Leo looked. The scoreboard had two big numbers on it. One number was for each team. The blue team had the bigger number.

"The blue team is winning!" said Leo. He clapped his hands.

The red team kicked the ball into the net. The scoreboard changed. Now the numbers were the same.

"It's a tie!" said Willa.

"Look at that," said Leo. "The scoreboard always knows. I never have to remember!"

Leo dreamed of the day he would play in a big game too. But for now, he sipped his milk and watched the numbers go up and up.

"Willa, check the scoreboard," he said. "Quick, quick!"

The blue team scored again. Leo jumped up and did a happy dance.

Athena ran to the scooter. Gurasees was already on it. Athena grabbed the handle. "My turn!" she said. Gurasees held on tight.

Mr. Gagnon came over. He had a little sand timer. "When the sand runs out, the turn is over," he said. He turned it over. The sand began to fall. Gurasees rode in a circle. Athena watched the sand. It went down, down, down. The sand ran out. Gurasees stopped. "Your turn now," he said.

Athena got on the scooter. She rode to the fence and back. She peeked at the timer. The sand was almost gone. Athena stopped all by herself. "Sand is done!" she said. Gurasees laughed and took his turn.

Then Athena and Gurasees built a big sand hill together. They dug with their hands. Athena said, "I am hungry." Mr. Gagnon smiled. "Snack time," he said. "First, brush the sand off." Athena brushed off her hands. Then she sat with Gurasees and ate crackers, side by side in the sun.

Ethan went to the store with his dad. It was snowy outside. The store had a big shelf of books. Ethan wanted a book about a red lamp.

He found one. He sat down to read it. He opened the back page first. He ran his finger from right to left. The words felt mixed up. "Dad, the story is broken," he said.

His dad sat close beside him. "Turn to the front cover first," he said. Ethan turned the book around. He put his finger at the left side of the page. Then he slid it to the right. The words went in a row, one after another. It sounded like a real story.

A girl named Maksim from his class peeked over. "That is my favorite book," she said. Ethan smiled and read on. His finger moved across the page, left to right, all the way to the end.

Brooklyn had a cold. Her nose was stuffy and runny. She sat on the couch with a soft blanket. Her tummy made a little rumble. "I want a snack," she said.

Her mom put crackers and apple slices on a plate. Brooklyn took a tissue. She blew her nose. It made a big honking sound. Then she reached for a cracker.

"Wait," her mom said. "Your hands need soap and water first." Brooklyn felt a bit sad about waiting. But she slid down from the couch. She went to the sink. She pumped the soap. She rubbed her hands under the water. Bubbles grew between her fingers. "I will tell my teddy," she said. "He should wash his paws too."

Then Brooklyn sat back down. She picked up a cracker with clean hands. She crunched it. The apple was sweet and juicy. Her mom smiled and tucked the blanket around her. Brooklyn gave one apple slice to her teddy, and pretended he took a big bite.

Everly had a sparkly pink dress. She wore it all day at Katelyn's party. She twirled. She jumped. She ate cake until her tummy was full.

Now it was dark. Everly did not want to take off her dress. "I want to sleep in my dress," she said. Her dad helped her change anyway. He put on her soft pajamas. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in," he said.

Everly got into bed. The pajamas felt warm and cozy. Her dress had been scratchy. The pajamas were soft like a blanket. She snuggled down and felt safe. Her dad tucked her in.

"Night night," he said.

Everly closed her eyes. "Night night, dress," she whispered. "You can come out tomorrow."

And soon she fell fast asleep.

Milo sat at the little table in the backyard. He had a big paper pumpkin to paint. He looked in the paint box. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. But there was no orange paint. "Where is the orange?" he wondered.

His friend Hayes came over. Hayes held up the red jar. "Want to paint it red?" asked Hayes. Milo shook his head. He wanted a real orange pumpkin. Then he had an idea. What if the paints could mix?

Milo put a dot of red on his brush. Then he put a dot of yellow next to it. He picked up the brush and swirled them together. Round and round they went. The red spread into the yellow. The yellow spread into the red. Then something new appeared. Orange! Bright, orange paint!

Milo dipped his brush in the orange. He painted the pumpkin. He painted the stem green. He touched the wet paint with one finger. It felt a little slimy. He laughed and wiped it on the paper. "Look, Hayes! Red and yellow made orange!" said Milo. Hayes grabbed a brush too. "My turn to mix!"

Lily ran into the playroom. Blocks were everywhere! Red blocks. Blue blocks. Yellow blocks. Green blocks. What a mess.

"Clean-up time!" said Ms. Bouchard. "Let's sort by color," said Cora. "That means all the same color blocks go together in one group."

Lily grabbed a red block. She put it in the red pile. Thunk! She grabbed another red block. Thunk! Soon the red pile was big and tall. Then she made a blue pile. Then a yellow pile. Cora made a green pile.

Lily looked at the red pile. Wait! One block was hiding in the wrong pile. It was blue! Lily picked it up. She walked it over to the blue pile. Thunk! Now every block sat with blocks just like it.

Cora clapped her hands. "All sorted!" she said. Cash held up a green block and grinned. "Look! Green pile wins. It's the tallest!"

Then Lily heard a quiet flutter by the window. A little bird spread one wing, then the other. It pecked at a yellow block on the sill. "The bird likes yellow too!" said Lily, and she waved hello.

Kinsley rode the bus with her mom. They were going to the big library. Today Kinsley would get her very first library card.

At the library, Kinsley wanted a book about trucks. She looked and looked. She saw books about cats. She saw books about the sea. But no trucks. Where could they be?

Then she saw a woman at a desk. Books were stacked all around her. Kinsley asked, "Do you work here?"

"Yes, I do," the woman said. "I am the librarian. I help people find books."

"Can you help me find truck books?" asked Kinsley.

The librarian walked to a shelf. "Here they are." There were so many trucks!

Kinsley picked a big red one. She shut the book under her arm. She held her new card up high.

On the bus home, she whispered, "I found it all by asking."

Nova was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Grandma held up Nova's thick red coat.

"Can you put it on by yourself?" Grandma asked.

Nova pushed her arm in one sleeve. Then the other arm. The coat was on! But the coat was open. Cold air came in at her tummy.

Nova pulled the little zipper tab up. Zzzzzip! The coat closed. Nova was warm now.

Nova and Grandma went out to the yard. There was a big puddle by the gate. Nova stomped in it. Splash! Her boots got wet and shiny.

Then Nova ran and ran. She ran to the fence and back. Now she was hot. Too hot! Sweat ran down her back.

Nova pulled the zipper tab down. Zzzzip! The coat opened. Cool air came in. Nova felt better.

"You did that all by yourself," said Grandma. "Yes I did," said Nova. "Down makes it open."

They walked to the gate. Nova pulled the tab up again. The coat closed and she was warm. She pulled it down. The coat opened and she was cool. Up and down, up and down.

"Time to come in, little one," said Grandma. Nova held her hand. They stepped over the puddle together.

Brooklyn went to the store with Mom. First they got bread. Then they got apples. Then they got milk. The milk case was cold. "Brrr," said Brooklyn. "My hands feel cold." The bread shelf was near a warm oven. A worker pulled hot rolls out with big gloves. Brooklyn stayed back and watched.

Brooklyn wanted to see the toy aisle. She looked and looked. Then she turned around. Mom was not there. Brooklyn could not see Mom anywhere. Where did Mom go?

Brooklyn remembered something. She walked to the front of the store. A worker in a red vest stood by the checkout. "I can't find my grown-up," said Brooklyn. "Can you help me?" The worker smiled. She used the big speaker. Soon Mom came running. "There you are!" said Mom. She gave Brooklyn a big warm hug. The worker put the bread in the bag. Brooklyn held Mom's hand all the way home.

Zoey sat on the playroom floor. "Let's make piles," said Ms. Holloway. "One pile for animals. One pile for toys. One pile for food." Zoey picked up a toy apple. It went in the food pile. Then she found a toy cat with soft fur. She threw it, and it did not run away. It just sat where it fell.

Zoey held a toy dog. "Woof," she said. She put it in the animal pile. Then she stopped. The toy dog did not wag its tail. It did not blink. "It is not alive," said Cassius, sitting next to her. Zoey tapped the toy dog. It stayed very still. She picked it up. She put it in the toy pile instead.

"Good sorting, Zoey," said Ms. Holloway. Ayoub clapped his hands. Zoey smiled and patted the toy dog on its soft head.

Lucy made a card at school. It said "Good Morning" on it. She wanted to give it to her friend Neriah. But where was Neriah?

"Not here now," said Ms. Santos. "She will come tomorrow."

Tomorrow. Lucy tapped her foot. When was tomorrow? Yesterday they had painted together. Today Neriah was not at school. So tomorrow must be the next day.

The next morning, Lucy woke up. She peeked out of her room. The family was at the table eating breakfast. Morning was here! It was the part of the day when they woke up and ate. So today had come.

"Good morning!" Lucy said.

At school, Lucy held her card tight. The door opened. Neriah peeked in.

"I came today!" said Neriah.

Lucy ran to her. "A card for you. Good morning, Neriah!"

Samuel was drawing at his desk. He made a big red ball. Then he made a messy blue sky. His crayons rolled under the desk. He had to reach far to get them.

"Time for the park," said Dad. Samuel ran to the door. He could see the swings across the road. The swings looked fun. Samuel wanted to run. He stopped at the curb and waited.

"Hold a grown-up's hand when you cross the street," Dad said. Samuel held Dad's big hand tight. They looked left. They looked right. They walked across together. Then Samuel let go and ran to the swings. Rosa was there too. "I held my dad's hand all the way," Samuel said. Rosa smiled and pushed the swing for him. "Higher, please!" Samuel said. His shoes touched the sky, almost.

Willow sat at Grandma's big chair. She had a long piece of paper and a box of crayons. She wanted to draw a picture for Grandma. It would be the garden and the sky.

Willow drew red flowers. She drew yellow flowers. She drew green grass, so green and soft. Then she picked up a gray crayon. "The sky is gray," she said. She made one gray line.

Grandma looked out the window. "What a sunny day," she said. Willow looked too. The sun was bright and warm on her face. The sky was not gray at all. The sky was blue! Willow put the gray crayon back. She took the blue crayon. She filled the whole top of her page with blue.

"Look, Grandma!" said Willow. Grandma held the picture up to the window. The blue on the paper met the blue in the sky. "It matches," said Grandma. Willow smiled and drew one yellow sun.

Kayden's class was having a shape hunt. Mr. Mehta gave each child a card. Kayden's card had a circle on it. So did Mohamed's card.

"I will find the big circle," said Mohamed. He ran to the wall clock. "Look! The clock is a circle."

Kayden looked down at his shirt. He saw a tiny button. He held it up. "My button is a circle too," he said.

Mohamed shook his head. "No way. Your button is too small. The clock is a circle."

Mr. Mehta came over. He was calm and kind. He put the button near the clock. "Put them side by side," he said.

Kayden looked at the big clock. He looked at his tiny button. He turned the button around. He traced it with his finger. Round and round it went. Round and round the clock went too.

"Both are circles!" said Kayden. "Big circle, small circle, both circles."

Mohamed traced the button too. "Both circles," he said. He smiled.

Then the boys counted their circles. One clock. Two buttons. Three stickers on the door. Kayden found a cookie in his lunch box at snack time. "The cookie is a circle too," he said. It was a cool find.

Mr. Mehta laughed. "Good hunting, boys," he said. Kayden put his button back on his shirt. He would remember this day.

"One circle," said Mohamed.

"Two circles," said Kayden.

"All circles," they said together.

Ethan was playing cars in the playroom. Angel was there too. They had lots of shiny cars. Ethan wanted his cars to be magic.

"I know," said Ethan. "Let's make a road!" He put down a yellow scarf. It looked like a big sunny road. Angel put down a blue scarf next to it. Now the road was long.

Then Lily-Rose held up a green card. "Green means go!" she said. Ethan pushed his little red car fast, fast, fast. It zoomed down the scarves. Then Lily-Rose held up a red card. "Red means stop," she said. Ethan stopped his car. It stopped right away, like magic!

Angel smiled. She drove a yellow truck to the end of the road. There sat a stuffed bunny. The bunny held a paper flower. "Truck, take the flower to the bunny!" said Ethan. Lily-Rose held up the green card. The truck went. She held up the red card. The truck stopped.

The cars stopped and went all morning. Stop, go, stop, go. Then Ethan's dad came to the door. "Time to go home, Ethan." Ethan picked up his red car. "Can we play again tomorrow?" he asked. His dad smiled and said, "Yes, we can." Ethan waved the little car at his friends. "Beep beep," said the car.

Mia stood on the big grass field. Mr. Kelly put a hoop on the ground. He gave her a small red beanbag. Mia threw it. It missed. It landed in the messy grass.

"Try again," said Mr. Kelly. Mia counted, "One, two, three." She swung her arm back. She threw it soft and slow. The beanbag went up. Then it went down. It fell right into the hoop. "I did it!" said Mia. Lilith clapped. Cynthia clapped too.

Then Mr. Kelly rolled a big ball to Mia. The ball hit her hands. It bounced out. It bounced away. "Oh no," said Mia. Mr. Kelly rolled it again. The ball hit her hands. It bounced out again.

Then Mia had an idea. She waited with her arms open. The ball came. She caught it. Then she hugged it to her chest. The ball did not bounce out. It stayed right there. "One, two, three, I got it," said Mia. Mr. Kelly rolled it again, faster this time. Mia caught it and hugged it tight. The ball stayed.

Lilith ran over. "Can I try?" she asked. Mia opened her arms wide and smiled.

Brooklyn ran to the living room. The Christmas tree stood tall and green. "We decorate a tree at Christmas," said Grandma.

A big box sat on the floor. It was full of ornaments. Brooklyn picked up a shiny red ball. She hung it on one branch. Then she hung a snowman there too. Then a little drum. Soon one branch was full.

"Look, Mama!" said Brooklyn. "My branch is so pretty."

Maci, her cousin, came close. "The tree is empty on top," Maci said. "Only one branch has ornaments."

Brooklyn looked up. Maci was right. She took a golden star from the box. She hung it high on another branch. Then a bell. Then a silver bird. Her hands reached out, one branch at a time.

Grandma plugged in the lights. Brooklyn stood back with Maci. The whole tree danced with tiny lights.

"Now it is a dream tree," said Brooklyn. Maci laughed and held her hand.

Declan ran to the window. "Rain!" he shouted. Big drops hit the glass. Plip, plip, plip.

"I want to splash in puddles!" said Declan. He ran to the door. He opened it fast. He ran straight out into the yard.

The rain fell on his head. The rain fell on his shirt. It was cold and wet. Declan was wet all over. He ran back inside fast.

His mom held up a red coat. "Your raincoat," she said. "Put it on." Declan pushed his arms in. He zipped it up. He pulled the hood on too.

Then he ran back out. The rain fell on the hood. Plip, plip. The rain fell on the coat. Plip, plip. But Declan stayed dry under it. Not wet at all!

He touched his sleeve. The rain sat on top. It did not go through. "Dry!" he yelled. He jumped in a big puddle. The water went splash.

Maci came by in her yellow boots. "Look at all that rain!" she said. "My coat keeps me dry too!" They stomped and stomped. Two dry kids, two big puddles, one happy rainy day.

Olivia got a small blue card. It had her name on it. "Your first library card," said Grandpa. "Now you can touch a book, take it home, and keep it a while."

They went to the library. Grandpa helped her pick a book about ducks. "This one," said Olivia. She held it tight all the way home.

At home, Olivia read the duck book many times. She read it to her teddy bear. She read it to Grandpa. Then Grandpa said, "Time to take it back. But we will get a new book too."

At the library there was a little hole in the wall. "That is the book return slot," said Grandpa. "A book return slot is a place to drop off books when bringing them back to the library." Olivia held the duck book. She did not want to let it go.

"I will miss it," said Olivia. "You can pick a new one right away," said Grandpa. Olivia held the book up to the slot. She waved to the ducks. "Bye bye, ducks," she said. Then she dropped the book in. It slid down, down, down. It was gone.

Olivia looked at the slot. The book had gone in, and now the slot was empty. She had put it in, and it had gone away. She jumped a little jump. "I did that!" she said.

Then she ran to the shelf. She touched the covers, one by one. "This one," said Olivia. It was a book about a loud, bumpy truck.

Anna sat on the big couch in the living room. Mama was beside her. Greyson and Bruno sat on the floor. They were all watching the big game on TV.

"Who is that man?" Anna asked. He wore a striped shirt. He kept running and looking at the players.

"That is the referee," said Mama. "The referee watches the game and makes sure the players follow the rules."

One player grabbed the ball with his hands. The referee blew his whistle. He pointed his finger. The player looked sad and let go of the ball.

"He saw it!" said Bruno.

"Yes," said Anna. "The referee watches everything."

Anna stayed awake until the end of the game. The referee blew his whistle one more time. The game was over. Mama gave Anna a warm hug. Then Anna looked at the picture of a referee she drew in her book, and smiled.

Ezra went to the library with his dad. He wanted a book about rocket ships. The library had big gray shelves and soft carpets. Ezra marched down the aisle. He saw a book with a red rocket on it. "This one!" he said.

Callan was there too. "Let's play rocket ship," said Callan. They stood by the carpet squares. Callan began to count. "Ten, nine, eight, seven." Ezra listened. The numbers went down, one by one. "Six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" Both boys jumped up high. A girl named Agathe clapped. "That's a countdown," she said. "You count backward from ten down to one."

Ezra wanted to try. He took a deep breath. "Ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one. Blast off!" He jumped so high his socks almost flew off. Ms. Leblanc, the librarian, smiled. Ezra held his rocket book tight. "Ten, nine, eight," he whispered all the way home.

Isaiah ran to the playground. His brown shoes went clip, clip on the path. He was excited to see the big drum.

Ms. Okonkwo had put the drum by the sandbox. Isaiah hit it once. Boom! He hit it again. Boom, boom! He laughed. "One boom, two booms, three booms," he counted.

Then Lilith came near. She put her hands over her ears. "Too loud," she said. Her face looked scared. Isaiah stopped his hands. He felt sad that his friend felt scared.

But Oakleigh ran over. She was smiling big. "I love the drum!" she said. She hit it too. Boom! Isaiah looked at Lilith. He looked at Oakleigh. Same drum. One friend was happy. One friend was scared.

"Ms. Okonkwo," said Isaiah, "can Lilith and I play something quiet?"

"Yes," said Ms. Okonkwo. "The sandbox is a quiet spot."

Isaiah and Lilith dug in the brown sand. One scoop, two scoops, three scoops. Oakleigh kept the boom, boom, boom far away by the fence. Lilith smiled now. Isaiah was happy too.

"We can all play," said Isaiah. "Loud over there. Quiet over here." Lilith patted the sand. "This is just right."

Eloise was at school. It was naptime. The room was quiet. But Haylie had a drum. She banged it loud. The loud drum woke Martha up. Martha rubbed her eyes. She looked mad.

Mr. Swampy walked over. He sat down next to Haylie. "Loud and quiet are opposites," he said. "Can you play the other way?" Haylie thought hard. Then she tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. The tap was quiet. Martha did not wake up again. She went back to sleep.

Eloise watched the whole thing. She wanted to try too. She picked up a small drum. First she played it loud. The loud sound made Martha stir. Then Eloise played quiet, quiet, quiet. Nobody stirred. A flower on the shelf stood still. "I need the quiet drum for naptime," Eloise whispered. Tap, tap, tap.

Riley looked out the glass door. The sky was gray. "Rain," said Dad. Riley put on her rain boots. The rain made a tap-tap sound on the roof.

The rain stopped. Riley ran to the backyard. Vyom was there too. "Look!" said Vyom. He pointed at the ground. A big puddle sat in the grass. Riley stepped in it. Splash! Her boot went down in the water. She laughed and jumped again. Splash, splash. The puddle got smaller and smaller.

Soon the sun came out. It was sunny now. The wind started to blow. It blew Riley's hair all around. "My puddle is going," said Riley. She filled her glass of water and poured a little on the ground. A tiny puddle came back. "There you are," she said, and she jumped one more splash.

Grandpa came to stay at Maya's house for a whole week. Each morning they walked to the park together. Grandpa pushed Maya on the swing, way up high. "I can see a big white cloud," Maya called. Grandpa laughed and pushed her again.

They sat on the warm bench and shared a full bag of bread crumbs. The ducks came running. Maya dropped a crumb, and a duck gobbled it up. Then she dropped another crumb, and another duck ran over. "One crumb, one duck," said Grandpa.

One day Grandpa packed his suitcase. Maya felt sad. "I will miss you," she said. At home, Maya drew a picture of the big white cloud. Her mom helped her put it in an envelope. They walked to the mailbox together. Then Grandpa called on the phone, and Grandma waved on a video call. Maya held up her cloud picture to the screen. "I will draw you more," she said. Grandpa smiled.

Eliana turned four today. Her party was at the big swimming pool. Himmat and Willa came too.

First they swam in the shallow end. Eliana kicked her legs fast. Her kicks made big splashes. The water went up and came down on Willa's head. Willa laughed and wiped her eyes.

Then Mommy called them out of the pool. There was a cake on the picnic table. It had a soft, furry teddy bear sitting next to it. One little candle stood on top.

"I will blow it out," said Eliana.

"Not yet," said Mommy. "First, everyone count."

They counted the candle. "One!" said Himmat.

"I was three yesterday," said Eliana. "Today I am four."

"That's how birthdays work," said Ms. Harper, the lifeguard, smiling.

Eliana took a big breath. She blew hard. The flame went out. Smoke curled up like a little gray cloud. Everyone clapped.

Then Eliana saw something. Willa was shivering. Willa's towel was far away on the bench. Eliana ran and got it. She wrapped it around her friend.

"Thank you," said Willa.

Eliana sat close beside her. Then she ate her cake, all of it, down to the last bite.

Dinner was outside tonight! Mom set the table on the grass. Luka ran to his seat. But his shoes felt tight and bumpy. "Ouch," he said. He sat down and could not wiggle his toes. Mom helped him pull off his shoes and socks. "Now your feet are safe and free," she said. Luka put his bare toes on the grass. The grass tickled! "My feet can feel it!" he laughed. "Soft grass under bare toes!" He sniffed the soup. It smelled like carrots. He heard Dad slurp, loud and silly. He saw steam rise up. He touched his warm cup with one finger. Then he tasted the soup. Yum! "My feet liked the grass," said Luka. "Can we eat out here every night?" Mom laughed. "Yes, little bare-feet boy."

Milo woke up in the tent. "Eggs today!" he shouted. Dad laughed. "Yes, you can help."

At the little camp table, Milo held a big brown egg. He tapped it on the bowl. Tap, tap, knock. The shell cracked. Milo pulled the shell open. The egg slid out! "It came out!" he said. "Look, Dad, it came out!"

But a little piece of shell fell in too. It sat in the yellow egg like a tiny boat. "Oh no," said Milo. Dad gave him a spoon. Milo dipped the spoon in. He fished out the piece of shell. "Got it!"

"Ready to cook?" said Dad. Dad lit the little camp stove. Milo stood back, far from the hot pan. He watched the egg go round and flat. "It makes a circle!" said Milo. "It makes a sun shape!"

The egg went onto a plate. Milo carried the plate to the tent, low and slow, both hands holding tight. "Breakfast!" he called. Mom sat up and smiled. "For me? Thank you, Milo!"

Milo grinned. "I cracked the shell. The egg came out!"

Riley went to the park with Dad. There was a little tent there. Kittens sat in a big pen. One small kitten had white paws. It looked at Riley. "This one," said Riley. Dad said, "We can take her home today."

At home, Dad put a box on the floor. It had soft sand inside. Riley pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked. "A litter box," said Dad. "The kitten goes to the toilet in it."

Riley watched the kitten. The kitten sniffed the sand. The kitten moved her paws. Then the kitten used the box. Riley clapped. "Good kitten!" she said.

At night the kitten sang a little song. Riley gave her water. She petted her softly. "Careful," said Dad. "Her claws are sharp." Riley touched the kitten very gently. The kitten purred and purred. "Good kitten," Riley said again.

Evan was at daycare. He had a big red box. He put a toy bear in the box. He put a little car in the box. He put a shiny ball in the box. The box was his soup pot. "This is bear soup," he said. "It is hot soup!" But then Andreas ran up. Andreas took the bear out. Andreas took the car out. Andreas took the ball out too. The soup pot was empty. Evan wanted his soup back. He put the bear in again. Andreas took it out again. In, out, in, out. "Hey!" said Evan. "You take out. I put in." Ms. González smiled. "In and out are opposites," she said. Evan looked at the box. Then he had a neat idea. He turned the box upside down. All the toys stayed under it. "No more out!" said Evan. Andreas tapped the box like a drum. Boom, boom! "Now it is a drum," said Andreas. Evan laughed and tapped too.

Layla and her dad went to the pharmacy. The shelves were tidy and bright. "We need a new toothbrush," Dad said. "You see the dentist today."

Layla picked a small blue toothbrush. The cashier put it in a bag. Layla held the bag all the way to the dentist.

The dentist's room had a big window. Layla sat in the chair. A bright light shone down above her. Layla squeezed her eyes shut. It was too bright!

"Here," the dentist said. She gave Layla tiny sunglasses. Layla put them on. Now she could open her eyes. The light did not hurt.

"Say ahh," said the dentist. Layla opened her mouth wide. The light above the chair helped the dentist see inside. "Nice teeth," the dentist said.

Layla looked at herself in a little mirror. A girl in sunglasses, at the dentist. She laughed. "I look funny," she said.

On the way home, Layla stirred her shoe in a puddle and smiled. "Can I wear the sunglasses again tomorrow?" she asked Dad. Dad laughed and held her hand.

Louis ran to the park with his mom. He wanted to build a big pile of leaves. "I will make it big," he said. Inayah was there too. She had a small purple bag.

Louis found a big rock. He pushed it. The rock did not move. He pushed again. It still did not move. "It is too heavy," said Louis. Inayah pushed too. Still no. It stayed right there.

Then Louis found a feather pillow by the blanket. He picked it up. Up it went, so easy! "This is light," he said. "The rock is heavy, and the pillow is light," said Inayah. "Heavy and light are opposites."

Louis put the pillow on the grass. He put light leaves on top. The pile grew and grew. He jumped in. The leaves flew up. "Soft fall," said Louis. His mom clapped. "Time for a cold drink," she said. Louis smiled and gave Inayah the first cup.

Charlie was at Grandma's house. It was cold outside. Charlie wanted to play in the snow.

"Put on your coat," said Grandma. Charlie tried to zip it up. The zipper did not move. She tried again. Still no zip. Charlie felt like crying a little.

"You can get it," said Grandma. "Try it again." Charlie put the zipper in the little slot. She pulled it up slowly. Zip! It worked! Charlie smiled big.

She put on her striped boots too. Then she and Grandma went outside. Charlie zipped her coat all by herself again at the door. The snow was soft and white.

"I did it, Grandma!" said Charlie. Grandma clapped her hands.

Hannah went to the music room at the community center. Mr. Wright had a drum there. He also had a big paper with dots and lines on it.

"What are the dots?" Hannah asked.

"Those are notes," said Mr. Wright. "Written music uses notes to show which sounds to play." Hannah tapped a note. She made a boom on the drum. She tapped a short note and made a quick boom. She tapped a big dot and made a long, loud boom. One dot made one sound. She tapped two dots fast. Boom, boom!

Colter came in. "Play with me," said Hannah. He tapped the notes. She played his sounds. He tapped high, she played high. He tapped low, she played low.

Mr. Wright smiled. "You two can play at the party on Friday."

"I know a song now," said Hannah. She tapped one note and waited. Colter hit the drum. Boom. Hannah laughed and clapped her hands.

Joshua ran into the doctor's office. He saw a big fish tank. "Look, Mom, a blue fish!" he said. A sign on the wall said "Shots Today." Joshua held his mom's hand tight. The nurse called his name.

"Time for your shot," the nurse said. Joshua sat very still. The nurse touched his arm. Then, pop! The shot was done. "That was fast!" said Joshua. The nurse gave him a crunchy cracker. Joshua munched it all up.

In the car, Joshua bumped his arm on his seat. "Ow!" he said. "My arm hurts." Mom looked at him. "The spot where you got your shot can feel sore for a little while," she said. Joshua rubbed the spot gently. Then he squeezed his toy dinosaur. "You can be sore too," he told the dinosaur. "It will feel better soon."

Maeva was at school. It was drawing time. She wanted the red color. Joelle had the red color.

Maeva hid behind the big paper shelf. She peeked out at Joelle. She did not say anything. Joelle did not look up. Joelle kept drawing her cat.

Mr. Shin walked over. "Say hello," he said to Maeva, softly. Maeva peeked out again. "Hello, Joelle," she said. Joelle looked up and smiled. "Hello, Maeva!"

"Please can I have the red color?" asked Maeva. "Yes, here you go," said Joelle. "Thank you," said Maeva.

Maeva began to draw. Her hand bumped the cup. Dirty water spilled on the table. "Sorry," said Maeva. "It is okay. I will help," said Joelle. They wiped the table together.

Hello, hello, hello. Maeva said it again at play time, to Maxime too. Everyone smiled back. Then Maeva sat down and drew a big red flower. "Hello, flower," she whispered.

Charlie had a red ball. His dad put a hoop on the fence. "You score when the ball goes through the hoop," said Dad. Charlie threw the ball. It hit the fence. It did not go through. "Oh no," said Charlie.

His friend Quentin came to play. Quentin threw the ball too. It went over the hoop. It did not go through. "The ball keeps missing!" said Quentin. Charlie made a mad face. Then he stuck out his tongue at the ball. "Bad ball," he said, and he laughed.

They practiced and practiced. Charlie threw the ball up, up, up. It went through the hoop. It dropped down. "It went in! We scored!" said Charlie. Quentin clapped his hands. "My turn, my turn!" said Quentin. He ran to get the ball.

Avery sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. Her mama held her hand. On the wall was a picture of a yellow duck. Avery liked the duck. But her tummy felt jumpy.

"The nurse will come soon," said Mama. Avery did not want a shot. She wanted to go home. She looked at the duck some more. Her legs swung fast under the chair.

The nurse came in with a small tray. Avery hid her face on Mama's shoulder. "I am scared," she said. "Let's try something," said Mama. "Breathe in slow, like you are smelling a flower." Avery sniffed a big, slow breath in. "Now blow out slow, like you are blowing out a candle." Avery blew out, slow and long.

They did it again. Sniff the flower. Blow the candle. One more time. Avery's shoulders came down. Her tummy felt less jumpy. "I feel better," she said. The nurse said, "Ready?" Avery held still and kept breathing slow. The shot was quick, like a tiny pinch. Then it was done.

Avery got a bright bandage with stars on it. On the road home, she practiced her slow breaths again. Sniff the flower. Blow the candle. "Look, Mama," she said. "I can do it all by myself."

Peyton ran into the art studio. She wore her favorite shirt. It was blue with a little pig on it.

"Time to paint," said Mr. Hughes. "Put on your aprons."

Abygael put on her apron. It was loose and big. Peyton wanted to paint a pig, so she began right away.

The brush dripped. Red paint fell on her blue shirt. Peyton looked down. Her pig was covered in red.

"Oh no," she said. "Will it come out?"

Mr. Hughes brought her an old shirt. "Wear this," he said.

Peyton put it on. It was long and loose. She dipped her brush again. Drip, drip. The paint fell on the old shirt. Her blue shirt stayed clean underneath.

"Look at that," said Abygael.

Peyton painted her pig. More drips fell. None got on her clothes.

Evelyn went to the store with her dad. The sky outside looked stormy. Evelyn wanted the big red apple on the shelf. It was too high up.

A boy named Bryson stood by the juice. "Give me juice!" he said. His mom shook her head. Then Bryson said, "Juice, please." His mom smiled and put the juice in the cart.

Evelyn slid her hand along the cool shelf. Then she looked up at the store man. "Apple, please," she said. The store man smiled big. He reached up and put the apple in her hand.

"Thank you," said Evelyn. "You are welcome," said the store man. Outside, the stormy sky began to clear. Evelyn held the apple all the way home. "Apple, please!" she said again, at her own house, just to hear it once more.

Aria put on her red shirt. She loved her red shirt. Then she ran to the big field with her dad.

The game was about to start. One team wore blue shirts. The other team wore red shirts, just like Aria. A man with a big horn looked at Aria. "Yay, red team!" he said. He gave her a red flag to wave.

But Aria did not want the red team. She wanted the blue team. Lachlan was there, waving a blue flag. "Blue team is my team," he said. "I wear blue so everyone knows."

Aria looked down at her red shirt. That was why the man cheered at her! So she ran to her dad. "Can I wear my blue sweater?" she asked. Her dad pulled it from the bag. Aria put it on over the red shirt. Now she looked all blue.

The man with the horn looked again. He laughed. "Blue team too?" he said. He gave her a blue flag. A dog near the fence gave one happy bark. The crowd got loud, then quiet, then loud again, like a big ocean of voices.

Aria waved her blue flag high. "Go, blue team!" she called.

The big game was on TV. Wesley sat on the rug in the living room. Dad was there. Raavi was there too. Alexandria sat on the small chair.

A player ran with the ball. He threw it up high. It went right through the hoop! The crowd went wild.

"He threw the ball through the hoop," said Wesley. "That is how they score!"

"Can I try?" asked Wesley. Dad found a soft ball and a toy hoop. He held it up high on the wall.

Wesley threw the ball. It hit the wall and fell down. He tried again. Too far to the left. Raavi was quiet. Then Wesley stepped closer. He threw the ball up.

Swish! Through the hoop it went. The ball dropped to the floor.

"I did it!" said Wesley. "I scored!"

"Good throw," said Alexandria. She clapped her hands.

"Again," said Wesley. He picked up the ball.

Adam sat at the big table. His friend Thalia sat next to him. Up on the wall was a big, bright screen. A soccer game was on. Adam's dad had brought a gray hat for Adam. It was a little gift for game day.

A player ran with the ball. He kicked it hard. The ball flew low. Adam held his breath. "It has to go over the net," Adam said. Thalia shook her head. "No, watch," she said.

The ball went into the net. The net moved and bulged out. The whole restaurant shouted, "Goal!" Adam clapped his hands. "The ball goes in the net," Adam said. Thalia smiled. On the screen, the player ran and jumped. Adam waved his hat in the air.

Rose went to the big library with her dad. It was dark and quiet inside. "Can I really take a book home?" she asked. "Yes, today you get your own library card," Dad said. Mr. Yilmaz made the card. It had Rose's name on it. Rose picked a book about a red triangle. She sat down and opened it. She found a crayon in her pocket. She wanted to draw a cat on the page. Then she saw small fingerprints on the paper. Other kids had read this book too. Mr. Yilmaz came over. Rose asked, "Do other people read this book?" "Many people share it, so we take care not to tear it or write in it," he said. Rose listened. She put the crayon away. She drew her cat on her own paper instead. Then she held her new card tight and checked out the triangle book all by herself. "See you soon, book," she whispered.

Amira sat at the big table in math club. Ms. Perera put down two trays of apples. "Which tray has more?" she asked.

Avi counted the red apples fast. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven!" But Amira looked closely. He had counted one apple two times. "Try again," she said. "Point at each apple once." Avi pointed carefully. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six apples, not seven.

Amira counted the green tray next. She touched each apple one time. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight." She counted it two times, just to be sure. Eight was more than six. "The green apples have more!" she said in a loud, happy voice.

"Good counting," said Ms. Perera. Shanaya giggled. "Avi, your apple was tricky!"

Avi laughed too. "You silly apple," he told it. Then he tapped it once, like a drum.

Anthony went to the library with his mom. Ms. Bui smiled at the big desk. "Would you like your own card?" she asked. Anthony nodded. The card was orange and shiny. It had his name on it. He held it with both hands.

Anthony found a book about dinosaurs. It smelled like paper and old glue. He hugged it tight. "I want to keep it forever," he said. Ms. Bui shook her head gently. "It has to come back by a certain day," she said. "That day is called the due date." She stamped a little paper. One book, one card, one due date.

Anthony read the book at home, one page, two pages, three pages. Then he met his friend Alaia at the library. She wanted to read the dinosaur book too. Anthony gave it to Ms. Bui at the desk. "Here you go," he said. Alaia took it next. "My turn," she said. Anthony picked a new book about trucks. His mom took his hand, and they walked home together.

Lydia was at home. Her friend Laith came to play. Laith had big tears on his face. He was crying.

"Why are you crying?" Lydia asked.

"I lost my dog toy," Laith said. "He was my best toy. Now I feel so sad."

Lydia felt sad too. She did not want Laith to cry. She ran to her room. She looked under her bed. She looked in her toy box.

Then Lydia found her favorite dog. It was brown and soft. She held it tight. It was hard to give it away. But Laith was still crying.

"Here," Lydia said. "You can hold my dog."

Laith wiped his eyes. He hugged the soft dog. His tears stopped. Then he smiled a big smile.

"Thank you," Laith said. "I feel happy now."

Lydia smiled too. She saw one thing. When Laith felt sad, he cried. When he felt better, the crying stopped.

"Can my dog spell too?" Laith asked. "I can spell my name. L, A, I, T, H."

Lydia laughed. "Dogs cannot spell. But my dog can sit!"

Lydia made the dog sit on the rug. Laith clapped his hands. He was excited.

They played until it got late. Then Laith's dad came to the door.

"Time to go home," his dad said.

"Can I keep the dog?" Laith asked.

"You can borrow him," Lydia said. "Bring him back soon."

Laith waved from the car. Lydia waved back from her window. Her mom gave her a warm hug.

"You were kind today," Mom said.

Lydia held her mom's hand. "Laith can bring my dog tomorrow," she said.

Arya went to the library with her family. She wanted the big red book about trucks. But Nolan had it first. "Can I have it?" asked Arya. "After me," said Nolan. "One turn for you, one turn for me."

Arya watched Nolan turn the pages. One page, two pages, three pages. Then Nolan held out the book. "Your turn," he said. Arya smiled and took it.

Nearby, a family sat by the window. The mama was rocking a baby. The baby was sleeping. Arya got excited and shouted, "Trucks!" The baby woke up and began to cry. The mama rocked and rocked. Arya felt bad. The crying sounded scary.

Ms. Nikolaidis came over. She bent down close. "The baby is sleeping," she whispered. Arya looked at the baby. She looked at Ms. Nikolaidis. Then she made her voice very small. "One truck," she whispered. "Two trucks. Three trucks."

The baby's eyes closed. The crying stopped. The mama rocked some more. Soon the baby was sleeping again. Arya turned one page, then another, all in her quiet voice. Nolan came back and sat close. "Trucks," he whispered. Arya nodded and slid the book so they could both see.

The baby slept and slept. The library was quiet and warm.

Gianna stood in the playroom with a big box of things. "Let's make groups," said Mr. Eze. "Put toys here. Put foods there." Gianna picked up a soft brown bear. She put the bear with the toys. Then she found a red apple. The apple went with the foods.

Ilyas held up a long orange carrot. "Where does this go?" he asked. He put the carrot with the toys. Gianna looked at it. She touched the smooth carrot. It did not look like her bear. "Are you a toy?" she asked the carrot. She sniffed it. It smelled fresh, like a snack.

Then she looked at the apple. She looked at the bread next to it. The carrot looked like food, too. Gianna picked up the carrot. She carried it across the rug. She set it down with the apple and the bread. "Foods," she said. Boston clapped his hands. Mr. Eze gave her a clean plate for the carrots. "Snack time," he said.

Milan sat on his bed with his big dog book. He loved the dog with one brown eye. "Who drew this dog?" he asked.

He took the book to his mom. "Can you help me look?" She opened the front cover. She turned to the first page. There was a name there. "Here it is," she said. "The person who draws the pictures for a book is called the illustrator."

"An illustrator," said Milan. "She drew my dog!" He ran back to his room. He held the book up high.

The next morning, Ariella came to play. Milan showed her the book. He started at the front. He turned the pages one by one. "See? The illustrator made this," he said. He pointed at the little puppy with a bite taken from its bone. Ariella laughed. "Show me again," she said. "From the front."

The lights went out. It was dark in the backyard. Juliette could not see her toys. She wanted her teddy bear on the chair.

Juliette ran to the chair. Bump! Her leg hit the chair. "Ow," she said. It was too dark to run.

Dad came out with a big flashlight. He turned it on. Juliette could see the chair. She could see her teddy, too. "My leg bumped the chair," Juliette said. "It was not a mean chair. The dark made me bump it."

"In the dark, walk slowly," said Dad. He held out his hand. "Hold my hand so nobody trips." Juliette held Dad's hand. They walked slowly, step by step, back across the grass. Nothing bumped them at all.

They sat on the step together. Juliette found a feather on the ground. It was soft and white. She let it go and watched it float down. Dad shone the flashlight on it. The feather danced in the light. Juliette laughed and let it float again.

Soon the lights came back on. The house glowed. "Now we can see everything," said Juliette. She held Dad's hand all the way to the door and carried her teddy inside.

Everett woke up in his bed. The sun was bright in his window. He heard a clink and a pour. Was someone in the kitchen? He wanted pancakes today.

He padded down the hall. Mom and Dad sat at the table. There were plates and cups and a big pancake stack. "Good morning," said Everett.

"Good morning," said Mom. "It is morning now. Morning is when we wake up and eat breakfast." She put a warm pancake on his plate. Everett took a big bite. Yum.

Yesterday there were no pancakes. Yesterday they had eggs. "Pancakes today," said Everett. "Eggs yesterday." Dad laughed. "That's right. And tomorrow we can have pancakes again, if you want."

"Tomorrow is after I sleep again?" asked Everett. Dad nodded. "Yes. First today, then sleep, then tomorrow." Everett thought that was a funny order. But he liked it.

After breakfast, Everett wanted to play a game. "Can we play now?" he asked. "We can play later," said Dad. "First the dishes go in the sink." Everett helped carry his cup. He was careful and slow.

Then it was time for the game. Everett and Dad sat on the rug. "I go first," said Everett. He rolled the dice. He moved his little piece two spaces. "Your turn, Dad," he said. Dad smiled and rolled the dice too.

Everett yawned a big yawn. Morning was for pancakes. Later was for games. Sleep would come after that. He leaned on Dad's arm and whispered, "Good morning was good." Dad said, "Good morning still is." Everett rolled the dice one more time.

Eleanor sat at the paint table at summer camp. She wanted to paint green grass. But there was no green paint. All the pots were empty except yellow and blue. How would her grass look right?

Rudy sat next to her. He was painting a blue lake. "No green," said Eleanor. "My grass needs green." She looked and looked at the pots.

Then she had an idea. What if the paints could be friends? She dipped her brush in the yellow pot. She dabbed yellow on the paper. Then she dipped the same brush in the blue pot. She swirled the wet blue into the wet yellow spot.

The spot turned green! Real green, like real grass. "Look, look!" said Eleanor. Rudy leaned over. "Green!" he said. "How did you do that?" Eleanor made a big green field. She even gave her painting a green coat of grass at the bottom.

Mr. Wu came to see. "That is lovely grass," he said. Eleanor held up her wet brush. "Yellow and blue made it," she said. "Yellow plus blue." Then she dipped her brush again. "Can blue and yellow make more?" she asked. Mr. Wu smiled and slid two full pots down the table toward her.

Today was Eliana's birthday. Her mom brought cupcakes to school. Ms. Goldberg said, "We will sing for you." Eliana felt worried. She did not like loud singing. She asked her mom, "Will it be very loud?" Her mom said, "Not too loud. Just wait and listen."

Robyn and Clementine helped set out the napkins. Eliana helped too. She carried one cupcake very slowly. Then she had to sneeze. The cupcake began to drop. Clementine caught it with a plate. "Safe!" said Clementine. The cupcake was fine.

Then everyone stood up. They sang, "Happy birthday to you." Eliana waited. Then she heard it. They sang, "Happy birthday, dear Eliana." They were singing her name. She hid her big smile behind her hands. Her cheeks felt warm and happy.

After the song, Ms. Goldberg gave out the cupcakes. Eliana looked at hers. There was a tiny toy duck sitting on top. "A duck!" said Eliana. "For me?" "Yes," said Ms. Goldberg. "It is yours to keep." Eliana put the duck in her pocket. She held up her cupcake and said, "Sing again, please. I want to hear my name one more time."

Beau ran to the story rug at daycare. Story time! Story time! He sat down next to David and Lev.

Mr. Sutherland held up a big book. Then he put on his glasses. "Why do you put those on?" asked Beau. "Glasses help me see more clearly," said Mr. Sutherland. Beau looked with his eyes. The glasses looked shiny.

Then Beau listened with his ears. Mr. Sutherland read about a soft feather. He passed around a real one! Beau touched it with his fingers. So smooth! He sniffed it with his nose. It smelled like nothing at all.

At snack time, Beau tasted a sweet apple. Yum!

Then Mr. Sutherland carried the book close to Beau's face. "Too fuzzy," said Beau. He held up the glasses. "Can I try?" He put them on. Now the pictures looked big and clear!

"My turn!" said David.
"My turn!" said Lev.
Beau smiled and passed the glasses on.

Charlotte ran into the art studio. She had on her new shirt with the stars. Mr. De Vries waved her over to the paint table. "Today we paint!" he said. Charlotte saw red paint. She saw yellow paint. She saw blue paint. "Can I paint now?" she asked. "First, put on this apron," said Mr. De Vries. "An apron keeps paint off your clothes." Charlotte put it on. Her star shirt stayed clean under it.

Charlotte got a brush. She dipped it in blue. Then she dipped it in yellow. She stirred them on her paper. "What is this new colour?" she asked. Sadie leaned over. "That's green!" she said. Charlotte gasped. Blue and yellow made green!

A dot of green paint flew up. It landed on her apron, not her shirt. Charlotte laughed and laughed. Then she dipped her brush in red. "Yellow, your turn!" she said.

Madelyn found a book on her bed. It was a book about a puppy who could chase butterflies.

She opened the book from the back. "That is funny," she said. The puppy was already home. The butterflies were gone. The story was all mixed up!

"What a mixed-up day," said Madelyn. She turned a page. Now the puppy was wet. Then he was dry. Then he was sleepy. "What a mixed-up day," she said again.

Grandpa peeked in the door. "That story sounds funny," he said. He sat down on the bed with her. Madelyn showed him the pages. Grandpa turned the book around in his hands.

Madelyn looked at the front. She saw the puppy at the start. He was a small puppy, waking up. She turned the pages one by one. The puppy chased a blue butterfly. He ran past a nice red flower. He splashed in a puddle. At the end, the puppy went home to sleep.

"So that is his day," said Madelyn. She patted the back cover. "Good night, puppy." Then she hugged the book tight.

Grandpa came to stay with Hazel for a whole week. On Monday they went to the big park near her house. Grandpa brought a small box. Inside was a card game. "You go first," said Grandpa. Hazel put down a card. Then she reached to go again. "Wait," said Grandpa. "Now it is my turn." Grandpa put down his card. Then he pointed to Hazel. "Your turn," he said. They went back and forth like that. One card for Hazel. One card for Grandpa. "We are taking turns," said Grandpa. Hazel laughed and clapped.

Hazel's friend Valerie came over to play. Valerie wanted to go first every time. Hazel felt a little mad. Then she had an idea. "One card for you," said Hazel. "Then one card for me." Valerie tried it. It worked! The game was fun for both of them. After the game, they picked a yellow flower and gave it to Grandpa. "Thank you," said Grandpa. "Shall we mix up the cards and play one more time?"

Elliot ran to the bathroom at summer camp. He used the toilet. Then he ran out fast. The water slide was calling him. "Wait for me, Theia!" he shouted.

Theia was at the sink. She was rubbing soap on her hands. "We always wash our hands after using the toilet," she said. She made soap bubbles shaped like a cloud. Elliot giggled and ran back.

Ms. Chowdhury was by the sinks. She helped Elliot pump the soap. "Now we count to twenty," she said. They sang the camp song twice. Elliot scrubbed and scrubbed. The soap smelled like lemons. He sniffed his hands. His nose was happy. "Not yucky anymore!" he said.

Mavrick zoomed out of the bathroom without washing. "Come back, Mavrick!" Elliot called. Mavrick ran back to the sink. He washed his hands too. All three friends sang the song together.

Then they ran to the water slide. Splash! The water was cold. Elliot's hands were clean and wet. Theia held up her soapy-smelling hands. "Twenty seconds, best seconds," she said. Elliot laughed. "Wash first, splash after!" he said. And he brought his clean hands all the way to the top.

Asher stood by the grocery store door. His coat was on, but the zipper was stuck at the bottom. He pulled it up, up, up. It went a little way and stopped. He pulled again. This time it slid all the way to his chin. "I did it," he said. His mom clapped.

One red mitten fell off the shelf by the door. Asher picked it up. Where was the other one? He looked under the cart. He looked by the bread. "Mom, where do mittens go?" he asked. She smiled and pointed at his coat. "Look at your side," she said. Asher patted his hip. There was a little door there. He opened it. Inside was the other red mitten!

Asher tucked both mittens into the pocket. He pushed the little door shut. They fit just right. He patted the pocket. It felt squishy and soft, like two small pillows.

The cart rolled past the soap aisle. Asher smelled flowers and lemons. Then a spot of dust slid under his shoe. He swept it away with his toe. At the checkout, Asher pulled both mittens out of the pocket. "Look, Ms. Cashier," he said. "My pocket kept them safe!" He put them back in, one, two, and zipped his coat up all by himself again.

Luke went to the park early with his dad. The sun made everything warm. Luke touched the slide. The slide felt hot. He pulled his hand back fast. "That part is in the sun," his dad said. They waited under a tree. Luke watched the shade creep over the slide. He touched it again. Now it was cool.

Zoya and Daxon came to the park too. They all ran to the sandbox. Luke stayed where his dad could see him. He found a picnic table under a big tree. On the table sat a small bag. Little round things spilled out of it. They were red and yellow and green. They looked like candy.

Luke wanted to pick one up. They were so pretty, like a tiny rainbow. But he stopped his hand. He remembered what his mom had told him. Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy.

"I will go get a grown-up," Luke said. He did not touch the little round things. He walked back to his dad. His dad held his hand. They went to the table together. His dad looked at the bag. "These are pills," his dad said. "You did the right thing."

A woman came running back. She had been looking for her bag. She thanked Luke. "I did not touch them," Luke said. She smiled at him. Zoya and Daxon clapped. Then they all went back to the sandbox. Luke dug a deep hole. It felt cool and soft under his hands.

Ava was playing in the playroom with her friend Navy. They built a big tower with pink blocks. Ava made the sky out of a blue blanket on the floor. It was a good game.

Then the bell rang. It was time for a snack. Navy ran out fast. Ava started to run too. But then she stopped. The blocks were all over the floor. The blanket was in a heap. Nobody had cleaned the toys.

Ava picked up one block. Then another. Mr. Zhou, her neighbor, was at the door with her mom. He smiled at Ava. "Can I help?" he asked. "Yes please," said Ava. They put the blocks in the basket together.

Then Navy came back. She looked at the blocks. "Those are mine too," said Navy. She picked up the last pink blocks. She put them away all by herself. Ava folded the blue blanket. The floor was clean now.

"Snack time," said Mom. Ava and Navy sat at the table. They ate apple slices together. "We clean the toys we played with," said Navy. Ava nodded and took a big bite.

Zachary looked out the window. Snow was falling on the backyard. "No school today," said his dad. "It is a snow day."

Zachary put on his boots. He put on his red mittens. He went outside to play. The snow was soft and cold. It squeaked under his boots. He patted a big snowball. It was round like a ball.

"I want to keep this snowball," Zachary said. His dad helped him carry it inside. They put it in a bowl on the table. Zachary wanted to save it for tomorrow.

Zachary played with his toy butterfly. He painted a picture of the snow. He waited a long time. Then he looked at the bowl. The snowball was small now. The bowl was not empty. There was water in it. "Dad, come look!" said Zachary. "The snow turned into water."

"The snow melted in here," said his dad. "It is warm inside." Zachary touched the water. It was cool on his finger.

Zachary had an idea. He got a fresh snowball from the yard. He put it in a cup. He carried the cup outside to the cold porch. "Stay there, snowball," he said.

The next morning, Zachary checked his cup. The snowball was still there, big and white. Zachary smiled and patted it with his mitten.

Harper ran to the park with her dad. "I want to play ball!" she said. But her hat flew off in the wind. It landed near the sandbox. Her sock slipped off too and fell in the sand.

Kiaan was digging in the sandbox. He found the sock. He put it with his trucks and shovels. "A new toy!" he said.

Harper ran over. She looked at the pile. She saw trucks. She saw shovels. She saw her sock. She laughed and laughed.

"That is not a toy," she said. "Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes!" She picked up her sock and shook off the sand. Kiaan picked up her hat. He put both things in her bag.

"Now let's play ball!" said Kiaan. Harper threw it high. Kiaan caught it, and they both cheered.

Isla sat at the big kitchen table. She was painting a picture. She painted a red bird. She painted a yellow sun. She painted a blue sky.

Now she wanted grass. Grass is green. She looked in the green paint pot. It was empty! "Oh no," said Isla. "My grass will be white. That is not right."

Her friend Aurora peeked at the picture. "Silly white grass!" she laughed. "The sheep will be confused."

Isla dipped her brush in the blue pot. She painted a blue stripe. Then she dipped in the yellow pot. She painted yellow on top. She stirred with her brush.

The paint turned green! Isla peeked at the pot. "Aurora, look! Blue and yellow make green!" She painted long green grass under the tree in her picture. "It is true. The grass looks perfect now," said Isla. Aurora clapped her hands.

Milan ran to the big pool with his bear under his arm. He could not wait to swim! Ms. Mercado waved at the water. "Jump in when I say go," she said.

Milan splashed in near Adalyn and Vincenzo. He kicked his legs. He blew bubbles. The water went up and down. "Look!" said Milan. "When I kick, the water jumps!" Adalyn laughed and kicked too. The water jumped even more.

Then Milan wanted to get out. He grabbed the side of the pool. He pulled and pulled. His arms slipped. It was too high to climb over the edge. Vincenzo pointed to the corner. "Try the ladder," he said. "It helps you get in and out of the water."
