Milan held the rail. He climbed one step, then two, then three. Step by step, he was out! That was so much easier. "That ladder is neat!" said Milan. He held his bear up high and let his legs swing in the air.

"Can I climb down the ladder too?" Milan asked. Ms. Mercado smiled. "Yes," she said. So Milan went down the ladder, step by step. He jumped back in the water with a big splash. Adalyn shouted, "Again, again!"

Grandma was coming to stay for a week. Ali wanted to make her feel happy. He got out a big bowl. Mom said, "I will pour the milk. You can pass me the spoon." Ali passed the spoon. Mom stirred pancake batter. The stove was hot, so Mom stood near it. Ali stood back and watched.

Then Ali saw a photo on the fridge. It showed Grandma holding Mom's hand. Mom was little in the photo. Ali frowned. "That is the wrong photo," he said. "Grandma is not your mom." Mom laughed softly. "Yes, she is. Grandma is my mom." Ali looked at the photo again. So Grandma was a mom two times!

The doorbell rang. Grandma came in with her bag. Ali ran to hug her legs. "You are Mom's mom!" he said. Grandma smiled a big smile. "That is my best hug today," she said. Then they all ate warm pancakes together.

Alexander stood in the big school gym. Mr. Dang put a hoop on the floor. He put three beanbags in a red basket. "Try to throw one in," said Mr. Dang. Alexander threw the first beanbag. It landed far from the hoop. He threw the second one. It bounced off the edge. Would the third one go in? He threw it. It went in! Alexander clapped his hands. He liked the sound of the beanbag landing inside.

Then Mr. Dang brought out a big yellow ball. He rolled it to Axton. Axton caught it. He rolled it to Harley. Harley caught it. Then it was Alexander's turn. The ball came rolling fast. Alexander's hands were tucked in his pockets. The ball bumped his legs and rolled away.

"Try again," said Mr. Dang. He rolled the ball again. This time Alexander held his arms out. His hands were open and wide. The big ball came right into them. He caught it! "I caught it!" said Alexander. He looked at his open hands. Arms out, hands open. That is what got him ready.

They played a counting game around the circle. One roll for Axton. One roll for Harley. One roll for Alexander. Around and around the ball went. Then the ball rolled past everyone. It rolled under the snowy coats hanging on the wall. It stopped on a sneaker. Whose sneaker was that? Out stepped the coach. "Looking for this?" he said, holding up the big yellow ball.

Amira was on a big train with her dad. They were going to Grandma's house. It was far, far away from home.

Amira looked out the window. She saw white clouds. She saw a river with water in it. "Can I have a drink?" she asked. Her dad gave her a water bottle. One sip, two sips, three sips.

Then Dad looked worried. "Oh no," he said. "Which stop is ours? I forgot." A lady in a blue coat came by. Her name was Ms. Desir. She pointed to a big paper on the train wall. "Look here," she said. "This is a map."

Amira stood up and looked. The map showed little dots for places. It showed the road the train went on. Amira put her finger on the map. She found the river on the map. She found the river out the window. "There!" she said. "The river is here, so we are here." Then she moved her finger along. One dot, two dots, three dots. "This dot is Grandma's town."

Dad smiled. "The map shows us the way," he said. The train went on. Soon a voice said, "Next stop, Grandma's town." Amira held her dad's hand. The train slowed down and stopped.

There was Grandma, waving on the platform.

Jasper stood in the kitchen. The toast was ready. Mama had made it with the toaster, and now it sat on his plate.

"I want to spread the butter," said Jasper. Mama gave him a small knife with a rounded end. Jasper dipped it in the butter. He spread it across the toast. It went bump, bump, bump. Little lumps sat on top. He spread them flat. The toast was all shiny now.

Next came the milk. Jasper held the cup. He poured and poured. The milk came up to the very top. He walked to the table. Oh no! The milk tipped over the edge. It made a puddle on the floor.

Mama wiped the puddle. "Try again," she said. Jasper poured once more. This time he stopped before the cup was full to the top. He walked slowly to the table. Not one drop fell out. He sat down and took a big bite of buttery toast and a big sip of milk.

Then something small and funny happened. The cat trotted in and licked the last bit of spilled milk right off the floor.

"That was Onyx's treat," Jasper said with a laugh. Onyx bumped his leg and purred.

Jaxson looked out the window. The sky was white. Snow was falling on the backyard.

"Snowy day," said Mom. "Put on your boots."

Jaxson pulled on his boots. He zipped his big coat. He ran outside into the snow. His friend Jaiden was already there. Jaiden wore a hat, a scarf and red mittens.

"Let's make a snow wall," said Jaiden.

They patted the snow. They stacked it up. Soon they had a big white wall. It was tall as their knees.

Then Jaxson tried to roll a snowball. The snow felt cold. His hands turned red. They hurt. He dropped the snowball and held his hands.

"My hands are cold," he said.

Jaiden held out his red mittens. "Mittens keep my hands warm," he said. "Try yours."

Jaxson looked down. His mittens were in his coat pocket. He pulled them on. He rolled a new snowball. His hands felt warm. He patted it onto the wall.

From the door, Ms. Suzuki, the neighbour, called, "Cocoa is ready!"

The boys went in slowly. Their legs were sleepy from playing. Mom set two warm cups on the table.

Jaxson took a sip. Something was floating in his cocoa. It was a tiny marshmallow snowman, with little stick arms.

"He looks just like us," said Jaxson, and he waved at it.

Jaxon sat on his bedroom floor. He had a new wallet. Inside was his new card. It had his name on it. "Jaxon," he read out loud. He felt shy about it. He hid it under his pillow.

At the library, Jaxon found a big red book. It had a bear on the front. He hugged it tight. "Can I keep it?" he asked his mom.

"Ask the lady at the desk," she said.

Jaxon felt shy. He walked slowly. He slid his card across the desk. "What is this for?" he asked.

The lady smiled. "It is a library card. It lets you borrow books and take them home."

Jaxon's eyes got big. "Take it home? To my room?"

"Yes," she said. "You can bring it back soon."

Jaxon gave her his card. She zipped it through a machine. Beep! She put the red book in his hands.

"You mean it is mine now?" he asked.

"It is yours for a while," she said.

Jaxon held the book all the way home. He ran to his bedroom. He sat on his bed. He opened the red book. The bear smiled at him. Jaxon smiled too.

"Mom," he called. "My card made this happen. Can we go back tomorrow?"

Brielle went to the park with her red ball. She wanted to kick it to Reginald. She kicked it high. The ball went into the cozy little playhouse at the park.

The playhouse was dark inside. Brielle stepped in to find her ball. She looked and looked. "It is hard to tell what color things are in here," she said. Everything looked the same dark gray. She touched something round. Was this her ball? She could not tell.

She carried it out into the sun. In the bright light, she could see. The ball in her hands was green, not red. It was Reginald's green ball! Then Reginald called from the doorway. He held up a red ball. "Is this yours?" he asked. "Yes!" said Brielle. They traded balls and laughed. Then they kicked the balls by the duck pond. The red ball went far. The green ball went far, too. Brielle read her name on the red ball. It was her ball, for sure.

Leo went to the farm with his class. Ms. Foster said, "Today we will name our five senses." Leo wanted to try them all before snack time.

First Leo used his eyes. He saw a cow with a short tail. Then he used his nose. He sniffed hay, and it smelled sweet. He touched a soft leaf on a plant. He used his tongue to taste his apple at snack time.

Then a big truck rumbled by. The noise was loud. Leo put his hands over his ears. The sound got quieter, just like that. He took his hands off. The truck was loud again. He put his hands back on. Quiet again!

"Ms. Foster, my ears can hear," said Leo. "And my hands make it quiet." Asha laughed and covered her ears too. The cows went back to munching their hay.

Joshua was in the backyard with Grandma. Grandma was staying for a whole week. Joshua had a red ball. "Grandma, play with me!" he said. Grandma threw the ball, but it went weak and slow. "I am tired," she said. "I need to rest." Joshua found her a chair in the shade.

Joshua still wanted to play. "I wish someone could play ball," he said. Grandma smiled. "I know a story instead," she said. "It is about your dad." Joshua sat down. "Dad is big," he said. "Dad was little once," said Grandma. "He had a small blue bike. He fell off. He cried. Then he got on again."

Joshua laughed. "Dad on a little bike!" he said. "Tell more!" Grandma told about Dad and his sister, who hid Dad's shoe. Joshua asked, "Can you tell stories every day this week?" "Every day," said Grandma. Joshua ran to get her a blanket for her lap. "Story time!" he called. "Story time!"

The cultural center was full of people. Theo held his dad's hand. The night was coming, and lanterns glowed up high. "Stay close," said his dad. "It is a big crowd."

Theo saw a food stall. It smelled sweet. He let go of his dad's hand. He took one step. Then two steps. The people were tall and thin between him and the stall. He could not see his dad. Theo's tummy felt small.

He stopped walking. He looked back. There was his dad! Theo ran to him and grabbed his hand. He held on tight. "I stayed close," said Theo. His dad smiled. They walked to the food stall together, hand in hand. "One sweet bun, please," said his dad.

Juliette went to the park with her mama. Jimmy was there too. He had a big cardboard box.

"I want to sit in it," said Jimmy. He sat down inside.

Juliette wanted a turn. She waited. Then Jimmy got out.

Juliette sat in the box. She held the sides. "Beep beep!" she said. "This box is my car!"

Jimmy looked sad. "I want it to be a car too."

"Okay," said Juliette. "You can ride in my car."

Then Jimmy had an idea. "Let's make it a boat," he said. He turned the box and rocked it side to side. "Row, row!"

"The box can be a house too," said Juliette. She tipped it up on one side. It made a little wall. Jimmy laughed and crawled in behind her.

Rosie came over with her toy elephant. "The elephant needs a home," she said. She set the elephant in the box. Juliette patted it gently, like a baby.

Ms. Lewandowski, the neighbour, waved from the bench nearby. "That looks like a nice house," she said.

Rosie almost dropped the elephant. Juliette caught it with both hands. "Got you," she said softly.

The sun went down a little. Mama called, "Time to go home."

Juliette gave the box a pat. "Bye, house. Bye, car. Bye, boat."

Jimmy helped tip the box back down. They all held hands and walked to the gate.

Maria sat in a big chair. It was a waiting room. Today she would see the dentist for the first time. She squeezed her mama's hand. "Will it hurt?" she asked.

A boy sat down next to her. His name was Justin. He had a loose tooth. He wiggled it with his finger. Maria watched. When he wiggled it, his whole mouth moved. She wiggled her own tooth too. Nothing happened. Her tooth stayed still. Why did his move and not hers?

The dentist called Maria in. He looked at her teeth with a little mirror. "Say hello to your front teeth," he said. "Front teeth are for biting food. Back teeth are for chewing it." Maria bit down on a soft fruit snack. Snip went the front teeth. Then she chomped with her back teeth. Chomp, chomp. The snack got small.

On the bus home, mama gave Maria an apple slice. Maria bit it with her front teeth. Then she chewed it with her back teeth. "It works!" she said. "I can feel it getting smaller." The boy across the aisle smiled at her. "Want to share mine too?" he asked. Maria took one polite little bite. Then she chewed. Chomp, chomp, chomp.

Henry ran out to the backyard. "Where are my toys?" he said. He wanted to build a big tower before lunch. But the toy box was empty! "Oh no," said Henry. Then he saw something funny. A string was tied to the swing. It went behind the big tree. Henry pulled the string. Out came his blocks, one by one. His dog had moved them! Henry laughed. He put the blocks in the toy box. "Blocks are toys," he said. Then he pulled again. Out came his doll. "Dolls are toys too!" He put the doll in the box. Out came his red ball. "And balls are toys!" said Henry. The box was full at last. Anais came through the gate. "Can we play?" she asked. "Yes!" said Henry. He lifted the red ball up high. "Watch me throw it far!"

Aaron went to the playground with his mom. He wanted to play on the big slide. But a new boy stood by the slide. Aaron did not know him. Aaron felt a bit scared, so he hid behind his mom.

Mr. Wanjiru walked by with the new boy. Mr. Wanjiru waved at Aaron. "Hello there!" he said. Aaron peeked out from behind his mom. Would the wave still work if he hid? He stepped out a little. "Hello," said Aaron in a small voice.

Mr. Wanjiru smiled a big smile. "Hello! This is Jensen," he said. Jensen smiled too. "Do you want to send the toy elephant down the slide?" asked Jensen. He held a toy elephant. "Yes, please!" said Aaron.

Up the steps they went. Aaron slid down first. Then he sent the elephant down to Jensen. "Thank you!" said Jensen. Aaron looked at his mom. His hello had made a new friend. What else could a hello do? He waved at the swing. "Hello, swing!" he said. Jensen laughed and laughed.

Jacob sat on the small blue chair. Ms. Kang handed him a recorder. It was long and white, with little round holes.

Jacob put his fingers on the holes. He blew hard. The recorder made a squeak. It sounded like a duck with hiccups. Vincent laughed. "Your duck is back," he said. Jacob laughed too. He tried again. Squeak, squeak!

"Look at your thumb," said Ms. Kang. Jacob peeked at his thumb. It was half off the back hole. He pressed it down all the way. He blew softly. A sweet, low note came out. Vincent's eyes went wide. Jacob lifted one finger. He blew again. Now the note was high, like a little bird. He lifted another finger. The bird flew even higher.

"Each hole makes a new sound!" said Jacob. He played low, then high, then low. Vincent clapped his hands. Jacob wiggled his fingers like a spider walking. The recorder sang a silly, jumpy tune. "Play it again," said Vincent. "It's my favorite song of the day." Jacob took a big breath and played the duck, the bird, and the spider, all in a row.

Rehmat ran to the bikes at the park. Her friend Lilah was already there. Rehmat jumped onto a red bike. She put her feet on the pedals. Then she stopped. She slid off the bike and ran back to the bench. "My helmet!" she said. She put it on her head. She clicked the strap under her chin. Then she got on the red bike again.

Lilah had no helmet on. "I want to ride now," Lilah said. Ms. Wardak held up a blue helmet. "Wait," said Ms. Wardak. Lilah took the helmet. She put it on too.

The two girls rode round and round the path. The sun was warm in the blue sky. A gentle wind blew on Rehmat's face. Rehmat saw her mama waving from the bench. Rehmat waved back and stayed close. Then she rang the little bell on her bike. Ding, ding! Lilah laughed. "Race you to the tree!"

Nora's baby brother came home today. He was very small. He had tiny hands and tiny feet.

"Can I pat him?" Nora asked.

"Yes, but gently," said her mom.

Nora patted the baby. Pat, pat. The baby began to cry. Nora stopped. "Was that too hard?" she asked. "Yes, it was," said her mom. "A new baby must be touched very gently."

Nora looked at her hand. What could she do? She put out one finger. She stroked the baby's tiny hand. Soft, soft, soft. The baby stopped crying. The baby looked at Nora.

"Does he like soft touches?" Nora asked.

"He does," said her mom.

The window was cloudy outside. Nora saw the baby close his eyes. Soon he began to sleep. Nora whispered, "Sleep, little baby. Sleep."

Naomi woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. She wanted milk in her big blue cup. "I can do it myself," she said.

Her mama put two warm slices of toast on a flat plate. She gave Naomi a soft round spreader. Naomi dug the butter. The toast tried to slip away. Naomi held the plate with one hand. She spread slow and soft. The butter went all over. Every bit of the toast turned yellow.

Next came the milk. Naomi held her cup in one hand. She poured with the other. The cup wobbled. Milk made a little puddle on the table. Naomi got a cloth and wiped it up.

Then she set the cup down on the table. She let go. The cup sat still. She poured again. The milk went right in. Not one drop spilled.

Naomi took a bite of toast. She took a sip of milk. "I did it all by myself," she said. Her mama smiled. Naomi gave her cup a little pat.

Isaiah stood in the bathroom next to the big tub. Dad turned the silver tap. The water came out fast. "That side is hot," said Dad. He put his hand under the other tap. "This side is cold." Isaiah touched only the cold water. It felt like snow from the sky. Dad filled the tub with warm water. Isaiah put in his blue boat. The boat went round and round.

After his bath, Isaiah and Dad went to the store. Isaiah wanted to see the apples. He looked at the red apples. Then he looked up. Dad was not there. Isaiah looked down the aisle. He saw shoes. He saw carts. He did not see Dad.

Isaiah remembered a word Dad had taught him. The word was "worker." A worker wore a green vest. Isaiah saw a woman in a green vest at the checkout. He walked to her and held the edge of her counter. "I can't find my grown-up," he said.

The worker spoke into her phone. Soon Dad came around the corner. He knelt down and hugged Isaiah. "You did it just right," said Dad. Isaiah held Dad's hand. The apples were red and shiny in the cart.

Evan woke up early. Today was his big day. He was going to the dentist for the very first time. "I get to sit in a big chair!" he told his gray cat. He counted his teeth with his finger. "One, two, three, all the way to twenty!"

He packed his small pillow in a bag. He wanted to hug it in the car. Mom smiled and buckled him in. The seat clicked.

At the dentist, a kind lady waved. Evan looked at her hands. Her hands were blue! "Why are your hands blue?" he asked. The dentist held them up. "These are my gloves. I wear gloves when I put my fingers or tools in your mouth."

Evan touched one glove. It felt smooth and stretchy. The dentist pulled it and let go. Snap! Evan laughed out loud. He opened his mouth wide, just like a lion.

At home, Evan put his pillow on the couch. He snapped his own pretend gloves on his hands. "Open wide, cat!" he said. The cat yawned big.

Jules wanted to build a big tower at daycare. He found a heavy box. He pulled it. He pushed it. The box did not move. "It is so heavy," said Eloi.

Ms. Tan brought a pillow. "Try this," she said. Jules lifted it up high. It was light. "Heavy and light are opposites," said Kaya with a giggle.

Jules put the light pillow on top of the heavy box. The tower stood tall. It did not fall down.

Jules colored a small piece of paper. He stuck it on the box like a flag. "Our tower!" he said. Kaya clapped. Eloi patted the box. Jules stood very proud, next to his big, tall tower.

Kinsley went to the library with Mama. She wanted a book about pink flowers. Ms. Dlamini showed her a little shelf.

Kinsley found a book. She held it up. The bear on the page stood on his head. The words sat at the bottom of the sky. "Look, Milo!" she said. "The bear is upside down!" Milo came over and laughed.

Ms. Dlamini turned the book around. Now the words sat at the bottom of the page. The bear stood on his feet. Kinsley blinked. She turned the book upside down again. The bear stood on his head again. The words flew up to the top. "Funny bear," she said. She turned it back. The bear sat down. The words sat at the bottom, all in a row.

Kinsley put her finger on the row. "These are the words," she said. "They tell about the bear." Milo leaned in close. Kinsley turned to the first page. "This is the front," she said. She opened it and began. "Bear woke up. Bear saw pink flowers."

Ryan sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy felt funny. "The shot might hurt," he told his mom. "Just a little pinch," said the nurse. "Then I have a surprise for you."

The nurse cleaned Ryan's arm with a cool, wet wipe. Ryan counted with his mom. "One, two, three." The pinch came. It was small, like a bug kiss. Then it was done.

Ryan saw the nurse open a small paper wrapper. She put a small bandage over the spot on his arm. The bandage had yellow stars on it. "A star bandage!" said Ryan. He could not stop looking at it. The spot felt better already.

Afterward, Mom took Ryan to the ice cream shop. Ryan got pink strawberry ice cream in a cup. It was cold and sweet on his tongue. A man at the next table waved. "Nice stars," he said. Ryan held up his arm to show him. "One, two, three, four, five stars," he counted.

Conner from school came in with his dad. Conner ran over to see. "I got a shot too," Conner said. He pulled up his sleeve. His bandage had blue dinosaurs on it. Ryan laughed. "Next time, I want dinosaurs," he said, and he took another big bite of ice cream.

Arthur was going next door. Ms. Doyle was having a big game day. Arthur wanted to wear his red shirt. But where was it? Not in his drawer. Not on his bed. Not on the hook. Arthur was mad.

At Ms. Doyle's house, everyone wore green shirts. Parker wore green. Christine wore green too. "Why does everyone wear green?" Arthur asked. Parker pointed at the TV. "Green is our team's colors. We wear them to show we cheer for our team." Arthur looked down at his blue shirt. Hmm.

Then Christine ran to the toy box. She found a green cape. She held it out. "You can wear this!" Arthur put it on. One, two, three tucks, and it stayed.

The game started. The team got a goal. Everyone stood up to clap. Ms. Doyle gave out cookies. Arthur clapped with his cookie in his hand. "We all match," said Parker. Arthur grinned under his green cape.

Matthew held his dad's hand at the street festival. There were red lanterns everywhere. There was a big dragon made of paper. There was food and drums and so many people.

"Can we dance too?" Matthew asked.

"Watch first," said his dad.

The drums went boom, boom, boom. The dancers hopped and turned. The dragon spun around. Zavier from Matthew's class was dancing too! He held his mom's hand and hopped. Ms. Tang waved from the stage. "The music makes us dance!" she called.

Then the music stopped. The dancers stopped too. Everything was quiet and still.

The music started again. The dancers danced again!

"The music makes the dancing!" said Matthew. "That is how it works!"

"Yes!" said his dad. "Dancing goes with the music."

Matthew pulled his dad's hand. "Let's dance now!"

They hopped and turned. Matthew saw a spider web shine on a lantern, slippery with rain drops. He laughed and spun again.

Boom, boom, boom went the drums. Matthew went hop, hop, hop.

Eleanor had a bath. The water was warm and smooth. Mama washed her hair. Then Mama helped her put on her soft pajamas.

Eleanor picked two books. Mama read them slow. Eleanor looked at every picture. Then Mama kissed her head. "Time to sleep," Mama said.

Eleanor got in bed. She pulled the blanket up. She closed her eyes. Then she sat up fast. "My teeth!" she said. "I forget to brush!"

Eleanor hopped out of bed. She walked to the sink. She got her little toothbrush. Mama put the paste on it. Eleanor brushed up and down. She brushed the front and the back.

"Teeth get brushed two times," said Eleanor. "In the morning and before bed." Mama nodded and smiled.

Eleanor rinsed the brush. She looked in the mirror. Her teeth were clean and shiny. She yawned a big yawn.

Back in bed, Eleanor snuggled down. The house was quiet. The blanket was warm. Mama hummed a little song.

"Good night, Eleanor," Mama said.

"Good night, teeth," said Eleanor.

Dylan stood at the snack table. Big kids were all around it. He wanted the red cup of juice. He could see it. He could not reach it.

Dylan tried to squeeze past a big kid. The big kid did not move. Dylan tried again. Still no room. He frowned and stood still. He did not know what to do. Then he heard a voice behind him.

"Excuse me," said Inaaya. She was trying to get past too. The big kid heard her and stepped aside. Inaaya walked right through. Dylan opened his mouth. He wondered if those words were magic.

Dylan took a little breath. "Excuse me," he said. The big kid looked down at him. The big kid moved to the side. Dylan walked past and picked up the red cup. "Thank you," he said to the big kid. The big kid smiled.

At the paint table, Dylan sat next to Aurelie. She was painting an old shoe box. It was the color of the sky. "Can you help me open the glue?" Dylan asked Mr. Eze. "Of course," said Mr. Eze. He opened the cap for him.

Dylan dripped a dot of glue. He pressed down a yellow leaf. It stuck. The leaf stayed on the box. Dylan looked at it and grinned. "Excuse me," he whispered to the leaf, "you live here now."

Abigail stood at the basketball court. She held a soft red beanbag. Ms. Moretti put a small hoop on the ground. "Try to get it in," said Ms. Moretti. Abigail threw the beanbag. It fell far from the hoop. She threw again. It missed again.

Her friend Grady ran over to meet her. "I keep missing," said Abigail. "Why does it fall short?" She took three little steps closer to the hoop. Then she threw the beanbag. It went in! "It went in!" she said. She pushed her hair out of her eyes and smiled. She threw again from close by. In it went again.

Next Ms. Moretti rolled a big ball to Abigail. Abigail held out both hands. She opened them wide. The ball came right into her arms. She hugged it tight. "Again!" said Abigail. Ms. Moretti rolled the ball again.

Eli stood in the kitchen. He wanted his bath now. He could hear the water running. It made a noisy sound. "Bath time soon," said his dad.

Eli climbed one step toward the tub. "Stop," said his dad. "I check the water first." Dad put his hand in the tub. He waited. Eli held his toy rock and waited too.

"Too hot," said Dad. "We make it warm." Dad turned the tap. Cold water ran in. Eli watched. Then Dad put his hand in again. "Now it is warm," he said. "Warm, not hot. You can get in."

Eli touched the water with his toes. It felt nice. It was not hot. Dad helped him sit down. The water went splash. Eli made his rock swim. "The rock likes warm water," said Eli. Dad laughed and clapped. Eli splashed again.

Riley waited at school pickup. She held her coat in her arms. She wanted to put it on all by herself. One sleeve hid inside the coat. It was like a little puzzle. "Where did my sleeve go?" she asked. Her friend Liyana looked too. "It went inside," said Liyana. Riley pulled the sleeve out. Then her arm slid right in. She had caught the sleeve just in time.

"Time to wash hands," said Ms. Buchanan. "Then we can eat our snack." Riley rubbed the soap. She added water. The soap made bubbles on her hands. The bubbles grew and grew. Riley made a bubbly beard on her chin. Liyana giggled. Riley giggled too. She was not afraid of the soap now. It felt soft and light.

The water rinsed the bubbles away. Riley dried her hands on the towel. "Bubbles need soap and water," Riley said. Ms. Buchanan smiled. Riley zipped up her coat. Then she waved to Liyana. "See you tomorrow," said Liyana. Riley held her parent's hand and walked to the car.

Audrey sat on the grass in the backyard. Her teddy bear, Boo, lay beside her. His tummy was muddy from a fall in the flower bed. "Oh no," said Audrey. "Boo is sick."

She wondered what to do. Mom was hanging up towels on the windy day. Audrey asked, "Can Boo have pretend medicine?" Mom smiled and found a small cup. "Here is his medicine," she said. Audrey held the cup to Boo's mouth. "Drink it all up," she said. She touched his forehead. It felt soft and warm.

Then Audrey got a towel from the pile. She wrapped Boo up like a blanket. "Now Boo needs a bed," she said. She patted the grass flat and laid him down. "Sleep tight, Boo." She patted his head very gently.

Boo lay still under the towel. The wind made the corners flap. Audrey waited and waited. Then she peeked under the towel. Boo's eyes looked shiny and happy. "All better!" said Audrey. She hugged him tight. "Time for a pretend snack, Boo."

Liam stood at the edge of the backyard pool. The water was blue and cool. His tummy felt funny. "I want to float," he said. "But what if I sink?"

Mr. Warsame stepped into the pool. "I will hold you," he said. "My hands go under your back. Now you can let go of me."

Liam lay back in the water. He felt Mr. Warsame's hands under his back, like a soft plastic mat. Liam opened his eyes. The sky was up there. A cloud looked like a big white dog. Was the water holding him too?

"I'm floating!" Liam said. "I'm not sinking!" Aanya clapped from the pool steps. "Next it's my turn," she said.

Then Mr. Warsame took one hand away. Liam did not sink. He did not go under. He just lay there, light as a leaf.

"Can you take your other hand away?" Liam asked. Mr. Warsame smiled and let both hands go. Liam floated all by himself. He saw the cloud drift by, slow and slow.

"Look at me, Aanya!" Liam called. Aanya kicked her legs in the water. "Can a cloud ride on the sky like that?" she asked.

"Maybe it can," Liam said. He lay still and watched it go.

Grace was at daycare. It was snack time. There was juice and bread on the table.

Theo grabbed for the bread. His hand went right past Grace's nose. Mr. Do shook his head. He held the bread plate up high.

"Try again," said Mr. Do.

Theo sat up tall. He looked at Mr. Do. "Bread, please," he said.

Mr. Do smiled. He gave Theo a big piece. Grace's eyes went wide. Theo grabbed, and nothing. Theo said please, and bread! Was that how it worked?

Grace wanted some bread too. She reached out her hand. Then she stopped. She put her hand down. She tried it the other way.

"Bread, please," said Grace.

Mr. Do gave her a piece right away. "Here you are, Grace."

Grace took a bite and began to chew. The bread was soft and warm. One piece for Theo. One piece for Grace. One, two, pieces on the table.

Siena came to the table. No bread for her yet. What would she do? Siena thought and thought. Then she said, "Bread, please."

Mr. Do laughed. "Bread for everyone who asks so nicely."

Grace drank her juice. Please, bread. Please, bread. She said the magic word all day long. "Juice, please." "Crayons, please."

At home time, Grace waved to Theo. "See you tomorrow, please."

Luke stayed at Grandpa's house. He ran to the bath and put one foot near the water. "Too hot!" said Grandpa. He held his hand in the water first. Then he turned the tap and added more cool water. Luke watched. The steam went away. Grandpa felt the water again. "Now it is just right," he said.

Luke got in. The water was warm and wet on his toes. He splashed a little. He washed his arms and his tummy. Grandpa gave him a duck to float. On the window, a flower sticker smiled at him. "Look, a yellow flower," said Luke. Grandpa laughed and washed Luke's hair.

After the bath, Luke got dressed in soft pajamas. Then he ate bread and milk with Grandpa. His eyes felt sleepy. Grandpa tucked him into bed. Luke yawned. "The duck can sleep too," he said. He closed his eyes and held the duck tight.

Naomi went to the store with her dad. She wanted to find a small blue lamp. Dad held her hand in the big store. The store had bright lights and long shelves.

Naomi saw a shelf with lamps. One lamp was not plugged in. Dad picked it up. "This one?" he asked. Naomi nodded. It was blue and small.

Near the shelf there was a little hole in the wall. It was an outlet. Naomi pointed at it. "Hole," she said. Dad crouched down. He put the plug into the outlet. The lamp made light. Naomi clapped her hands.

Naomi reached out her little finger toward the outlet. Dad held her hand softly. "No fingers in there," he said. "Only plugs." Naomi watched again. Dad took the plug out. The light went off. He put it back in. The light went on. Naomi laughed.

At home, the lamp sat by her bed. Dad plugged it in, ready for her nap. Naomi touched only the lamp's cool shade. "Night night, lamp," she said.

Leon stood in the kitchen. He wanted to help make soup. Dad had the big pot on the stove. The stove was hot, so Leon stayed back. "You can wash the carrots," said Dad. Leon carried a carrot to the sink. The water was cold. Brrr, cold water on his little hands.

Then a red ball rolled under the table. Leon ran to the far end of the kitchen. It was dark back there. He could not see Dad. Dad could not see him. Leon looked around the corner. No Dad. "Dad?" he called. No answer came. Leon picked up his ball and ran back fast. Now Dad could see him. "There you are," said Dad. "Stay where I can see you, okay?" "Okay," said Leon. "I will stay right here."

Dad spoke a soft word. "Look now." He turned the lid. Hot steam rose up and away. Leon did not touch. Then, surprise, inside the pot was a carrot shaped like a star! Dad had cut it just for him. Leon laughed. "My star!" he said. He sat on his little stool, close to Dad, and watched it swim in the soup.

Grandpa came to stay for a whole week. Matthew wanted to make something with him, something just theirs. In the kitchen, Grandpa got out a big bowl. "I will show you my special bread," he said. "My mother made it, and her mother made it too. Our family has made it for a long time."

Matthew poured the flour. Grandpa showed him how to mix and press the dough. Matthew pressed it flat, then folded it, then pressed again. It was soft and warm, like a cloud. They put the dough in the bowl and covered it with a towel. Then they had to wait. Matthew wanted to peek. "Not yet," said Grandpa, and they sat down to talk about the park instead.

After a long time, Grandpa lifted the towel. The dough was big now. Matthew's eyes went wide. His pressing had helped make it grow. Dad put the pan into the hot oven, and Matthew watched from far away. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

The next day they took the bread to the park. Marion was there by the lion statue, and Ariel was on the swings. Matthew gave them each a piece. "My grandpa taught me," he said. "It is our family bread." Ariel took a bite and smiled. "Can I help next time?"

Rain was falling on the window. Audrey put her hand on the glass. The drops made little lines slide down. Was it rainy outside? Yes, it was rainy outside.

Audrey put on her boots. Dad held a big umbrella. It looked like a triangle. "Can it catch the rain?" Audrey asked. "It can," said Dad. They walked to daycare under it. The rain tapped on top. Tap, tap, tap. Audrey stayed dry. Her head was dry. Her coat was dry. "The umbrella keeps rain off my head," she said.

At daycare, Ms. Farah looked out the window. The wind blew. It was windy too. A leaf flew past, fast. Audrey laughed and pointed. Later the rain stopped. The sun came out. Now it was sunny. Audrey and Elianna played outside. The sun felt warm on her face.

Dina was at the craft table. She made a snowman picture with cotton balls. "Snow!" said Dina. "Snowy," said Audrey. She wondered: when it is snowy, do you need mittens? "Yes, you need mittens," said Dina. Audrey looked at the umbrella rack by the door. The umbrellas sat there, still and quiet, waiting for the next rainy day.

Zoe wanted to ride the small red trike. It was the best one in the yard. There was only one trike and many kids.

Mohamed was first in line. Then came Kaya. Then came Zoe. Zoe watched Mohamed zoom around the cones. He laughed and pedaled fast. Zoe waited in her spot.

Then a boy ran up. He pushed past Kaya. He jumped onto the trike. "Hey!" said Kaya. "That was not your turn." The boy looked at the line. He got off the trike. He walked back to his spot. Mr. Bui said, "A line means you stay in your place until it is your turn."

The boy waited at the end. Mohamed had one more ride. Then Kaya had her turn. She rode slowly and smiled. Then it was Zoe's turn at last.

Zoe pedaled the red trike. The wind tickled her face. It felt just like her dream. "My turn came!" she called. Kaya clapped for her. Mohamed clapped too. After that, Zoe went to the back of the line and waited again.

Aaron sat in the backyard with his markers. He was drawing a big red truck on paper. Flynn sat next to him, drawing a sun.

Aaron reached for the blue marker. It slipped in his hand. The blue tip touched his skin. Now his hand had a blue stripe on it.

Aaron looked at the stripe. His lip began to wobble. "It won't come off," he said. He thought he might cry.

Mr. Goh was watering the flowers nearby. He came over and looked at Aaron's hand. "Let's try soap and water," he said. "These markers are washable. Washable means they wash off."

Aaron went to the outside tap. Mr. Goh put soap on his hand. Aaron rubbed and rubbed under the water. The blue stripe got smaller. Then it was gone. His hand was clean.

Aaron laughed. "It went away!" He ran back to Flynn. "Look, one stripe, two stripes, three stripes!" he said, drawing on his paper. "And if I get one on my hand, I can wash it off."

Flynn smiled and drew a big yellow snowman with a bumpy carrot nose. "The snowman has no snow," Flynn said.

"Then we will draw him some," said Aaron, and he picked up the white marker.

Avery sat in her car seat. Her father was driving. They were going home early from the park. Avery wanted to sleep in the car. But she could not sleep. There was a big truck outside. It made a loud sound. "Too loud," Avery said. She covered her ears.

Next to her sat Lilly. Lilly had a small toy drum. Lilly hit the drum hard. It went boom, boom. That was loud too. Avery's eyes stayed open. The baby in the back was awake now too. He made a loud cry.

"Lilly, can you make it quiet?" Avery asked. Lilly tapped the drum softly. Tap, tap. That was quiet. The truck went far away. That got quiet too. Soon the car was all quiet. The baby closed his eyes. Avery closed her eyes too.

"Did the quiet help him sleep?" Avery whispered. Lilly smiled and tapped one more soft tap. "We win," she whispered back. Avery felt the slow, soft taps on her arm. Then she fell fast asleep.

Eva sat at the big table. It was cooking class at school. Mr. Quinn put warm toast on her plate. Eva wanted to spread butter all by herself.

She picked up her knife. The butter was cold and hard. It came straight from the fridge. Eva pushed the hard butter on her toast. The butter made a hole in the toast. "Oh no," said Eva. Timothee looked over. Beckham looked over too.

"Let the butter sit out," said Mr. Quinn. "We will wait a bit." So they waited. They poured milk into cups while they waited. Eva poured slowly, slowly. Not one drop spilled. Outside, the rain tapped on the window.

Then Eva touched the butter. It was soft now. She pushed the soft butter on her toast. It spread and spread. No holes! The toast was smooth and sweet-smelling. Eva took a big bite. "Yum," she said.

Eva looked at the cold butter dish. She looked at the soft butter dish. She pushed the soft butter on one more piece of toast. Smooth again. "Soft butter is the best," said Eva. Beckham clapped his hands. Timothee laughed. Mr. Quinn smiled and said, "One more round of toast for everyone."

The lights went out. Henri stood still in the dark. "Mama?" he called. "I am here," said Mama. She found him and held his hand. The house was very quiet. No fridge hum. No fan.

Henri wanted light in his room. Mama lit a candle on the table. The flame was small and orange. Henri reached for it. He wanted to carry it with him. "Only a grown-up lights candles and looks after them," said Mama. She took the candle away. She put it in a safe spot. Then she gave Henri a flashlight instead.

Henri pressed the button. Click! The light came on. He shone it on his teddy bear. The bear looked bright in the dark. Henri laughed. The candle gave one orange glow. The flashlight gave a big white beam. His mama watched the candle. Henri watched his beam.

They sat together on the back step. The sky outside was soft and dark. Henri held the flashlight on his lap. Soon the lights came back on. "All done," said Mama. Henri gave his teddy bear a goodnight squeeze under his blanket.

Addison sat at the kitchen table. The bowls were warm. The spoons were shiny. Mama set down the rice, and Addison grabbed her spoon fast.

"Wait," said Mouhamed, her friend. "We say Bismillah first."

"What is Bismillah?" asked Addison.

"It means in the name of God," said Mouhamed. "Many Muslims say it before they eat."

Addison put her spoon down. She folded her small hands. The steam rose up, thin and white, like a little spring from the bowl. "Bismillah," she said. The word felt good in her mouth.

Mama smiled. "Now we can eat," she said.

Addison took one big bite. The rice was warm and soft. Then she spoke again, quiet and happy. "Bismillah," she said, "before my next bite too."

Mouhamed laughed and clapped his hands. "You said it all by yourself."

Addison held her spoon up high like a flag.

Hailey put on her swimsuit. She was on the swim team now. Today was the big meet at the pool.

"I want to swim fast right now," Hailey said. Ms. Kaya smiled. "First we warm up," she said. "Teams warm up before a game."

Hailey watched the team run around the pool. Then they stretched their arms way up high. Hailey peeked at her friend Andrei. He was stretching too. So Hailey ran with him. She stretched her arms and legs.

"Race time," said Ms. Kaya. The whistle blew. Hailey jumped in. Her arms felt strong. Her legs felt strong too. She swam all the way to the wall.

She looked up. Andrei was clapping. So was Davis. "You were so fast," said Andrei. "I warmed up first," said Hailey. "That helped me."

After the race, Hailey sat on the towel. Her little brother was asleep in the stroller. Ms. Kaya gave her a warm hug. "Next race soon," said Hailey, and she jumped back to the pool.

Kinsley sat at Grandma's big table. The bowls were full of corn. The corn was yellow and a little salty. Everyone held hands. It was time for the family blessing.

Kinsley did not know the blessing yet. She opened her mouth. Nothing came out. She looked down at her lap.

Grandma squeezed her hand. "Take your time," said Grandma. "We can wait." They all waited. The room was quiet and warm.

Kinsley thought about the corn. "Grandma, where did the corn grow?" she asked. "On a farm," said Grandma. "A farmer picked it for us."

Kinsley thought about that. The farmer had pulled the corn from the tall plants. Then the corn came all the way here. Kinsley took a big breath.

"Thank you for our food," she said. "Thank you for the corn. And thank you to the farmer." Grandma smiled wide. "That is a good blessing," she said. "It says thank you."

Then Grandma passed the bread. Kinsley took a warm piece and ate it all up. "Can I say it again tomorrow?" she asked. Grandma laughed and squeezed her hand one more time.

Rehmat stood by the pool in her red swimsuit. Today was game day! Ms. González held a big box. Inside were beanbags and a hoop. "First we throw," said Ms. González. "Then we catch. Then we jump in and drink our juice."

Rehmat grabbed a beanbag. She swung her arm high and let go. The beanbag flew way over the hoop. It landed near Marvin's feet. "Too far!" laughed Marvin. "One, two, three misses," counted Paige.

Ms. González picked up the beanbag. She held it low, near her knees. Her arm swung from down low, forward and up. The beanbag went up and dropped into the middle of the hoop. "Try that way," she said.

Rehmat held her beanbag down low. She counted, "One, two, three!" Her arm swung forward and up. The beanbag sailed through the air. Plunk! It landed in the hoop.

"You did it!" said Paige. "One, two, three baskets!" said Marvin. Now it was catch time. Paige threw the big beach ball. Rehmat opened both arms wide. She caught it and hugged it tight. The ball smelled like sunscreen and felt bumpy.

Then everyone jumped in the pool. The water was cool and splashy. Rehmat was so tired and happy. After juice, she yawned a big yawn. "You might fall asleep right here," said Ms. González. Rehmat laughed and hugged her wet beanbag. "More hoop tomorrow!"

Alice wakes up in her soft, warm bed. The sun is bright at her window. She hears Dad making breakfast in the kitchen. "Eggs today," he says. Alice wants to help, but first she has a small problem. She needs to use the toilet.

Alice sits on the toilet. Then she pulls up her pants and runs to the kitchen. But wait. The toilet is still full. She forgot something! What did she forget? Alice runs back to look.

"First we flush," says Dad, following her. Alice presses the big silver handle. Whoosh! The water spins round and round. She watches it all go down. That was the first step. But there is one more step after that.

"Now we wash our hands," says Dad. He turns on the tap. Warm water runs over Alice's little hands. The soap is slippery and smells like flowers. One, two, three, four, five bubbles. She counts them all. Then she dries her hands on the blue towel.

Now her hands are clean. Now she can help Dad. Alice sits on her chair and cracks nothing, but she does open the egg box for him. "Nice work, Alice," says Dad. Alice smiles and eats her warm egg.

Audrey sat at the dinner table. The bright lamp made a warm circle of light. Her dad set down three bowls. One was for animals. One was for toys. One was for foods.

Audrey picked up a carrot. "Food," she said. She dropped it in the foods bowl. Then came a little cow from her farm set. "Animal," she said. Clunk. Then a soft toy dog. She held it near the animal bowl. Her dad waited. She squeezed its furry arm. It did not wiggle. It did not bark. It just sat in her hand.

"Not alive," said Audrey. She moved it over. "Toy dog." Clunk, into the toy bowl. Her dad smiled and swept the crumbs off the table with his hand.

"Now dinner," he said. Audrey put one strawberry in her own bowl. "Food," she said. She took a big bite.

Ethan stood at the school gate. His tummy felt funny, like little butterflies. His mom held his hand tight.

"My tummy feels fluttery," Ethan said.

Mom knelt down. "That means you feel nervous. It is okay to feel nervous on the first day of school. I felt nervous on my first day too."

"You did?" said Ethan.

"Yes! And then I saw my teacher and it got better."

Just then, a boy named Salem ran up to the gate. He was holding a special red truck. He rolled it on the ground and sent it right to Ethan's feet.

"Want to play trucks?" said Salem.

Ethan picked up the truck. The butterflies in his tummy flew away. Across the street, the school bell rang, warm and loud.

"Let's go together," said Salem.

Ethan smiled and took his new friend's hand. "Let's go!"

Mya stood in the kitchen. Her tummy said it was breakfast time. She wanted toast with butter, all by herself. Her dad put two warm pieces of toast on her plate. Then he handed her the butter knife.

Mya dug the knife into the soft butter. She spread it across the toast, one, two, three strokes. The butter made shiny lines. Some spots were bare. She spread some more. Now the toast was covered, and it smelled yummy.

Next came the milk. Mya held the small cup. She poured the milk slowly, slowly. The milk rose up in the cup. Then her hand wiggled. A little white puddle sat on the table. Mya's lip went down at the corners.

She reached for the curly blue cloth. She wiped the puddle, one wipe, two wipes. The table was dry again. Mya poured one more time. This time her hand was steady. Not one drop spilled. She took a big bite of buttery toast and a big sip of milk. "I did it," said Mya, "all by myself."

Aubrey sat in her seat in the family car. Click, click went her buckle. The car hummed under her feet. Today was shot day at the doctor. Aubrey did not like shot day. "I am afraid," she said.

Mom kept driving. "We will go together," said Mom. "I will be with you the whole time." Aubrey looked out the window. One tree, two trees, three trees went by. Then the car stopped. They were at the doctor's office.

In the office, Aubrey climbed on the big, high table. It felt cold and too big. Her legs swung in the air. The nurse came in with a little tray. Aubrey's eyes got wide. She started to cry.

"Come here," said Mom. Mom sat on a chair and pulled Aubrey onto her lap. Mom's arms went around her, warm like a blanket. Aubrey held Mom's hand. She squeezed it tight. The nurse counted, "One, two, three." The shot was done, that fast. It barely hurt at all.

They walked back to the car. The seat felt cozy now. The sun made a warm spot on her knee. "My turn for a sticker," said Aubrey. She stuck it right on her shirt and smiled.

William loved the playroom floor. It had a big striped rug with squares on it. He wanted to build a house for his toy bear.

He found a round plate. "That is a circle," he said. He put it down for a wall. Then he found a tiny button. Mackenzie shook her head. "That can't be a circle," she said. "It is too small. The plate is a circle."

William held the button up. He looked at the plate. Then he looked at the button. Both went round and round, with no corners at all. "Look," he said. He spun the button on the floor. It rolled just like the plate rolled.

"Big circle, tiny circle," said Mackenzie. She clapped. They used the button for a little window. William found a triangle block for the roof. The bear had a house at last.

Beatrice came home from Grandma's house. She had a big blue bag. The trip was over now.

"Time to unpack," said her mama. Beatrice put her bag on the floor. She opened it up. Out came her shirt. Out came her soft bunny. Out came her little red shoes.

She tipped her shoe upside down. Sand fell out! Sand from the beach at Grandma's house. Beatrice laughed and laughed. The sand made a small pile on the rug.

"That is beach sand," said her mama. She helped sweep it up. Beatrice put her shirt in the drawer. She put her bunny on the bed. She put her shoes on the shelf. The bag was empty at last.

Beatrice smelled her shirt. It smelled like Grandma's flowers. Her feet felt funny without shoes, like something new.

"Unpack, unpack," sang Beatrice. She hugged her empty bag. "All done!"

Wesley was at Grandma's house. He sat at the big table. Emmie sat next to him. They were painting pictures.

"One cat," said Wesley. "Two cats. Three cats." He painted three orange cats. Emmie painted three orange cats too. Grandma put the paintings in the sun to dry. The paint began to shine.

Then Wesley wanted his painting. But there were two papers. Both had three orange cats. "Which one is mine?" he asked. He looked and looked. He could not tell.

Emmie held up her paper. Her name was on it. Letters at the top said Emmie. "Look," she said. "I wrote my name." Wesley picked up a crayon. He wrote W-E-S on his paper. Now everyone knew which painting was his.

"How did you know?" he asked Emmie. "Grandma helped me," she said. Wesley smiled. He carried his cats to Grandma. "This one is mine," he said. "It says Wesley."

Ryan went to the bank with his mom. It was cold outside. Ryan held his coat in his hands.

"I will put it on myself," Ryan said. He pushed one arm into a sleeve. Then he pushed his other arm in too. Both arms went into the same sleeve! The coat looked like one long tube. Ryan laughed and laughed. He waved his arms like a big flipper.

His mom smiled. "Try again," she said. Ryan shook the coat out. This time he looked at it. One arm went into one sleeve. The other arm went into the other sleeve. Each arm had its own sleeve. The coat sat just right on his shoulders.

Now the zipper. Ryan pulled it up, up, up. It stuck near the top. He pulled again, slow and steady. Click. The zipper closed all the way.

At the bank, the warm air felt good. Ryan patted his chest. "I did it," he said. "All by myself."

His mom said, "Next time, we can work on your hat."

"Maybe," said Ryan. "But the coat was my big dream today." He zipped it down and zipped it back up, just to hear the sound.

Eliana ran to her cubby at daycare. She touched the tag on it. The tag said "Eliana." "That is my name," she said.

Ms. Boateng held out a card. "This came for you today." The card was smooth and red. Eliana opened it. It was from Louie. The card said "Eliana" at the top.

Eliana looked at the cubby. Then she looked at the card. "Same!" she said. "The letters are the same." Ms. Boateng smiled. "Louie can spell your name."

Jane came over. "How do you spell it?" she asked. "E, L, I, A, N, A," said Eliana, pointing at each letter. The letters went in the same order both times.

Eliana turned the pages of the card, one by one, front to back. On the last page, there was a picture of bread. It was a picture of bread with a candle in it.

"Happy birthday, Eliana!" said Louie, running in the door.

Rosalie took the big road with her dad. They walked to the wide doors of the temple. Inside, Ms. Chaudhry was waiting with her drum.

"Hello, Rosalie," said Ms. Chaudhry. "Today we will clap and sing. You will meet the beat."

Ryan and Reese sat on the mats too. Ms. Chaudhry tapped the drum. Rosalie began to sing right away. But Ryan and Reese did not sing yet. Rosalie sang all alone. She stopped and her face felt warm.

"Wait for the count," said Ms. Chaudhry, kindly. "I will say one, two, three, four. Then we all start singing together."

Ms. Chaudhry lifted her hand. "One, two, three, four." Ryan and Reese began to sing. Rosalie began too, right on four. Now they all sang at the same time.

Then they clapped. Ms. Chaudhry tapped the drum, boom, boom, boom. Rosalie clapped her hands on each boom. She saw that when her hand went down, the drum went boom. Clap, boom. Clap, boom.

They sang "Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star." Rosalie knew all the words. She did not look at anyone. She sang them all by herself.

"Again!" said Rosalie.

Ms. Chaudhry smiled and lifted her hand. "One, two, three, four."

Aiden was busy in the playroom. He wanted his red ball. He looked under the little chair. He looked behind the big plant. "Where is my ball?" he asked. His dad said, "Look in the toy box."

The toy box was full of everything. Blocks were on the floor. A doll was on the rug. The ball was under the teddy bear. Aiden put a block in the box. The box had one less thing on the floor. He put in another block. Now the floor had more room.

Aiden held up the doll. "Doll goes in," he said. Dad said, "Yes, it does. Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys." Aiden smiled. He put the doll in. He picked up the ball. "Ball goes in too!" he said.

Then Aiden wanted to make a picture. Dad got the glue and some paper. Aiden spread the glue with a stick. He stuck on a red circle. He pressed it down. The paper was heavy with glue, so it sank down flat on the table. Aiden held his ball up high. "My ball can sit here," he said, and he set it right on top of the full toy box.

Jaxon walked in the forest with Ms. Ricci. He saw a box under a big tree. The box had a hat, a scarf, and some shiny boots. "Who wears this?" he asked. "You can wear it," said Ms. Ricci. Jaxon put on the big hat. He stood very tall. "Now I am a firefighter!" he said. "The dress-up clothes make me someone new."

His friends Shepherd and Judith came down the path. "Look, look!" said Jaxon. "I am a firefighter!" Judith put on the scarf. "Now I am a mama," she said. Shepherd put on the boots. "I am a farmer now," he said. They all laughed.

The farmer had a carrot. "My baby bunny is hungry," said the mama. The firefighter helped. "I will bring the carrot fast!" said Jaxon. He ran, but not too fast, and gave the carrot to the soft toy bunny. The bunny was not hungry anymore. "Is the bunny okay now?" asked Jaxon. "Yes, all better," said Judith.

Then the pretend phone rang. Beep, beep! "Come quick!" said Shepherd. "A little cat is stuck!" The firefighter put on his big hat again. He held his toy hose. He sprayed pretend water on a pretend fire. The cat was saved. The mama hugged the cat. The farmer clapped. Jaxon took off the big hat at the end of the day. He was just Jaxon again. But he smiled all the way home. "Can we play again soon?" he asked Ms. Ricci. "Yes," she said. "Tomorrow we play again."

Carter went to the playground with his mom. First he went down the slide. Then he ran in the green grass. "One slide, two swings, three big steps," he counted. His mom waved from a bench.

After play time, they walked to the little store next to the playground. Mom said, "Stay close." Carter saw apples. He saw a big tower of cans. Then he looked up. Mom was not there. The tall shelf had hidden her.

Carter remembered what his dad had taught him. He walked to the front. The cashier had curly hair. "I can't find my grown-up," Carter said. The cashier called out, and Mom came running around the shelf. "You told a store worker," Mom said. "That was just right."

Then a small surprise came. Azalea from his class popped out from behind the juice boxes. "Carter! We play at my house next door," she said. Carter counted again: "One apple, two friends, three happy people." Mom held his hand all the way to the door.

Luke had a toy snake at school. It was green and long. He loved that snake.

At play time, Luke saw Liana. She sat by the wooden blocks. Tears ran down her face. She was crying. Luke felt sad too.

He ran to his cubby. He got his toy snake. He held it out to Liana. "You can hold him," Luke said. Liana wiped her eyes. She took the soft snake. She hugged it close.

Then Liana smiled a big smile. "His name is Sam," she said. Luke sat down next to her. They made a little home for Sam out of blocks. Mr. Lin came over and helped them cover the snake with a small blanket.

"More blocks," said Liana. She handed one to Luke.

Emmett hurried to the dress-up corner at school. He wanted to wear the firefighter hat. But his shoe felt funny. One sock was gone!

"Where is my sock?" Emmett asked. He looked under the chair. No sock. He looked in the short basket of hats. No sock. He looked in the toy box. Yes! His sock was lying on top of a teddy bear.

Emmett picked up the sock. He laughed. "A sock is not a toy," he said. "It goes with clothes. Shirts, socks and hats are all clothes."

Yousuf came over. He was holding his shirt. "My shirt fell in the toy box too," Yousuf said.

"Then we can fix it," Emmett said. He put his sock in the clothes basket. He counted out loud, "One sock, one shirt, one hat." Yousuf added his shirt. "Now two shirts!" he said.

Ms. Munro smiled. "You made the corner neat," she said. "Thank you, boys."

Emmett put on his sock and shoe. Then he put on the firefighter hat. He looked out the window at the big tree. "Firefighter to the rescue!" he said.

Theodore sat at the paint table at summer camp. He wanted to paint the long grass by the lake. But there was no green paint in his tray. He had red, yellow, and blue. He looked and looked. Still no green.

His friend Khaled sat down next to him. "I need green for the grass," Theodore said. "I only have yellow and blue." Khaled pointed at the jars. "Yellow is a sun colour," he said. "Blue is a sky colour."

Theodore dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He painted a big yellow stripe on his paper. Then he dipped the same brush in the blue paint. He made a blue stripe right on top. He swirled his brush round and round. The colours touched. The wet paint moved together.

The stripe turned green! Theodore jumped up. "Khaled, look! It's green!" He painted long green grass all the way across his paper. He even gave the stick figure in his picture green shoes. Ms. Pérez came over and smiled. "What lovely grass, Theodore." Theodore held up his wet painting so she could see. "It's yellow and blue," he said.

Riley stood in the restaurant kitchen. The cook had made hot toast, and it sat on a plate. "Now you can butter it," the cook said. Riley took the knife and scooped soft butter. She spread it slow, corner to corner. "Look, shiny toast!" she said. Mr. Kaminski smiled. "Nice work, Riley."

Next came the milk. Riley held a cup in one hand. She poured with the other hand. The cup wiggled. Milk plopped onto the table. "Sorry, milk," Riley said. Mr. Kaminski handed her a cloth. Riley wiped it up.

Then she set the cup down on the table. She let go of it. The cup sat still. Riley poured, and the milk went right in. Not one drop spilled. Riley hopped up and down. "The cup stays still when I put it down!" Jolene clapped from the door. "Can I try too?"

Leah was almost asleep. Then she heard a sound. Tap. Tap. Tap. It came from under her bed. Leah sat up fast. Her heart went boom, boom. She was scared. She pulled the blanket up high. The sound came again. Tap. Tap. Tap. Leah did not like it one bit.

She thought for a minute. She was a young girl, but she knew something good. When you are scared, you can tell a grown-up you trust, and they can help. So she called out, "Mom! I hear a sound!" Mom came in fast. She sat on the bed. "I'm scared," Leah said. "It goes tap, tap, tap." Mom held her hand. Leah pointed one finger down at the floor. "It's under there," she said.

Mom got down on her knees. She looked under the bed. Then she laughed a little laugh. Out came the cat! He had been batting a toy. Tap. Tap. Tap. That was his little game all along. The cat jumped up on the bed. He curled up by Leah's feet. His tail was soft and warm.

Leah was not scared anymore. She felt happy and sleepy too. Mom kissed her head. "Call me any time," Mom said. "I will always come." Leah closed her eyes. The cat purred by her toes. It sounded like a tiny motor. Tap. Tap. Tap, said the toy on the floor. The cat did not care. He was already asleep.

"Good night, cat," Leah whispered.

Isla went to the garden center with her dad. She picked a small bag of seeds. "Carrot seeds," she said. She held the bag like a little ball all the way home.

In the yard, Isla dug in the dirt. She made the soil clean and soft. Her dad helped her break up the big lumps. Isla patted the seeds down into the dirt. Then she gave them a drink of water.

Every day Isla ran outside to look. She saw only brown dirt. She saw a worm. She saw a leaf blow by. But no carrots came up. "Too slow," said Isla. Her dad laughed. "Wait more days," he said.

At last, Isla saw something tiny and green. It was poking up out of the soil. She ran to the fence. "Hector! Come see my sprout!" she called. Hector ran over fast. "A sprout?" he said. "Yes," said Isla. She pointed at the little green tip. "That is a sprout. My seeds made it." Hector bent down low. "It is so small," he said. "It will grow big," said Isla. She gave the sprout one more drop of water.

David sat in his car seat. He looked out the window. The sun was out. It was a sunny day. David wore his sunglasses.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain fell on the window. Tap, tap, tap. "Rainy now," said David. His dad turned on the wipers. The rain went away, swish, swish.

"Where is my hat?" David asked. "We might need it." His dad said, "Look at the trees."

The trees swayed back and forth. Leaves blew all around. They blew across the road. They blew past the car. "It is windy!" said David. He counted the leaves as they flew. One, two, three. The wind took them far away.

"Wind makes the trees dance," said David. His dad smiled. The last leaf flew up, up, up. Then it landed on a big hill.

"The hill is white," said David. "Snow!" His dad said, "Yes. We will need warm coats."

David hugged his hat. "I am ready," he said.

Adam wanted to draw a farm picture. He had paper and crayons. But he needed a shape for the barn door. "I need the door shape," he said. "But which one is it?"

Mom was cooking at the stove. Adam stayed back from the hot stove. He looked around the sunny kitchen. He saw a plate. "That is a circle," he said. He saw a window. "That is a square." He saw a slice of toast. "That is a triangle!" But no door shape yet.

Then Adam looked at the big kitchen door. He ran to it. He touched one side. Then another side. "One, two, three, four sides!" He poked each corner. "One, two, three, four corners. And they are square corners!" The dog barked, as if to say yes. "A rectangle has four sides and four square corners," said Adam, "like the shape of a door!"

Adam ran back to the table. He drew four sides and four square corners. He drew a red barn around it. He drew a sunny sky and a cow. "The farm is done!" he shouted. Mom clapped her hands. The dog barked again, loud and happy.

Penelope sat at the dinner table. Her plate had peas, cheese and bread. Under her chair, her boot tapped the floor. One boot was on. One boot was lost somewhere.

"I want a book about animals," said Penelope. "The cat book. With the big tiger."

"We can go to the library tomorrow," said her dad. "The animal books sit together on one shelf. The toy books sit on another shelf."

Penelope looked at her plate. She had an idea. The dinner table could be a library!

She pushed all her peas into one group. "These are the animal peas," she said. She pushed her bread into another group. "These are the toy breads." The cheese got its own spot too. "Food books," she said, and giggled.

Then she dropped some cheese, and it went splat. "The cheese is glue now," she said. "It sticks my groups down."

Her dad laughed and helped wipe the table. "Now the table is clean again," he said.

The next day they went to the library. Penelope held her dad's hand. She found a big shelf full of animal books. Tigers, cats and elephants, all together. She picked the tiger book and hugged it tight.

"Peas go with peas," she said. "Animal books go with animal books."

She found her other boot by the door on the way out. She sat down and put it on, right there on the library steps.

"Tiger time," she said.

Juliette wanted to wash her hands all by herself. But the sink was too high. Her hands could not reach the water. "Too high, too high!" she said.

Her dad brought a step stool. "Here is your step stool," he said. He stayed close by her side. Juliette climbed up. Now her hands could reach the water. "I can do it!" she said.

She put soap on her hands. She rubbed and rubbed. "Bubbles, bubbles!" she sang. She counted to twenty. It took a long, long time. The bubbles went down the drain. Her hands were clean and shiny.

"Now we can eat," said Dad. He held up a cookie. Juliette looked at her hands. "Clean hands get a party treat!" she said. Dad laughed. "A cookie party for two." Juliette rode her step stool down and ran to the table. She clapped her soapy-clean hands. "Cookie time!"

Lena sat at her big table. She had a pile of crayons. She wanted to draw the sky.

She found her blue crayon. But it was dark like the night sky. "I need light blue," she said.

Erica was there to play. She held up a navy crayon. "This one is blue," said Erica.

Lena shook her head. "That one is too dark. Blue is light like the sky."

They put all the blues on the table. There were five blue crayons. Lena lined them up. The palest one went first. The darkest one went last. They made a long row, light to dark.

"Look," said Erica. "They are all still called blue."

Lena smiled. She picked the lightest blue crayon. She drew a big sky shape with soft clouds. Then she drew the sea with the dark blue crayon. The sea was still blue too.

At bath time, Lena splashed the water with her hand. The water looked light blue in her little cup. The big tub looked dark blue in the shadow. "Two blues," said Lena. "One light, one dark."

Charles went to the library with his dad. He wanted the big white book about trucks. It sat on the shelf, and Charles could see it from far away. He began to walk faster and faster. Then he ran right to the front of the line of kids. Safa and Dani were standing there, waiting for their turn.

"Charles, you went past us," said Safa. Ms. Korhonen knelt down beside him. "This is the line," she said. Charles looked behind him. So many kids, all standing one after another. He wondered, what is a line for? He went back to his spot, behind Dani. His feet stayed still. It was hard to wait. He counted the flowers on Dani's shirt, one, two, three, four.

A boy at the front got his book. Then it was Safa's turn. Then it was Dani's turn. And then it was Charles's turn. He held out his hands. Ms. Korhonen gave him the big white truck book. "My turn," said Charles, and he hugged it tight.

David woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! "No school today," said Mom. David jumped up and down. "Snow day!"

He put on his boots and his red hat. Mom took him to the big sledding hill. His friend Kingston was there too. They sled down fast, fast, fast. Whee!

Then David tried to walk to the sled hill steps. His feet slipped. He sat down in the snow with a plop.

Mr. Cruz was shoveling a path. He pushed the snow away with his big shovel. "Try walking here," he said. David walked on the clean path. He did not slip at all!

"Can I help?" David asked. Mr. Cruz gave him a small shovel. David pushed snow off the path. The mail carrier came by and waved. "Thank you!" she said.

Then Mom called, "Time to go cook soup!" David slid down the hill one more time. He heard the sound of Kingston laughing all the way down.

Parker went to the library with his dad. Mr. Janssen had a table with tablets on it. Parker wanted to draw a cat on one.

"Can I try?" Parker asked.

"Yes," said Mr. Janssen. "First we turn it on." Parker pressed the round button. The screen lit up. His tap made it wake!

He tapped the little paint app. It opened. The app was open, just like a book. One tap, one picture page. Another tap, a new color. It was like magic, but it was not magic. His finger did it.

Parker drew a big orange cat. Then Tiago sat down beside him. Tiago set his juice cup on the table. It sat right by the tablet.

"Not there," said Mr. Janssen. "Tablets stay away from water and drinks." Tiago moved his cup to the next table. Parker looked at his own cup. He moved it too. Far away.

He drew the cat a pillow to sleep on. Then it was time to go. Parker pressed the button and held it. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in the basket, flat side down.

"Bye, tablet," said Parker. "Bye, cat."

Anna wanted to wash her toy duck. She went to the bathroom with her dad. The water ran into the sink. Dad felt it first. "Hot," he said. "Too hot for you." He turned the tap. Now the water felt warm and nice.

Anna washed the duck. It went splash, splash. Then she saw a little box on the wall. It had small holes in it. It was near the sink, close to her elbow.

Anna pointed at it. "What is that?" she asked.

"That is an electrical outlet," said Dad. "Never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet."

Anna looked at her fingers. She kept them on the duck. Dad plugged in his razor, and it made a noisy hum. Anna heard it buzz.

Dad put a little sign over the outlet. "There," he said. "Now it is covered."

Anna washed the duck some more. Splash, splash. "All clean," she said.

"Good girl," said Dad. "You told me. You did not touch."

Elias went to Grandma's house. Today was a big party day. There were so many people there. There were lanterns and red paper on the door.

Elias held Mama's hand at the door. Then he saw a big table of food. There were his favorite dumplings. He let go of Mama's hand. He walked toward the dumplings all by himself.

The room was full of legs and coats. Elias could not see Mama. He could not see Grandma. His tummy felt funny. He stood still and thought. At a big party, he must stay close to his grown-up. Grandma found him by the food table. She took his hand. "Stay with me, little one," she said.

Grandma walked with him past all the people. Grandpa was lighting a candle. Grandma held Elias back from the candle. "Only grown-ups touch fire," she said. Elias watched the candle from far away. It was pretty and safe.

Then they found the dumplings together. Elias ate three dumplings. Mama sat right beside him. Grandma gave him a red envelope with money inside. Elias held Mama's hand again. The party was loud and happy. "This is my favorite day," said Elias. Grandma smiled and squeezed his hand.

Florence was at Grandma's house. On the shelf sat a little tablet. Florence wanted to draw on it.

Grandma showed her the round button. Florence pressed it with one finger. The screen lit up. A picture appeared!

"Now the drawing part," said Grandma. Grandma tapped the blue spot. Florence tapped it too. A big white page opened. Florence picked the red crayon on the screen. She drew a red cat. She drew a sleepy sun going down.

Soon Florence got tired of drawing. She put the tablet on the soft couch. Then Grandma came in to sit down. "Wait!" said Florence. The tablet was right where Grandma would sit!

Florence picked up the tablet. "Where does it go?" she asked. Grandma pointed to the shelf. "When you are finished, the tablet goes back in its special place," said Grandma. Florence set it on the shelf. It fit just right in its spot.

Grandma sat down on the couch. Florence climbed up beside her. On the fridge hung a plastic magnet shaped like a star. Florence pointed at it. "That star can be my next picture," she said. "A red one."

Alexander wanted the rabbit book. It had a fuzzy cover. He hugged it to his chest. He carried it to Ms. Kamau.

"Read it, please," he said. Ms. Kamau sat down on the small red chair. She opened the front cover first. Then she turned the pages one by one. She read the words out loud. "The rabbit hopped to the garden," she read. The words sat under the picture, small and black.

Then she turned to a page with only a picture. The rabbit drank milk in the sun. Alexander waited. But Ms. Kamau was quiet.

"Read this one too," said Alexander.

"There are no words on this page," she said. "There is nothing written here to read."

Alexander leaned close. He looked and looked. He touched the page with his finger. There were marks on other pages, but not here. Only the rabbit and the milk.

"Turn it," he said. Ms. Kamau turned to the next page. The words came back. She read them all the way to the back cover.

Alexander clapped. Then he opened his fuzzy book again, at the front, all by himself. He traced the little black words with one finger.

"These say rabbit," he told Lachlan. "You wait. I will learn to say them too."

Milo ran into the bright backyard. "Let's play hide and seek," said Zak. Milo put his hands over his eyes. "Now you can't see me," he said. Zak laughed. "I can still see you, Milo. Your eyes are the only thing that can't see."

Milo peeked through his fingers. Zak was right. He could see the swing, the grass and Zak's big grin. He ran and hid behind the big tree. He could feel the bark, rough on his fingers. He could smell the flowers by the fence. He could hear Zak counting. "Ready or not, here I come!" Could Zak hear his feet on the grass?

Zak found him fast. "How did you know I was here?" asked Milo. "I saw your shoes," said Zak. Milo looked down. His shoes stuck out from the tree.

They played again. This time Milo tucked his feet in. Zak walked right past him. "Where is Milo? Maybe he is a dream!" Zak called. Milo held his breath and waited, smiling in the dark behind his safe tree.

Livia wanted to help in the kitchen. Mom was busy at the stove. "The pot is hot," Mom said. "You stay back here." Livia stood far from the hot pot. She could see Mom. Mom could see her.

"I will get the big spoon," Livia said. She ran to the far end of the pantry. It was dark back there. Livia looked out. She could not see Mom. "Mom?" she called. Mom did not answer. Livia did not like the far end. She hurried back fast. Then Mom could see her. And Livia could see Mom.

"I like it here," Livia said. Mom gave her a brush. "Brush the crumbs off the table," said Mom. Livia brushed. The crumbs went slide, slide, into her hand. "Good helper," said Mom. Livia smiled and brushed some more.

Isla wanted to see the pot bubble. Her dad put the pot on the stove. Then the water began to hum. "Can I guess what is inside?" Isla asked. "Just water," said her dad. White puffs rose up from the pot. They curled like little clouds. Isla stepped closer to peek. Her dad held out his hand. "Stay back," he said. "The steam is hot. It can burn you." Isla stopped. She stood by the door, far from the stove. The steam rose higher and higher. It faded before it touched the roof. "Wow," said Isla. "It goes up so fast!" Her dad smiled. He stirred the pot with a big spoon. Isla watched the bubbles pop and roll. They were round and small. She clapped her hands. Then her dad turned off the stove. He poured pasta into a strainer. Isla helped by holding the bread bag. She pulled out two soft slices. "The steam went away," she said. Her dad nodded. "It will come back next time we cook." Isla wondered where the steam would go. "Can we watch again tomorrow?" she asked. "Yes," said her dad. "You can be my young helper. You stand right there, and you watch." Isla stood very still. The pot sat quiet and cool now. "All done," she said, and patted the counter gently.

Hazel was at Grandma's house. Grandma had a small box for her. "This is for you," said Grandma. Hazel opened it fast. Inside was a red hat with a white pompom.

Hazel put the hat on. She ran to the mirror. "Not ugly at all!" she said. She spun around and around. Then she ran outside to show Madden, her friend from next door.

Madden looked at the hat. "Grandma gave you that?" he asked. Hazel nodded. "Was it a present?" he asked. Hazel nodded again. Then she stopped. She had not said the magic word to Grandma. Her mother had taught it to her. You say it when someone gives you something. Hazel ran back inside. Grandma was washing cups at the sink. Hazel waited by the door until Grandma looked up. "Thank you for my hat," said Hazel. Grandma smiled big. She gave Hazel a hug. "You are so welcome," said Grandma. Hazel held the pompom and smiled too.

Parker came home with a small puppy. The puppy had soft brown fur. Parker named him Buddy.

Then Buddy wiggled out the door. He ran across the yard. Parker called and called. Buddy did not come back. Parker felt like crying.

His dad said, "Let's check his collar." Buddy had a tag on his collar. His dad read the tag out loud. It said their phone number. A neighbour found Buddy down the street. She saw the tag. She called the number. Parker and his dad ran to get Buddy.

Parker hugged Buddy tight. "Your tag helped you come home," Parker said. Now Parker held Buddy's leash every day. He filled the water bowl. He gave Buddy soft pats. Parker was a proud big helper. At night, Buddy slept in his new bed. Parker whispered, "Good night, Buddy." Buddy wagged his little tail.

Hailey was drawing in the backyard. It was a sunny day, but the sky was getting dark. Then the lights in the house went out. "A power cut," said Dad. "The power is off."

Hailey went to the back door. She stood very still. "It's so quiet," she said. Dad nodded. "The fridge stopped humming. The power made it go."

Hailey listened hard. She heard a bird in the tree. She heard her own breath. She heard a little tap, tap, tap. "Dad, what is that?" she asked. They listened together. "Rain," said Dad. "It's starting to rain."
