Hailey put out her hand. The drops fit right in her palm. Then the rain stopped. The sun came back. Inside, the fridge began to hum again. "The power is on!" Dad called. Hailey laughed. The hum filled the house like a song. "I missed you, fridge," she said. Dad gave her a big hug.

Ayla sat at the kitchen table. She had a pencil and some paper. Mom sat next to her with a towel and a cup of tea.

"Can you write your name?" Mom asked.

Ayla wanted to try. She held the pencil with her whole fist. She made a big round A. Then the paper slid away. Her line went crooked. The letter looked wobbly.

"My paper keeps moving," Ayla said.

She tried again. She pressed hard. The paper slid again. She frowned and put her head down.

Mom sat close by her side. "You can try again," Mom said softly. "Your hands can work together."

Ayla sat up. She put her left hand flat on the paper. She held the paper still. Then she drew with the pencil.

The paper did not slide. Her A stood up straight. Her Y had two neat arms. Her L had a good tall line.

"Mom, look!" said Ayla. "I did it!"

She wrote the whole name. A Y L A. All four letters, neat and small.

Mom clapped her hands. "Let's ask Dad to come and see," she said.

Dad came to the table. He looked at the paper. "That's your name!" he said. "You wrote it all by yourself."

Ayla smiled big. She turned the paper toward him. "This is me," she said.

Rose sat on the little red mat. Mr. Lim tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. Rose clapped along with the taps. Her claps went the same speed as the drum.

"Now let's sing," said Mr. Lim. "The cat sat on the mat. The cat wore a big red..."

Amelya stopped. "I forgot the word!"

"Ask Rose," said Mehreen. "Rose knows it."

Rose thought hard. The cat wore a big red... She tried a word. "Mat?"

Amelya laughed. "A red mat on his head? That is so silly!"

"The word ends like cat," said Amelya. "Cat. Hat!"

"Hat!" said Rose. "The cat wore a big red hat!"

They sang it again. Tap, tap, tap went the drum. Clap, clap, clap went Rose. "And next he found an egg," sang Mehreen.

"A red egg?" said Rose. "You are so mean to that cat!"

Everyone giggled. Mr. Lim tapped faster. Rose clapped faster to keep up. "My hands can go fast too!" she said.

Louis stood in the kitchen. The toast was on his plate. Mom had made it warm for him. Louis wanted to butter it all by himself.

He took his knife. He poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast tore. Little crumbs went everywhere. "Oh no," said Louis. Mom handed him a new piece of toast. "Try the flat side," she said.

Louis looked at the flat side. He pushed it across the bread. The butter came off the knife. It spread out smooth and shiny. "It works!" said Louis. He pushed again and again. Soon the toast was all covered.

Next came the milk. Louis held the cup with two hands. He poured slowly. One little drop spilled on the table. But the cup did not tip over. "I did it!" said Louis.

Mom smiled at him. Louis took a big bite of his toast. "Yummy," he said. "Can I do it again tomorrow?"

Aiden was at Grandma's house. Snow was falling outside. He wanted to play in it fast!

Grandma gave him his red coat. Aiden pushed one arm in. Then he wiggled and wiggled. He could not find the other sleeve. The coat fell down. "Oh no!" said Aiden.

Just then his friend Amal came to the door. Amal had her coat on already. "Watch this," she said. She laid her coat on the floor. She put her arms in the sleeves. Then she flipped it over her head. The coat was on!

Aiden laid his coat on the floor. He put his arms in the sleeves. He flipped it over his head. The coat was on him! He pulled the zipper up, up, up. It went zzzzzip!

"I did it!" said Aiden. "We can go far in the snow!" said Amal. Grandma waved from the window. Aiden ran out the door into the white, white snow.

Willow went to the park today. Yesterday it rained, so she could not come. The grass was still wet and shiny.

Willow saw the big yellow swing. She wanted to ride on it. But Ava was on it now. Willow asked, "Can I have a turn?"

"Soon," said Ava. Willow frowned. "What does soon mean?"

Ms. Nowak was sitting on a bench nearby. "Soon means in a little while," she said. Willow sat on the wood chips to wait. She counted the birds. One, two, three.

Ava pumped her legs. The swing went up and down. Then Ava jumped off. "Your turn now!" she said.

Willow ran fast. She climbed on and rode the swing. Her hair flew in the wind. She touched the sky with her toes.

Then Khadijah came by with a little carton of milk. She sat down on the wood chips. "I want a turn too," she said.

"You can have it soon," said Willow. Ava pushed the swing soft and slow. Khadijah watched the swing go up. Willow counted to three again.

Then Willow jumped down. "Now it is your turn," she said.

Khadijah clapped her hands and ran to the swing.

Harrison ran to the pretend kitchen at the playground. Belle was already there. "I am cooking soup," she said. She stirred a pot full of red and yellow leaves. Harrison picked up a tiny cup. He poured pretend tea. The cup felt bumpy in his hands. The leaves smelled like dirt and rain.

Then it was time to go home. Ms. Wanjiru rang the bell. Harrison started to run. But Belle stopped. She put the leaves back in the pot. She set the cups in the middle of the little shelf. "We have to clean up," she said. "When pretend play is finished, the toys get put away." Harrison looked at the messy kitchen. So that was the rule!

Harrison picked up the spoon. He put it in the pot. He set the little plates in a neat row. The kitchen looked new again. Would Ms. Wanjiru see it? She smiled and clapped her hands. "What a tidy kitchen," she said. Harrison hugged his pretend pot. "Bye bye, kitchen," he whispered. "See you tomorrow."

Lennon sat at the big table. Her fries were hot and salty. Lisa sat next to her. Penelope sat across. On the wall was a huge screen. A soccer game was on.

"Look at the blue team run!" said Lennon. "They run so fast. They run the most."

The blue team ran and ran. But the ball went in the other net. The red team jumped up high.

Lennon frowned. She pointed at the screen. "Wait. The red team did not run much."

"That is the score," said Lisa. She pointed to the numbers.

Lennon looked. Red had two goals. Blue had zero. The wind blew a plastic napkin off the table and Lennon caught it, giggling.

Then red scored one more. The whistle blew. The game was over.

"Red wins!" said Penelope. "They have more points at the end!"

Lennon clapped her salty hands. "So running fast is not the game. Points are the game!"

She ate another fry and waved at the screen. "Goodbye, blue team. Practice your kicks!"

Elias ran out to the school yard. It had rained all morning. Now the sun made the puddles shine like little blue mirrors. A big puddle sat by the gate. A small puddle sat by the wall. Elias stomped right into the big one. Splash! Cold water went into his shoe. His sock was wet. Very wet.

"Wet and dry are opposites," said Mr. Grant. "Come with me." Elias walked slow through the hall. Squish, squish, squish. Mr. Grant found a dry pair of socks in the big box. Elias pulled off the wet sock. He blew on his cold toes to warm them up. Then he put on the dry sock. It felt soft and warm. Then came a surprise. The lamp on the shelf blinked on. The lamp had a plug on a timer, and it buzzed a little. "What made the lamp go on?" Elias asked. Mr. Grant smiled. "Something inside," he said. Elias sat under the warm lamp until his other shoe dried.

Mackenzie woke up in the tent. "Toast time!" she shouted. At the campsite table, her dad set down warm bread. Mackenzie took the butter knife. She spread and spread. The butter got stuck in one lump. She tried again, slow and small. One, two, three little strokes. Now the butter covered the whole slice!

Next came the milk. Mackenzie wanted to pour it all by herself. She tipped the cup high. Milk went glug, glug, glug, right up to the very top. She grabbed the cup with both hands. She took one step. The milk wobbled. Then the milk spilled all over the table. "Oh no," said Mackenzie.

She got a towel and wiped it up. Then she tried again. This time she poured and stopped before the cup was full to the top. She left some room. Mackenzie picked up the cup. One step, two steps, three steps. The milk stayed in! "I did it!" she said. Kaysen clapped from his seat. Mackenzie took a big drink and smiled. "More milk, please," she said.

Theo went to the store with Dad. Today they needed apples and bread. Yesterday the bread was all gone. Tomorrow they would have toast.

Theo wanted to roll the cart. "Can I push it now?" he asked. "Later," said Dad. "First we get the apples." Theo looked up. There was a big clock on the wall. It had hands and numbers.

"When is later?" Theo asked. Dad pointed at the clock. "The clock shows what time it is," he said. "When the big hand moves to the top, we will go home." Theo watched the hand. It ticked and ticked. Then it reached the top. "Now it is time!" he said. Dad smiled. "Yes. You watched the clock with your own eye." They rolled the cart to the door. "Can we come back tomorrow?" Theo asked. "Tomorrow," said Dad, "we will get jam."

Grayson woke up and looked out the window. The snow was loud on the glass. "Mom, come see!" he called.

It was a snow day. No school today. Grayson wanted to build a snowman. He ran to the door in his pajamas. He opened it fast. The cold air came in. His fingers got cold right away. "Brrr," said Grayson. He ran back inside.

Mom helped him get dressed. He put on warm boots. He put on a big warm coat. Mom found his hat. "Where are your mittens?" she asked. Grayson looked and looked. He could not find them. He almost forgot all about his snowman.

There they were, under the chicken puzzle. Grayson pulled them out. "My mittens!" he said. Mom helped him put them on.

Grayson went outside. His boots went crunch, crunch. His fingers were warm in the mittens. He patted snow onto a big ball. He patted more and more. Soon his snowman stood up tall.

Grayson put his hat on the snowman's head. The snowman wore a hat, just like him. "Goodbye, snowman," said Grayson. He waved his mitten hand all the way to the door.

Aria looked out the window. The sky was white and the snow fell down. "It is a snowy day," said Aria. She put on her boots. She put on her red coat. She ran outside to play.

The snow was soft and bumpy in spots. Aria made a snowball with her bare hands. The snowball was round like a triangle was not. She laughed and threw it at a post.

Then her hands felt cold. Very cold. Her fingers hurt a little. Aria ran back inside. "My hands are cold," she said. Her mom got her mittens. They were blue with white stars.

Aria put the mittens on. She went back out. She made another snowball. Her hands stayed warm this time. The wind blew, but her mittens kept her hands cozy. Aria made one snowball, then two, then three. "Snowball mountain," she said. She stacked them up tall. Then she gave the top one a little nose made of snow. "Hello, snow friend," said Aria.

Zayn stood in the garage with his dad. It was cold outside. Snow was on the ground near the big door.

Zayn had a new coat. He wanted to put it on all by himself. He pushed his arms in. One arm went in. The other arm went in too. Now for the zipper. He pulled it up, up, up. It stuck halfway. His dad waited quietly. Zayn pulled again. Zip! It went all the way to the top.

"I did it!" said Zayn.

Then he saw his mittens on the floor. He had dropped one. He picked it up. Where could it go? He found a little pocket on his coat. He tucked both mittens inside. The pocket held them tight.

"Ready to meet Beckett at the lake?" his dad asked.

"Yes!" said Zayn. He patted his furry mittens in the pocket. Then he held his dad's hand and walked out into the snow.

Zachary stood at the front door. He put on his red hat. The trees outside were bending. The leaves flew all around. "It is windy," said his mom. Zachary stepped outside. The wind pushed his hair. Then the wind blew his hat right off his head.

The hat rolled across the grass. Zachary ran after it. "Come back, hat!" he called. His friend Danika was walking by. "I will help you," she said. She ran too. The hat flew high. Then it landed in a bush. Zachary grabbed it. He held it tight.

He ran back to the door. His dad gave him a clip. The clip held the hat to his coat. Zachary jumped in the wind again. The hat stayed on his head. He laughed. Zachary felt tired from running. "That was fun," said Danika. Zachary smiled and waved. "See you tomorrow!"

Zoe went to the library with her dad. Today was Saturday. She found a book about a plane. The plane was big and red. "I want to read this now," said Zoe.

Brock was there too. He had a toy plane in his hand. "Come to my house and play," said Brock. "We can zoom our planes together."

"I want to go now," said Zoe. Her dad knelt down beside her. "Today we go home after the library," he said. "You slept last night, and that was yesterday. Tonight you will sleep again. Tomorrow is the day after today. Tomorrow you can go to Brock's house."

Zoe made a sad face. "Tomorrow feels far away," she said. Brock smiled. "I will draw you a picture," he said. He drew a red plane with a cute round nose.

That night, Zoe slept in her cozy bed. When she woke up, the sun was bright. "Is it tomorrow now?" she asked. Her dad laughed. "Yes. It is today, and today is Brock day."

At Brock's house, the two planes zoomed across the rug. Then Zoe heard a pop. A little bubble had popped right out of Brock's toy plane. A tiny puppy was hiding inside the box. "A surprise!" said Zoe. The puppy licked her hand, and she giggled. "Tomorrow was worth the wait," said Zoe, and she zoomed her red plane up, up, up.

Scarlett sat on the red mat at school. She had big news. Her cat had kittens last night. One kitten ripped a hole in the paper bag. It drank milk from a little bowl. So yummy, the kitten purred.

Ms. Wong was talking. "Today we will paint," she said. Scarlett jumped up. "My cat!" she called. Ms. Wong kept talking. Liyana could not hear. Avyaan put his hand over his ear.

Scarlett sat back down. She put her hands in her lap. She looked at Ms. Wong. She waited. Her toes wiggled. Her tummy felt buzzy. She waited some more.

At last Ms. Wong stopped. "Now it is your turn, Scarlett." Scarlett took a big breath. "My cat has kittens!" Liyana clapped. Avyaan smiled.

"Tell us more," said Ms. Wong. And Scarlett did.

Jasmine sat in her car seat. The sun was bright outside. "Sunny day!" said Jasmine. Her dad nodded. "Yes, it is sunny," he said.

They were going to the park. Jasmine wanted to run and play. But first, dad stopped the car. He opened the door. "Wait," he said. "Sunscreen first." Jasmine wiggled her toes. "Why?" she asked. Dad said, "Sunscreen helps protect your skin from sunburn." He rubbed the white cream on her arms. It smelled like summer.

Then the wind blew. "Windy!" said Jasmine. Her hat flew off her head. "I will fetch it," said dad. He ran and got the hat. He put it back on her head. The wind could not take it now.

At the park, Jasmine found a big tree. Its root stuck out of the ground. She sat on the root and ate a snack. Her apple was sweet, not sour. Then rain began to fall. "Rainy!" said Jasmine. Dad held up a big umbrella. They sat under it together. Jasmine watched the rain drip, drip, drip off the edge.

No sunburn, no wet clothes. Dad said, "Ready to go home?" Jasmine held his hand. "Yes," she said. "The sun will come back tomorrow."

Declan ran to the playground. He wanted the red truck. It sat by the sandbox. Axelle had it in her hands.

"Give me the truck!" said Declan. Axelle held it tight. She turned away. Declan frowned. He did not get the truck.

Then Declan heard Winifred speak. "Ms. Pierre, may I have a turn on the swing, please?" Ms. Pierre smiled. "Yes, you may, Winifred." Winifred got the swing.

Declan looked at the square sandbox. He thought hard. He walked back to Axelle. "Can I have the truck, please?" he asked. Axelle smiled at him. "Yes. Here you go." She put the truck in his hands.

"Thank you," said Declan. He pushed the truck in the sand. Later, Axelle bumped his arm. "Sorry," she said. "It's okay," said Declan. He made room for her in the sand. They took turns with the truck, one kind push at a time.

Norah put on her sparkly shoes. Today was Eid. The community hall had balloons and a big banner.

Mom held her hand at the door. "Say Eid Mubarak," Mom said. Norah tried the words in a small voice. "Eid Mubarak." Her aunt hugged her. Everyone smiled.

Inside, Norah saw her friends. Camelia was drawing a bee on paper. Fern was helping Ms. Chaudhry set out plates. Norah whispered to Fern, "Watch this." She walked to the door. An uncle came in. "Eid Mubarak!" Norah said, big and loud. "Eid Mubarak!" the uncle said back. He gave her a sweet.

Norah tried it again and again. Say the words, get a smile. Say the words, get a hug. Camelia tried it too. Then Fern tried it. "Eid Mubarak!" they said together.

At snack time, Norah took one cookie. There was a bowl of something green. She took a tiny bite. Yucky! She put it down and drank her water instead. Ms. Chaudhry laughed kindly and gave her a plain cracker.

Before they left, Dad read a card out loud. Everyone clapped. Norah waved at the door. "Eid Mubarak!" she called one more time. The whole hall called it back to her.

Edouard stood by the bathroom sink. He wanted to see his whole face up close. His dad lifted him up. Edouard leaned over the sink and looked in the big mirror. He saw his eyes, his ears, his nose, his mouth. He touched the cold tap with one finger. He heard water drip, drip, drip.

Then Edouard looked at his nose. "What are these little holes?" he asked. His dad said, "They are called nostrils. Your nose has two openings."

Edouard counted them. "One, two," he said. His nose had two nostrils. He breathed in. He could smell the soap. He stuck out his tongue. He could taste a little soap. "Yuck," he said, and laughed.

A small string from his towel was on the sink. Edouard watched it crawl toward the drain as water ran past. "Where is it going?" he asked. "Down the drain," said his dad. Edouard waved at his face in the mirror. The face in the mirror waved back with wild, wet hands. "Hello, Edouard," he said.

The lights went out. The whole house went dark. Jacob and his dad went out to the backyard. It was getting dark there too.

Dad put three candles on the picnic table. He struck a match and lit them. Jacob watched the little flames. They made soft yellow light.

"I want to take a candle to my room," said Jacob. He reached for one.

"Not this time," said Dad. "Only a grown-up lights candles. Only a grown-up looks after them." Dad gave Jacob a flashlight instead. Jacob pressed the button. The beam was big and bright. He shone it on the grass and on the fence.

Dad set a bucket of water on the table. "This stays near the candles," he said. Jacob looked into the bucket. A small snail sat on the rim. Its shell was shiny. Jacob touched it very gently. "Slimy," he said, and laughed.

A voice came from the next yard. It was Mr. Bennett. "Are you okay over there?" he called.

"We have candles and a flashlight," said Jacob.

"Good for you," said Mr. Bennett.

Jacob shone the flashlight at the sky. Then he moved it slowly on the grass, making a long white circle. The lights came back on in the house. The windows glowed warm and yellow.

Jacob turned off the flashlight. He put it in his pocket, just in case. Then he picked up the snail's leaf and set it near the flowers, away from the table.

"You finish the candle time," Jacob told Dad. "I will keep the snail safe."

James woke up and saw white everywhere. "Snow day!" said Dad. James ran to the window. The backyard was all white and soft. Dad put James's plastic sled by the door.

James wanted to sled right away. He lay down on the sled. He put his head at the front. Dad shook his head. "Not head first," said Dad. "Sit up and face the front. Hold on here." Dad helped James sit up. Dad stood and watched.

James held the rope. Dad gave one little push. The sled slid down the small hill. It did work! James sat up tall the whole way. "Again!" he said. Dad laughed and watched again. A lazy cat sat in the snow and blinked at them. James slid past the cat, sitting up, facing the front, all the way to the fence.

Ibrahim wanted the big red book. It was about a bear. He saw it on the shelf yesterday. The cover showed a bear in sunny yellow boots.

Today the book was not there. Many books sat on the shelf. Some were blue. Some were green. Ibrahim pulled one out. He opened the front cover. He peeked at the pages. No bear. He put it back.

Everleigh came to help. "Which book do you want?" she asked. "The bear one," said Ibrahim. "The big red one." Everleigh looked at the shelf. She could not find it either.

Mr. Okonkwo walked over. "The bear book has a name," he said. "It is called Sleepy Bear." Ibrahim looked at him. A book had a name? He wanted to see. Mr. Okonkwo pointed to a book. "The name is here, on the front," he said.

They went to the library desk together. "May we have Sleepy Bear, please?" asked Mr. Okonkwo. The teacher behind the desk smiled. She held up the big red book. The bear on the cover had sunny yellow boots. "These words say Sleepy Bear," she said. Ibrahim traced the letters with his finger. Then he hugged the book to his chest. "Found you, Sleepy Bear," he whispered.

Evelyn sat in her car seat. "Are we there yet?" she asked. "Almost," said Dad. "Are we there yet?" she asked again. Then the car stopped. They were at the park.

Evelyn saw a boy with a red balloon. The balloon began to float away. Evelyn ran to him. She grabbed the string just in time. Her hands were sticky from her snack, so the string stuck tight.

"Gracias," said the boy. His name was Amari.

"Grassy ass?" said Evelyn.

"Gracias," Amari said again. "It means thank you. It is Spanish."

Evelyn smiled big. "Gracias," she said. "That means thank you too!"

"Can we pet your dog?" Evelyn asked. "Please?" A fluffy dog sat by Amari's feet.

"Yes!" said Amari. "Thank you for my balloon."

"You're welcome," said Evelyn. Then she patted the dog, soft as a cloud.

Andrew was painting a dragon at daycare. The dragon needed green grass to sit on. But the green paint pot was empty. Andrew showed the pot to his friend Agathe. "No green left," she said.

Andrew looked at his cups. He had blue paint and yellow paint. He poured some blue into a big cup. Then he poured some yellow in too. He stirred it with his brush. The paint turned green! Andrew gasped. "It's green now!"

Mr. Hassan came to look. "Perfect green for your dragon," he said. Andrew painted tall grass all around. He gave the dragon a furry green belly too. Then Edgar asked for green for his frog. Andrew mixed blue and yellow again. "Here you go," he said. "More magic green, coming right up."

Muhammad went to the playground with his dad. He marched straight to the slide. Then he saw a little door low on the wall. It looked funny, like a tiny face with two round eyes.

"What is that?" Muhammad asked.

His dad crouched down. "That is an outlet," he said. "Never put fingers or things into it. Fingers do not go in there."

Muhammad looked at his own small fingers. He hid them behind his back. Just then, the juice machine went quiet. No juice came out.

Ms. Huang, the playground teacher, came over. She had a plug in her hand. "The plug fell out," she said. Muhammad watched her push the plug into the outlet. Click! The machine hummed again. Juice poured into her cup.

The plug went in. The machine turned on. Muhammad clapped his hands.

"More juice, please," he said. He kept his fingers far, far away.

Mila found a big red book at school. She opened it from the front. She turned page after page. On each page was a yellow bee flying over flowers.

"Who made this bee?" Mila asked. She wanted to know. She turned back to the front of the book. She looked. She looked again.

Mr. Mensah came to help. He was careful with the old pages. "The name is here," he said. He pointed to small black words. "These words say who drew the pictures. That person is called an illustrator."

Mila touched the small words. The words had a name in them. "The illustrator drew my bee!" she said.

Then she ran to Hubert. "Come see," she said. They sat down together. Hubert opened the book from the front. Mila stacked two more books beside them.

"Turn the page slowly," said Mila. "Be careful with the bee."

Grandma was coming to stay for a week. Luka wanted to give her the guest bedroom. But the bed was covered with his toy cars. "Too many cars," said Luka. "Grandma needs room to sleep."

He moved the cars one by one. He put them in a deep basket by the door. Now the bed was clear. He put a soft pillow at the top. He put his teddy bear in the corner. Then his mom came in.

"Is Grandma your mom?" Luka asked. "Yes," said Mom. "Grandma is my mom!" Luka laughed. "So Grandma is a mom to you," he said. "And a grandma to me!" He counted on his fingers. "One, two. Two jobs for one Grandma!"

The doorbell rang. Grandma hugged Luka tight. He showed her the room. "Look, no cars on your bed!" he said. "I moved them all by myself." Grandma picked up the teddy bear. "Does this bear need a number too?" she asked with a smile. "Every car has a number. The bear can be car number one," said Luka.

Gabriel sat in his car seat. The car went fast on the big road. Then it went slow on the small street. Outside, the weather was cold and snowy. Gabriel rubbed his hands. The heater blew warm air on him.

"I am cold," said his friend Edgar. Edgar sat in the seat next to him. Their dad was driving them to school. Gabriel's dad reached back with a scarf. "Here you go," he said. Gabriel had his own scarf in his bag. He pulled it out.

The two boys put on their scarves. Gabriel's scarf went around his neck once. It still hung down to his knees. Edgar's scarf went around twice. It stopped at his chin. "Yours is long," said Edgar. "Yours is short," said Gabriel. "Long and short are opposites," said Edgar. Gabriel laughed. He stood his scarf up like a tall snake. Then he squished it down small.

"Let's share," said Gabriel. He wrapped his long scarf around Edgar too. Now both boys were warm. The car stopped at school. "Race you to the door," said Edgar. "Slow like turtles!" said Gabriel. They walked slowly together, all wrapped up.

Eliana was at team practice. Mr. Traoré put out one big red ball. "One ball for all of us," he said.

Onyx held the ball first. He hugged it tight. Eliana wanted the ball so much. She ran over and grabbed it out of his hands.

Onyx's face went red. His eyes got watery. He sat down on the grass and started to cry. "My ball," he said. "I had it first."

Eliana looked at Onyx. She looked at the ball. Grabbing the ball made Onyx cry. She did not want that. She walked back to him slowly. "Here, Onyx," she said. "You can have it."

Onyx wiped his eyes. "Do you want a turn?" he asked.

"Yes, please," said Eliana.

"Okay. You can have it after me." Onyx kicked the ball to Rory. Rory kicked it back. Then Onyx rolled the ball right to Eliana. "Your turn," he said.

Eliana kicked the ball high. "That was nice of you, Onyx!" she said.

After practice, they sat on the bench. Eliana had a sandwich in her bag. She could smell the cheese. She broke it in two pieces. "Half for you," she said to Onyx.

Onyx smiled. "We take turns," he said. "Turns are fun."

Noah was at Grandma's house. It was his birthday. The soft brown cat slept by the door. Grandma carried in a big cake.

Noah counted the candles. "One, two, three, four," he said. He counted again. One, two, three, four. His friend Bryson came to look. "I am five today," said Noah. "But there are only four candles."

Mom stopped and looked at the cake. She smiled. She took a little candle from the drawer. She put it in the middle. "One candle for each year," she said. "You are five. Now you get five."

Noah counted one more time. "One, two, three, four, five!" He counted the candles at Grandma's house, at the table, on the cake. Dad lit the candles with a match. Noah did not touch. He just watched the flames.

The cat woke up and stretched. Bryson sang the birthday song. Noah blew out his five candles, one, two, three, four, five. "Happy birthday, Noah!" said Grandma.

Aubrey went to the big church with her family. There was a Christmas party inside. In the corner stood a tall green tree. "Can I help?" Aubrey asked. Her dad smiled and gave her a box of ornaments.

Aubrey hung a red ball on one branch. Then she hung a star there too. Then a little bell. "Why is the branch bending?" she wondered. She watched it dip down low. All the ornaments were on one spot. That was too heavy for the little branch!

So Aubrey moved them. One ornament here, one ornament there. She spread them all over the tree. The branch popped back up. The tree looked round and full. Sun came through the window and made the red ball shine. Aarav ran over. "The tree is so pretty," he said. Aubrey touched a soft squishy ornament and hung it where it would not be missed, high on a fresh green branch. "All done," she said.

Jules stood in the backyard with his red ball. Today his baby sister was coming home. Jules wanted to show her the ball. He wanted to roll it to her. "Babies can't catch," said his dad. "But she can watch me," said Jules. "She will see my wild throw!"

The car pulled up. Dad carried a little basket. Inside was the baby. Jules ran over fast. "Wake up, baby!" he said. "Time to play ball!" But the baby's eyes were closed. She was sleeping again. "New babies sleep for much of the day," said Dad. Jules frowned. "Again? She slept in the car too."

So Jules waited. He stirred the dirt with a stick. He found a small surprise, a round white stone, just like a tiny ball. He put the stone in his pocket. He waited and waited. Then the baby opened her eyes. Jules held up the red ball. The baby looked and looked. Then she made a small smile. "She saw my ball!" said Jules. He put the stone beside her blanket. "This one is yours," he said. "For when you wake up."

Scarlett swept her bedroom floor. She was making a library! Her books sat in a row on the bed. The clock ticked as she worked. Ms. Chan came in with a little card. "Your first library card," she said. It had one loose corner. Scarlett pressed it flat.

"I HAVE A CARD!" Scarlett shouted. Mom looked up from her book. Cole looked up from his book on the rug. Ms. Chan put a finger to her lips. "The library asks for quiet voices so others can read," she whispered. Scarlett whispered too. "Can I take a book home?" she asked. "Yes, with your card," whispered Ms. Chan. Scarlett picked the dinosaur book. "Stomp, stomp," she whispered to it. "Dinosaurs can be quiet too."

Cole lined up for a turn. "Quiet voices," whispered Scarlett. "Quiet voices," whispered Cole. Mom smiled behind her book and turned the page.

Charlie was going on a big trip. The car drove onto a big boat. It was a ferry. The boat went "Honk!" Charlie looked out of the window. He could see water. He could see white waves.

Charlie was so excited. He jumped in the car. He wanted to see the sea gulls. But Dad did not start the car. "Click first," said Dad. "Why?" asked Charlie. "A car seat buckle keeps you safe," said Dad. So Charlie pulled his buckle. He pulled it across his tummy. Click! Dad smiled. Then Dad started the car.

The car had a bit of dirt on the window. Dad gave it a quick wipe with a cloth. "Fixed," said Dad. The ferry began to move. The water splashed. The boat rocked, and Charlie rocked too, safe in his seat. "Look," said Charlie. "The waves make the boat go up and down."

Thomas held his little blue bag. His family was at the airport. The bag had wheels. Thomas made it slide across the shiny floor. Whoosh. It went far, and Thomas laughed.

"Thomas, time to go," said his dad. The big plane sat by the window. Thomas walked slowly. He waited in a long line. The line moved a little, then stopped. Thomas held his bag and waited some more. Waiting was not fun, but it was easy if he watched the planes.

Then the line moved again. The door opened. Cool air blew on Thomas's face. The plane was big and white. Thomas found his seat by the window. He looked out at the clouds for a long, long time.

After the trip, the family got home. Thomas's mom said, "Now we unpack." She opened the big bag. Thomas opened his blue bag too. He pulled out his shirt. He pulled out his socks. He put them away in his drawer, one by one. Then he shook his shoes. Sand fell out on the floor. "Beach sand!" said Thomas. He poked the little pile with his finger. "It came home with me."

Austin went with Grandpa to the phone repair shop. The shop had little phones in glass boxes. A phone began to ring on the counter. Austin laughed at the funny sound.

Ms. Chanthavong worked at the shop. She had a big gray tablet. Austin wanted to draw on it. But the tablet was dark and still. "It needs power," said Ms. Chanthavong. She held up a charger. Austin picked up the charger. It was a squishy little box at the end. He carried it to Grandpa. A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall, so Grandpa did that part. Austin watched the cord go into the wall. Then the screen lit up bright.

Ms. Chanthavong touched the button. The tablet turned on. Austin tapped one time. The drawing app opened. He drew a red circle and a blue line. His finger made the colors appear.

Then the tablet made a soft sound. The picture was done. "Time to put it away," said Ms. Chanthavong. Austin pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He helped put the tablet on the shelf. "Bye, circle," said Austin. Grandpa took his hand.

Florence sat in a big chair at the doctor's office. She wanted the bear sticker on the desk. But first, the doctor had to check her.

"Look here," said the doctor. Florence used her eyes to see a little picture of a duck. "Now listen." Florence used her ears to hear a soft beep. "Sniff this." Florence used her nose to smell soap. "Touch my hand." Florence used her fingers to touch the doctor's warm hand.

"Last one," said the doctor. He held out a small lemon slice. Florence thought it would taste sweet like her orange juice. She took a little lick. Her whole face scrunched up!

"It's sour!" said Florence. The doctor laughed and laughed.

Then Florence got her sticker. She held it tight so it would not fall. "Safe in my hand," she said.

Jack wanted his soft pig. The pig was small and it sat up on his bed. Jack was at the bottom of the stairs.

"Too high," said Jack. "My pig is way up there."

Mom held his hand. "You can try," she said. "One step at a time."

Jack went up, up, up. His legs felt slow and tired. At the top, he grabbed the soft pig. It was not big, but it felt big in his arms.

"Now we go down," said Mom.

Jack went down, down, down. The steps went fast. His feet found the floor. The pig was safe and warm next to him.

"Up and down," said Mom. "They are opposites."

Jack laughed and did it again. Up, up, up to get his pig. Down, down, down to his mom.

He held the soft pig close. "Opposites," said Jack. "Again, please!"

Felix sat at the little red table. He had a big pencil in his hand. He wanted to write his name on his paper.

"Hold it like this," said Ms. Delgado. She showed him. "Pinch it near the tip."

Felix pinched the pencil. His hand felt hard and tight at first. He wrote a wobbly F. Then E. Then L. Then I. Then X.

"Five letters," said Rhea next to him. "F, E, L, I, X. That's a lot!"

The next day, Felix wrote his name again. F, E, L, I, X. The X looked like two sticks kissing.

"Mine looks like a spider fell in the ink," said Melissa. Everyone laughed.

Every day Felix wrote his name. One, two, three, four, five letters. The F stood up straight. The E got straight lines.

At dinner he told his dad, "I can write Felix!"

The next morning he touched his pencil to the paper. He wrote his name all by himself.

"Look, Ms. Delgado!"

"Now that," she said, "is a fine, fine Felix."

Zoe stood in the kitchen. Dad had made warm toast. Zoe wanted to do it herself.

First Zoe spread the butter. The knife slid across the toast. "Look, Dad! The butter goes soft!" She made it cover all the toast.

Then Zoe picked up the big milk carton. It was too heavy. Milk sloshed near the edge of the cup. Dad held her hands steady. "Let's try something," he said. He poured some milk into a little jug.

Zoe held the little jug. It was light. She tipped it, and the milk went into the cup. Not one drop spilled.

"Is the little jug easy for me?" Zoe asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Small hands like small jugs."

Zoe drank her milk and ate her toast. "I did it all by myself!"

Zayn stood in the kitchen. He wanted a snack before Gracelyn came over.

Mom got out two pots. One pot was big. One pot was small. "Can I help?" Zayn asked.

"You can put the big apple in the small bowl," said Mom. Zayn tried. The apple did not fit. It rolled away fast, fast, fast. Zayn chased it slow, slow, slow.

He picked up the apple. He put it in the big bowl instead. It fit! "Big bowl, big apple," said Zayn.

Then the doorbell rang. It was Gracelyn. She ran inside the house. "Let's play a game," she said. "I say a word. You shout the opposite!"

"Opposites are two words as different as can be, like big and small," said Gracelyn.

"Big!" she shouted. "Small!" said Zayn.

"Hot!" said Gracelyn. She pointed at the stove. The grown-ups were cooking there. "Cold!" said Zayn. He touched the cold milk cup.

"Fast!" said Gracelyn. "Slow!" said Zayn, walking like a turtle.

"I lost the next word," said Gracelyn. "Oh wait. Found it. Up!"

"Down!" said Zayn. Then he sat down and ate his apple slices.

Mom helped Gracelyn close the fridge door. "One more?" said Gracelyn. "Night!"

"Day!" said Zayn, and he waved his apple slice like the sun.

Beau put on his red shirt. It was a hot day on the soccer field. His team ran and kicked the ball. Beau liked playing with Gregoire and Zyon.

Beau kicked the ball into the net. But a man blew his whistle. Beau did not get the point. He stomped his foot. "Why?" he asked. The coach knelt down beside him. "That man is the referee," the coach said. "The referee makes sure players follow the rules." Beau looked at the referee. The referee showed where Beau had kicked from. It was the wrong spot.

Beau ran back to the right spot. He waited for the whistle. Then he kicked the ball again. It went in! Beau jumped up like a spring. His shoes seemed to sink into the soft grass as he landed. Gregoire clapped for him. Zyon clapped too. The referee smiled and gave a thumbs up.

Lucy ran to the playground. There was a big new puddle under the swing. Mohammad was jumping in it. Splash, splash! Lucy wanted to jump too.

But first she had news. Ms. Njoroge was talking to a dad by the slide. Lucy pulled her sleeve. "Ms. Njoroge! Look at my new boots!" Ms. Njoroge kept talking to the dad. Lucy pulled again. "Look! Look!" Still no answer. Lucy waited. She looked at her boots. Then Ms. Njoroge stopped talking. There was a quiet little pause. Lucy spoke in the pause. "I have new boots today." Ms. Njoroge smiled. "What lovely red boots! Thank you for waiting, Lucy."

Lucy said, "Sorry I pulled your sleeve." Then she asked, "Can you help me with my boots? The buckle is stuck." Ms. Njoroge fixed it. "Please can I jump in the puddle now?" said Lucy. "Yes, you may," said Ms. Njoroge. Lucy ran to Mohammad. Splash! The water was cold on her toes. The other kids made a loud happy shout. Lucy laughed and jumped again. At home, her mom said, "Those feet need a bath!" Lucy wiggled her toes in the warm water and told her mom about the big puddle, waiting happily for her mom to finish her own sentence first. "Then Mohammad fell down," said Lucy. "He said sorry to the puddle!"

David needed to wash his hands. The bathroom was quiet. He was not alone. His dad stood by the sink.

David saw a little hole in the wall. It was near the tub. It had two small slots. He counted them. One, two.

The wind came in through the window. It made David shiver. "Cold," he said.

"Dad, what is that?" David asked.

"That is an outlet," Dad said.

David reached out one finger. Dad caught his hand softly. "We never put fingers or things into an electrical outlet," Dad said. "Come, tell me when you see one. That is your job."

David nodded. His job felt big.

Dad turned the tap. Steam rose up. "Hot," said Dad. "I will hold your hands under the warm water. Not too hot."

One pump of soap. Two scrubs. Three rinses.

"All clean," said David, and he smiled at his hands.

Clara stood by the big window at daycare. She wanted to see the sun. "Where is the sun?" she asked. Ms. Ramírez said, "Look up at the sky." Clara looked up. The sky was full of gray clouds. The clouds were hiding the sun. Clara made a grumpy face. Stanley came to look too. "The sun is playing hide and seek," he said. So they waited. One cloud, two clouds, three clouds. They named the clouds. "That one looks like a hat," said Clara. "That one looks like a sock," said Stanley. Then the wind blew. The clouds moved slowly, slowly away. The sun came out! It was sunny now. Ms. Ramírez smiled. "Time for hats and sun cream," she said. Clara put on her yellow hat. She felt like she could win a race in the sun. "Hello, sun!" she called. The sun shone on her face, warm and bright.

Levi wanted to ride his bike in the yard. He ran to the door. His dad called, "Levi, wait." Levi stopped and looked back.

"Where is your helmet?" his dad asked. Levi patted his head. His hair was soft and bare. He ran back to the porch. His helmet sat on the step. It was blue with a white stripe, straight and shiny. He put it on. Dad helped snap the strap. It clicked under his chin.

Then Levi rode his bike on the grass. The wheels went bump, bump. A big truck drove past the house. Levi stayed near Dad the whole time. After the ride, Levi washed his hands. Dad filled the sink. The water was warm, not hot. Levi dropped in his little boat. It did float! Levi laughed and pushed it gently across the water.

"Again," said Levi, and he sailed the boat back.

Luca had been sick with a cold. Today he got to go back to the doctor's office. Ms. Vargas, the nurse, looked in his ears. "All better," she said with a big smile. Luca hopped down from the big chair.

At home, Luca sat on his pillow. His nose felt funny. He blew his nose into a tissue. Then he saw crackers on the table. He reached out his hand.

Then he stopped. He remembered Ms. Vargas washing her hands. Luca went to the sink. He used soap and water. He rubbed and rubbed. The bubbles felt warm.

Then he ate his crackers. His dad gave him a thumbs up. "Look," said Luca, holding up his clean hands. "Soap and water!"

Arthur sat in the playroom with a big box of blocks. His friend Alina came to play too. "Let's sort them," said Alina. She put all the red blocks in one pile. She put all the green blocks in another pile. Arthur tipped the box. Some blocks began to spill out. "Oh no," said Arthur. "Don't worry," said Mr. Demir, who was sitting nearby. "We can pick them up together."

Arthur picked up the blocks. Then he looked at the piles. He had an idea. "Can I sort them my way?" he asked. "Yes, you can," said Alina. Arthur put the big blocks in one pile. He put the small blocks in another pile. The same blocks, but in new piles! "Why do they look different?" Arthur asked. "Because this time I sorted by size, not by color," he said.

Then Alina clapped her hands. Under the blocks was a small paper map. It showed where a toy animal was hiding. Arthur and Alina followed the map to the toy box. There was a little green frog toy waiting. Arthur hugged the frog. "Sorting is fun," he said. Mr. Demir smiled. "Frog says ribbit," said Arthur, and he made the frog jump onto the big pile of blocks.

Lincoln put on his swim shorts. They were tight at first. Then he pulled and pulled. Now they fit just right. "Are we going to the pool?" he asked. "Yes," said his dad. "The pool at the community center."

At the pool, Lincoln saw his friend Calum. Calum started to run to the water. Then Calum's feet slid out. He landed on his bottom. Splash, right on the wet floor. Mr. Rao came over fast. "The floor is wet and slippery," said Mr. Rao. "We walk, not run." Calum stood up slowly. He nodded.

Lincoln looked down at his feet. The floor was shiny and wet. So that was it. Wet floor, then a slide. He tried one little step. Then one more. No sliding. "I walk, I walk," he said. He said it like a song.

Lincoln got in the water at the steps. He held the rail tight. He practiced kicking. One kick, two kicks, three kicks. Calum practiced too. They counted together. "One, two, three. One, two, three."

When it was time to go, Mr. Rao helped them out. The floor was still wet. So Lincoln walked, slow and steady, step by step. "Look at me, Calum," he said. "I did not slide at all." Calum walked beside him. Their feet went pat, pat, pat all the way to the towels.

Michael was going to the dentist. It would be his first time. "What will the dentist do?" he asked his mom. "The dentist will look at your teeth," she said.

So Michael practiced at home. He stood by the big mirror. He opened his mouth. Then he wanted to talk, and his mouth went shut. The mirror showed no teeth at all. He tried again. He opened his mouth wide. His mouth went shut again when he said "hello" to the mirror.

His mom had an idea. "Point to a picture of a lion," she said. Michael pointed to the lion in his book. The lion had its mouth open wide for a big roar. Michael tried the roar. "Roooar!" His mouth stayed open. He could see every tooth in the mirror. One open mouth made every tooth show up. "Cool," said Michael.

At the dentist, a kind man looked into Michael's mouth. Michael did not talk. He opened his mouth wide, like a lion. Every tooth was easy to see. "Roooar," said Michael, very quietly, with his mouth still open.

Noah sat at the big table in the library. His friend Mateo sat next to him. Mr. Johansson put out paper and fat pencils.

"I want to write my name," said Noah. He held the pencil tight. He made a small n. Then o, a, h. He looked at his paper. "noah," it said.

Mateo held up his paper. It said "Mateo" with a big M at the start. Noah looked again. His tummy felt funny. "Mine looks wrong," he said.

Mr. Johansson smiled. "Watch this," he said. He took a new paper. He wrote "Noah" with a big N at the start. "A name gets a big letter at the start," he said.

Noah grabbed his pencil. The pencil almost did slip out of his hand. He held it again. He made a big N. It was rough and wobbly, but it was big. Then o, a, h. "Noah!" he read out loud.

The big clock on the wall went tick tock. Noah wrote his name again. Big N, o, a, h. "Now it matches Mateo's," he said. Mateo clapped. Noah slid the paper across the table to show him.

Michael wanted a warm bath. His dad turned the tap. The water poured into the tub. White steam floated up. It looked like tiny clouds.

"Can I touch the steam?" Michael asked. He stepped close to the tub.

His dad held out a hand. "Stay back, Michael. Steam is hot. It can burn you." Michael stopped his feet. He took one big step back.

From far away, Michael watched the steam. It rose up and up. Then it went away into the air. He blew at it. The steam moved a little. He clapped his hands. The steam did not clap back.

His dad put his own hand near the steam. "Hot," he said. Then he held Michael's hand under the cold tap. "This is cold." The cold water felt like winter on his fingers.

The tub filled up slow. The steam got smaller and smaller. Soon it was all gone. His dad felt the water with his elbow. "Just right now," he said.

Michael put one toe in the water. It was warm like a blanket. He slid in and made a splash. "The steam went away," he said. "Where did it go?"

His dad smiled and pointed up. "It flies up high, past the ceiling." Michael looked up. He waved at the ceiling.

Maverick ran into the kitchen at Grandma's house. The room smelled like soup. Grandma was stirring the big pot. Grandpa carried the bread to the table.

"Sit down, Maverick," said Grandma. "First we say our word."

Maverick sat. But he did not know the word. He felt his face go hot. What if he said it wrong?

Grandpa clapped his hands. "Bon appétit!" he said.

Maverick's mouth popped open. "What is that?"

Grandma laughed. "It is what people in France say before a meal. It means we wish everyone a good meal."

Maverick took a big breath. "Bon... appétit!" he said. Grandma clapped. Grandpa clapped. Even the soup seemed to bubble louder.

"I said it!" said Maverick. "Bon appétit, soup!"

Grandma poured the soup into his bowl. "And bon appétit to you too," she said, with a wink.

Hudson was at daycare. It was a sunny morning. He wanted to build a big tower with Celeste.

Hudson stacked one block. Then two. Then three. The tower grew tall. "Look, Celeste!" he said. "So tall!"

Then the tower fell down. All the blocks went down. Boom.

Celeste looked at Hudson. Her mouth turned down. Her eyebrows came together. Hudson saw her face. "Celeste, are you sad?" he asked.

"Yes," said Celeste. "The tower fell."

Hudson looked at her face some more. Now her mouth made a little smile. "Are you happy now?" he asked.

"Yes! Let's build it again," said Celeste.

So they tried again. One block. Two blocks. Three blocks. Slow and careful. The tower grew tall again.

Ms. Nowak came over. "Nice work, friends," she said.

Celeste laughed. Hudson laughed too. Then they gave the blocks a big hug, all around the tall tower, so it would feel safe.

"Tomorrow we build it taller," said Celeste.

"Okay," said Hudson. He put the last block on top.

Georgia was awake from her nap. She wanted a snack. Ms. Ahmed had a box of crackers on the shelf.

Georgia could not find the crackers. There were many boxes. She picked one up. It had little words on it. "Ms. Ahmed, what does this say?" she asked.

"That says pasta," said Ms. Ahmed. Georgia put it down. She passed it to James.

Georgia picked up another box. It said crackers. Ms. Ahmed read it out loud. "Crackers," she said. "That is the one you want."

Georgia smiled. The words had told her! She opened the door of the snack cupboard. She took the cracker box to the little table.

James held up a jar. "What does mine say?" he asked.

Ms. Ahmed looked. "Yours says jam," she said.

Georgia passed him a spoon. She pointed at the label. "Jam," she said. "The words say jam."

Hallie clapped her hands. Georgia munched her crackers and looked at the box again.

Elijah ran onto the basketball court. His team wore blue shirts today. Zion wore blue too. Josiah wore blue too.

The game began. Mr. Castillo blew his whistle. Elijah got the ball. He saw a green shirt nearby. He passed the ball to the green shirt. But the green shirt was on the other team! The boy in green ran away with the ball.

Elijah stopped and looked around. He saw Zion waving. Zion wore a blue shirt, just like him. "Here, Elijah! Pass here!" Elijah passed the ball to Zion. Zion caught it and shot. The ball went in the hoop.

The coach clapped. Elijah smiled. He looked down at his own blue shirt. Then he looked at Zion's blue shirt. Same color. Same team.

Later, the ball came to Elijah again. This time he looked for blue. He found Josiah in a blue shirt. He passed. Josiah passed back. Elijah took a short shot. The ball bounced on the rim. Then it dropped in.

After the game, Mr. Castillo gave each player a paper ribbon. Elijah held his up high. Zion held his up high too.

"Blue shirts win," said Josiah, and he laughed.

Elijah laughed too. "Same shirt, same team," he said.

Ayla rode on a big train. She sat by the window with Mama. The train went choo, choo. Ayla held her small bag. Inside was a cookie for later, and her red shoes from the beach.

The train stopped. Then it went again. Ayla watched the trees go by. "We go home now," said Mama. Ayla looked out at the wooden fence by the track. It went fast, fast, fast.

At last they got home. Mama said, "Now we unpack our bags." Ayla unpacked her small bag. She put her pants in the drawer. She put her shirt in the drawer. Then she shook out her red shoes. Sand fell out! Sand from the beach was hiding in her shoe. Ayla laughed and laughed. "Sand came home with me!" she said. Mama gave her the cookie. Ayla sat on the rug and ate it all up, while sand covered her toes like tiny stars.

Liam sat on the couch with a blanket. His nose was red. His cough came back, one, two, three times.

His mom brought him warm soup. Liam took a little sip. It felt good on his throat. Then his nose tickled. A sneeze was coming. It was going to be a big one.

Liam sneezed right into his hand. His hand felt wet. He frowned. "That was bad," he said.

His mom sat down next to him. She lifted her arm and bent it. "Watch me," she said. "I use my elbow." She tapped her elbow. "Elbow, elbow, elbow."

Liam had a question. "My elbow?" he asked. He bent his own arm and tapped. "This part?"

"Yes," said his mom. "Try it now."

Liam practiced. He made a fake cough, one, two, three. He put his elbow over his nose each time. His mom clapped. "You got it!"

Then the tickle came back for real. Liam moved fast. He bent his arm. He sneezed into his elbow.

"My hand stayed clean," said Liam. He held it up to show her.

Mom clapped again. "Good job, Liam."

Liam snuggled back into the blanket. He kept his arm bent and ready. "Elbow, elbow, elbow," he said softly, and took one more sip of soup.

Michael played on a basketball team. It was winter, but the court was warm inside. His friends Lucca and Izabella played too. Mr. Sokolov was the coach.

The ball came to Michael. He tried to shoot. The ball hit the rim. It missed.

Michael's face went hot. He wanted to cover his eyes with his hands. Then he heard a sound.

Lucca clapped. Izabella stomped her feet. "Go, Michael, try again!" they cheered. The whole team clapped too.

Michael looked up. They were smiling at him. The ball came back. He held it with both hands. He bent his knees. He pushed the ball up.

The ball went up, up, up. It went through the net. Swish!

"Yay, Michael!" the team cheered. "Yay, Michael! Yay, Michael!"

Michael ran to his friends. "Next time you miss," he said, "I will cheer for you."

After the game, Dad gave Michael a big orange slice. It was cold and juicy. Michael shared half with Lucca.

"One for you," said Michael. "One for me."

Kinsley loved the library. It felt like a big purple castle full of books. Today she was excited. Story time was about dragons!

Her friend Hoorain ran to get a seat. Then Hoorain tripped. She fell down near the book swing, the little seat that hung by the window. Hoorain's face turned sad. A tear rolled down her cheek.

Kinsley ran over. She bent down low. "Are you okay?" she asked. Hoorain looked up. Her sad face grew soft. "My knee hurts," she said. "But you asked me. That makes me feel better."

Kinsley held her hand. Mr. Demir, the librarian, brought a small ice pack. He placed it on Hoorain's knee. Soon Hoorain smiled again.

Then the dragon story began. The dragon was big and green. He was scared of mice! Hoorain laughed so loud that a shush came from behind the shelves. Kinsley laughed too. She held Hoorain's hand and whispered, "Dragons can be scared, just like us."

Hoorain whispered back, "And friends can be brave, just like us."

Owen sat at the dinner table. His cup was red. He was happy. "Yum, noodles!" he said.

Then he heard a loud noise. BANG! It came from the kitchen. Owen jumped. His tummy felt tight. He was scared. "Too loud," he whispered.

Mom saw his face. "You look scared, Owen." Owen nodded. "Scared of the bang." Mom held his hand. "You can tell me. I will help." They walked to the kitchen together. Mom looked under the sink. A pot had fallen down. Mom picked it up and put it high on the shelf.

"No more bang," said Mom. Owen smiled big. Now he felt excited. "I want to catch the noise next time!" he said. Mom laughed. "You are quick, Owen. But just tell me first. I will always come."

Back at the table, Owen ate his noodles. Then he saw something in his bowl. A little carrot looked just like a worm! Owen giggled. "A worm in my noodles!" Mom smiled. "That is just a carrot, cut long." Owen took a big bite. "I ate the worm!" he said.

Bennett sat in the living room. The big tablet was on the rug. He wanted to draw a rock on it. But first he had to turn it on. Where was the button? He looked and looked. There! A little round button on the side. He pressed it. The screen lit up. The whole thing glowed. "It works," he said.

Now he needed the drawing app. He tapped a red square. No, that was not it. He tapped a blue circle. No. Then he tapped the green paint pot. Yes! A white page came up. He drew a big gray rock. Then he drew a cat sitting on the rock. The cat was orange.

Bennett picked up the tablet with one hand to put it away. It tipped and slid. It almost fell on the rug! He caught it with a squeak. Then he tried again, this time holding it with two hands. It stayed nice and steady, like a book. He carried it to the shelf. He set it down and pressed the button. The screen went dark.

"Is that a little pop sound?" he wondered. He put his ear close to the shelf. Then his dad called, "Bennett, come see this!" On the window, a butterfly was sitting very still. Bennett tiptoed over. The butterfly opened its wings. They were blue, like the sky. "Hello," Bennett whispered.

Jackson sat on the small blue chair. A lamp glowed beside him. In his hands was a recorder from Mr. Zhang's music studio.

"Blow soft and slow," said Mr. Zhang.

Jackson blew. Squeak! The sound was loud and funny. Jackson felt upset. Zach laughed next to him, but then he patted Jackson's arm.

Mr. Zhang bent down. "Look at your thumb," he said. "It slid off the hole."

Jackson looked. His thumb had moved. The hole was half open. He put his thumb back on the hole. He locked it there, flat and tight.

He blew again. A round note came out. Not a squeak. A real note.

Jackson lifted one finger. He blew. A new note came out, higher. He put the finger back down. He blew. The low note returned.

Zach clapped. "Do it again!"

Jackson lifted a different finger. He blew. That hole made a new note too. He tried all the holes, one by one.

Mr. Zhang smiled and turned on the lamp, so Jackson could see his fingers better.

Jackson played a low note, then a high note. Zach tried to copy him.

"Your turn," said Jackson. "Cover the hole all the way."

Addison sat at the dinner table. Her dad put a plate in front of her. "Lemon slices," he said. Addison looked with her eyes. The slices were yellow and shiny. She sniffed with her nose. They smelled like juice, sweet like her morning orange juice.

Addison wanted a sweet taste. She picked up a slice with her fingers. It felt cool and bumpy. She took a little bite with her tongue. Ooh! Her whole face scrunched up. The lemon was sour, not sweet!

"Daddy, it bites my tongue!" she said. Her dad laughed softly. "Lemons are sour," he said. He gave her a glass of water. Addison drank it all up. One, two, three sips. Then her tongue felt better. Her dad sat close by her side. Addison patted the table with her hand. Dinner was warm. The kitchen was cozy. "One more tiny taste?" asked her dad. Addison shook her head. "Water, please!"

Louis wanted his bath. He wanted his yellow fish toy in the bath too.

Dad turned the water on. Louis saw steam go up, up, up. "In now?" asked Louis. He put one foot near the tub.

"Wait," said Dad. Dad put his hand in the water. "Too hot. We must wait." A grown-up checks the water first, so it will not be too hot.

Louis waited. He counted with Dad. "One, two, three." The steam went away. Dad put his hand in again. "Now it is just right."

Louis got in. He held his fish. "Fish says swim, swim, swim," said Louis. Dad smiled and washed his hair.

After the bath, Louis put on his pajamas. They had neat blue stars. Dad tucked him into bed. Louis yawned. "Night night, fish," said Louis. He closed his eyes and went to sleep.

Eva sat on the train with her mama. Her shoes were on tight. Her bag was on her lap. "One bag, one bear, one hat," she said. "And one mama!"

They were going to the sea. Eva looked out the window. A cow stood in a field. The train went fast, and the cow went zoom, backwards. Eva laughed. "The train makes the cow go back!"

At the sea, Eva met a boy named Scott. They dug a big hole. An ant ran over the sand. "Hello, ant," said Eva. The ant tickled her toe.

Then the trip was over. The train took them home. Eva missed the sea. She missed the big hole. She wanted to cry a little.

Mama had an idea. "Let's look at our trip photos." Click, click, went the screen. There was the cow. There was the hole. There was Scott. There was the tickly ant!

Eva clapped. "The photos stay!" she said. "The sea can go zoom away, but the photos stay right here."

She looked at the ant picture one more time. "Hello again, ant," she whispered.

Lennon sat at the big table at the library. Mr. Nkosi put out paper and paint. Lennon wanted to paint a pumpkin. But there was no orange paint in the jar.

She looked and looked. There was red paint. There was yellow paint. Hmm, she thought. What if she mixed them? She put red on her brush. She put yellow on top. She gave the paint a little stir.

The paint turned orange! "Look, look!" said Lennon. Her friend Theodora came to see. "That is so neat," said Theodora. Lennon painted her pumpkin all orange. Theodora gave the painting a kiss with her fingertip. Then they hung it up to dry. "Orange," said Lennon, with a big smile.

Aaron went to the park with his little toy mouse. The mouse was small and grey and very cute. Aaron threw a ball with his friend Cedric. Then Aaron looked in his pocket. The mouse was gone.

"I lost my mouse," said Aaron. "Where did it go?" He looked by the bench. No mouse. He looked by the tree. No mouse. He looked under the slide. It was dark under there. He could not see anything. "Too dark," said Aaron.

Ms. Wong came over with a flashlight. "Try this," she said. She clicked it on. Aaron shined the light under the slide. "A flashlight helps you see into dark spots!" The light made the dark spot bright. There was his mouse, sitting in the leaves. "Mouse!" said Aaron. He picked it up and hugged it tight. "All safe now," said Ms. Wong. "Let's go tell Cedric." Aaron ran across the grass with the mouse in his hand. "Look, Cedric! My mouse was under the slide!"

Kayden went to the store with his dad. He wanted new socks. He saw socks with a star on them. "I want blue," said Kayden. The sock bin sat in a very dark corner. The light there was off. Kayden dug in the bin. He held up two socks. He could not tell what color they were. The dark made it hard. "I can't see," he said. Mr. Farah-Ali worked at the store. He turned on the light. The corner got bright. Now Kayden could see! One sock was red. One sock was green. Not blue at all. Kayden laughed. He dug again. He found two blue socks with a star. He put the red one and the green one back. All the picking made Kayden thirsty. Dad bought him a little juice. "We can leave now," said Dad. Kayden held his blue socks all the way home. "Star socks," he said.

Charles ran to the toy shelf. He was excited to play trucks. But then he heard a sound. It was a small, sad sound. Marley sat by the blocks. Her face was wet with tears. Charles felt scared to ask. He held his truck tight.

He looked at Ms. Torres. She smiled and nodded. Charles walked over slow. He held out his red truck. "Want to share?" he asked. Marley wiped her eyes. She took the truck. Then she smiled a big smile.

Ms. Torres said, "That was kind, Charles." Charles felt happy in his chest. Daxton came with a bone toy for the toy dog. One truck, one bone, one smile. Marley laughed. Charles said, "Sharing is easy." Then he pushed the truck across the rug to her.

The lights went out. Hayden stood in the dark. "I can't see," he said. Mom found her phone. The little light was warm on the wall. But then the phone went dark too, to save its power.

Hayden held Mom's hand. The dark was very big at first. He could not see the sofa. He could not see his toy truck. He waited with Mom on the soft rug. Slowly, the dark began to feel smaller. A little while went by. Then Hayden could see the big shape of the sofa. Next he saw his truck, right by his feet. "Mom! My eyes can see now!" he said. "In the dark, they got used to it. I can see more and more!"

He crawled to the truck and rolled it on the floor. "Vroom," he whispered. The wheels clicked in the quiet room. Outside, a neighbor started a car, and its lights swept across the ceiling. Then the house lights came back on, all at once. Hayden blinked at the bright lamp. He waved at the sofa. "I saw you," he said. "I saw you in the dark."

Mia sat at the kitchen table. Mom put down two bowls. One bowl had strawberries. One bowl had crackers.

"Which bowl has more?" Mom asked.

Mia looked and looked. She pointed at the strawberries. Then she pointed at the crackers. "I don't know," she said.

"Try counting them," said Mom.

Mia counted the crackers. "One, two, three, four." Then she looked away to grab her cup. When she looked back, she forgot. Was it four? Was it five?

Mom held up her hand. "Watch me," she said. She put up one finger for each cracker. "One, two, three, four." Four fingers stood up tall.

Mia tried it. She touched a cracker and put up a finger. "One." She touched the next one. "Two." Then "Three." Then "Four." Her four fingers stayed up. She could see them.

Then she counted the strawberries the same way. "One, two, three, four, five, six." Six fingers stood up.

Mia looked at her hands. One hand had six fingers up. One hand had four fingers up. Six was taller than four.

"The strawberries have more!" she said.

"Yes," said Mom. "Six is more than four."

Mia drank some water from her cup. An ice cube clinked inside. "The ice is cold," she said.

Mom laughed. "You can count them too, if you like."

Mia sipped slowly. Then she put her cup down. "Can we count again?"

"We can count all day," said Mom.

Mia put up one finger. "One strawberry for me, please."

The wind howled outside the apartment. The big tree by the window began to swing its branches. Then, click, all the lights went out.

"Strong wind can knock out the power," said Dad. He lit a little lantern. "So we wait." Wren held her toy bunny tight. She could not watch her show. She could not have warm toast. The room felt dark and quiet.

Wren listened to the wind. It howled and howled. Then it grew soft. It grew still. Click, the lights came back on. Wren clapped her hands. The lamp glowed again. "The wind stopped," she said. Dad smiled and got out the bread. Wren watched from her chair as he made warm toast. It was a pretty golden color. She took a big bite and said, "Hello again, lights."

Sebastian looked out the window. The rain was falling on the street. "Rainy day," he said with a sigh.

Then the rain stopped. The sun came out. "Sunny now!" said Sebastian. He put on his rubber boots. Mom said, "Let's check the backyard."

In the backyard, the wind blew a little. Sebastian's hat almost flew off. "Windy too!" he said. Then he saw it. A big puddle sat on the ground near his sandbox. It was wide and brown and dirty.

Yara came over with her boots on. "Look!" said Sebastian. "Rain makes puddles on the ground!" He stepped in. Splash! Water went up on his legs. Yara stepped in too. Splash! They laughed and jumped together.

Then Yara slipped and sat down in the mud. Her lip began to shake. "I might cry," she said. Sebastian ran to her. He held out his hand. "Hold on," he said. "I'll pull you up." Up she came, splash-free and smiling.

"I'll get a towel," said Mom. She wiped Yara's dirty hands. "Thank you," said Yara. The wind blew again. "Brrr," said Yara. "My jacket is all wet." Sebastian ran inside. He came back with his warm, puffy coat. He gave it to Yara to wear.

Yara zipped it up. They jumped in the puddle one more time. "Splash!" they said together.

The lights went out. Madison stood still in the dark. "The power is off," said her dad. He found a big flashlight and turned it on. The beam made a bright circle on the floor.

Madison looked around. The house felt strange. "Why is it so quiet?" she asked. Dad said, "Listen. What do you hear?" Madison listened hard. She heard no humming. The fridge was not humming. The fan was not humming. All the machines were sleeping. That made the house quieter.

Then Madison heard a new sound. Drip, drip, drip. It came from the sink. "I never heard that before!" she said. Next door, her neighbour Mr. Bondarenko called from his yard, "Is your power out too?" "Yes!" said Dad. Madison held the flashlight up high, her neck stretched tall, still wide awake. Drip. Drip. Drip.

Jasmine stood at the school gate. Her tummy felt funny. Today was her very first day.

Her new backpack was on her back. But it was very heavy. Jasmine fell forward a little bit. "Too heavy," she said.

Her dad knelt down beside her. "Let's look inside," he said. They opened the backpack. Jasmine had packed her teddy bear, a toy mouse, and three big books.

"Your backpack is a bag you carry on your back," said Dad. "It goes on your back, so it must not be too heavy."

Jasmine took out the teddy bear. She took out the toy mouse. Now the backpack was light. She could stand up tall.

"Can I pay for milk at school?" Jasmine asked.

"Yes," said Dad. "Ms. Friedman will help you."

Just then, a girl ran up to the gate. "Hi! I'm Valeria!" she said. "Want to hold hands?"

Jasmine smiled. Her tummy felt better now. She held Valeria's hand, and they walked through the gate together.

Wyatt sat in the big waiting room chair. His legs swung back and forth. Today he would see the dentist for the first time. He held his old red ball tight.

Zoha sat down next to him. "I like your ball," she said. Wyatt rolled it to her feet. She rolled it back. Then a nurse called, "Wyatt!"

The dentist smiled at Wyatt. Wyatt looked at her hands. "Your hands are blue!" he said. "These are my gloves," said the dentist. She pulled one finger of the glove. Snap! Wyatt laughed. "Gloves keep things clean when fingers or tools go in your mouth," she said, and put on a fresh one. Wyatt opened his mouth wide, just like a lion. "Say ah," said the dentist. Wyatt said, "Ahhh!" The dentist gave him a sticker. It was a shiny tooth. Zoha clapped when he came back out.

Sara had a new baby brother. He was small and warm. He made tiny sounds.

Sara sat next to him. She held her cracker up. "Do you want some?" she asked. The baby did not take it. His little mouth turned away.

"Why won't he eat it?" Sara asked. Her mom smiled. "Babies drink milk or formula," Mom said. "Not regular food."

Sara watched Mom feed the baby. The baby drank and drank. His eyes closed. His tummy went up and down. "Milk makes him sleepy," Sara said.

Then the baby grabbed Sara's finger. His hand held on tight. He was stuck to her finger like a little spider on a web! Sara laughed.

"Can I do that again?" Sara asked. "Yes," said Mom. So Sara gave her finger back. The baby held on one more time.

Scarlett wanted a cat book. At the library, she found a green book with a cat on the cover. She sat down fast. But when she opened it, the pages looked all mixed up. The cat came before the kitten. The ending came first. "This book is broken," she said.

Her friend Muhammed came over. He looked at her book. Then he looked at his own book. "Mine starts here," he said. He pointed to the front cover. Scarlett turned her book over. Now the front cover was on top. She opened it again. One page, two pages, three pages. The cat came first. Then the kitten. Then a nap in the sun.

"Fixed!" said Scarlett. She counted the pages as she turned them, all the way to the back cover. Ms. Becker smiled and gave them each a sticker. "Thank you," said Scarlett, very polite. The cat on the sticker winked at her. Or maybe it was just the light.

Levi ran to the park with his dad. The grass smelled fresh and green. Levi was excited to play on the slide.

His friend Braxton was there. Braxton had the only red truck. Levi wanted it too. He grabbed the truck. Braxton shouted and his face turned red. He stomped his feet. He was angry. He began to cry big tears.

The park helper, Ms. Pereira, knelt down beside Braxton. "Let's try slow, deep breaths," she said. She breathed in slowly. She breathed out slowly. Braxton copied her. In. Out. In. Out. His face got calm. He stopped crying. He handed the truck to Levi.

Levi took a turn with the small truck. Then he gave it back. Braxton smiled. "Your turn," Levi said. They rolled the truck in the sand together. The warm sun shone on their heads.

Ellie sat at Grandma's big table. The bowls were full of soup. Ellie picked up her spoon. She was ready to eat.

Then everyone stood up. They all reached out their hands. Grandma reached for Ellie's hand. Uncle Ben reached for her other hand. Ellie was still holding her spoon. She could not hold hands and a spoon too. What should she do?

Ellie looked at the spoon. Then she looked at the hands. She set the spoon down by her bowl. Now her hands were free. Grandma smiled and held one hand. Ellie held Uncle Ben's hand too. Everyone made a big circle around the table. They closed their eyes and said the blessing together. After that, Grandma gave Ellie a kiss on her head. Ellie picked her spoon back up and poured nothing, because soup needs a spoon! She laughed and took a big bite.

Would her friend Orion's family do this too? Ellie wanted to ask him tomorrow.

Amelia was at Grandma's house. She found a big jar of buttons. "I want to count them all," she said. "One, two..." Then she stopped. What came after two? She tapped her finger on her chin. The number word would not come out.

Grandma sat down next to her. "Let's sing it," said Grandma. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." Amelia laughed. The words rhymed! Shoe went with two. Door went with four. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight." Amelia sang along. The rhymes helped the numbers stick in her head, like glue.

"Nine, ten," sang Grandma. "A big fat hen!" At that moment, something went cluck outside. A real hen was at the window! Amelia jumped up. "Grandma, the song sent us a hen!" Grandma laughed her gentle laugh. "Maybe she wants to count too."

Amelia picked up one button at a time. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." She laid the buttons in a row. When a button rolled off the table, she watched it sink deep into the couch cushions. "Button, come back!" she called. The hen clucked twice, as if she was counting too. "One, two," said Amelia. "Even the hen knows the song."

John sat on the red rug at school. Ms. Walker said, "We will sing a rhyme today." John wanted to clap and sing it all by himself. He did not know it yet.

Tiara and Andrew stood up to sing. Ms. Walker sang fast, fast, fast. The words got all tangled. Andrew said, "My tongue is in a knot!" Tiara giggled and fell down on the rug.

Ms. Walker said, "A song can be sung fast or slow. Let us try slow." She sang very slow. Clap, clap, clap went John's hands. The beat was steady like a big drum. John peeked at his white shoes. They tapped the floor too. John sang the whole rhyme, all alone. He clapped the last clap. "Again!" he said.

Jack wanted to zip his coat by himself. He pulled the zipper up. It stopped halfway. It would not go any farther.

"Let's try again," said his dad. Jack pulled it down. Then he pulled it up. It stopped again. Jack sat on the step and frowned.

"You can practice," said his dad. "Zipping takes practice." So Jack practiced. He tried at breakfast. He tried after he got dressed. He tried before they went to the bank. Sometimes it stuck. Sometimes it went up.

At the bank, Jack put on his coat. He held the zipper. He pulled it slow. Up, up, up it went. It went all the way to the top. Jack smiled big. "I did it!" he said. His dad clapped. Outside, they saw a big sign with a yummy bread on it. "We can eat a snack now," said Dad. Jack zipped his coat all by himself, and off they went.

Sadie woke up and saw white snow. "No school today!" said her dad. It was a snow day. Sadie wanted to play in the park. So Dad helped her hang her coat on the hook. Then they put on boots and walked to the park.

At the park, Sadie saw her friend Ari. Ari lay down in the snow. He swept his arms up and down. He swept his legs out and in. Then Ari stood up. His boot made a big smudge. His angel had a mark right in the middle.

"What happened?" Sadie wondered. Did the boots do that? Ari lay down in a new spot. This time he swept his arms and legs again. Then he rolled to the side, far away from his picture. He stood up next to it. The angel was clean. Its wings were soft and whole.

"Now me," said Sadie. She lay down in the snow. She swept her arms. She swept her legs. Then she rolled to the side. She stood up next to her angel. "Look!" she said. "A snow angel!" Ari clapped his mittens. "Mine has a smudge," he laughed. "Let's make ten more," said Sadie. Dad smiled and sat down on the bench to watch them.

Mya stood at the bus stop. She held her yellow hat in her hands. The sun was out, and it made the road hot. "Jalen is coming on the bus," said Mya's mom. "I want to show him my hat."

Then the wind came. The wind blew Mya's hair. The wind blew a paper down the street. Mya held her hat tight so it would not fly away.

Then a big cloud moved in the sky. The clouds hid the sun. The road was not hot anymore. "Where did the sun go?" asked Mya. "Look up," said her mom. "The clouds hide the sun sometimes." Mya watched and waited. Rain began to fall. Mya's mom put up her umbrella.

The bus came. Jalen jumped down. He wore his rain boots. "My mom glued my boot strap," he said. "It broke on the swing yesterday." The rain made little taps on the umbrella. Mya gave Jalen her hat. "It will keep the rain off your head," she said. Then the cloud moved away. The sun came back out. Mya pointed up at the bright sky and smiled.

Logan was at Grandpa's house. He found a big book on the soft chair. The book had a frog on the cover. Logan wanted Grandpa to read it.

"Read the frog book," said Logan. Grandpa sat down next to him. He opened the book from the front. He read the first page out loud. Logan saw little marks under the picture. Grandpa pointed at the marks as he read.

Then they came to a page with no words on it. It was just a picture of a pond. "Read this page too," said Logan. Grandpa shook his head. "There is nothing written here to read," he said. "I can tell you about the picture instead." Logan felt a little sad. He wanted words on that page too.

Grandpa turned to the next page. More little marks! Grandpa read them out loud. The frog said, "Croak!" Logan blew on the page like a pretend wind. Grandpa laughed. Logan turned the page himself, from the front to the back, all the way to the end. "The end," said Grandpa. Logan clapped his hands. "Again!"

Mackenzie did not want to sleep. "When is tomorrow?" she asked. Mom pointed at the tall clock on the wall. "The clock shows what time it is," Mom said. "See the little hand? When it gets to the eight, it is bedtime."

"Is it eight now?" asked Mackenzie.

"Not yet. It is seven now," said Mom. "So it is bedtime later."
