Mackenzie watched the clock. The hand moved a tiny bit. Her puppy wagged his tail on the bed. "He wants to wait too," she said.

Yesterday Mackenzie had cried at bedtime. Today she did not cry. She watched the clock instead.

"Is it eight now?" she asked again.

"Now it is eight," said Mom.

Mackenzie hugged her puppy close. "Tomorrow we can watch it again," she said. Mom turned off the light.

Olivia sat in her bed. It was a rainy night. Rain tapped on the window. Tap, tap, tap. Her book was on the blanket. It had a bunny on the front. The bunny had big soft ears.

"Who drew this bunny?" Olivia asked. She hugged the book. "I want to know." Her sister came in to say good night. "Open the front cover," her sister said. "The name is inside." Olivia opened the front cover. She turned the pages one by one, front to back, just like at story time. There it was. Words on the page. "Drew Byrd," she read slowly. "Who is Drew Byrd?" "The person who painted the pictures," her sister said. "That is called the illustrator."

Olivia clapped her hands. "Drew Byrd made my bunny!" she said. She looked at the words again. The marks on the page had told her a name. The rain went tap, tap, tap. Olivia yawned and chewed the corner of her blanket. She held the book up high. "Good night, Bunny," she whispered. "Good night, Drew Byrd."

Max was at Grandma's house. He could not find his red car. It was his favorite toy. He looked under the big chair. He looked by the door. No red car.

Max scratched his head. Where could it be? He asked himself, "Did I leave it outside?" He peeked out the window. He saw only grass and flowers. His car was not there.

Max felt like giving up. Then he heard Dad in the kitchen. Grandma was there too, making soup. Max ran to them. "My red car is lost," he said. "Will you help me look?"

"Of course," said Dad. Dad looked in the hall. Grandma wiped her hands and looked near the couch. Max looked in the toy box. Now three people were looking, not just one!

"I see something red!" said Grandma. She reached behind the couch cushion. Out came the red car. It had been hiding all along.

"You found it!" said Max. He hugged Grandma fast, then hugged Dad. "When we all look, we find it," he said. He pushed the car across the floor. "Vroom!" said Max. "Who wants to race?"

Harrison ran to the swings at the playground. The big swing was taken. Annabelle was on it. Harrison wanted that swing a lot.

He asked, "Can I have a turn, please?" Annabelle jumped off. "You can go now," she said. Harrison smiled. Then he had an idea. "You can have my snack," he said. He held out his crackers.

Annabelle took one. "Thank you," she said. She stood very quiet. She did not know what to say back. Ms. Dlamini was sitting on the bench. Harrison waved to her. "Please help," he said.

Ms. Dlamini came over. She whispered to Harrison. Harrison nodded. He had heard his dad say it at home. "You're welcome," he said to Annabelle. Annabelle smiled big. "You're welcome," she said back to him.

Then Kaysen ran up with a glue stick in his hand. "My paper bird lost a wing," he said. "Can you help, please?" Harrison and Annabelle helped glue the wing. "Thank you," said Kaysen. Harrison said, "You're welcome." Annabelle said it too. The three friends sat on the quiet grass and shared the crackers, one by one.

Harrison ran to the playground with his mom. The sun made the slide hot. He touched the slide with one finger. "Ouch," he said. The slide was too hot. His mom poured water on it. The water made the slide cool. Harrison slid down and laughed.

Then he saw Kimberly by the bench. She was looking at something on the ground. It was a little bottle. Bright dots fell out of it. They were red and yellow. "They look like candy," said Kimberly. She reached out her hand.

"Stop," said Harrison. "Only a grown-up gives you medicine, even if it looks like candy." Kimberly pulled her hand back. They did not touch the dots. They ran to the coach. The coach picked up the bottle with a tissue. "Thank you," she said. "You two did the right thing."

Harrison jumped down from the bench. He landed on his knee, then stood up fast. He was okay. Kimberly clapped for him. On the way home, Harrison held his mom's hand. He saw one small bug crawl up a green leaf. He wondered, where do red and yellow bugs go at night?

James got a drum in music class. Mr. Cheung showed him how to tap it. Tap, tap, tap went James. Ahmad played bells. Remy played a little horn.

"Time for a show," said Mr. Cheung. James wore his spotted shirt for the big day. He tapped his drum for the class. Tap, tap, boom! The children clapped and clapped. Remy jumped up and down. But James just stood there. Then he saw Remy bow. The clapping got even bigger. Ahmad bowed too. So James bowed too. More claps! More claps!

"Again," said James. He tapped his drum one more time. Then he bowed fast and low. The class clapped, and James smiled.

Juliette stayed at Grandma's house. She wore her pink party dress all day. She twirled in the kitchen. She ate an apple at the table. She carried her shoes to the door. At night, Grandma said, "Time for bed."

"I want to sleep in my party dress," Juliette said. Grandma held her hand. They went to the cozy room. Grandma laid out soft pajamas with stars on them. "These are pajamas," Grandma said. "Pajamas are clothes we wear to sleep in."

Juliette touched the party dress. It was stiff and tight. She touched the pajamas. They were soft like her blanket. She pulled on the pajamas. They felt warm and snug. She climbed into bed. Then she saw something in her pocket. It was a tiny star sticker from the party! Juliette stuck it on her pajama sleeve. "My pajamas have a star now," she said. Grandma smiled and turned off the light.

Joseph went to the pharmacy with his dad. He had to use the toilet. Then he rushed out fast. He wanted to look at the candy.

Mr. Guo the pharmacist called out, "Wait, Joseph. We always wash our hands after using the toilet." Joseph stopped. He turned back to the sink.

He pumped the soap into his hands. Mr. Guo said, "Now rub for twenty seconds. I will count." Joseph rubbed and bubbled. "Ten, eleven, twelve," said Mr. Guo. The bubbles grew big and white. "Nineteen, twenty!" Joseph rinsed the soap away. The germs went down the drain too.

Then came a surprise. Mr. Guo held out a little spoon. On it was a taste of honey. "A smart boy who washes so well gets a treat," he said. Joseph had wished for candy, and this was even better. He licked the spoon. It was sweet and warm on his tongue. Joseph smiled at his shiny, clean hands. "Twenty seconds is not too long," he said. Mr. Guo laughed and put a sticker of a happy soap bottle on Joseph's shirt.

Nolan went to the farm with his dad. They had seeds to plant. Nolan wanted to grow his own carrots.

"Can we plant them now?" he asked.

"Yes," said his dad. "First we dig."

Nolan dropped the little seeds into the dirt. He patted the soil on top. Then he watered the ground with a small can.

Every day Nolan came back to look. He saw brown dirt. He saw more brown dirt. "Where are my carrots?" he asked. "Just wait," said his dad. "Seeds take time."

One morning Nolan ran to the garden. There in the soil was a small green tip. It was tiny and new. Nolan had never seen one before.

He ran to the big tree by the barn. His friend Oscar was there. "Come see!" said Nolan. They ran to the garden together.

Oscar bent down low. "That little green thing is called a sprout," said Oscar. "My mom grows beans. Sprouts come up first."

Nolan smiled big. "My sprout!" he said. He gave it one drop of water, very gently.

The farmer walked by with a snowy white duck under his arm. "Well done," he said. "Watch it grow tall."

Nolan and Oscar sat in the shade and watched the sprout stand up in the sun.

Addison sat at the dinner table. Baby Ben was asleep in his little seat. Addison had big news. She had shared her lunch with Mario at school. Mario had shared his apple back. It was kind.

Addison opened her mouth wide. "I SHARED MY..."

Daddy put one finger to his lips. Then Daddy whispered, "Baby Ben is sleeping. When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice."

Addison looked at Ben. His eyes were shut. His tiny hand was curled up like a ball.

Addison tried again, very small. "I shared," she whispered.

Daddy smiled and whispered back, "Thank you, Addison." Ben kept sleeping, soft and warm.

After dinner, Daddy would sweep the crumbs. Addison could help hold the dustpan. But first, she whispered to Ben one more time. "One, two, three, shh."

Ben made a little sleep sound. Addison giggled, very, very quietly.

"Shh," she said.

Victoria went to the store with her dad. She wanted a book about ducks. On a shelf she saw a little red book. The cover had words on it. Dad read the words out loud. "Duck, Duck, Sleep," he said. The words told them what the book was. Victoria hugged the book. It was hers.

At home, after dinner, Victoria sat on the rug. She peek at the pages. But the duck looked funny. The duck was upside down. So were the words. Victoria laughed and laughed. "Silly duck," she said. Dad smiled. Victoria turned the book around. Now the duck stood right side up. The words stood up too.

She turned the book upside down again. The duck flopped. She turned it back. The duck stood. "Again," said Victoria. Dad said, "You read it front to back." Victoria opened page one.

Henri was grumpy at daycare. His sandwich was cut in a strange way. It was not a square anymore. It had pointy bits.

Felix sat next to him. "That is a triangle," said Felix. Henri touched the sandwich. He counted the corners. One, two, three. He counted the sides too. One, two, three. The same number!

Henri took a small bite. Now his sandwich had a new shape. He counted again. One, two, three, four. "A square has four," said Zayd.

Ms. Huang brought a plate of crackers. Some were circles. Henri found a circle and put it on the table. He spelled his name with string at the craft table. Then he made shapes with the string too. He made a triangle with three loops. One, two, three.

"Look, Felix," said Henri. "My string has three sides." He smiled and munched his cracker.

Olivia went to Ivan's house. Ivan had a big red drum. He banged on it. Boom, boom, boom!

Olivia wanted to bang the drum too. She grabbed for it. Ivan held it tight. "My turn," he said.

Ivan's mom came in with sandwiches. "Let me tell you something," she said. "You can take turns. Taking turns means one person plays for a while, and then the other person gets to play."

"Okay," said Olivia. She sat on the floor. She waited.

Ivan played for a while. Boom, boom, boom. Then he stopped. "Now you," he said. He let Olivia hold the drum.

Olivia played for a while. Boom, boom, boom. Then she stopped too. "Now you," she said.

They took turns and took turns. Ivan's mom smiled. "Time for cold milk," she said.

Olivia drank her milk. "Taking turns is fun," she said. Ivan banged the drum one more time. Boom, boom, boom!

Stella ran to the line in the gym. It was ball day in gym class. Ms. Visser put a bat in Stella's hands.

"Wait," said Ms. Visser. "You need a helmet first."

"A helmet?" said Stella.

"In baseball, the batter wears a helmet," said Ms. Visser. "It protects your head." She set the blue helmet on Stella's head. It felt snug, like a hat for winter.

Stella swung the bat. Ping! The ball flew far. Her friend Saint clapped. "Nice hit!" he said. Then Saint ran to bat fast, with no helmet.

"Saint, come back!" called Ms. Visser. Saint ran back. She put a red helmet on his head. He smiled and gave the bat a big rip swing. Ping! The ball rolled past Saige.

Stella was happy. She patted her helmet with her hand. "My head is safe," she said. "My turn again!"

Rowan lost his small red dinosaur at Grandma's house. He ran to the kitchen. He ran to the bedroom. He ran to the den. No dinosaur anywhere.

Grandma was in the kitchen. "Can I help feed the birds?" Rowan asked. "First let's find your dinosaur," said Grandma. She held out her hand. "Let's look in one room at a time."

They started in the kitchen. Rowan looked under the table. He looked behind the big chair. He looked in the warm bread basket. No dinosaur there. They went to the bedroom next. He looked under the bed. He looked in the shoe basket. Then he saw it! His dinosaur was stuck to a magnet on the fridge door in the den.

"One room at a time," Rowan whispered. "That is how you find things." He hugged the dinosaur tight. "Now can we feed the birds?" Grandma laughed and filled the little cup with seeds.

It was Lea's first day of school. She rode the bus with her father waiting at the stop. Lea felt a little sad. She wanted to wave to him out the window. She stood up in her seat. She bounced on her toes. The driver looked back. "Sit down please," the driver said. "On the school bus, children stay sitting in their seats." Lea sat down fast. She waved from her seat. Her father waved back big. Lea smiled. Staying sitting still let her wave and wave.

At school, Lea walked down the hallway. She held her little backpack tight. A boy named Shawn stood by the door. He was looking for his classroom. "I lost my room," Shawn said. Lea saw the teacher, Mr. Lindqvist. She took Shawn's hand. They walked to Mr. Lindqvist together.

"Can you help us?" Lea asked. Mr. Lindqvist smiled. He showed them the room. There were tiny chairs and red cups. Lea let go of Shawn's hand. He smiled too. Liya was already at the paint table. "Come paint with us," Liya said. Lea sat down next to her. She picked up a brush and made a long blue line.

Declan sat in a big red seat. The basketball game was starting below him. Ziyad sat near him. They both held a bag of popcorn.

A player ran with the ball. He threw it up high. The ball went right through the hoop. The crowd went wild.

"They scored!" shouted Ziyad.

"They threw it in the hoop," said Declan. "I want to do that too."

After the game, they found a little hoop by the door. It was just their size. Declan held his ball. He threw it up. It hit the rim and fell off. He laughed.

"Too high, silly ball," he said.

Ziyad tried too. His ball went through the hoop and dropped down. "I did it!" said Ziyad.

Ms. Torres, who was walking by, clapped her hands. Declan stirred his feet in a happy dance, then threw again. This time the ball went through the hoop.

"Through the hoop!" Declan shouted. "Just like the big game."

Everett was three years old today. His party was at the big hall in town. Balloons hung by the door. A thick red curtain stood on the stage.

Everett marched in with his box of invitations. He had drawn a cake on each one. His friends came through the door one by one.

Harriet stopped outside. She looked worried. "I got lost on the way," she said. "I did not know where to go."

Everett ran to her. He held up his invitation. "Look," he said. "It says the party is at the big hall." Harriet looked at the paper. She saw the hall on it. She saw a time too. "It says three o'clock," she said. "That is now!"

"So you came to the right place," said Everett. Harriet smiled big. She put the invitation in her pocket.

Mr. Qureshi set out cups of juice. Anita picked a blue balloon. Everyone sat at the long table. The cake came out with three candles. A grown-up lit them carefully. Everett blew hard. The candles went out. All his friends clapped and cheered.

Harriet waved her invitation in the air. "Best paper ever," she said. "Now let's eat cake!"

Ivy sat with Grandma's big cat book. She wanted to hear the cat story again. Grandma was in the kitchen making tea. So Ivy turned the pages herself.

She turned the pages front to back, one by one. Some pages had words. Some pages had only pictures. She pointed at the words, but the words did not say anything to her.

"Grandma, can you read this page?" asked Ivy.

Grandma came over. She sat down. She read the words out loud. "The little cat jumped into a deep, dark box."

Ivy smiled. Then she found a page with no words at all. Only a big orange cat sat there. "Read this page too!" said Ivy.

Grandma looked at it. "There are no words here," she said. "There is nothing written to read. But we can make up our own words if you like."

Ivy nodded. "The cat took a nap," she said slowly. Grandma laughed. Then Grandma read the next page, and Ivy turned it.

Mateo sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. His tummy hurt a little. "Time for your checkup," said Ms. Pérez. First Mateo had to use the toilet. Then Ms. Pérez showed him the little sink. "Now we wash," she said. "We count to twenty." She squirted soap on his hands. One, two, three! The soap got bubbly and white. The bubbles slipped down his fingers. Ten, eleven, twelve! Mateo rubbed and rubbed. Twenty! The water washed all the soap away. His hands looked shiny and clean. Before that, dirt had been on them. Now the dirt was missing! "Lunch time," said his dad. He held out crackers. Mateo looked at his clean hands. "Wash first!" he said. He ran back to the sink. "One, two, three..."

Benjamin went to the library with his dad. Ms. Weber had three tablets on a table. "Can I use one?" Benjamin asked. "Yes," said Ms. Weber. "I will show you how."

Benjamin pressed the round button. The screen lit up. He had made that happen. He tapped the blue square with the crayon on it. A drawing app opened. He made a big deep blue lake and a yellow sun. "One sun, two ducks, three fish," he counted as he drew.

Then the screen went black. "Oh no," said Benjamin. He pressed the button again. Nothing happened. He tried once more. Still nothing. "The tablet ran out of power," said Ms. Weber. "It needs charging." She plugged the charger into the wall. Benjamin watched. The little battery picture came back on the screen.

"Now we wait," said Ms. Weber. They read a book while the tablet sat still. After the book, the screen was awake again. "Summer!" said Benjamin, and he drew a green tree. When he was done, Ms. Weber helped him press the button, slide the tablet into its box, and put it back on the shelf. "Goodbye, tablet," said Benjamin. "I will press your button next time."

Nicholas was in the playroom with his friend Quinn. On the floor there were three big circles made of string. Mr. Kamau had made them after breakfast. "Let's sort," he said. "Put animals here. Put toys here. Put foods here."

Nichels picked up a toy bear. Was it an animal? No, it was a toy. It went in the toy circle. He counted as he sorted. "One bear, two balls, three blocks." Quinn found a cat puzzle piece. "Cat!" said Quinn. It went with the animals.

Then Nicholas found a carrot. He put it in the toy circle. Mr. Kamau shook his head. "Where does the carrot go?" he asked. Nicholas looked and looked. There was an apple in one circle. There was bread in the same circle. Apples and bread were there, and they were foods.

Maybe the carrot was a food too? Nicholas picked it up. He moved it next to the apple and the bread. He counted again. "One apple, two breads, three carrots." All foods!

Then Mr. Kamau held up something furry with long ears. "What is this?" he asked. It was a rabbit, a real soft rabbit! The rabbit hopped over and sniffed the carrot. "He likes foods too," said Nicholas. The rabbit took a tiny nibble.

Ibrahim sat on the playroom floor. He had a bowl of crackers next to him. Aaron sat close by, building with blocks.

Ibrahim held up a cracker. "Is this a square?" he asked.

Aaron looked at it. "I don't know," he said.

Ibrahim found a piece of string. He laid it along one side of the cracker. Then he held the string up. "Now let's see," he said. He laid the string on the next side. It was just the same. He laid it on the third side. The same again. One more side to go. He laid the string down. The same!

"Four sides," said Ibrahim. "All the same length. It's a square!"

Aaron clapped his hands. "A square cracker!" he said.

Ibrahim took a bite. Crunch. The cracker was gone. He reached into the bowl for another one. This one was long, not square. "Hmm," said Ibrahim. He got the string again. He laid it on each side. One side was long. The short sides were not the same.

"This one is not a square," said Ibrahim.

"Maybe it's a rectangle," said Aaron.

Ibrahim put the long cracker down. He picked up a block. It was black and square. He laid the string on all four sides. All the same length. "Square!" he said.

Aaron held up a block too. They laughed and lined up their squares on the floor, one, two, three, four.

Ibrahim finished his last cracker. "Square," he said, and smiled.

Jordan sat in his car seat. Colson sat next to him. They were going to the park.

Jordan's mom handed back a bag of snacks. "Would you like a cheese stick, Jordan?"

"Yuck!" Jordan shouted. He pushed the bag away.

Colson spoke in a small, quiet voice. "No, thank you," he said to the cheese sticks. Then Colson held up a thin cracker. "May I have this, please?"

"Of course," said Jordan's mom. She smiled at Colson.

Jordan thought about that. He took a breath. "No, thank you," he said to the cheese stick. "May I have a cracker, please?"

"Yes, you may," said his mom. She passed him the crackers.

Jordan took a small bite. "They taste good," he said. He ate another one.

Then he saw a gray mouse by the fence at the park. It ran under a thin bush. Jordan waved at it through the window.

"Thank you for the crackers, Mom," said Jordan.

"You are welcome, sweetheart," she said. She parked the car, and the boys ran out to play.

Sarah and her dad drive to the pharmacy. Sarah thinks they are going to see her doctor. "I do not like shots," she says. Dad smiles. "Today we see someone new," he says. The cashier hands Dad a little paper bag.

At the new place, a big chair waits. It goes up and down. A kind woman looks in Sarah's mouth. She counts Sarah's teeth. One, two, three. She looks and looks. She does not look at Sarah's arm. She does not give a shot. "You only looked at my teeth," says Sarah. The woman nods. "A dentist is a doctor who takes care of teeth," she says.

Sarah gets a new toothbrush. It is her favorite color, red. "Open wide," she tells her teddy at home. Teddy stays very awake.

Clara sat on the big red couch. Her teddy bear sat on her lap. Mr. Toussaint's TV showed a big game. Everyone was shouting and clapping. "Kick the ball!" said Loan. Loan sat next to Clara. Gurfateh sat on the floor.

Clara looked at the TV. She saw lots of running. But she could not tell the two teams apart. "Who has the ball?" she whispered to Loan. "I don't know," said Loan. "All the players look the same to me."

Mr. Toussaint laughed. He sat down beside them. "Look at the shirts," he said. "One team wears blue. One team wears red. Each team wears its own colors." Clara looked hard. The blue team had the ball! "The red team has the ball!" she said. "No, blue!" said Gurfateh. They all laughed.

Clara held up her teddy bear. The bear's ribbon was red. "You are on the red team," she told the bear. She patted the bear's rough paw. On the TV, a blue player kicked the ball. The crowd went wild. Clara jumped up on the couch. "Blue scored! Blue scored!" she shouted.

Grandma came to stay for a whole week! Clara gave her the white blanket from her bed. Grandma hugged her tight.

On Saturday they went to the market. "We need flour," said Grandma. Clara counted the bags as they went in the basket. One, two, three! A big wooden owl watched from a stall, and Clara laughed at it.

At home, Grandma rolled up her sleeves. "My mother made this bread with me," she said. "Now I will make it with you." Clara poured the flour. Grandma mixed it with water. Clara patted the soft dough with her hands. Then they put it in a bowl and waited.

The dough grew big and puffy! Clara peeked again and again. "It got so fat!" she said.

The oven was hot, so Grandma slid the pan in herself. Clara watched from her chair. Soon the kitchen smelled warm and sweet.

The bread came out golden. Clara took one bite and jumped up and down. "It tastes like your bread, Grandma!"

"It is my bread," said Grandma. "Now it is yours too."

Clara held out a slice. "You have to try it!"

Margot was at Grandma's house. She sat at the big table. She wanted to paint a turtle. She picked gray paint. She painted a big gray turtle. The turtle looked like it could swim in the sea.

Her friend Oceane came to play. Oceane painted a turtle too. It was big and gray, just like Margot's. They set the paintings side by side. "Which one is mine?" asked Margot. The two paintings looked the same. She could not tell.

Grandma brought a marker. "People often write their name on their artwork," she said. "Then everyone knows who made it." Margot wrote M-A-R-G-O-T on her paper. Oceane wrote her name too. Now Margot saw her name and smiled. She pointed and said, "This one is mine!"

Sophia went to the store with her dad today. She wanted the ocean book with the blue fish. Yesterday she had seen it on the shelf. Today it was still there.

"When can we get it?" Sophia asked. "Now? Or later?"

Her dad pointed up at the wall. "See the clock? The clock shows what time it is," he said. "Now the big hand is at the top. Later it will point down. Then we pay."

Sophia watched the clock. She watched the fish book too. Slowly, the big hand moved. It crept past each number.

"It moved!" she said. "It is later now!"

Her dad smiled. "Yes. Now we can pay."

They took the book to the cashier. Tomorrow Sophia would read it at home. She held it tight all the way to the car.

Florence sat on the big low couch in the living room. She wanted to draw a flower on the tablet. But the screen was dark and still. She pressed her finger on it. Nothing happened.

Her dad sat down next to her. "Tap the little button on top," he said. Florence tapped it. The screen lit up. There were small pictures everywhere. "The small pictures on a tablet screen are called icons," her dad said. Florence looked and looked. One icon had a paintbrush on it. She tapped the paintbrush. The drawing app opened. "I did it!" she said.

She drew a big yellow flower with a green stem. Then she drew a small red flower too. When she was done, she put the tablet on the table. "All done," Florence said, and she tapped the screen dark again.

Isaiah stood in the playroom. The toy box was empty. Toys were all over the floor.

"Time to clean up," said Ms. Bakker. "Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys. Every toy goes in the box."

Isaiah picked up a red block. He dropped it in. Clunk. He picked up a blue block. Clunk. Samara held up a doll with yellow hair.

"Is this a toy?" she asked.

"Yes," said Isaiah. "Dolls are toys." Samara put the doll in the box.

Amin rolled a bright green ball across the floor. It bumped Isaiah's foot. Isaiah laughed and picked it up. The ball went in too. Bounce, plop.

Then Isaiah found something under the chair. It was a red apple from snack time. "Is an apple a toy?" he asked.

Amin shook his head. "No. Apples are foods. Foods go on the plate."

Isaiah put the apple on the snack table. Then he looked around the room. A wooden dog, a small cat, a drum, a tiny car. He pointed at each one.

"Animals, drum, car," he said. "All toys!" He put them in one by one.

Soon the box was full. The floor was clean. Ms. Bakker smiled.

"Nice work," she said. "Now who wants to share the drum?"

"Me!" said Isaiah. He sat down next to Samara. He tapped the drum softly. Tum, tum, tum.

Luca ran into the playroom. "A sorting game!" he shouted. Mr. Grant had put out three big boxes. One box was for animals, one for toys, one for foods.

Luca peeked in the toy box. "One car, two cars, three cars," he counted. Then he saw something yellow. It was a banana! The banana did not belong there. "You are the odd one out," Luca told the banana. He picked it up and put it in the foods box. Then he clapped.

Ocean came over with a loud laugh. "Look at the animals!" A feather was hiding under the toy lion. "One lion, two bears, three ducks," said Ocean. "The feather is the odd one out!" She put the feather in her pocket.

Amy closed the door of the toy box. "All done!" she said. Mr. Grant held up the banana. "Snack time!" Luca jumped up and down. "Banana for the odd one out finder!" he said.

Charles went to the playground with his friend Jace. They found the mud kitchen by the sandbox. It had pots, cups, and spoons.

"I will make soup," said Jace. He put leaves and water in a red pot. He stirred it with a big spoon. "Mud soup!" he said.

Charles wanted some too. He made his own soup with tiny stones and water. The stones were sticky from mud. Charles lifted the spoon to his mouth. He wanted to taste it.

Mr. Ong ran over fast. "Stop, Charles!" he said. He took the spoon away. "Pretend food is for pretending to eat, not for putting in your mouth."

Charles looked at his soup. Then he made a big slurping sound. "Slurp! Yum!" he said. He did not put the spoon in his mouth at all.

Jace laughed and slurped too. "More soup?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Charles. They stirred and slurped and pretended all morning long.

Elias went to the store with his dad. They went to shop for paint. Elias held a little paper pumpkin. He wanted to paint it orange. "I need orange paint," he said. He looked and looked. He saw red paint. He saw yellow paint. He saw blue paint and green paint too. But no orange paint anywhere. His bottom lip went down, down, down.

Then his friend Luka came by with his mom. Luka had paint cups in his hands. "No orange?" asked Luka. "No orange," said Elias. "Want to see a trick?" said Luka. "Watch me."

Luka got two small pots, one red and one yellow. He dipped his brush in the red paint. He swirled it in a cup. Then he dipped his brush in the yellow paint. He swirled it in the same cup. Round and round went the brush. "Stir, stir, stir," said Luka. Elias leaned in close. The red and yellow mixed. The cup turned orange! Orange like a pumpkin. Orange like a carrot.

"It's orange!" said Elias. "You made it!" "You try," said Luka. Elias dipped his brush in the red. He dipped it in the yellow. He stirred and stirred. His cup turned orange too. He laughed a big laugh. "My turn worked!" he said.

Elias painted his paper pumpkin orange. He painted one big green leaf on top. Then he saw a toy elephant on a shelf. It was stuck behind a big box. Elias pulled and pulled. Pop! Out came the elephant. It was blue. "A blue elephant!" said Elias. Luka giggled. "Elephants aren't blue," he said. Elias hugged the elephant anyway. "My elephant is blue," he said. "My pumpkin is orange. Stir, stir, stir!"

The lights went out. Isaiah's whole apartment went dark. "Mama," he said. "The lamp is off." "The power is out," said Mama. She felt for the flashlight. It was not on the shelf. It was not under the bed. Isaiah felt shy in the big dark. He held Mama's hand tight. Then he remembered. "The kitchen drawer!" he said. Mama opened the drawer. Her fingers found the flashlight. She pressed the button. Click. A bright beam shot out. The flashlight still shone! It did not need the power at all. Isaiah laughed. "It works, Mama!" Mama swept the light across the room. Isaiah planted his feet and reached for the beam on the wall. He made a dog shadow with his fingers. Then the light found something small on the couch. It was the cat, curled up in Mama's sweater. "There you are," said Mama. Isaiah sat close. The cat purred. The little beam glowed on the wall. Isaiah pointed at the circle of light. "Mama, can we make a big sun?" he asked. Mama moved the flashlight near the wall. The circle grew and grew. "Wow," said Isaiah. "The sun is in our house."

Audrey was at daycare. She had a big bucket of wet sand. She patted it and patted it. Soon she had a tall sandcastle with a brown paper flag.

Leah came running with a truck. She did not see the castle. The truck bumped it. The tall tower fell down. Leah stopped. Her face went sad. "Sorry, Audrey," she said. "It was a mistake. I feel bad I broke your castle."

Audrey looked at the flat sand. Then she looked at Leah. "It is okay," said Audrey. "You can help me build it again." Leah smiled. She scooped up more sand. Audrey patted the tower. Leah made two small walls.

Ms. Lin brought a glass of water for the seeds. "Please may we have one more tower?" asked Audrey. "Thank you," said Leah. They put the flag back on top. Then they sang a happy building song together. "Best castle ever," said Leah.

Luna had a cold. Her nose ran and her head felt warm. She sat at the kitchen table in her striped pajamas. Her stuffed animal, a little zebra, sat beside her.

Luna wanted to feel better. She saw the medicine bottle on the counter. It was small and purple. She reached for it.

Her mom came in fast. "Only a grown-up gives a child medicine," Mom said. She picked up the bottle. "You can hold your zebra while I pour it."

Mom poured the purple medicine into a little cup. One spoon, two spoons, three. "All done," said Mom.

Luna drank it down. It tasted like grapes. She hugged her zebra and counted his legs. One, two, three, four.

Mom made warm soup. Mom poured it into a red bowl. Luna took one sip, then another.

Soon Luna felt less sniffly. She yawned big. Mom carried her to the couch, zebra and all. "Sleep tight," Mom whispered.

Julia woke up in her dark room. She jumped out of bed. "Morning!" she shouted. "Park time!" She ran to the window and looked out. The sky was dark. The stars were out. Her mom came in and smiled. "It is still night, Julia. Day and night are opposites. Night comes first, then day." Julia frowned. "I want day," she said. "You must wait," said Mom. So Julia went back to bed.

Soon the sky turned light. "Day!" cried Julia. "Park time for real!" Mom laughed. At the park, Julia saw the big slide and the small slide. She counted them. "One big slide, one small slide!" Julia ran fast down the big one. Then she walked slow up the steps. "Fast and slow," she said. Her friends Mehreen and Aria were there. Mehreen had a cold drink. Aria had a warm bun from home. "Cold drink, warm bun," said Julia. They sat in the shade because the sun was hot.

Mr. Menon was mixing sand and water in the sandpit. Julia and Mehreen helped him mix. They made a tall triangle tower. "One triangle, two triangles, three triangles!" said Julia. Aria patted the sand flat. Then Julia tipped over her bucket and the tower fell. The bucket was empty now. "Sand all gone!" said Julia. The sun went down. The sky grew dark again. Julia yawned. "Night is back," she said. Mom took her hand. "See you tomorrow, park," said Julia, waving all the way home.

Elijah was at the playground with his mom. The sun was out. "It is sunny," said Elijah. He wore his sun hat. Vaughn was there too. Vaughn wore a big cap. "Your hat is neat," said Vaughn.

Then the wind came. The wind blew Elijah's hat off. Elijah ran to get it. He put it back on. The wind blew it off again. He held it with his hand this time.

Then the sky got dark. "Rain is coming," said Mom. She opened a big red umbrella. Elijah stood under it with her. The rain fell all around them. But Elijah's head stayed dry. "The rain can't get me," said Elijah. He smiled up at the umbrella.

They walked home in the rain. Elijah held the umbrella handle too. "I want to wear my boots," said Elijah. "Next time," said Mom. "We can jump in puddles then." Elijah looked back at the wet playground. "Bye, playground," he said. "See you when it's sunny again."

Owen stood on the soccer field. Ms. Chukwu held up a big red hoop. "Throw the beanbag in, Owen," she said. Owen threw it. The beanbag hit the edge and dropped. Neil got his beanbag in. Annabella got hers in too. Owen frowned. "I missed," he said. Ms. Chukwu said, "I missed lots of times when I was small. Try again and again." Annabella handed Owen the beanbag. "You can share my turn," she said.

Owen threw the beanbag. It missed. He threw it again. It missed again. His hands felt sticky from his juice box at snack time, and the beanbag felt slimy on one side. He wiped his hands on his shorts. Then he locked his eyes on the hoop. He threw it one more time. The beanbag went in! "I did it!" Owen shouted. Neil clapped.

Next came the big yellow ball. Ms. Chukwu rolled it to Owen. He held out both hands. The ball bounced off. She rolled it again. It bounced off again. Then Owen pulled both hands together and caught it. "Big ball, both hands," he said. Ms. Chukwu smiled. "Again?" she asked. Owen hugged the ball to his chest. "Again," he said.

Emilia planted seeds with her dad. She put carrot seeds in one row. She put tomato seeds in another row. Then she watered them all.

A few days later, tiny green leaves popped up. Emilia forgot which row was tomatoes. She felt worried. "Dad, I don't know where the tomatoes are!"

Her dad smiled. "We can fix that," he said. Emilia drew a red tomato on a card. She drew an orange carrot on another card. They stuck the cards in the soil. "The label shows what is planted in each spot," her dad said. Now every row had a picture label.

Her friend Elliana came to see the garden. A fuzzy caterpillar sat on a leaf. Emilia gave a little wave to Elliana at the gate. "Look!" said Elliana. "Your tomato row has little tomatoes!" It was a happy surprise.

Maeve stood at the edge of the backyard pool. The water looked cool and beautiful. "I want to swim," she said. The coach held her hand. "Kick your legs," said the coach. Maeve kicked. The kicking made her move forward through the water. She kicked again. She moved some more. "I did it!" she said.

Maeve saw a tall chair by the pool. A lifeguard sat up high in it. "Why do you sit up there?" Maeve asked. "My job is to watch the swimmers," said the lifeguard. "I help anyone who needs it." From up high, she could see everyone.

Maeve let go and kicked all by herself. Splash, splash, splash. She moved all the way to the pool wall. The water touched her lips. It taste like summer, she thought. The lifeguard waved from her tall chair. "Look at me!" called Maeve to the whole world. "I am swimming!"

Lucas peeked under the toy box. He found a feather there. It was small and gray.

"A bird must have lost it," said Marvin. "Birds are animals that have feathers."

Lucas looked at his toy shelf. He saw a toy duck. He saw a toy bear. "Did my toys lose it?" he asked.

Marvin touched the toy duck. "No feathers here," he said. "It is soft, but not feathers."

Lucas touched the toy bear too. No feathers. Then he looked out the playroom window. A wet bird sat on the fence. It shook its wings. Little feathers puffed out.

"Look!" said Lucas. "The bird has feathers!"

The bird dropped one more feather. It floated down like a little boat.

"Hello, bird," Lucas called. "That one is yours."

The bird flew away. The feather stayed on the grass.

Ezra was hungry. He wanted his sandwich now. "One minute," said his dad. He cut the sandwich with a safe knife. Ezra watched from his chair.

Dad put the plate down. The sandwich was not squares today. It had pointy pieces. "What shape is this?" Ezra asked. "A triangle," said Dad. Ezra touched one piece with his finger. He counted the corners. "One, two, three." He slid his finger along each line. "One, two, three." Three sides and three corners.

Ezra took a big bite. One corner was gone. He counted again. "One, two, three, four. Four corners now!" He laughed. Dad laughed too. "You made a new shape, Ezra." Ezra held up the piece. "Triangle had three," he said. Then he chased the last crumb around the plate with his finger and popped it in his mouth.

Eloise sat at the little red table. Mr. Georgiou put down two plates. One plate had cookies on it. The other plate was empty.

"Count with me," said Mr. Georgiou. Eloise pointed at each cookie. "One, two, three, four, five." Five cookies. She looked at the other plate. She counted anyway. "One, two..." But there was nothing to point to. The empty plate had no cookies at all.

Desmond sat down next to her. He was hungry. He ate a cookie. Eloise counted again. "One, two, three, four." He ate another one. "One, two, three." Then another. "One, two." Then one more. "One." Desmond picked up the last cookie. He ate it all up.

"Now count," said Desmond. Eloise looked at the plate. It was empty. Not one cookie was left. "It has none," she said. "Zero," said Mr. Georgiou. "Zero means none." Eloise said the new word slowly. "Zero." The empty plate had zero cookies on it.

Then Mr. Georgiou held up both plates. "Which plate has more?" Eloise pointed at the plate with the new cookies, the ones he had just set down. "That one," she said. "It has more. The empty one has zero." Clover clapped her hands. On the shelf, a toy sheep stood by a little bell. Eloise reached up and made the bell ring, ding, ding, ding. Mr. Georgiou laughed and gave her a fresh cookie, still cool, not frozen at all. "One," said Eloise, and she took a big happy bite.

Maeva and her family drove to the national park. There was a lake there with little waves. Maeva wanted to splash right away.

"Wait," said her dad. "A child goes near the water only with a grown-up watching. Come hold my hand." Maeva held his hand. They walked down to the water together.

Maeva looked at the waves. She touched one with her toe. The water went splash on her loose shoelace. Her wet shoe made a footprint on the rock. Each wave made a new splash. Each splash made her giggle. "The wave came to me!" she said. Dad laughed and held her hand tight. "Again!" said Maeva, and the next wave came.

Claire went to the farmers' market with her dad. She saw a big gray bucket full of little seed packets. She picked one with a carrot on it. "Can we plant these?" she asked. Her dad said yes.

At home, Claire dug a small hole. She dropped the seeds in the dirt. Then she gave them water from her little can. The next morning, Claire ran outside. She looked and looked. There was only dirt. No sprout. Claire felt sad.

Her neighbor Ms. Schneider came by. "Keep giving them water," she said. "A sprout does not come up right away." So Claire watered the seeds every day. She told her friend Kilian, "My seeds have a name. They are carrots." One morning, Claire saw a tiny green tip in the dirt. "It came up!" she said. She clapped her hands and ran to get her watering can.

Hayden was at Grandpa's house. Grandpa had a big game box. On the box was a picture of an eye, an ear, a nose, a mouth and a hand. "This is my senses game," said Grandpa. "Can you play?"

Hayden opened the box. Out fell a feather, a pinecone and a small clock. "First, use your hands," said Grandpa. "Close your eyes and touch." Hayden touched the feather. It was soft. He touched the pinecone. It was rough. "The feather is soft!" said Hayden. "The pinecone is rough!"

"Now use your nose," said Grandpa. He held up a jar. Hayden sniffed it. "Cookies!" he said. "My nose knows cookies." Grandpa laughed. He rang the little clock bell. "My ears hear that!" said Hayden.

Then Grandpa hid the cookie jar behind his back. "Something is missing," said Hayden. "Where are the cookies?" Grandpa held one up. "Use your eyes," he said. "Look, then use your mouth." Hayden took a small bite. He smiled big. "Yum! My tongue tastes sweet!" Grandpa clapped his hands. "Five senses, all found," said Grandpa. "Want to play again?" "Yes!" said Hayden, picking up the soft feather.

Emmett was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to count the apples in the big bowl. He counted, "One, two," and then he stopped. He could not think of what came next.

His cousin Mac was there too. Mac wanted to know the number after two. "I forgot it," Mac said.

Then Grandpa began to sing. "One, two, buckle my shoe. Three, four, shut the door." Emmett listened. The song went on. "Five, six, pick up sticks. Seven, eight, lay them straight."

Emmett sang along. When he got to "nine, ten," he laughed. The words rhymed, and that helped him remember. "Three comes after two!" he said. Mac clapped his hands.

Emmett pointed at the bowl. "One, two, three, four, five." There were five red apples. Grandpa gave each boy a good apple to eat.

Emmett sang the song all the way to the kitchen door.

Jade sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. The nurse held a small tray. Jade saw the tiny needle. Her tummy felt tight.

Grandpa sat next to her. He held her hand. "Smell the flower," he said. "Breathe in slow. Then blow out slow." Jade smelled the flower. She breathed in slow like smelling a flower. Then she blew out slow. Her shoulders came down. Her tummy felt calm. The nurse said, "All done!" Jade blinked. She had not even felt the pinprick much at all. "I breathed like a flower," Jade said.

Afterward, they went to the ice cream shop. Grandpa poured hot fudge on top. The man scooped a high pink tower for Jade. A butterfly sticker sat on her arm where the bandage was. Naomi waved from the next table. "Did the shot hurt?" she asked. Jade held up her sticker and smiled. "I smelled a flower," she said.

Caleb woke up and saw snow. Lots of snow! No school today. It was a snow day.

Dad took Caleb to the sledding hill. The snow was deep and white. It looked like a big, quiet ocean. Caleb saw Lilianna there with her green sled.

Caleb climbed to the top. He lay down on his sled. He wanted to go down head first, like a penguin.

"Wait," said Dad. "Not like that. Sit up on the sled. Face the front. Hold on with both hands."

Caleb sat up. He faced the front. He held on tight.

"I will watch from right here," said Dad.

Whoosh! Caleb went down the hill. He sat up the whole way. He did not tip over. He landed in the soft snow and laughed.

Lilianna lay down on her sled next. Then she sat up too. She faced the front and held on. Dad watched her too. Whoosh! Down she went.

"My turn again!" said Caleb. He pulled his sled up the hill, one small step at a time.

Ava sat on Grandpa's big soft chair. The soccer game was on the TV. Her friends Arnaaz and Zariah sat on the rug. Grandma brought sticky buns on a plate.

The blue team ran and ran. They ran so fast. "The blue team runs the most," said Ava. "They will win."

The game ended. The blue team still ran more. But Ava looked at the screen. The numbers said red two, blue one.

"Red has more points," said Zariah. "Red wins the game."

Ava clapped her hands. She had a small problem in her head, and now it was solved. Running a lot did not win. More points won.

Then Grandma called, "Snack time. Come and feed your tummies." The kids ate sticky buns. Arnaaz said, "Next time I will watch the numbers." Ava smiled and took one more bun.

Penelope sat on her bedroom floor. Her teddy bear had a hole in his arm. Fluff was coming out. That made Penelope sad.

She got her toy toolbox. It was hard to find the right tool. The wrench was too big. The hammer was too heavy. Then she found a big safe plastic needle and some yarn. She asked her dad to help thread it. He sat with her on the rug.

Penelope tried to fix the hole. The yarn slipped out. She tried again. It slipped again. She took a deep breath and waited a bit. Then she tried one more time, slowly. The yarn went through.

Just then her friend Zakary came in. His mouth was turned down and his eyebrows were bumpy. Penelope looked at his face. She saw he felt sad. "What is wrong?" she asked.

"My truck is at home," said Zakary. "I wanted to show you."

Penelope smiled at him. "Teddy has a hole, but I fixed it," she said. She held Teddy up. Zakary's mouth turned up into a big smile. Penelope saw his happy face and laughed. "Do you want to help Teddy find his hat?" she asked. Zakary clapped his hands.

Leo sat on the living room rug. The tablet lay dark in front of him. He tapped the dark screen. Nothing happened. He tapped it again and again. Still nothing.

Dad sat down next to him. "This little button turns it on," Dad said. He showed Leo the button on the side. Leo pressed it. The screen lit up. Leo laughed. One press, and the dark screen woke up!

Leo tapped the drawing app. He drew a big spotted cat. Then he drew a cat with a bump on its head, like a funny hat. "More cats," Leo said. He drew one more cat.

Soon it was time for dinner. "All done," said Dad. Leo pressed the button again. The screen went dark. He put the tablet in its basket, soft and safe. "Night night, tablet," Leo whispered.

Chloe put on her swim cap. Today was her first swim team day. The pool was big and blue.

Ms. Nielsen stood at the edge. "I am your coach," she said. "A coach teaches the team. I help you learn the game."

Chloe did not know where to stand. She stood by the wrong wall. Ms. Nielsen showed her the spot with a red cone. "Stand here," she said. Chloe stood there. It was the right spot!

"Now we kick," said Ms. Nielsen. "Hold the rail. Kick, kick, kick." Chloe held the rail. She kicked one, two, three times. She made big white splashes. Her kicks made the water fly up!

"I did that!" said Chloe. Malcom kicked next to her. He made splashes too. Celina kicked and laughed.

They kicked one, two, three, over and over. Then it was time to get out. Chloe was a polite swimmer. She said, "Thank you, Ms. Nielsen."

She put on her warm sweater. It was soft and cozy. Her hair was still wet.

"One, two, three," said Chloe. She gave three big waves to the pool.

Logan sat on the big red mat. Music class was starting at the community centre. Ms. Mehta had her drum. Lorelei and Ishaan sat close by.

Ms. Mehta tapped the drum. Bump, bump, bump. Logan clapped whenever he wanted. His claps went everywhere. They bumped into Ishaan's ear by mistake. "Ow," said Ishaan, and he laughed. Logan stopped. He felt his face go warm.

"Lorelei, how do you clap so well?" Logan asked. Lorelei clapped with the drum. Bump went the drum, clap went her hands. "I clap at the same time as the beat," she said. Logan put his hands in his lap. He listened. Bump went the drum. Clap went Logan. Bump, clap. Bump, clap. "You did it!" said Lorelei. Ishaan clapped with him too, and their hands made one big sound.

Then Ms. Mehta sang a song about a star in the dark sky. Logan sang too. He knew the words all by himself. Lorelei clapped for him. Logan took a little bow and fell over sideways on the mat.

Emma went to the library with her dad. The library had a big tree painted on the wall. There was a playroom too. Emma wanted to play there, but the toy box was empty. "Where did the toys go?" she asked.

Blocks and dolls and balls were all over the floor. Justin had dumped them out. Gideon was hiding under the table. "Too many toys!" said Justin. "They go everywhere."

Ms. Rajapakse came in. She knelt down by the box. "Let's put them back," she said. Emma picked up a block. "Block," she said, and dropped it in. "That's a toy," said Ms. Rajapakse. Emma picked up a doll. "Doll," she said, and put it in. Justin threw a ball. The ball bounced off the wall and rolled back. Emma caught it. "Ball," she said. "Ball is a toy too." She put it in the box.

Gideon came out from under the table. He picked up a book. "Book?" he asked. "The book goes on the shelf," said Ms. Rajapakse. So Gideon put the book on the shelf, not in the toy box. Soon the floor was clear. The box was full. Emma yawned. She was tired now. She sat on her dad's lap by the big tree. "One more story," she said. Her dad opened a book and began to read.

Violet stood in the backyard with a red beanbag. She wanted to throw it into the hoop. Her friend Nimrat held the hoop up high. Violet threw the beanbag. It hit the grass. She threw it again. It went in! "Yay!" said Nimrat. "The beanbag went through!"

Then Mr. Kim rolled a big ball to Violet. She put out her hands. The ball hit her hands and bounced away. It rolled past a spider on its web. Mr. Kim rolled the ball again. The ball bounced out of her hands once more. "Hmm," said Violet. "The ball is too big for my hands."

Then she had an idea. She held her arms out wide. The ball came. She caught it and hugged it to her chest. The ball stayed! No bounce at all. "Look, Mr. Kim!" she said. "I hug it, and I hold on to it!" She got a little dizzy spinning around with the ball. Mr. Kim laughed and rolled the ball again.

Blake woke up hungry. She wanted toast with butter. Her dad put two pieces of toast on a plate. "Can I butter it?" Blake asked. "Yes," said Dad. "I will get the butter for you."

Blake took the hard butter from the fridge. She pushed it on the toast. The butter tore a big hole in the bread. "Oh no," said Blake. Dad smiled. "Let's try again. This butter sat out on the counter. It is soft now."

Blake spread the soft butter. It went on smooth and easy. No holes! Then she poured milk into her cup. She poured slowly. Only one little drop spilled. Dad clapped. Then Cara knocked at the door, holding a jar of jam. "We made fresh jam at my house," Cara said. Blake held up the knife. "Look, I can spread it myself."

Eleanor went to the pool with her dad. She rode her bike there first, and her dad pushed it along. At the pool, her friend Noa was already in the water. Noa could float on her back.

"I want to float too," Eleanor said. But she sat on the step and did not move. The water felt big. She was not angry, just scared.

Then Ms. Chaudhry came over. "I will hold you while you float," she said. Eleanor lay back. She felt Ms. Chaudhry's hands under her back. The hands held her up. Eleanor opened her eyes and watched the ceiling. The water did not pull her down.

"Now one hand," said Ms. Chaudhry. Then she took that hand away too. Eleanor was floating all by herself. Noa splashed and cheered. Eleanor kicked her feet a little and laughed.

David ran to the park. The sun was warm on his face. His hat went flying off. "Wow, it is windy!" he said. He picked up his hat and put it back on.

Then the sky turned gray. Rain began to fall. Drip, drip, drip. David got wet fast. His friend Katelyn ran by in her red raincoat. She stayed dry. "How are you not wet?" David asked. "My raincoat keeps me dry," she said.

David ran home. He put on his blue raincoat. He ran back to the park. The rain tap-tapped on his coat. His face smiled. His tummy was dry. His arms were dry too. "Rain, rain, you can't get me!" he called. Katelyn laughed and splashed in a puddle. David stomped in it too. Splish, splash, splosh.

Scarlett sat in her car seat. The sky had been sunny all morning. Now it looked cloudy and gray. "Rain is coming," said Dad. Big drops hit the window. Tap, tap, tap.

"I want to play at the park," said Scarlett. Then the wind blew hard. It made the trees bend and wave. "Windy!" said Scarlett. Rumble, rumble. Thunder! It was loud like a big drum. Scarlett covered her ears. Dad said, "When you hear thunder, you go indoors. We will play at home instead."

At home, Dad used a hammer. He fixed the loose board on the porch. Then it began to snow outside. Soft white flakes fell down. Scarlett and Dad watched from the warm window. "Snow," said Scarlett. She held her teddy bear tight. Dad gave her warm milk in her cup. "Safe and cozy," said Dad. Scarlett smiled and watched the snow.

Lennon stood on the soccer field. The sun felt warm on her arms. Ms. Haddad set out a big hoop. "Watch me," said Ms. Haddad. She tossed a beanbag up. It dropped right into the hoop. Lennon tried. Her beanbag fell short. She tried again. It went in. "I did it!" she said. Maren clapped.

Next they played catch with a big ball. Sam threw it hard. The ball flew past Lennon's hands. "Too fast," said Lennon. She had to crawl after it into the string net by the goal. Then Sam smiled. He tossed the ball gently. Lennon caught it with both hands. The soft toss was easy to hold.

"Again," said Lennon. Sam tossed it gently again. Lennon caught it. She felt brave. "Your turn now," she said to Maren. Lennon tossed the ball soft and slow. Maren caught it too. "Nice and easy," said Maren. Ms. Haddad blew her whistle. "Good catching, everyone," she said. Lennon held the big ball tight and smiled.

Cooper sat in the nursery room. There was a new baby at his house. The baby was his little sister. Cooper made a puzzle on the rug. Mr. Eze sat down next to him. "Where is your smile today?" asked Mr. Eze. "The baby took it," said Cooper. "The baby cries. Mom holds the baby. Mom can't hold me."

Amirah came over with a drum. "Bang it soft," she said. Cooper banged it soft. The drum made a little sound. Cooper banged it hard. The drum made a big sound. He banged it soft again. The sound got small again. "One bang makes one sound," said Amirah. Cooper nodded. He tried it again and again.

Mr. Eze said, "It is okay to feel left out when a new baby comes. Big brothers can feel that way." Cooper looked up. "Even me?" he asked. "Even you," said Mr. Eze. "You can tell Mom. She will listen."

Mom came to the nursery room. Cooper ran to her. "Mom, I miss you," he said. Mom sat down on the little chair. She pulled Cooper onto her lap. "I miss you too," she said. "We can sing together." They sang a song. Cooper felt warm. The baby was different, and that was okay. Cooper leaned his head on Mom. "Again," he whispered.

Harrison stood at the train station with his mom. Grandpa was coming today. He was going to stay for a whole week. Harrison looked down the long track. Where was the train?

The train came in with a big whoosh. Grandpa stepped off and gave Harrison a hug. He was carrying a small red bag. "I have a gift for you," Grandpa said. Inside the bag was a card game. "We can play this together," said Grandpa. "We take turns."

They went home and sat on the floor. Harrison wanted to go first. He grabbed all the cards. "Me first! Me first!" he said. Grandpa shook his head. "My turn, then your turn," he said. He put down one card. Then he waited. "Now it is your turn."

Harrison put down a card too. Then it was Grandpa's turn again. Back and forth the cards went. "This is how taking turns works," said Grandpa. Harrison smiled. The game filled the whole afternoon with fun.

The next morning, Harrison ran to Grandpa's room. "Cards again?" he asked. Grandpa laughed. "You can go first this time," he said. Harrison clapped his hands. "Your turn, then my turn," he said. Grandpa dealt the cards, and they began to play.

Arlo ran to the park with his grandpa. He wanted to find the blue slide. First he looked with his eyes. He saw Malakai and Eesa by the swings. He heard them laugh with his ears. He smelled popcorn with his nose. He could almost taste it with his tongue.

Then Arlo found a duck sitting on a big wheel. It was an old wagon wheel by the pond. Arlo touched it with his hands. The metal felt cold and bumpy. "Look, Grandpa!" he called.

Grandpa squinted and shook his head. "I can't see it yet," he said. He took his glasses out of his pocket. He put them on his face. "Ah, now I see the duck on the wheel!" He waved at Malakai and Eesa too.

Arlo's eyes went wide. Glasses helped Grandpa see! Arlo pointed at a far bird. "Can you see that one now?" he asked.

Grandpa smiled. "Yes! I see its little red feet."

Arlo grabbed his hand. "Come see the popcorn too!"
